questions.concept_tag: Data interpretation - ratio from two columns
questions.question_text:
Four firms report their yearly revenue and number of employees.

| Firm | Revenue (₹ crore) | Employees |
|---|---|---|
| A | 480 | 160 |
| B | 350 | 70 |
| C | 600 | 150 |
| D | 270 | 45 |

Which firm earns the most revenue per employee?

options.A: Firm C
options.B: Firm B
options.C: Firm D
options.D: Firm A

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Revenue per employee (₹ crore per person): A = 480/160 = 3; B = 350/70 = 5; C = 600/150 = 4; D = 270/45 = 6. D is highest. Shortcut: divide each revenue by its own employee count before comparing. Trap (A): this is the firm with the largest total revenue, not the largest revenue per employee. Trap (B): its ratio of 5 is the second highest, not the highest. Trap (D): this firm has the largest workforce and a low ratio of 3.

questions.question_text:
The table gives road lengths (km) between five towns. A dash means no direct road.

| Road | Length |
|---|---|
| A-B | 4 |
| A-C | 2 |
| B-C | 1 |
| B-D | 5 |
| C-D | 8 |
| C-E | 10 |
| D-E | 2 |

What is the length of the shortest route from A to E?

options.A: 11 km
options.B: 12 km
options.C: 10 km
options.D: 15 km

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Compare routes to E through D, since the last leg D-E is cheap: A-C-B-D-E = 2 + 1 + 5 + 2 = 10; A-B-D-E = 4 + 5 + 2 = 11; A-C-D-E = 2 + 8 + 2 = 12; A-C-E = 12; A-B-C-E = 15. The shortest is 10 km. Shortcut: work backwards from E: the cheapest way in is D-E (2), then find the cheapest way to D. Trap (A): uses A-B-D-E and misses the shortcut B-C that makes A-C-B cheaper. Trap (B): takes A-C-E using the direct road, or A-C-D-E, without comparing other routes. Trap (D): takes A-B-C-E, going through the long final road C-E.

questions.question_text:
A family's yearly budget of ₹4,80,000 is divided as follows.

| Head | Share |
|---|---|
| Food | 25% |
| Rent | 30% |
| Transport | 15% |
| Savings | 20% |
| Miscellaneous | 10% |

How much more is spent on rent than on transport and miscellaneous together?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Transport + miscellaneous = 15% + 10% = 25%. Rent exceeds it by 30% - 25% = 5% of ₹4,80,000 = ₹24,000. Shortcut: subtract percentages first, then apply the total. Trap (A): compares rent with transport alone (15%) and forgets miscellaneous. Trap (B): compares rent with miscellaneous alone (10%). Trap (C): reports transport plus miscellaneous (25%) instead of the difference.

questions.concept_tag: Matching puzzle - three owners, three vehicles
questions.question_text: Kiran, Lata and Manoj each own exactly one vehicle, and the three vehicles are a car, a scooter and a bicycle, all different. Kiran does not own the car. Lata does not own the scooter or the bicycle. Manoj does not own the bicycle. Who owns the scooter?

options.A: Kiran
options.B: Manoj
options.C: Lata
options.D: It cannot be determined

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Lata owns neither the scooter nor the bicycle, so she owns the car. Manoj does not own the bicycle, and the car is taken, so Manoj owns the scooter. Kiran owns the bicycle, which agrees with his clue. Shortcut: start with the person with the most restrictive clue. Trap (A): Kiran owns the bicycle, since Lata has the car and Manoj has the scooter. Trap (C): Lata is left only with the car. Trap (D): the clues fix exactly one assignment.

questions.question_text:
Meera must reach town T. Her options are:

| Option | Departure | Journey time | After arrival |
|---|---|---|---|
| Express bus | 9:00 | 2 h 10 min | none |
| Local bus | 8:20 | 2 h 55 min | none |
| Train | 8:40 | 2 h 20 min | 15 min walk to town T |

What is the earliest time she can reach town T?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Express: 9:00 + 2:10 = 11:10. Local: 8:20 + 2:55 = 11:15. Train: 8:40 + 2:20 = 11:00, plus a 15-minute walk = 11:15. The earliest is 11:10. Shortcut: add every leg of the trip, including the walk, before comparing. Trap (B): ignores the 15-minute walk after the train. Trap (C): picks the local bus or the train with the walk, whose times tie, instead of the express. Trap (D): mis-adds 2 h 10 min to 9:00 as 11:05.

questions.question_text:
Four students' marks are shown. The final score weights Maths 60% and English 40%.

| Student | Maths | English |
|---|---|---|
| P | 80 | 50 |
| Q | 70 | 70 |
| R | 85 | 40 |
| S | 60 | 90 |

Who ranks second on the final score?

options.A: Q
options.B: P
options.C: R
options.D: S

questions.pedagogical_explanation: P = 0.6 × 80 + 0.4 × 50 = 68; Q = 42 + 28 = 70; R = 51 + 16 = 67; S = 36 + 36 = 72. Order: S, Q, P, R. Second is Q. Shortcut: compute weighted totals for all four, then sort. Trap (B): ranks by Maths marks alone, where P is second. Trap (C): picks the Maths topper. Trap (D): picks the overall topper (72), who ranks first, not second.

questions.question_text:
Four flats share a monthly electricity bill of ₹2,400. ₹400 is a fixed charge divided equally among the flats; the remaining ₹2,000 is divided in proportion to units used.

| Flat | Units used |
|---|---|
| 1 | 150 |
| 2 | 90 |
| 3 | 60 |
| 4 | 100 |

What does Flat 2 pay?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Fixed share = 400/4 = 100. Total units = 400, so the variable rate = 2,000/400 = ₹5 per unit. Flat 2: 100 + 90 × 5 = ₹550. Shortcut: split the bill into its fixed and variable parts before allocating. Trap (A): divides the whole bill in proportion to units, ignoring the equal fixed charge. Trap (B): splits the whole bill equally. Trap (C): includes only the variable part and leaves out the fixed charge.

questions.question_text:
Direct flights operate between these pairs of cities (each works both ways): A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, D-E, B-E.

How many different routes go from A to E using at most 3 flights, without visiting any city twice?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Two flights: A-B-E. Three flights: A-B-D-E and A-C-D-E. The route A-C-D-B-E needs 4 flights, so it is excluded. Total 3. Shortcut: list routes by number of flights and stop at 3. Trap (A): misses the 2-flight route A-B-E. Trap (C): includes the 4-flight route A-C-D-B-E. Trap (D): counts routes that revisit a city.

questions.question_text: A purse holds 12 coins, all of ₹1, ₹2 or ₹5, with a total value of ₹33. Exactly three of the coins are ₹5 coins. How many ₹2 coins are there?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The three ₹5 coins are worth ₹15, leaving 9 coins worth ₹18. If every one of these were a ₹2 coin, the value would be 18. So all 9 are ₹2 coins and there are no ₹1 coins. Shortcut: remove the known coins, then compare the average value needed with the denominations. Trap (A): 6 forgets to take the three ₹5 coins out of the coin count and solves x + y = 12, x + 2y = 18. Trap (C): treats all 18 remaining rupees as 9 coins of ₹2 but miscounts by one. Trap (D): reports the number of ₹5 coins.

questions.question_text:
Five meetings are booked at these times.

| Meeting | Start | End |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | 9:00 | 11:00 |
| M2 | 10:00 | 12:00 |
| M3 | 11:00 | 13:00 |
| M4 | 12:00 | 14:00 |
| M5 | 10:30 | 11:30 |

A meeting ending at a time and another starting at that time can share a room. What is the minimum number of rooms needed?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Check the busiest moment. Between 10:30 and 11:00, M1, M2 and M5 run together (3 meetings). Between 11:00 and 11:30, M2, M3 and M5 run together (3). No moment has 4 meetings, so 3 rooms suffice and are needed. Shortcut: the minimum rooms equals the maximum number of meetings running at one moment. Trap (A): counts only two of the three meetings that overlap at 10:30. Trap (B): counts M3 as overlapping with M1. Trap (C): gives each meeting its own room.

questions.question_text: Three machines make the same item at these rates: Machine A 12 per hour, Machine B 18 per hour, Machine C 30 per hour. An order of 540 items must be finished as fast as possible using exactly two machines working together. Which pair should be used?

options.A: B and C
options.B: A and B
options.C: A and C
options.D: A, B and C

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The combined rates are A+B = 30, A+C = 42 and B+C = 48 per hour. The highest rate gives the least time: B and C take 540/48 = 11.25 hours. Shortcut: rates add; the pair with the biggest sum wins. Trap (B): picks the two slowest machines. Trap (C): pairs the fastest machine with the slowest, assuming balance matters. Trap (D): uses all three machines although the order allows exactly two.

questions.concept_tag: Data interpretation - growth in a table
questions.question_text:
Yearly sales (₹ lakh) of Company Y:

| Year | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sales | 80 | 88 | 110 | 121 | 145 |

Between which two consecutive years was the percentage growth the highest?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Growth rates: 2019-20: 8/80 = 10%; 2020-21: 22/88 = 25%; 2021-22: 11/110 = 10%; 2022-23: 24/121 ≈ 19.8%. The highest is 25% for 2020 to 2021. Shortcut: divide each increase by its own starting value. Trap (B): picks the largest absolute increase (24) instead of the largest percentage. Trap (C): treats the first step as the fastest. Trap (D): 2021 to 2022 rose by 11 on a base of 110, only 10%; choosing it means comparing rises without dividing by the base.

questions.question_text: A 3-digit code uses three different digits from 1 to 6. Clues about guesses: 123 has 0 digits right in the right place and 1 digit right in the wrong place; 124 has 0 right in place and 2 right in the wrong place; 136 has 1 digit right in place and 1 right in the wrong place. What is the code?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Clues 1 and 2 together mean the code contains 4 and exactly one of 1 or 2, and never 3 (if 3 were present, clue 2 could not reach two digits). Testing the remaining codes against clue 3 (one digit of 1, 3, 6 in its place, another present elsewhere) leaves only 416. Shortcut: use every clue as a filter on the small set of 120 codes. Trap (A): satisfies the first two clues but fails the clue about 136 (it has no digit in the right place). Trap (B): swaps the first two digits; it fits the first two clues but fails the clue about 136. Trap (D): has the digit 4 in the last place, which breaks the clue about 124.

questions.question_text:
Exactly one of three suspects stole a phone, and exactly one of the three statements below is true.

Raju: "Sonu stole it."
Sonu: "I did not steal it."
Tina: "Raju is lying."

Who stole the phone?

options.A: Raju
options.B: Tina
options.C: Cannot be determined
options.D: Sonu

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Test each thief. If Sonu is the thief: Raju is true, Sonu is false, Tina is false: exactly one true. If Raju or Tina is the thief: Raju is false while Sonu and Tina are both true: two true. Only Sonu works. Shortcut: test each suspect in turn and count true statements. Trap (A): with Raju guilty, both Sonu's and Tina's statements are true, giving two true statements. Trap (B): with Tina guilty, Raju's statement is false, but Sonu's and Tina's are both true. Trap (C): assumes the statements are insufficient without testing each case.

questions.question_text:
Three colleagues list the weekdays on which they are free this week (✓ = free).

| Day | Asha | Bilal | Chitra |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | ✓ | | ✓ |
| Tue | | ✓ | ✓ |
| Wed | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Thu | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Fri | ✓ | | ✓ |

On which is the earliest weekday that all three are free?

options.A: Monday
options.B: Thursday
options.C: Tuesday
options.D: Wednesday

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Check each day for all three ticks. Mon: Asha, Chitra; Tue: Bilal, Chitra; Wed: Asha, Bilal; Thu: all three. Thursday is the earliest and the only day. Shortcut: scan each row for three ticks. Trap (A): only Asha and Chitra are free on Monday. Trap (C): only Bilal and Chitra are free on Tuesday. Trap (D): only Asha and Bilal are free on Wednesday.

questions.question_text: Three parcels P, Q and R are weighed in pairs: P and Q together weigh 14 kg, Q and R together weigh 17 kg, and P and R together weigh 19 kg. What is the weight of R?

options.A: 11 kg
options.B: 8 kg
options.C: 6 kg
options.D: 25 kg

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Adding the three equations: 2(P + Q + R) = 50, so the total is 25. Then R = 25 - 14 = 11 kg (P = 8, Q = 6). Shortcut: total = (sum of pair weights)/2; subtract the pair that excludes the one you want. Trap (B): reports the weight of P. Trap (C): reports the weight of Q. Trap (D): reports the total weight of all three parcels.

questions.question_text:
Daily movements of Item B in a store (units):

| Day | Opening stock | Received | Issued |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50 | 20 | 30 |
| 2 | carry over | 0 | 15 |
| 3 | carry over | 40 | 25 |

What is the closing stock of Item B at the end of Day 3?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: End of Day 1: 50 + 20 - 30 = 40. Day 2: 40 + 0 - 15 = 25. Day 3: 25 + 40 - 25 = 40. Shortcut: roll the closing stock forward day by day. Trap (A): stops at the end of Day 2. Trap (C): adds the receipts to the opening stock and ignores the issues. Trap (D): uses only the net movement of Day 3.

questions.question_text: A van can carry at most 50 kg per trip. Six boxes weigh 40, 30, 25, 20, 15 and 10 kg. What is the minimum number of trips needed to carry all the boxes?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total = 140 kg, so at least 3 trips are needed (140/50 = 2.8). Three trips suffice: 40 + 10, 30 + 20 and 25 + 15 (each ≤ 50). So the minimum is 3. Shortcut: lower bound = ⌈total/capacity⌉; then try to match large with small. Trap (A): loads boxes greedily in the order given and wastes space. Trap (B): divides the total 140 kg by 50 and rounds down. Trap (D): pairs only the boxes that are adjacent in the list.

questions.question_text:
A walker moves from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell of a 3 × 3 grid, moving only right or down, one cell at a time. The centre cell is blocked.

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| Start | | |
| | BLOCKED | |
| | | End |

How many different paths are there?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: All paths: C(4, 2) = 6. Paths through the centre: 2 ways to reach it × 2 ways to leave it = 4. Remaining: 6 - 4 = 2 (the two edge paths). Shortcut: total paths minus paths through the blocked cell. Trap (A): counts all paths and ignores the blocked cell. Trap (B): subtracts too few paths, forgetting the blocked cell lies on 4 paths in total. Trap (C): counts only paths along one side plus one more.

questions.question_text:
Marks of 40 students:

| Marks | Students |
|---|---|
| 0-10 | 5 |
| 10-20 | 12 |
| 20-30 | 9 |
| 30-40 | 8 |
| 40-50 | 6 |

In which class does the median mark lie?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The median is between the 20th and 21st students. Cumulative frequencies: 5, 17, 26, 34, 40. The 20th and 21st fall in the third class, 20-30. Shortcut: build the cumulative frequency column and locate n/2. Trap (A): picks the modal class (largest frequency) instead of the median class. Trap (B): counts from the top and stops one class early. Trap (D): picks the last class.

questions.concept_tag: Colouring argument - dominoes on a damaged board
questions.question_text: A 6 × 6 chessboard has two opposite corner squares removed; both removed squares are the same colour. Dominoes, each covering exactly two squares that share an edge, are placed on the board without overlapping. What is the largest number of dominoes that can be placed?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Colour the board in the usual way: 18 black and 18 white squares. Removing two squares of the same colour leaves 16 of that colour and 18 of the other. Every domino covers one square of each colour, so at most 16 dominoes fit. A tiling pattern achieves 16 (leaving two squares of the majority colour uncovered). Shortcut: count the two colours; each domino uses one of each. Trap (B): divides the remaining 34 squares by 2, which would need equal numbers of both colours. Trap (C): divides the full 36 squares by 2. Trap (D): stops one short of the maximum that a careful placement achieves.

questions.question_text:
One of four children - Amit, Bina, Charu or Dev - broke a vase. Their statements:

Amit: "Dev broke it."
Bina: "Amit did not break it."
Charu: "Bina broke it."
Dev: "Amit is telling the truth."

Exactly two of the four statements are true. Who broke the vase?

options.A: Amit
options.B: Charu
options.C: Bina
options.D: Dev

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Test each child as the culprit and count true statements. Amit: none true. Bina: Bina's and Charu's true (2). Charu: only Bina's true (1). Dev: Amit's, Bina's and Dev's true (3). Only Bina gives exactly two. Shortcut: Dev copies Amit, so those two statements are always true or false together. Trap (A): if Amit broke it, all four statements are false (Bina's is false because Amit did break it). Trap (B): with Charu guilty only Bina's statement is true, which makes one true statement, not two. Trap (D): with Dev guilty, Amit, Bina and Dev are all truthful, so three statements are true.

questions.question_text:
Four workers must each be given exactly one of four tasks. The hours each would take:

| Worker | T1 | T2 | T3 | T4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| W1 | 14 | 6 | 11 | 6 |
| W2 | 9 | 11 | 6 | 5 |
| W3 | 15 | 5 | 8 | 8 |
| W4 | 5 | 12 | 11 | 11 |

What is the minimum total number of hours?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Try the assignments systematically. W4 is cheapest on T1 (5) and W3 on T2 (5). Then W1 and W2 share T3 and T4: W1-T4 (6) with W2-T3 (6) gives 5 + 5 + 6 + 6 = 22. Checking all 24 assignments confirms nothing is lower. Shortcut: lock the clearly cheapest pairs, then check that the leftover pairing cannot be improved. Trap (A): giving each worker in turn their cheapest free task (W1-T2, W2-T4, W3-T3, W4-T1) leaves W4 a poor choice and costs 24, not the optimum. Trap (C): adding the cheapest entry of each column (5 + 5 + 6 + 5) breaks the one-task-per-worker rule. Trap (D): assigning W1-T1, W2-T2, W3-T3, W4-T4 down the diagonal ignores the costs.

questions.question_text:
Sales (₹ lakh) of a company in four regions:

| Region | Year 1 | Year 2 |
|---|---|---|
| North | 40 | 28 |
| South | 10 | 33 |
| East | 35 | 80 |
| West | 15 | 54 |

Which region's share of the company's total sales rose by the most percentage points from Year 1 to Year 2?

options.A: West
options.B: East
options.C: South
options.D: North

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Totals: Year 1 = 100, Year 2 = 195. Shares in Year 1: 40%, 10%, 35%, 15%. Shares in Year 2: 14.4%, 16.9%, 41.0%, 27.7%. Changes: North -25.6, South +6.9, East +6.0, West +12.7 points. West rises the most. Shortcut: convert both years to shares before comparing; the total changes too. Trap (B): East has the largest rise in rupees (45 lakh), but the total also grew, so its share rises by only about 6 points. Trap (C): South's share rises by only about 7 points. Trap (D): North's share actually falls.

questions.question_text: Five jobs A, B, C, D and E are done one at a time. A and B must both be done before C; C must be done before D; and B must be done before E. In how many different orders can the five jobs be done?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Listing by the order of A, B and C: A, B, C or B, A, C (C always third among them, and D after C). E only needs to come after B. With A first: ABCDE, ABCED, ABECD. With B first: BACDE, BACED, BAECD, and BEACD (E can sit between B and A). Total 7. Shortcut: count orders of the chain A,B before C before D, then slot E after B. Trap (A): dropping the requirement that A be before C (or B before E) leaves more orders than allowed. Trap (B): ignoring the rule that A precedes C counts orders the rule forbids. Trap (D): ignoring the rule that C precedes D counts far too many orders.

questions.question_text: Five jobs need 8, 7, 6, 5 and 4 hours. Two identical machines work side by side; each job runs without a break on one machine. What is the least time in which all the jobs can be finished?

options.A: 15 hours
options.B: 17 hours
options.C: 18 hours
options.D: 21 hours

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total work = 30 hours, so no schedule beats 15 hours. A split of 8 + 7 on one machine and 6 + 5 + 4 on the other gives 15 each, so 15 is achievable and optimal. Shortcut: least possible time is at least total work divided by number of machines; look for a split that meets it. Trap (B): giving each job to whichever machine is free first, longest job first, ends with 8+5+4 on one machine. Trap (C): putting jobs on the machines alternately (8, 6, 4 and 7, 5) leaves one machine with 18 hours. Trap (D): putting the three biggest jobs together (8 + 7 + 6) overloads one machine.

questions.question_text:
A project has six activities.

| Activity | Duration (days) | Needs completed first |
|---|---|---|
| A | 3 | - |
| B | 4 | A |
| C | 2 | A |
| D | 6 | B and C |
| E | 2 | C |
| F | 3 | D and E |

What is the minimum time to complete the project?

options.A: 20 days
options.B: 13 days
options.C: 10 days
options.D: 16 days

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Earliest finish: A = 3; B = 7; C = 5; D starts when B and C are done (7) so D = 13; E = 7; F starts when D and E are done (13) so F = 16. The longest path is A-B-D-F = 3 + 4 + 6 + 3 = 16. Shortcut: the project length equals the longest chain of dependent activities. Trap (A): adding all six durations assumes the activities cannot overlap. Trap (B): the path A-B-D ignores that activity F must still be done after D. Trap (C): the path A-C-E-F is short, but the project cannot end before the longest path does.

questions.question_text:
A bag can carry at most 10 kg. The items available:

| Item | Weight (kg) | Value (₹ hundred) |
|---|---|---|
| A | 6 | 13 |
| B | 5 | 10 |
| C | 5 | 10 |
| D | 3 | 5 |

Each item can be taken at most once. What is the largest total value that can be carried?

options.A: ₹18 hundred
options.B: ₹23 hundred
options.C: ₹15 hundred
options.D: ₹20 hundred

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Value per kg: A 2.17, B 2, C 2, D 1.67. Greedy takes A (6 kg) and then D (3 kg) for 18. But B + C weigh exactly 10 kg and give 20. Checking every feasible set confirms 20 is the maximum. Shortcut: greedy by ratio can waste capacity; test the combinations that fill the bag exactly. Trap (A): taking the item with the best value per kg first (A) and then filling with D gives only 18. Trap (B): taking A and B together weighs 11 kg and breaks the limit. Trap (C): taking B and D weighs only 8 kg and leaves capacity unused when B and C fit together.

questions.question_text: You have an unmarked 3-litre jug and an unmarked 5-litre jug and unlimited water. One step is one of: fill a jug to the top, empty a jug, or pour from one jug into the other until the source is empty or the receiving jug is full. What is the least number of steps needed to get exactly 4 litres in one of the jugs?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Writing states as (5-litre, 3-litre): fill the 5-litre jug (5,0); pour into the 3-litre jug (2,3); empty the 3-litre jug (2,0); pour the 2 litres across (0,2); fill the 5-litre jug (5,2); pour into the 3-litre jug until it is full (4,3). That is 6 steps. Starting with the 3-litre jug needs 8 steps. Shortcut: write each state as (5-litre, 3-litre) and search level by level. Trap (A): starting by filling the 3-litre jug reaches 4 litres only after 8 steps. Trap (B): this leaves out one of the pours; no 5-step sequence gives 4 litres. Trap (D): a 7-step sequence does not reach 4 litres.

questions.question_text: A machine gives change only in ₹1, ₹6 and ₹10 coins. What is the least number of coins that make exactly ₹12?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Greedy picks 10 and is then forced into two ₹1 coins: 3 coins. But 6 + 6 = 12 uses 2 coins. One coin is impossible because there is no ₹12 coin, so 2 is the minimum. Shortcut: greedy fails for unusual coin sets; check combinations of the middle coin. Trap (A): taking the biggest coin first (10 + 1 + 1) uses three coins. Trap (B): 6 + six ₹1 coins misses that two ₹6 coins finish the job. Trap (C): using only ₹1 coins is the slowest way.

questions.concept_tag: Network flow - maximum through a pipe system
questions.question_text: Water flows only in the directions shown. Pipe capacities (units per minute): S to A 12, S to B 9, A to B 6, A to T 5, B to T 10. What is the greatest rate at which water can reach T from S?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The pipes into T carry at most 5 + 10 = 15. This is reachable: A to T carries 5; S to A carries 11 (5 into A to T and 6 into A to B); S to B carries 4, so B receives 10 and B to T is full. Total into T = 5 + 10 = 15. By max-flow min-cut, the smallest cut, {A to T, B to T}, equals 15. Shortcut: find the smallest set of pipes whose removal disconnects S from T. Trap (B): adding the two pipes leaving S ignores the narrower pipes into T. Trap (C): this adds the pipes leaving the set {S, A} (9 + 6 + 5), which is not the smallest cut. Trap (D): this adds S to A and B to T (12 + 10), which is a cut but not the smallest.

questions.concept_tag: Scoring - correct answers from net marks
questions.question_text: A test has 30 questions. A correct answer earns 4 marks, a wrong answer costs 1 mark, and an unattempted question earns 0. Kabir attempts 24 questions and scores 66. How many of his answers are correct?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let c be correct, so 24 - c are wrong: 4c - (24 - c) = 66, so 5c = 90 and c = 18. Check: 72 - 6 = 66. Shortcut: each wrong answer swaps +4 for -1, a 5-mark swing from the all-correct score of 96. Trap (A): dividing 66 by 4 ignores the marks lost for wrong answers. Trap (C): this is the number of wrong answers, not the number correct. Trap (D): writing 4c - (24 - c) as 4c - 24 - c gives 30, more than the 24 attempted.

questions.question_text: A desk quotes: 1 AUR = 2 BEX, 1 BEX = 3 CIN, and 1 CIN = 0.18 AUR. A trader starts with 100 AUR, converts to BEX, then to CIN, and then back to AUR. How many AUR does the trader end up with?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 100 AUR gives 200 BEX, then 600 CIN, then 600 × 0.18 = 108 AUR. The rates multiply to 2 × 3 × 0.18 = 1.08, a gain of 8 percent. Shortcut: multiply the three rates; anything other than 1 means a gain or loss. Trap (A): assuming a round trip returns the starting amount ignores that the three rates do not multiply to 1. Trap (B): adding 18 for the rate 0.18 mixes a rate with an amount. Trap (D): this is the CIN holding before the last conversion.

questions.question_text: A lock accepts 4-symbol codes made from the letters X and Y, with no two X's side by side. How many different codes are possible?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: List by number of X's: none: YYYY (1); one X: 4 ways; two X's not adjacent: XYXY, XYYX, YXYX (3). Three X's cannot avoid touching. Total = 1 + 4 + 3 = 8. Shortcut: count by number of X's, since only 0, 1 or 2 are allowed. Trap (A): this counts all codes without the restriction. Trap (C): this allows at most one X, which is stricter than the rule. Trap (D): subtracting one forbidden code per position for XX misses the overlaps.

questions.question_text: Three bus routes leave a depot at 6:00. Route 1 buses leave every 12 minutes, Route 2 every 18 minutes and Route 3 every 30 minutes. Counting the 6:00 departure and a departure at 12:00, how many times between 6:00 and 12:00 do buses of all three routes leave together?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: All three leave together every LCM(12, 18, 30) = 180 minutes = 3 hours. Within 6:00 to 12:00 inclusive, that is 6:00, 9:00 and 12:00, which is 3 times. Shortcut: use the LCM of all three intervals, then count the endpoints. Trap (B): this omits the 6:00 start (or the 12:00 end) from the count. Trap (C): using only routes 2 and 3 (together every 90 minutes) counts too many. Trap (D): using only routes 1 and 3 (together every 60 minutes) counts too many.

questions.question_text: Four customers arrive together at one counter and need 5, 1, 2 and 4 minutes of service. They are served one at a time, and a customer's waiting time is the time before service starts. If the clerk picks the order that makes the average waiting time as small as possible, what is that average?

options.A: 4.75 minutes
options.B: 2.75 minutes
options.C: 6.25 minutes
options.D: 3 minutes

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Serve the shortest first: order 1, 2, 4, 5. Waiting times are 0, 1, 3 and 7, a total of 11, so the average is 11/4 = 2.75 minutes. Shortcut: shortest job first minimises average waiting. Trap (A): this is the average when the customers are served in the order listed. Trap (C): this is the average when the longest job goes first. Trap (D): this is the average service time, not the average waiting time.

questions.question_text:
A bus starts its route empty. The table shows the number of passengers boarding and alighting at each stop. At a stop, passengers alight first and then others board.

| Stop | Alight | Board |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 12 |
| 2 | 3 | 8 |
| 3 | 9 | 5 |
| 4 | 6 | 14 |
| 5 | 10 | 0 |
| 6 | 11 | 4 |

What is the largest number of passengers on the bus at any time while it is moving between stops?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Load after each stop: 12; 12 - 3 + 8 = 17; 17 - 9 + 5 = 13; 13 - 6 + 14 = 21; 21 - 10 = 11; 11 - 11 + 4 = 4. The maximum is 21, between stops 4 and 5. Shortcut: keep a running total with alighting subtracted before boarding is added. Trap (A): adds the 14 boarding at stop 4 to the 13 already on the bus without removing the 6 who alight there. Trap (C): stops at the first peak, after stop 2. Trap (D): adds all boardings, ignoring those who alight.

questions.question_text: Nine coins look identical, but one is slightly heavier. You have a balance scale with two pans and no weights. What is the least number of weighings that guarantees finding the heavy coin?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Split into three groups of 3. Weigh two groups: the heavier pan holds the heavy coin, or if balanced it is in the third group. Then weigh two coins of that group of 3 the same way. So 2 weighings suffice, and 1 is not enough because one weighing separates at most 3 coins. Shortcut: each weighing has 3 outcomes, so k weighings separate 3 to the power k coins. Trap (A): weighing 4 against 4 wastes the third outcome (balance), so this needs more weighings. Trap (B): this counts ceil(log2 9), assuming every weighing has only two outcomes. Trap (D): comparing coins one pair at a time is far slower than splitting into groups.

questions.question_text:
A 4 by 4 grid is filled with the digits 1 to 4 so that each row, each column and each of the four 2 by 2 corner boxes contains each digit once. Dots are blank cells.

| | C1 | C2 | C3 | C4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | . | 3 | . | . |
| R2 | 1 | . | 3 | 2 |
| R3 | . | . | . | 1 |
| R4 | . | . | . | 3 |

What digit goes in the cell R4, C1?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Row R2 is 1, _, 3, 2, so R2, C2 = 4. The top-left box then needs 2 in R1, C1. Column C1 now has 2 and 1, so R3, C1 and R4, C1 take 3 and 4. Row R4 already has 3 in C4, so R4, C1 = 4. Shortcut: fill the row that has three givens first, then follow the forced box. Trap (A): 1 already appears in column C1 (R2) so it cannot go in R4, C1. Trap (B): 2 is forced into R1, C1 by the top-left box and column C1, so it cannot be in R4, C1. Trap (C): 3 already appears in row R4 (column C4).

questions.question_text:
Staff of a firm by department and usual way of travelling to work:

| Department | Cycle | Bus | Car |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sales | 18 | 42 | 20 |
| Tech | 32 | 28 | 40 |
| Ops | 10 | 30 | 30 |

Of the staff who do not travel by car, what percentage are from Tech?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Non-car staff: Sales 18 + 42 = 60, Tech 32 + 28 = 60, Ops 10 + 30 = 40, total 160. Tech share = 60 / 160 = 37.5%. Shortcut: when the question says 'of those who...', that group is the denominator. Trap (A): this is Tech's share of all 250 staff, ignoring the condition. Trap (B): this divides Tech's non-car staff (60) by all 250 staff instead of by the 160 non-car staff. Trap (C): this is Tech's share of cyclists only, treating non-car as cycling.

questions.question_text: Four hikers must cross a narrow bridge at night. They have one torch, and the bridge holds at most two people at a time. A pair walks at the speed of the slower person, and someone must carry the torch back for the next crossing. The hikers take 1, 3, 6 and 8 minutes to cross alone. What is the least total time for all four to get across?

options.A: 19 minutes
options.B: 17 minutes
options.C: 18 minutes
options.D: 21 minutes

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Send 1 and 3 across (3 min), 1 returns (1), 6 and 8 cross together (8), 3 returns (3), 1 and 3 cross again (3). Total = 3 + 1 + 8 + 3 + 3 = 18. Sending the two slowest together means the 6 is hidden inside the 8. Shortcut: pair the two slowest hikers so only the larger time is paid. Trap (A): letting the fastest hiker escort each of the others and walk back alone each time (3 + 1 + 6 + 1 + 8) costs 19. Trap (B): adding 3 + 6 + 8 ignores the time spent carrying the torch back. Trap (D): sending the 3-minute hiker back and then escorting the slow hikers one at a time (3 + 3 + 6 + 1 + 8) costs 21.

questions.question_text:
A hall can host one event at a time, and an event that ends at a given hour allows another to start at that hour. Seven events request the hall; the table gives start, end (hours on a 24-hour clock) and fee (₹ thousand).

| Event | Start | End | Fee |
|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | 2 | 5 | 5 |
| E2 | 0 | 5 | 9 |
| E3 | 5 | 7 | 8 |
| E4 | 7 | 11 | 8 |
| E5 | 5 | 10 | 9 |
| E6 | 1 | 4 | 4 |
| E7 | 2 | 4 | 7 |

What is the largest total fee the hall can earn?

options.A: ₹25 thousand
options.B: ₹18 thousand
options.C: ₹20 thousand
options.D: ₹23 thousand

questions.pedagogical_explanation: E2 (0 to 5, 9) followed by E3 (5 to 7, 8) and E4 (7 to 11, 8) are all compatible, giving 25. No other compatible set does better: E7 with E3 and E4 gives 23 and anything with E5 forfeits E3 and E4. Shortcut: check whether a long, high-paying event blocks several short ones that add up to more. Trap (B): taking the highest fee first (E2, then E5, which fits) leaves nothing else that fits and earns only 18. Trap (C): taking the event that ends first (E6) and then each next compatible one (E3, E4) earns 20. Trap (D): taking events by best fee per hour (E3, E7, E4) earns 23.

questions.question_text:
A firm has 5 units of budget to split (whole units) among three projects. The total return (₹ lakh) for each number of units:

| Units | Project P | Project Q | Project R |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 3 | 1 | 6 |
| 2 | 6 | 5 | 7 |
| 3 | 7 | 6 | 8 |
| 4 | 10 | 8 | 9 |
| 5 | 13 | 10 | 13 |

What is the largest total return?

options.A: ₹16 lakh
options.B: ₹17 lakh
options.C: ₹13 lakh
options.D: ₹15 lakh

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Check all splits of 5 units. The split P = 2, Q = 2, R = 1 earns 6 + 5 + 6 = 17. The next best is 16 (P = 4, R = 1), so 17 is the maximum. Shortcut: returns are not smooth, so test the balanced splits rather than following the best next unit. Trap (A): adding one unit at a time to the project with the best next-unit gain ends at 4 units to P and 1 to R, which returns 16. Trap (C): putting all 5 units into one project returns at most 13. Trap (D): the split 1, 2, 2 units earns 3 + 5 + 7 = 15; moving a unit gains 2.

questions.question_text: Three boxes each hold two coins: one box has two gold coins, one has two silver coins, and one has one gold and one silver coin. A box is chosen at random and a coin is drawn at random from it. The coin is gold. What is the probability that the other coin in the same box is also gold?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: There are three gold coins that could have been drawn, and two of them lie in the gold-gold box. Given a gold draw, the other coin is gold with probability 2/3. (Bayes: (1/3 × 1) / (1/3 × 1 + 1/3 × 1/2) = 2/3.) Shortcut: count equally likely coins, not boxes. Trap (A): argues that only two boxes remain, so each is equally likely, forgetting that the gold-gold box offers two gold coins to draw. Trap (C): reports the chance of having picked the gold-gold box before the draw. Trap (D): reports the chance of picking the mixed box and drawing its gold coin.

questions.question_text: Two players take turns removing 1, 3 or 4 stones from a pile, and the player who takes the last stone wins. For how many starting pile sizes from 1 to 20 does the second player win with best play?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A pile is lost for the player to move if every move leads to a winning pile. Working up from 0: losing piles are 0, 2, 7, 9, 14, 16, 21, ... (pattern repeats every 7: 0 and 2 mod 7). In 1 to 20 these are 2, 7, 9, 14, 16, which is 5 values. Shortcut: find the losing piles from the bottom; the pattern repeats with period 7. Trap (A): this is the count for the usual 'remove 1 to 4' game, where only multiples of 5 lose for the first player. Trap (B): this rounds 20 times 2 over 7 up; the losing sizes in 1 to 20 are only 2, 7, 9, 14 and 16. Trap (D): this counts the sizes where the first player wins.

questions.question_text: A circular park has a fountain at the centre and five beds around it in a ring. Each bed touches its two neighbours in the ring and also the fountain. Four colours are available; the fountain and the five beds are each painted one colour, and any two touching areas must differ. In how many ways can the park be painted?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The fountain has 4 colour choices; the five ring beds must then use only the remaining 3 colours and be a proper colouring of a 5-cycle: (3 - 1)^5 + (-1)^5 × (3 - 1) = 32 - 2 = 30. Total = 4 × 30 = 120. Shortcut: colour the centre first, then count proper colourings of the ring from the remaining colours. Trap (A): treating the ring as a straight line (3 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 48) and ignoring that the first and last beds touch gives 192. Trap (C): 48 treats the ring as a straight line (3 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2) and forgets the 4 choices for the fountain. Trap (D): colouring the ring with all 4 colours ignores that no bed may use the fountain's colour.

questions.question_text: Twelve people numbered 1 to 12 stand in a circle. Starting from person 1 and counting 1, 2, 3 clockwise, every third person still in the circle leaves, and counting continues from the next person. Who is the last person remaining?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Order of leaving: 3, 6, 9, 12, then counting continues from 1: 4, 8, then 1, 7, 2, 11 and 5. Only person 10 is never removed. Shortcut: write the circle out and strike every third name; do not skip the wrap-around. Trap (B): this is the last person to leave, not the one remaining. Trap (C): this is the first person to leave. Trap (D): this assumes the last numbered person survives, but 12 leaves fourth.

questions.concept_tag: Switches in a row - fewest presses
questions.question_text: Five lamps in a row are numbered 1 to 5; lamps 1, 3 and 5 are ON and lamps 2 and 4 are OFF. Pressing a lamp's switch flips that lamp and its immediate neighbours (lamp 1 has one neighbour, lamp 5 has one). What is the smallest number of presses that turns all lamps OFF?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Press lamps 2, 3 and 4. Start 1 0 1 0 1; press 2 (flips lamps 1 to 3): 0 1 0 0 1; press 3 (flips 2 to 4): 0 0 1 1 1; press 4 (flips 3 to 5): 0 0 0 0 0. Two presses cannot work: a single press flips 11000, 11100, 01110, 00111 or 00011, and no pair of these combines to 10101. Shortcut: a press order does not matter, so test which set of lamps to press. Trap (B): no pair of presses produces the pattern 10101, so two presses never switch all lamps off. Trap (C): pressing every lamp once leaves lamps 1, 2, 4 and 5 on, so it does not switch all lamps off. Trap (D): a 3-press sequence already works, so 4 is not the least.

questions.question_text: The numbers 5, 3, 6, 1, 4, 2 are in a row. In one move you may swap two neighbouring numbers. What is the least number of moves needed to put them in increasing order?
questions.trap_type: Lower bound mistaken for exact value
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Each adjacent swap removes exactly one inversion (a pair in the wrong order). Inversions: 5 with 3, 1, 4, 2 (4); 3 with 1, 2 (2); 6 with 1, 4, 2 (3); 4 with 2 (1). Total 10 moves. Shortcut: minimum adjacent swaps equals the number of inversions. Trap (A): this is the number of pairs of numbers, which counts pairs already in order. Trap (C): this is the number of numbers that are out of place; a single swap may fix only one. Trap (D): this is half the total distance the numbers must travel, a lower bound that is not reachable here.

questions.question_text: Five married couples attend a party. Nobody shakes hands with their own partner or with themselves, and nobody shakes hands with the same person twice. The host asks each of the other nine people how many hands they shook and receives nine different answers. How many hands did the host's partner shake?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Each person can shake at most 8 hands (all but themselves and their partner), so the nine answers are exactly 0 to 8. The person with 8 shook everyone except their partner, so the person with 0 must be that partner. Remove that couple: the remaining people each lose one handshake and the argument repeats: 7 pairs with 1, 6 with 2, 5 with 3. That leaves the host and the person with 4: the host's partner shook 4 hands. Shortcut: pair 8 with 0, 7 with 1 and so on; the unpaired number is the host's partner. Trap (A): this ignores that the answers 0 to 8 pair off as (8, 0), (7, 1), (6, 2), (5, 3) leaving 4. Trap (B): the person who shook 5 hands is paired with the person who shook 3. Trap (C): the person who shook 8 hands is the partner of the person who shook 0.

questions.concept_tag: Pigeonhole - guaranteed five of a kind
questions.question_text: A bag holds 10 red, 8 blue, 6 green and 3 yellow balls. Balls are drawn one at a time without looking. What is the least number of balls that must be drawn to be certain of having five of the same colour?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In the worst case you hold 4 red, 4 blue, 4 green and all 3 yellow, 15 balls with no colour at five. The 16th ball must complete five of a colour. Shortcut: build the worst case first: the most balls you can hold without five of any colour, then add one. Trap (A): 4 × 4 + 1 assumes every colour can supply four balls, but yellow has only 3. Trap (B): allowing five of each colour in the worst case already counts five of a kind. Trap (C): this takes just 4 red, 4 blue and 4 green plus 1, forgetting the 3 yellow balls that can also be drawn without making five.

questions.concept_tag: Ants on a stick - passing through
questions.question_text: Four ants stand on a 120 cm stick at distances 20, 50, 70 and 100 cm from its left end. Each ant walks at 1 cm per second, either left or right, and the directions are chosen freely. When two ants meet, each turns round at once and walks the other way at the same speed. An ant falls off when it reaches an end of the stick. Over all possible choices of directions, what is the longest time before every ant has fallen off?

options.A: 100 seconds
options.B: 120 seconds
options.C: 70 seconds
options.D: 60 seconds

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Treat meetings as ants passing through each other: swapping labels changes nothing about when positions are occupied. Then each ant walks straight off an end. The longest possible time is the largest distance any ant must walk: for the ant at 20 cm it is 100 cm (to the right end), for the ant at 100 cm it is also 100 cm (to the left end). Longest time = 100 s. Shortcut: collisions do not matter: ants may be imagined to pass through one another. Trap (B): takes the full length of the stick. Trap (C): takes the largest distance for the two middle ants. Trap (D): takes half the length of the stick.

questions.question_text:
A workshop has one machine and four jobs. Each job has a processing time (hours) and a penalty weight; the cost of a job is its weight multiplied by the time at which it finishes.

| Job | Hours | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| J1 | 4 | 2 |
| J2 | 2 | 3 |
| J3 | 5 | 4 |
| J4 | 1 | 1 |

What is the smallest possible total cost?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Order jobs by weight divided by hours, largest first: J2 (1.5), J4 (1), J3 (0.8), J1 (0.5). Finish times 2, 3, 8, 12. Cost = 3×2 + 1×3 + 4×8 + 2×12 = 6 + 3 + 32 + 24 = 65. Shortcut: sort by weight per hour of work, highest first. Trap (A): running the shortest job first (J4, J2, J1, J3) gives 72. Trap (C): running the jobs in the order listed gives 82. Trap (D): running the job with the biggest weight first (J3, J2, J1, J4) gives 75.

questions.concept_tag: Regions of a plane - lines with a parallel pair
questions.question_text: Five straight lines are drawn in a plane so that exactly two of them are parallel to each other, no other pair is parallel, and no three lines pass through a common point. Into how many regions do the lines divide the plane?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Each new line adds one more region than the number of lines it crosses. Start with 1 region. Line 1 adds 1 (total 2). Line 2 (parallel to line 1) crosses none, adds 1 (3). Line 3 crosses 2 lines, adds 3 (6). Line 4 crosses 3, adds 4 (10). Line 5 crosses 4, adds 5 (15). Shortcut: regions = 1 + number of lines + number of intersection points. Trap (A): uses the count for five lines with no parallel pair. Trap (B): counts only the intersection points, not the regions. Trap (D): subtracts 2 for the parallel pair instead of 1.

questions.question_text: A child climbs a flight of 10 steps, taking 1, 2 or 3 steps at a time, but never two 3-step moves in a row. In how many different ways can the child reach the top?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Without the rule, the number of ways satisfies f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2) + f(n-3), giving 274 for 10 steps. Sequences with two adjacent 3-step moves number 24; removing them gives 250. Shortcut: count by the last move: keep one count for sequences ending in a 3 and one for those that do not. Trap (A): this counts all sequences, with no restriction on consecutive 3-step moves. Trap (B): subtracting each occurrence of two adjacent 3-step moves counts a run of three 3-steps twice. Trap (D): allowing at most one 3-step move is stricter than the rule.

questions.question_text: Ten coins lie heads up on a table. In each move you must turn over exactly three coins. What is the least number of moves needed to make all ten coins tails up?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Every coin must be turned an odd number of times, so the total number of turns is even (ten odd numbers add to an even number). Total turns = 3m, so m is even. Also 3m ≥ 10, so m ≥ 4. With m = 4 there are 12 turns: turn each of the ten coins once and two extra turns on one coin (3 turns in all). That is feasible, so the least number is 4. Shortcut: parity of total flips plus a lower bound from 3m ≥ 10. Trap (A): rounds 10/3 down; three moves turn only nine coin-flips, so one coin stays heads. Trap (B): takes an odd number of moves, but an odd number of moves gives an odd number of flips and cannot flip ten coins an odd number of times each. Trap (C): turns one coin per move in effect.

questions.question_text: A workshop makes two products. Product P needs 3 machine-hours and 1 assembly-hour and earns ₹50; product Q needs 2 machine-hours and 2 assembly-hours and earns ₹60. There are 24 machine-hours and 12 assembly-hours. Only whole numbers of products can be made. What is the greatest profit?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Both constraints bind at the best point: 3P + 2Q = 24 and P + 2Q = 12 give P = 6, Q = 3. Profit = 6 × 50 + 3 × 60 = 480. Other whole-number plans earn less (for example 8 P alone is 400). Shortcut: intersect the two limits and check that the corner is a whole number. Trap (A): making 4 of each earns only 440 and leaves machine-hours unused. Trap (B): making only P (8 units, limited by machine-hours) earns 400. Trap (D): making only Q (6 units, limited by assembly-hours) earns 360.

questions.question_text: A 3-digit number ABC (digits A, B, C with A greater than C) satisfies ABC - CBA = 297, and A + B + C = 14, and ABC is divisible by 11. What is ABC?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: ABC - CBA = 99(A - C), so A - C = 3. With digit sum 14: (A, B, C) = (4, 9, 1), (5, 7, 2), (6, 5, 3), (7, 3, 4), (8, 1, 5). The divisibility test (A - B + C = 0 or 11) holds only for 572: 5 - 7 + 2 = 0. Shortcut: the difference of a number and its reverse is 99 times (A - C). Trap (A): it satisfies the first two clues but 4 - 9 + 1 = -4, so it is not a multiple of 11. Trap (B): it satisfies the first two clues but 6 - 5 + 3 = 4, so it is not a multiple of 11. Trap (C): it satisfies the first two clues but 7 - 3 + 4 = 8, so it is not a multiple of 11.

questions.question_text:
100 voters rank three candidates. The ballot patterns:

| Number of voters | First | Second | Third |
|---|---|---|---|
| 36 | A | B | C |
| 33 | B | C | A |
| 25 | C | B | A |
| 6 | C | A | B |

The candidate with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated and those ballots go to each voter's next choice among the remaining candidates. How many votes does the winner have in the final count?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: First choices: A 36, B 33, C 31. C is eliminated. Of C's 31 ballots, 25 rank B next and 6 rank A next. Final: B = 33 + 25 = 58, A = 36 + 6 = 42. B wins with 58. Shortcut: eliminate the lowest, then redistribute only that candidate's ballots by their second choice. Trap (B): this is the leader's first-round vote count; the leader loses after C's votes are redistributed. Trap (C): this is the final count of the runner-up A. Trap (D): this is the winner's first-round count, before C's 25 votes are added.

questions.concept_tag: Tariff comparison - when is the flat rate cheapest
questions.question_text:
Four monthly plans for a service:

| Plan | Fixed fee | Included units | Rate per extra unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | ₹200 | 100 | ₹4 |
| P2 | ₹500 | 200 | ₹6 |
| P3 | ₹0 | 0 | ₹3.50 |
| P4 | ₹100 | 50 | ₹3 |

For how many whole-number usages from 0 to 300 units is Plan P3 strictly the cheapest of the four?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: P3 costs 3.5u. P4 costs ₹100 up to 50 units. P3 < P4 while 3.5u < 100, i.e. u ≤ 28. P1 costs at least ₹200 and P2 at least ₹500, so they cannot beat P3 in that range. Cheapest P3 for u = 0 to 28, which is 29 values. Shortcut: compare P3 with the plan that has the lowest fixed fee, since that plan is first to beat it. Trap (A): this leaves out usage 0, where P3 is also the cheapest (it costs nothing). Trap (B): at 29 units P3 costs ₹101.50, more than P4's ₹100. Trap (C): this compares P3 with P1 alone, ignoring that P4 becomes cheaper than P3 sooner.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'The town library should stay open until 9 pm on weekdays. At present it closes at 5 pm, and many working people live nearby. Opening later will therefore increase the number of people who use the library.' Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?

options.A: Every person in the town will use the library once it stays open until 9 pm
options.B: Some working people nearby cannot visit the library during its present hours but could visit in the evening
options.C: The library has more books than any other library in the district
options.D: Most people who work nearby already use the library before 5 pm

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Negation test: suppose no working person is prevented by the closing time. Then later hours add no users, and the conclusion collapses. So the stated option is needed. Shortcut: look for the gap between 'working people live nearby' and 'will use it later'. Shortcut: negate the option; if the conclusion falls, it is the assumption. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The argument needs only some additional users, not all. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The size of the collection is not connected to the claim about more users. Trap (D): Reversal. If most already used it, the extra hours would add few new users; the argument needs unmet demand in the evening.

questions.question_text: Read the passage: 'Because the river's water level rises sharply after heavy rain, and because the old bridge sits barely above the normal water line, the old bridge is at risk of flooding. The council should therefore build the new bridge on higher ground.' What is the main conclusion of the passage?

options.A: The river's water level rises sharply after heavy rain
options.B: The old bridge is at risk of flooding
options.C: The council should build the new bridge on higher ground
options.D: The old bridge sits barely above the normal water line

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The word 'therefore' flags the final claim: the recommendation about the new bridge. Everything before it is support. Shortcut: the conclusion is the claim the others are offered to prove, often marked by 'therefore'. Shortcut: find the claim that the others are meant to prove. Trap (A): Half-true. This is a premise that supports the conclusion. Trap (B): Half-true. This is an intermediate conclusion supporting the recommendation, not the final one. Trap (D): Half-true. This is a factual premise.

questions.question_text: All orchids in the greenhouse need shade. Some plants in the greenhouse are orchids. Which of the following must be true?

options.A: Some plants in the greenhouse need shade
options.B: All plants in the greenhouse need shade
options.C: Some plants that need shade are not orchids
options.D: No plant in the greenhouse other than orchids needs shade

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Some plants are orchids, and all orchids need shade, so those orchid plants need shade. Hence some greenhouse plants need shade. The other options claim something about plants that are not orchids, which the statements do not cover. Shortcut: chain 'some' with 'all' to get 'some'. Trap (B): Extreme scope. Only the orchids are stated to need shade; other plants are not covered. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The statements say nothing about shade-loving non-orchids. Trap (D): Reversal. This claims more than the statements say; they are silent on other plants.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'Our school should adopt a uniform, because uniforms reduce rivalry over clothes and so improve discipline.' Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.A: Uniforms are cheaper than ordinary clothes
options.B: Some students dislike wearing uniforms
options.C: In schools that adopted uniforms, the number of disciplinary complaints fell
options.D: The school building was recently painted

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The claim is that uniforms improve discipline. Evidence that discipline complaints fell after uniforms were introduced directly supports it. Other options deal with cost, dislike or paint, which do not bear on discipline. Shortcut: pick the option that links the cause to the stated effect. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Cost does not show an effect on discipline. Trap (B): Reversal. This is mildly against the proposal, not for it. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. It has no bearing on uniforms or discipline.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'After the town banned plastic bags, litter in its streets fell by a third. The ban therefore cut the amount of litter.' Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

options.A: The ban was announced a month before it took effect
options.B: Many shoppers now carry cloth bags
options.C: Plastic bags are cheap to make
options.D: In the same period the town started a daily street-cleaning programme that removed most litter

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A new street-cleaning programme gives another explanation for the fall in litter, so the fall may not be due to the ban. Weakening works by offering an alternative cause. Shortcut: look for another cause of the same effect. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The timing of the announcement does not offer another cause. Trap (B): Reversal. This supports the ban's effect. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The cost of making bags does not touch the cause of the fall in litter.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'Every time the market vendor lights incense in the morning, rain falls by evening. So the incense causes the rain.' What is the flaw in the reasoning?

options.A: It assumes that because one event came before another, the first caused the second
options.B: It relies on the opinion of a single vendor
options.C: It assumes that rain falls only in the evening
options.D: It proves that incense never causes rain

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The argument moves from 'incense, then rain' to 'incense causes rain'. Sequence alone does not show causation; there may be a common cause such as the season. Shortcut: before-and-after is not cause-and-effect. Shortcut: sequence is not causation. Trap (B): Half-true. The argument does not rely on opinion; it relies on a sequence of events. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The argument says nothing that requires rain to fall only in the evening. Trap (D): Reversal. The argument tries to prove the opposite.

questions.question_text: All lanterns in the shop are brass. No brass item in the shop is for sale. Which conclusion definitely follows?

options.A: Some brass items in the shop are for sale
options.B: No lantern in the shop is for sale
options.C: All items in the shop are brass
options.D: Some lanterns in the shop are for sale

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Lanterns are brass, and no brass item is for sale, so no lantern is for sale. The remaining options either overreach or contradict. Shortcut: link 'all A are B' with 'no B are C' to get 'no A are C'. Shortcut: all A are B, no B are C gives no A are C. Trap (A): Reversal. No brass item in the shop is for sale, so this contradicts the second statement. Trap (C): Extreme scope. Nothing is said about items that are not lanterns. Trap (D): Reversal. This contradicts the conclusion that follows.

questions.question_text: Passage: 'Some people say that pigeons are pests. Yet pigeons help to spread seeds and to clean up food waste in cities. We should therefore not regard them only as pests.' What role does the statement 'Pigeons help to spread seeds and to clean up food waste' play in the passage?

options.A: It is the main conclusion of the passage
options.B: It is a view that the author rejects
options.C: It is an example of a common opinion about pigeons
options.D: It is evidence offered in support of the conclusion

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The word 'therefore' marks the conclusion. The statement about seeds and waste is a reason for that conclusion, so it is a supporting premise. Shortcut: a statement before 'therefore' that supports the final claim is a premise. Trap (A): Half-true. The conclusion is the statement that begins with 'We should therefore'. Trap (B): Reversal. The author accepts it and uses it. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The common opinion is 'pigeons are pests', not this statement.

questions.question_text: Advertisement: 'Use Zesta toothpaste. Nine out of ten dentists in our survey said it is good for your teeth. So Zesta will give you healthier teeth.' Which of the following is an assumption of the advertisement?

options.A: What dentists say is good for teeth is likely to help the teeth of people who use it
options.B: Every person who uses Zesta will have perfect teeth
options.C: Zesta is the cheapest toothpaste in the market
options.D: The survey was conducted among people who do not use toothpaste

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Negation test: if dentists' approval says nothing about whether the toothpaste helps teeth, the ad's inference fails. So the link between approval and benefit is assumed. Shortcut: negate to test: if the conclusion collapses, it is an assumption. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The ad needs only that it helps, not that it makes teeth perfect. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. Price is not part of the argument. Trap (D): Reversal. This would undermine the survey, not support the ad.

questions.question_text: Most books in the school library are novels. Some novels in the library are very old. Which of the following can be concluded?

options.A: Most very old books in the library are novels
options.B: Most novels in the library are very old
options.C: At least one very old book in the library is a novel
options.D: No non-novel in the library is very old

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The only certain addition is that at least one very old novel exists, so at least one very old book is a novel. The other options claim proportions that are not given. Shortcut: 'some' gives only existence, not proportion. Trap (A): Half-true. The statements do not say how many old books exist or what they are. Trap (B): Extreme scope. Only some novels are stated to be old. Trap (D): Reversal. The statements do not exclude old non-novels.

questions.question_text: Rule: 'A student can enter the final round only if she has scored at least 60 in the preliminary round.' Meera has scored 72 in the preliminary round. Which of the following is correct?

options.A: Meera will certainly enter the final round
options.B: Meera cannot enter the final round
options.C: Meera meets the stated requirement, but it is not certain that she will enter the final round
options.D: Any student who scores 60 or more enters the final round

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Only if' makes 60 a necessary condition. Meeting it keeps her eligible, but nothing in the rule makes it enough. Hence we cannot say that she will certainly enter. Shortcut: 'only if' = necessary, not sufficient. Trap (A): Affirming the consequent confusion. A necessary condition does not guarantee entry; other conditions may exist. Trap (B): Reversal. Her score satisfies the condition. Trap (D): Extreme scope. 'Only if' states a necessary condition, not a sufficient one.

questions.concept_tag: Principle - what rule supports the argument
questions.question_text: Argument: 'Raj promised to return the book on Monday, so Raj ought to return it on Monday.' Which principle, if accepted, most justifies the reasoning?

options.A: People ought to do what they have promised to do
options.B: People ought to return everything they borrow immediately
options.C: People should never borrow books
options.D: People who forget things should not be trusted

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The argument moves from 'promised' to 'ought'. The principle that promises should be kept bridges that gap exactly. Shortcut: the principle should bridge premise and conclusion exactly. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The argument concerns a promised date, not immediate return. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The argument does not oppose borrowing. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. Nothing in the argument concerns forgetfulness.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'All birds in this park are sparrows. This creature is in the park. So this creature is a sparrow.' Which argument is most similar in its flaw?

options.A: All students in this hall are seniors. Sana is in the hall. So Sana is a senior student
options.B: Some students in this hall are seniors. Sana is in the hall. So Sana is a senior
options.C: No student in this hall is a senior. Sana is in the hall. So Sana is not a senior
options.D: Sana is a senior. All seniors are in the hall. So Sana is in the hall

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The flaw: the argument assumes that being in the park makes the creature a bird, though a creature in the park could be anything. The matching option makes the same move: being in the hall is taken to mean being a student. The matching option has the same structure: 'all X in a place, this thing in the place, so this thing is X', where the thing may not be an X at all. Shortcut: match the structure of the reasoning. Trap (B): Half-true. This has a different structure, as it begins with 'some'. Trap (C): Reversal. This is a valid argument. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. This is a valid argument with a different structure.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'In the town, ice cream sales and drowning accidents both rise sharply every summer. Therefore ice cream sales cause drowning accidents.' Which of the following best explains why the argument is weak?

options.A: Ice cream is a popular food
options.B: Drowning accidents are always avoidable
options.C: Ice cream sales rise only in the summer
options.D: Hot weather could be causing both more ice cream sales and more swimming, and hence more drowning

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A third factor, hot weather, can raise both ice cream sales and swimming. So the correlation does not show that ice cream causes drowning. Shortcut: look for a common cause. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Popularity does not explain the link. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. This is not about the cause. Trap (C): Half-true. This repeats the correlation and does not explain why it is not causal.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'I bought a mobile phone from Sagar Electronics last month and it stopped working in a week. All the phones sold by Sagar Electronics must therefore be faulty.' What is the flaw?

options.A: It assumes that Sagar Electronics sells only phones
options.B: It draws a conclusion about all phones from one instance
options.C: It argues that no phone can be faulty
options.D: It depends on the phone being expensive

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A single phone is too small a sample to show anything about all phones. Shortcut: 'one case → all cases' is a hasty generalisation. Shortcut: one case is not a rule. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The argument does not need this. Trap (C): Reversal. The argument claims the opposite. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. Price is not mentioned.

questions.question_text: Either the manager or the supervisor approved the leave request. It is known that the supervisor did not approve it. Which statement is certainly true?

options.A: Neither approved the leave request
options.B: Both approved the leave request
options.C: The leave request was rejected
options.D: The manager approved the leave request

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Either-or with one option eliminated leaves the other. So the manager approved it. Shortcut: eliminate one branch of an either-or. Trap (A): Reversal. The first statement says that one of them approved it. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The supervisor did not approve it. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The statements are about approval, and say nothing of rejection.

questions.question_text: A 'perennial' plant is one that lives for more than two years. The mango tree in Kavita's garden has lived for six years. Which of the following follows?

options.A: All trees are perennial plants
options.B: The mango tree will live for ten more years
options.C: Plants that live for less than two years are trees
options.D: The mango tree is a perennial plant

questions.pedagogical_explanation: By the definition, a plant that has lived for more than two years is perennial. Six years satisfies it. The other options go beyond the facts. Shortcut: apply the definition directly. Trap (A): Extreme scope. Only the definition and one tree are given. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. The definition does not predict future life. Trap (C): Reversal. The definition does not say what non-perennial plants are.

questions.question_text: Rohan is taller than Sameer. Sameer is taller than Tanvi. Which of the following must be true?

options.A: Tanvi is taller than Rohan
options.B: Rohan is taller than Tanvi
options.C: Sameer is the tallest of the three
options.D: Rohan and Tanvi are of the same height

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Taller-than is transitive. Rohan > Sameer > Tanvi, so Rohan > Tanvi. Shortcut: use transitivity. Trap (A): Reversal. This contradicts the chain. Trap (C): Reversal. Rohan is taller than Sameer. Trap (D): Reversal. The chain gives Rohan more height than Tanvi.

questions.concept_tag: Evaluate the argument - what to ask
questions.question_text: Argument: 'The company's new training programme must have worked, because the employees' average sales have risen since it began.' Which question would be most useful in evaluating this argument?

options.A: Do the employees enjoy their lunch breaks?
options.B: Is the training programme held in a large hall?
options.C: Did the employees' sales rise because of a factor other than the training, such as a new product or a seasonal demand?
options.D: Was the programme designed by a famous trainer?

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The argument infers cause from timing. The most useful question tests whether something else could explain the rise in sales. Shortcut: ask about other causes. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Lunch breaks are not connected to the argument. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. The venue does not bear on the effect of the training. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. Fame of the designer does not show that the training produced the rise.

questions.concept_tag: Strengthen - causal claim about a teaching method
questions.question_text: Argument: 'A school introduced weekly group-discussion classes in Class IX, and the pass rate in the next annual examination rose from 70% to 82%. The group-discussion classes therefore improved the students' results.' Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.A: The group-discussion classes were held in the afternoon
options.B: Class X, which did not get the discussion classes, showed no change in its pass rate over the same year
options.C: The examination paper in Class IX was made easier that year
options.D: Many students said they enjoyed the discussion classes

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A control group, Class X, with no change in results while Class IX improved, rules out general factors such as an easier year, so it strengthens the claim that the classes caused the rise. Enjoyment shows nothing about results. Shortcut: a comparison group that did not change supports the cause. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The time of the class does not bear on the cause of the rise. Trap (C): Reversal. This offers an alternative cause and weakens the argument. Trap (D): Half-true. Enjoyment does not show an effect on results, so it only mildly helps.

questions.concept_tag: Weaken - base rate in a statistic
questions.question_text: Argument: 'Of the 40 accidents recorded last year at the busy crossing, 30 involved cars with red paint. Red cars are therefore more dangerous than cars of other colours.' Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

options.A: The crossing has a poorly lit signal
options.B: Red cars make up about three-fourths of all the cars that pass through the crossing
options.C: Of the 10 remaining accidents, some involved lorries
options.D: Red paint is more expensive than other colours

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 30 of 40 accidents is 75%. If red cars are about 75% of all traffic, then they are involved in accidents in proportion to their numbers, so the figure does not show they are more dangerous. Shortcut: compare the share in accidents with the share in the population. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Poor lighting does not bear on whether red cars are more dangerous. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The vehicle types in other accidents do not change the share for red cars. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The cost of the paint is irrelevant to accident risk.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'The council should ban cars from the central market street. Without cars the street will be quieter and more pleasant, and so more shoppers will come, and the shopkeepers' sales will rise.' Which of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.A: The shopkeepers have asked the council to ban the cars
options.B: Cars are the main source of noise in the whole city
options.C: No shopper has ever complained about the noise of the street
options.D: The shoppers who now drive to the street will not stop coming merely because they can no longer bring cars

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Negation test: if drivers stop coming because they cannot park or bring cars, then the lost shoppers may exceed the new ones and the sales conclusion fails. So the argument assumes that they will not stay away. Shortcut: negate: if the loss of drivers cancels the gain, the conclusion fails. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Their request is not needed for the reasoning. Trap (B): Extreme scope. Only the market street is concerned. Trap (C): Reversal. Complaints would support the argument, and their absence is not needed.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'Either we ban all private cars in the city or we accept permanent smog. We cannot accept permanent smog. So we must ban all private cars.' Which of the following best describes the flaw in this reasoning?

options.A: It treats two options as the only ones, though other ways of reducing smog might exist
options.B: It assumes that smog is harmless
options.C: It confuses a cause with its effect
options.D: It rests on the authority of an unnamed expert

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The first premise offers only two options. If other measures, such as cleaner fuel or public transport, can reduce smog, the conclusion is not forced. Shortcut: check whether the 'either-or' really covers all options. Trap (B): Reversal. The argument treats smog as unacceptable. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The argument is not about cause and effect order. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. No expert is cited.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'Dr Mehra argues that the new bridge design is unsafe. But Dr Mehra was once fined for a parking offence, so his opinion about the bridge cannot be trusted.' What is the flaw in the reasoning?

options.A: It claims that parking offences are as serious as unsafe bridges
options.B: It relies on a survey of many engineers
options.C: It attacks the person who makes the claim instead of examining the reasons for the claim
options.D: It assumes that the bridge design is already built

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The argument rejects Dr Mehra's claim by pointing to something unrelated about him, and says nothing about whether the bridge design is safe. Shortcut: personal attack is not a rebuttal. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The argument does not compare the two. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. No survey is used. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. Nothing in the argument depends on this.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'Each player in our cricket team is an excellent batter. Therefore our team is an excellent batting side.' Which of the following most closely points out the flaw?

options.A: It assumes that there are no bowlers in the team
options.B: It relies on only one player's ability
options.C: It assumes that what is true of each part must be true of the whole
options.D: It assumes that the team will win every match

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Even if every member bats well, the team's batting could be weak if, for example, they bat in a poor order or fail to play together. A property of parts does not always carry over to the whole. Shortcut: parts to whole needs justification. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The flaw is not about bowlers. Trap (B): Reversal. The argument speaks of each player. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The argument is about the batting side, not winning every match.

questions.concept_tag: Resolve the paradox - lower price, lower revenue
questions.question_text: A bookshop reduced the price of its notebooks by 20% in order to increase its earnings. After the reduction, the number of notebooks sold increased by 10%, yet the bookshop's earnings from notebooks fell. Which of the following, if true, would help to resolve this apparent paradox?

options.A: The bookshop also sells pens and pencils
options.B: Customers like the new covers of the notebooks
options.C: The bookshop reduced the price of its pens by 5%
options.D: The rise in sales was less than 25%, so the extra volume did not make up for the lower price per notebook

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A 20% cut needs sales to rise by 25% to keep earnings the same: 0.8 × 1.25 = 1. A 10% rise falls short, so earnings fell. The option states this directly. Shortcut: check price × quantity. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Other items do not explain notebook earnings. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. Covers do not explain the fall in earnings. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The pens do not affect the notebook earnings.

questions.question_text: Statements: (1) If the festival is cancelled, the stalls will not be set up. (2) If the stalls are not set up, the vendors will lose income. The vendors did not lose income. Which conclusion must be true?

options.A: The festival was not cancelled
options.B: The stalls were set up but the festival was cancelled
options.C: The festival was cancelled and the vendors found another source of income
options.D: The stalls were not set up

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Chain: cancelled → no stalls → lost income. Contrapositive: no lost income → stalls were set up → festival was not cancelled. Shortcut: chain the conditionals, then take the contrapositive. Trap (B): Reversal. If the festival was cancelled, the stalls would not be set up. Trap (C): Reversal. Cancelled festival leads to lost income, which did not occur. Trap (D): Reversal. This leads to lost income, which did not occur.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'Hospitals should require all doctors to use the new diagnostic app, because it identified rare diseases correctly in a large trial.' Which of the following is an assumption of the argument?

options.A: No doctor can identify a rare disease without the app
options.B: The app will perform about as well in ordinary hospital use as it did in the trial
options.C: The app is free of cost for all hospitals
options.D: Rare diseases are the most common cause of death

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Negation test: if the app would do much worse in real use than in the trial, the trial result gives no reason to require it. So the argument assumes that trial performance carries over. Shortcut: trial to real life is the usual gap. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The argument needs only that the app helps, not that doctors cannot do without it. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. Cost is not part of the argument. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. This is not a requirement.

questions.question_text: In a society, 60% of the members voted in an election. Of those who voted, 50% voted for the same candidate, Uma. Which of the following must be true?

options.A: 30% of all the members voted for Uma
options.B: Uma won the election
options.C: 50% of all the members voted for Uma
options.D: 40% of all the members did not vote for Uma

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 50% of 60% = 30% of all members. The other options either confuse the base or claim a result which is not given. Shortcut: multiply the fractions: 0.6 × 0.5. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. The result depends on the other candidates' votes, which are not given. Trap (C): Reversal. Half of the voters is 50% of 60%, which is 30% of members. Trap (D): Reversal. Those who did not vote for Uma are 70% of members.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'Sales of the Zing energy drink doubled after its launch in the city, so the drink is popular with the city's residents.' Each of the following, if true, weakens the argument EXCEPT:

options.A: Most of the sales were to a single hotel for a conference
options.B: The sales figure includes sales to visiting tourists
options.C: The drink was sold at half the usual price for a month after launch
