options.D: Surveys show that most buyers who tried the drink bought it again

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Three options give reasons why sales could have doubled without popularity among residents. Repeat purchases support popularity, so that option does not weaken the argument; it is the exception. Shortcut: for an EXCEPT question, identify the three that do the task and pick the odd one. Trap (A): Reversal of function. This suggests that the rise is due to one bulk buyer, so it weakens. Trap (B): Reversal of function. This suggests that residents may not account for the rise, so it weakens. Trap (C): Reversal of function. This offers another reason for the rise in sales, so it weakens.

questions.question_text: Passage: 'The new law requires that every building should have a fire exit. Since the old market has no fire exit, it breaks the law. So the market owner may be fined.' Which of the following is an intermediate conclusion in the passage?

options.A: The new law requires that every building should have a fire exit
options.B: The market owner may be fined
options.C: The old market was built many years ago
options.D: The old market breaks the law

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The market breaks the law is derived from the law's requirement and the lack of exit, and it supports the final claim about the fine. So it is an intermediate conclusion. Shortcut: intermediate conclusion: supported by premises and itself supports the final claim. Trap (A): Half-true. This is a premise. Trap (B): Half-true. This is the final conclusion. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. This is not stated in the passage.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'If Anil studies hard, he will pass the exam. Anil passed the exam. Therefore Anil studied hard.' Which of the following arguments contains the same flaw?

options.A: If it rains, the ground gets wet. It did not rain. Therefore the ground is not wet
options.B: If it rains, the ground gets wet. The ground is wet. Therefore it rained
options.C: If it rains, the ground gets wet. It rained. Therefore the ground is wet
options.D: If the ground is wet, it rained. The ground is not wet. Therefore it did not rain

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The given argument affirms the consequent: from 'P then Q' and 'Q', it concludes 'P'. The wet-ground argument does the same. Other causes can produce the same result. Shortcut: P→Q and Q does not give P. Trap (A): Different flaw. This denies the antecedent, which is a different error. Trap (C): Valid. This is a valid argument. Trap (D): Valid. This is a valid argument by contrapositive.

questions.question_text: Ravi says: 'No one who plays chess well can be a poor mathematician.' Mala replies: 'My uncle plays chess very well, and he failed mathematics repeatedly.' Mala's reply proceeds by:

options.A: Attacking Ravi's character
options.B: Appealing to the opinion of most mathematicians
options.C: Offering a specific case that contradicts the general claim
options.D: Restating Ravi's claim in different words

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A universal claim is refuted by one case that violates it. Mala's uncle is such a case. Shortcut: one counterexample refutes a universal claim. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Mala does not comment on Ravi himself. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. No such appeal is made. Trap (D): Half-true. She does not restate it; she contradicts it.

questions.concept_tag: Conditional logic - only if and a fine
questions.question_text: Rule: 'A shopkeeper may be fined only if he sold an item above its marked price.' Hari, a shopkeeper, has been fined under this rule. Which of the following must be true?

options.A: Hari sold some item above its marked price
options.B: Hari sold every item in his shop above the marked price
options.C: Hari refused to give a receipt to a customer
options.D: Every shopkeeper who sells above the marked price is fined

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Fined only if above marked price' means fined → sold above marked price. Hari was fined, so he sold at least one item above its marked price. It does not follow that all sales were above, nor that all such shopkeepers are fined. Shortcut: 'X only if Y': X true means Y true. Trap (B): Extreme scope. One such sale is enough; the rule does not require all. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The rule says nothing about receipts. Trap (D): Reversal. 'Only if' gives a necessary condition and not a sufficient one.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'Since a ban on mobile phones in examination halls has cut cheating in our college, a ban on mobile phones in classrooms will improve attention in lessons.' Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.A: Classroom distraction in the college mainly came from students using their phones during lessons
options.B: The examination halls are larger than the classrooms
options.C: Teachers prefer to use whiteboards
options.D: Cheating in examinations has no link to attention

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The analogy works if the situations are similar. Showing that phones are the main source of distraction supports the claim that the ban will improve attention. Shortcut: strengthen an analogy by showing relevant similarity. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. Size does not link phones to attention. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. This does not link phones to attention. Trap (D): Reversal. This would make the examination ban an unsuitable comparison.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'Giving every employee a bonus raised morale at our sister firm, a small design studio. So giving every employee a bonus will raise morale at our factory with 5,000 workers.' Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

options.A: The studio is located in a different city
options.B: The bonus at the studio was paid in December
options.C: Many factory workers like their jobs
options.D: At the factory, bonuses are widely seen as an entitlement and not a reward, unlike at the small studio

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A relevant difference between the two situations undermines the analogy. If workers see a bonus as an entitlement, it need not raise morale. Shortcut: weaken analogies with a relevant difference. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Location alone does not show a different effect. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. The month is irrelevant. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. This does not show that a bonus will fail to raise morale.

questions.question_text: Statement: 'The match will go ahead unless it rains heavily.' It is known that the match did not go ahead. Which of the following must be true?

options.A: It rained lightly
options.B: It rained heavily
options.C: The ground was too dry for the match
options.D: The match would have gone ahead if it had rained lightly

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'A unless B' means 'if not B then A'. The contrapositive is 'if not A then B'. The match did not go ahead, so it rained heavily. Shortcut: 'A unless B' = 'if not A, then B'. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The statement is about heavy rain. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. Dryness is not mentioned. Trap (D): Half-true. This may be so, but it does not follow from the facts given as a certainty about the outcome.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'The city should repair the old stone bridge instead of building a new one, because repairing is cheaper and the bridge is of historical value.' Which of the following would be LEAST relevant in evaluating the argument?

options.A: The cost of the repairs compared with the cost of a new bridge
options.B: Whether the repaired bridge would be safe for traffic
options.C: The colour of the stone used in the old bridge
options.D: Whether experts agree that the bridge has historical value

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Cost, safety and historical value all affect the argument. The colour of the stone has no effect on any premise or on the conclusion. Shortcut: ask: would the answer change anything in the argument? Trap (A): Relevant. It bears on the cheaper-claim. Trap (B): Relevant. It bears on the conclusion that repair is adequate. Trap (D): Relevant. It bears on the historical-value premise.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. Therefore a feather cannot be dark.' What is the flaw in the reasoning?

options.A: It assumes that all feathers are of the same weight
options.B: It argues from a single feather to all feathers
options.C: The word 'light' is used in two different senses, one meaning not heavy and the other meaning not dark
options.D: It assumes that dark things are heavy

questions.pedagogical_explanation: In the first premise 'light' means of low weight, and in the second it means bright. The shift in meaning makes the conclusion unsupported. Shortcut: check that key words keep one meaning. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Weight in general is not the problem. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. The flaw is in the use of the word. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The argument says nothing about dark things being heavy.

questions.question_text: Rules: (1) If Anu attends the meeting, Bala attends. (2) If Bala attends, Charu does not attend. (3) At least one of Charu and Dev attends. Anu attends the meeting. Which of the following must be true?

options.A: Charu attends the meeting
options.B: Both Charu and Dev attend the meeting
options.C: Dev attends the meeting
options.D: Bala does not attend the meeting

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Chain: Anu → Bala → not Charu. Rule 3 says at least one of Charu and Dev attends; Charu is out, so Dev attends. Shortcut: follow the forced chain, then use the disjunction. Shortcut: follow the chain, then eliminate in the disjunction. Trap (A): Reversal. Anu attending leads to Bala attending, which means Charu does not attend. Trap (B): Reversal. Charu does not attend. Trap (D): Reversal. Anu's attendance forces Bala's attendance.

questions.question_text: Rule: 'A person may vote in the society's election only if he is a member, has paid his dues and has attended the general meeting.' Ravi voted in accordance with the rule. Which of the following must be true?

options.A: Ravi is a member, has paid his dues and attended the general meeting
options.B: Every member who has paid dues and attended the meeting voted
options.C: Ravi is a member who has paid his dues, but he may not have attended the meeting
options.D: Ravi was the only person who voted

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Only if' lists necessary conditions. If Ravi voted lawfully, all three conditions must hold. The other options treat the conditions as sufficient or drop one. Shortcut: 'X only if A, B, C' means X implies A, B and C. Trap (B): Necessary treated as sufficient. The rule lists necessary conditions; it does not say that every person who meets them voted. Trap (C): Half-true. Attendance is also a necessary condition. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The rule says nothing about how many voted.

questions.question_text: In a class, more than half the students play chess, and more than half the students play carrom. Which of the following must be true?

options.A: At least one student plays both chess and carrom
options.B: More than half the students play both games
options.C: Exactly half of the students play both games
options.D: No student plays only chess

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Two groups each larger than half of the class together exceed the class size, so they must overlap in at least one student. Nothing more can be stated. Shortcut: two majorities of the same group always intersect. Shortcut: two majorities of one group must overlap. Trap (B): Extreme scope. Overlap is guaranteed but not by such an amount. Trap (C): Extreme scope. No exact figure follows. Trap (D): Extreme scope. Some may play only chess.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'To win the election, a candidate must have the support of the public. Seema has the support of the public. Therefore Seema will win the election.' What is the flaw?

options.A: It assumes that Seema is the only candidate
options.B: It treats a condition that is needed for winning as if it were enough to win
options.C: It argues that public support is unimportant
options.D: It relies on a survey of Seema's friends

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Public support is necessary for winning, but the argument moves to 'will win' as if it were sufficient. Other conditions, such as votes on the day, may be missing. Shortcut: a requirement is not a guarantee. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The flaw is not about the number of candidates. Trap (C): Reversal. The argument treats public support as important. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. No survey is mentioned.

questions.concept_tag: Assumption - exposure in a vaccine trial
questions.question_text: Argument: 'The new vaccine is effective, because none of the 500 vaccinated volunteers caught the disease during the study.' Which of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.A: All the volunteers were of the same age
options.B: The vaccinated volunteers were exposed to the disease to a reasonable extent during the study
options.C: The disease is deadly
options.D: The vaccine was cheap to produce

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Negation test: if the volunteers were never exposed to the disease, the absence of cases says nothing about the vaccine. So exposure is needed. Shortcut: negate: no exposure means no evidence. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The argument needs exposure, not equality of age. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The seriousness of the disease is not part of the argument. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The cost is irrelevant.

questions.concept_tag: Weaken - overall rate versus category rates
questions.question_text: Argument: 'Hospital P has a higher overall death rate than Hospital Q. Hence P provides poorer treatment.' Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.A: P is much older than Q
options.B: P has more beds than Q
options.C: P's overall death rate is much higher than Q's
options.D: P treats mainly critically ill patients, and for critically ill patients and for other patients separately, P's death rate is lower than Q's

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If P receives more critically ill patients and does better in each group, the higher overall rate comes from the patient mix, not poorer treatment. Shortcut: compare like with like. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Age of the hospital does not affect the rate comparison. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. Number of beds is not linked to the death rate. Trap (C): Reversal. This repeats the premise and does not weaken it.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'People who wear heart-rate watches have healthier hearts than people who do not. So wearing such a watch improves heart health.' Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.A: In a trial, people given watches at random showed better heart health a year later than people who were not given watches
options.B: Heart-rate watches are expensive
options.C: People who buy heart-rate watches are usually already health-conscious
options.D: Many people wear watches for fashion

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Random assignment removes the possibility that health-conscious people simply choose watches, and so supports the claim that the watches cause the improvement. Shortcut: random assignment strengthens a causal claim. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. Price does not help the causal claim. Trap (C): Reversal. This offers another explanation, so it weakens. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. Fashion is not relevant.

questions.concept_tag: Resolve the paradox - safety rule and reported injuries
questions.question_text: A company introduced a compulsory helmet rule to reduce head injuries among its workers. In the first year after the rule, the number of head injuries recorded in the company's books rose. Which of the following, if true, best resolves the paradox?

options.A: The helmets are heavy and uncomfortable
options.B: The company hired more office staff in that year
options.C: Workers wear helmets for the whole shift
options.D: Before the rule, many minor head injuries went unrecorded, but after it every head injury had to be recorded

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If the way injuries are recorded changed, the recorded figure can rise even though actual injuries fell. This explains the paradox. Shortcut: look for a change in measurement. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Discomfort does not explain a rise in recorded injuries. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. Office staff do not wear helmets or face head injuries. Trap (C): Reversal. This would lower injuries, deepening the puzzle.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'Some doctors are researchers. All researchers are curious. Therefore some doctors are curious.' Which of the following is most similar in its reasoning?

options.A: All pilots are tall. Some tall people are heavy. Therefore all pilots are heavy
options.B: Some pilots are tall. Some tall people are heavy. Therefore some pilots are heavy
options.C: No pilot is tall. All tall people are heavy. Therefore no pilot is heavy
options.D: Some pilots are tall. All tall people are heavy. Therefore some pilots are heavy

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The structure is 'Some A are B; all B are C; so some A are C'. The pilots argument has the same valid form. In the other options the structure changes. Shortcut: match the logical form. Trap (A): Extreme scope. This has a different and invalid structure. Trap (B): Half-true. This replaces 'all' with 'some' in the second premise, which makes it invalid. Trap (C): Reversal. This has a different, invalid structure.

questions.question_text: Rule: 'The prize is awarded to a paper if and only if the paper is original and its author attends the ceremony.' The author of Paper X attended the ceremony, but the prize was not awarded to Paper X. Which of the following must be true?

options.A: Paper X is original but its author did not attend
options.B: Paper X is not original
options.C: The prize was awarded to another paper
options.D: Paper X is original

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'If and only if' means both conditions together are necessary and sufficient. The author attended, so if the paper were original the prize would have been awarded. It was not awarded, so the paper is not original. Shortcut: iff: both conditions together give the prize. Trap (A): Reversal. The author attended. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The rule says nothing about other papers. Trap (D): Reversal. If it were original, the author's attendance would lead to the prize.

questions.question_text: Rule: 'An employee who has completed one year of service and has no disciplinary record is entitled to the annual bonus.' Tara has completed two years of service but has a disciplinary record. Which of the following is correct?

options.A: Tara is not entitled to the bonus
options.B: Tara is entitled to the bonus because she has served for more than a year
options.C: The rule does not decide whether Tara gets the bonus
options.D: No employee with a disciplinary record can get the bonus

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The rule states a sufficient condition. Tara does not meet it fully, which means the rule does not apply; she may or may not be entitled on other grounds. We cannot conclude either way. Shortcut: sufficient condition not met means no conclusion. Trap (A): Sufficient treated as necessary. The rule gives conditions that are enough for the bonus, not conditions that are required for it. Trap (B): Half-true. Service is only one of the two conditions in the rule. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The rule does not say this.

questions.question_text: Passage: '(1) Several scientists say that the lake is shrinking because rainfall in the region has declined. (2) However, rainfall records for the last twenty years show no decline. (3) So the shrinking of the lake must have some other cause.' What role does statement (2) play?

options.A: It is the main conclusion of the passage
options.B: It is the claim that the author seeks to establish by (1)
options.C: It is an example of the scientists' own reasoning
options.D: It is evidence against the claim in (1) and supports the conclusion (3)

questions.pedagogical_explanation: (1) is the view being challenged. (2) gives data that undermines it, and (3), introduced by 'So', is the final conclusion that (2) supports. Shortcut: track claims: opponent's view, evidence against it, conclusion. Trap (A): Half-true. The main conclusion is statement (3). Trap (B): Reversal. The author argues against (1). Trap (C): Reversal. (2) is the author's evidence against the scientists' claim.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'No one has proved that the factory pollutes the river. So the factory does not pollute the river.' What is the flaw in the reasoning?

options.A: It treats the lack of proof that something is so as proof that it is not so
options.B: It assumes that every factory pollutes rivers
options.C: It argues from a single case to all factories
options.D: It uses the word 'pollute' in two different senses

questions.pedagogical_explanation: No evidence either way leaves the matter open. Absence of proof is not proof of absence. Shortcut: no proof is not disproof. Trap (B): Reversal. The argument concludes the opposite. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The argument concerns one factory. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The word has a single sense.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'The new highway has cut the travel time between town A and town B from five hours to two. So trade between the two towns will rise.' Which of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.A: The highway was built entirely with government money
options.B: Trade between the two towns was earlier nil
options.C: Both towns have the same number of people
options.D: The long travel time was a significant obstacle to trade between the two towns

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Negation test: if travel time never mattered for trade, a faster road would not raise it, and the conclusion fails. So the argument depends on travel time being an obstacle. Shortcut: negate: if time was no obstacle, the conclusion falls. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The source of funds is not relevant. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The argument needs only that trade can rise. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The size of the populations is not required.

questions.question_text: Argument: 'The students who followed Method M for exam preparation scored higher on average than the students who did not. So Method M is better than other methods.' Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

options.A: Method M takes two hours a day
options.B: Only students who were already top scorers chose to follow Method M
options.C: Method M was invented in another country
options.D: Some students who followed Method M scored very well

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If the students who chose Method M were already strong, their higher scores may come from that and not from the method. The argument ignores this. Shortcut: who chose the method matters. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Time spent does not bear on whether it is better. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The origin of the method is irrelevant. Trap (D): Reversal. This is consistent with the argument.

questions.concept_tag: Parallel flaw - no, some and some
questions.question_text: Argument: 'No honest person is a thief. Some officials are not thieves. Therefore some officials are honest.' Which of the following has the same flaw?

options.A: No cat is a dog. Some pets are not dogs. Therefore some pets are cats
options.B: No cat is a dog. Some pets are cats. Therefore some pets are not dogs
options.C: All cats are pets. Some pets are dogs. Therefore some cats are dogs
options.D: No dog is a cat. All pets are dogs. Therefore no pet is a cat

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The given argument moves from 'not thieves' to 'honest', though a person may be neither. In the matching argument, pets that are not dogs may be neither cats nor dogs, so the conclusion does not follow. Shortcut: check whether the leftover group could be neither. Trap (B): Valid. This argument is valid and does not share the flaw. Trap (C): Different flaw. This has a different structure. Trap (D): Valid. This argument is valid.

questions.question_text: Statements: Every member who supports Plan X also supports Plan Y. No member who supports Plan Y supports Plan Z. Rahul is a member who supports Plan Z. Which of the following must be true?

options.A: Rahul supports Plan Y
options.B: Rahul supports Plan X but not Plan Y
options.C: Rahul does not support Plan X
options.D: Rahul supports all three plans

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rahul supports Z, so he does not support Y. Since support for X implies support for Y, the contrapositive says no support for Y implies no support for X. So Rahul does not support X. Shortcut: contrapositive: not Y gives not X. Trap (A): Reversal. No member who supports Y supports Z, so Rahul does not support Y. Trap (B): Reversal. Anyone who supports X also supports Y. Trap (D): Reversal. This is impossible given the second statement.

questions.question_text: All the employees of a firm know at least one of Hindi and English. At least 70% of the employees know Hindi and at least 60% know English. What is the minimum percentage of employees who know both languages?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Hindi + English ≥ 130% while the total is 100%, so at least 30% are counted twice. Both = 70 + 60 - 100 = 30% at least. Shortcut: overlap = sum - total. Trap (A): Wrong subtraction. This subtracts 60 from 70 and ignores the 100% total. Trap (C): Max rather than min. This takes the smaller group as the overlap, which is the maximum, not the minimum. Trap (D): Max rather than min. This takes the larger group as the overlap.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Goods displayed in a shop window or on shelves with price tags are not an offer to sell. They are an invitation to treat, that is, an invitation to customers to make offers. The offer is made by the customer when he brings the goods to the counter and tenders the price, and the contract is formed only when the shopkeeper accepts it. Until then, the shopkeeper is free to accept or to refuse, and is not bound to sell at the price marked, even if the mark was wrongly written. The rule protects the shopkeeper from being compelled to complete every sale that a customer may choose to demand, and it lets him control to whom he sells. An advertisement is treated in the same way unless it shows a clear intention to be bound by the first person who accepts.

Facts: A bookshop displays a rare atlas in its window with a tag of ₹500; the tag was written by mistake and the intended price was ₹5,000. Meena takes the atlas to the counter and offers ₹500. The cashier refuses to sell. Meena claims that the shop must sell the atlas to her at ₹500. Decide.

options.A: The shop must sell, because the price tag was a binding offer which Meena accepted
options.B: The shop must sell, because it would be unfair to refuse a customer who paid the price shown
options.C: The shop need not sell, because the display was only an invitation to treat and Meena's offer was never accepted
options.D: The shop need not sell, because Meena ought to have realised that the price was a mistake

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A priced display is an invitation to treat. Meena's tender at the counter was the offer, which the shop was free to refuse. No acceptance means no contract. Shortcut: identify who made the offer and who accepted it. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. The principle says a priced display is not an offer. Trap (B): General morality. Fairness is not the test; the principle turns on offer and acceptance. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle does not depend on what the customer knew; it depends on the absence of acceptance.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - counter-offer ends the original offer
questions.question_text:
Passage: When a person to whom an offer is made replies with a different price or changed conditions, the reply is not an acceptance but a counter-offer. A counter-offer rejects the original offer and brings it to an end, so that the original offer cannot later be accepted unless the person who made it renews it. The counter-offer is itself a new proposal, which the original offeror is free to accept or to refuse. A mere inquiry whether the terms might be changed, made without rejecting the offer, is different and does not end the original offer. The rule keeps the parties' positions clear and prevents a person from holding open a fixed offer while testing the market for better terms.

Facts: Seema offers to sell her camera to Tushar for ₹10,000. Tushar replies: "I will give you ₹8,000." Seema refuses. The next day Tushar writes: "I accept your offer of ₹10,000." Seema declines to sell. Tushar claims that a contract exists. Decide.

options.A: There is a contract, because Tushar finally accepted the exact terms Seema had offered
options.B: There is no contract, because Tushar's reply of ₹8,000 was a counter-offer that ended the original offer
options.C: There is a contract, because Seema never expressly withdrew her offer
options.D: There is no contract, because ₹10,000 was too high a price for the camera

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Tushar's ₹8,000 reply rejected the ₹10,000 offer. Seema had not renewed it, so his later 'acceptance' had nothing to accept. Shortcut: a counter-offer is a rejection plus a new proposal. Trap (A): Ignoring the condition. The principle says the original offer ended when the counter-offer was made. Trap (C): Ignoring the condition. The counter-offer ends the offer without any withdrawal by the offeror. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The adequacy of the price is not part of the principle.

questions.question_text:
Passage: An offer is a proposal which, once accepted, becomes a promise. Until it is accepted, the person who made it is free to withdraw it. The withdrawal takes effect when it is communicated to the person to whom the offer was made, and it must reach him before he accepts. Once the offer has been accepted, it can no longer be withdrawn, and a contract has been formed. This remains the rule even where the offeror has said that his offer will stay open for a stated period, because a promise to hold an offer open is not by itself a binding promise unless the other side has given something in exchange for it.

Facts: On the 1st, Asha offers to sell her car to Bhanu for ₹2 lakh and says the offer will stay open until the 10th. On the 5th, Asha tells Bhanu on the phone that the offer is withdrawn. On the 6th, Bhanu says: "I accept." Bhanu claims a contract exists. Decide.

options.A: There is a contract, because Asha had promised to keep the offer open until the 10th
options.B: There is a contract, because Bhanu accepted within the period stated in the offer
options.C: There is no contract, because Bhanu delayed in accepting
options.D: There is no contract, because the offer was withdrawn and the withdrawal reached Bhanu before he accepted

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Asha withdrew on the 5th and Bhanu knew before accepting on the 6th. Her earlier promise to hold the offer open had no consideration. Shortcut: draw a timeline: offer, withdrawal known, acceptance. Trap (A): Ignoring the condition. The principle says that promise is not binding unless something was given for it. Trap (B): Ignoring the condition. The period does not prevent withdrawal before acceptance. Trap (C): General morality. Delay is not mentioned in the principle; the point is the earlier withdrawal.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person who commits a wrongful act is liable for damage that is the natural and probable result of the act, or that a reasonable person could have foreseen as likely to follow. He is not liable for damage that is highly unusual or too remote to have been foreseen, even if his wrongful act was one of the events leading to it. The test looks at the kind of damage and not at the exact way in which it happens. Where several consequences follow, the wrongdoer answers for those that were reasonably foreseeable and not for the others. The rule limits liability to a fair range, so that a person is not made answerable for every distant chain of events set off by a single careless act.

Facts: Rakesh carelessly leaves a manhole uncovered on a footpath at night. Sanjay, a passer-by, falls in and breaks his ankle. While he is in hospital for treatment, a fire caused by faulty wiring, which has nothing to do with Rakesh, breaks out in the ward, and Sanjay suffers burns. Sanjay sues Rakesh for both injuries. Decide.

options.A: Rakesh is liable for both injuries, because Sanjay would not have been in hospital but for the fall
options.B: Rakesh is liable for the broken ankle but not for the burns, because the burns were not a foreseeable result of his carelessness
options.C: Rakesh is not liable for either injury, because the fire was an accident
options.D: Rakesh is liable for both injuries, because it is only fair that the careless person bears all the loss

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A fall into an open manhole naturally causes injury like a broken ankle. A ward fire is unrelated and unforeseeable from his act. Shortcut: ask: could a reasonable person foresee this kind of harm from the act? Trap (A): Ignoring the condition. The principle requires foreseeability; being a link in the chain is not enough. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. The ankle injury is the natural and foreseeable result of the open manhole. Trap (D): General morality. The principle limits liability to foreseeable damage.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Private nuisance is an unreasonable and substantial interference with a person's use or enjoyment of his land. Whether an interference is unreasonable depends on its nature, how long and how often it continues, and the character of the locality: what is acceptable in an industrial area may not be acceptable in a residential one. Trivial or occasional annoyance is not enough, and a person cannot complain merely because he is unusually sensitive. The fact that the defendant's activity is lawful, or useful to the public, does not by itself excuse the interference if it is unreasonable to the neighbours. The remedy is damages, and in a proper case, an order to stop the activity.

Facts: A flour mill operates a noisy grinder every night until midnight next to Latika's house in a quiet residential colony. The noise is loud enough to keep her family awake on most nights. Latika sues the mill owner. Decide.

options.A: The mill owner is liable, because the noise is a substantial and repeated interference with the enjoyment of her home in a residential locality
options.B: The mill owner is not liable, because running a flour mill is a lawful business
options.C: The mill owner is not liable, because Latika could move to another colony
options.D: The mill owner is liable, because any noise a neighbour dislikes is a nuisance

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The interference is substantial (keeps the family awake), repeated (most nights) and unreasonable for a residential locality. Shortcut: test the three factors: nature, duration, locality. Trap (B): Ignoring the condition. The principle says lawfulness does not by itself excuse unreasonable interference. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. Moving away is not part of the principle. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The principle excludes trivial or occasional annoyance.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person who is injured by another's negligence may sue for damages. If the injured person's own failure to take reasonable care for his safety contributed to the harm, he is said to be contributorily negligent. In that case, he is not shut out from recovery, but the damages are reduced in proportion to the share of the harm which his own carelessness caused. If his carelessness was the sole cause of the injury, he recovers nothing, because the defendant's negligence then caused no harm. The reduction applies only to the part of the damage that his own fault contributed to, and not to damage that would have happened in any case through the defendant's negligence.

Facts: Kabir rides a motorcycle without a helmet and is hit by a car whose driver jumped a red light. Medical evidence shows that a helmet would have made his head injury much less serious, although his other injuries would have been the same. Kabir sues the driver for the whole of his loss. Decide.

options.A: Kabir can recover the whole loss, because the driver's red-light violation caused the accident
options.B: Kabir recovers nothing, because he was also at fault
options.C: Kabir recovers nothing, because motorcyclists accept the risk of the road
options.D: Kabir can recover from the driver, but his damages for the head injury are reduced to the extent his own failure to wear a helmet contributed to it

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Both parties were at fault. The driver is the main cause; the helmet's absence reduces the damages for the head injury only. Shortcut: contributory negligence reduces, it does not bar. Trap (A): Ignoring the condition. The principle reduces damages for the part of harm his own carelessness caused. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. The principle says contributory negligence reduces damages; it does not bar recovery unless his fault was the sole cause. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. Assumption of risk is not part of the stated principle.

questions.question_text:
Passage: An occupier of premises who invites visitors on to them owes them a duty to take reasonable care that they are reasonably safe in using the premises for the purpose of the visit. This includes a duty to warn visitors of dangers that the occupier knows of, or ought to know of, if those dangers are not obvious. A warning by a sign, a barrier or an attendant is enough. The occupier is not bound to warn of a danger which would be obvious to a reasonable visitor, such as an open flame, or a flight of steps in good light. The duty is one of reasonable care, so a visitor who is injured by a danger which was properly pointed out cannot claim from the occupier.

Facts: A shop owner mops the floor of the shop, which then looks dry after a few minutes, but does not put up any warning sign. A customer, Hari, slips on the damp surface and breaks his wrist. Hari sues the owner. Decide.

options.A: The owner is liable, because he knew of a danger that was not obvious and gave no warning
options.B: The owner is not liable, because floors are bound to be wet sometimes in shops
options.C: The owner is liable, because every injured customer is entitled to compensation
options.D: The owner is not liable, because Hari should have watched his step

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The owner created the danger, it was not obvious, and no warning was given. The duty to warn applies. Shortcut: ask whether the danger was obvious; if not, the duty to warn arises. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. Nothing in the principle excuses an unwarned, hidden danger because it is common. Trap (C): General morality. The principle depends on a duty to warn of non-obvious dangers, not on injury alone. Trap (D): Ignoring the condition. The floor looked dry, so the danger was not obvious to a reasonable visitor.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person abets the doing of an offence if he instigates another to do it, intentionally aids it, or joins in a plan to do it. Instigation means actively urging, encouraging or suggesting that the act be done. Mere presence at the place, silent approval, or a failure to prevent the act is not instigation. If the other person does the offence as a result of the encouragement, the person who encouraged him is liable as an abettor, whether or not he took part in the act himself. The law distinguishes the one who prompts the offence from the one who only looks on, and punishes only the first as an abettor.

Facts: Pankaj, Qadir and Rahul are standing near a parked bus. Qadir picks up a stone to break a window. Pankaj says nothing but watches. Rahul shouts, "Go on, smash it, nobody will see!" Qadir breaks the window. Apart from Qadir, who is liable as an abettor?

options.A: Pankaj alone, because he stood by and did not stop the act
options.B: Both Pankaj and Rahul, because both were present when the window was broken
options.C: Neither of them, because Qadir was the one who threw the stone
options.D: Rahul alone, because he actively urged Qadir to do the act

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rahul's shout was active encouragement, and Qadir broke the window as a result. Pankaj was only a silent onlooker. Shortcut: separate the one who urges from the one who merely watches. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. The principle says failure to prevent is not instigation. Trap (B): Ignoring the condition. Presence alone is not abetment; only active encouragement counts. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. The principle says the person who encouraged is liable whether or not he took part.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - accident in a lawful act
questions.question_text:
Passage: A crime generally requires both a wrongful act and a guilty mind. An act done by accident is not an offence if the following conditions are all met: it was done in the course of a lawful act, in a lawful manner, by lawful means, and with proper care and caution, and there was no criminal intention or knowledge that harm would result. The law does not punish a person for harm that he did not intend or foresee and could not have prevented by taking reasonable care. If any one of the conditions is missing, for example if the person was careless, or the act itself was unlawful, the protection is lost and the person may be answerable for the harm.

Facts: Farida is chopping vegetables in her kitchen with proper care when the blade comes loose from a handle that looked sound, and flies off, injuring a neighbour standing nearby. The neighbour complains that Farida committed an offence of causing hurt. Decide.

options.A: Farida has committed an offence, because her neighbour was injured by her knife
options.B: Farida has not committed an offence, because the harm was an accident in a lawful act done with proper care and without intention or knowledge
options.C: Farida has committed an offence, because she ought to have checked the handle with a hammer
options.D: Farida has not committed an offence, because accidents are never punishable

questions.pedagogical_explanation: All the conditions are present: lawful act, lawful manner, proper care, no intention or knowledge. So the accident is not an offence. Shortcut: tick off each condition for the protection. Trap (A): Ignoring the condition. Harm alone does not make an accident an offence if all conditions are met. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The principle requires proper care and caution; there is nothing to suggest more than ordinary care was needed. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The protection is lost if any of the conditions is missing, for example if she had been careless.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person who plans to commit an offence does not commit that offence by merely thinking or talking about it, and the law does not punish a person at the stage of intention. The law also separates preparation from attempt. Preparation consists of arranging or collecting the means needed for the offence, such as buying a tool or gathering information. It is not punishable on its own unless the law says so for a particular offence. Attempt begins when the person does an act that is a direct step towards committing the offence, and goes beyond mere preparation, such as using the means against the target. The point at which preparation ends and attempt begins depends on how close the act is to the crime.

Facts: Naresh buys a mask and a toy pistol and keeps them in a bag at home. He plans to rob a jeweller's shop next week. The police find the bag and arrest him before he leaves the house. Naresh is charged with attempt to commit robbery. Decide.

options.A: Naresh is guilty of attempt, because he clearly intended to rob the shop
options.B: Naresh is guilty of attempt, because he bought the mask and pistol for the robbery
options.C: Naresh is not guilty of attempt, because buying and keeping the means at home was only preparation
options.D: Naresh is not guilty, because a toy pistol cannot hurt anyone

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Gathering the means is preparation. Attempt requires an act that is a direct step towards the offence, such as going to the shop. Shortcut: find the last act and ask if it is 'using' the means against the target. Trap (A): Ignoring the condition. Intention alone is not an attempt; a direct step beyond preparation is needed. Trap (B): Half-true. Collecting the means is preparation, which the principle says is not an attempt. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle's test is the stage reached, not the dangerousness of the weapon.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - cheating needs dishonest intention at the start
questions.question_text:
Passage: A person cheats if he deceives another and thereby dishonestly induces that person to hand over property. The crucial element is deception that induces the delivery. The deceit must be present at the time the inducement is made, that is, when the promise or representation is given. A person who makes a promise intending to keep it, and later fails to keep it for reasons that arise afterwards, has broken his promise but has not cheated, because he had no dishonest intention at the time. Such a failure may entitle the other party to a civil remedy, such as a refund, but it is not a crime. The court looks to the state of mind of the accused at the time of the promise.

Facts: Sapna sells Tarun a phone and promises to deliver it the next day after he pays ₹10,000 at once. She honestly intends to deliver it, but her supplier lets her down and she cannot get the phone. Tarun alleges that she cheated him. Decide.

options.A: Sapna cheated, because she took the money and did not deliver the phone
options.B: Sapna cheated, because she ought to have checked her supplier first
options.C: Sapna did not cheat, because she must have refunded the money in full
options.D: Sapna did not cheat, because she had no dishonest intention when she took the money and promised delivery

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Cheating needs a dishonest intention when the promise is made. Sapna's failure came later through her supplier. Shortcut: look at the state of mind at the moment of the promise. Trap (A): Ignoring the condition. Non-delivery alone is not cheating; dishonest intention at the time of the promise is needed. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. Carelessness in planning is not dishonest inducement. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. The principle does not depend on a refund; it depends on intention at the time of the promise.

questions.concept_tag: Administrative law - right to be heard
questions.question_text:
Passage: Before an authority takes a decision that adversely affects a person's rights or interests, it must give him notice of the case against him and a fair opportunity to put forward his side. A decision taken without hearing the affected person can be set aside, however correct it may seem on the merits, unless the law expressly excludes a hearing. The right to be heard does not require a full trial with witnesses and lawyers: an opportunity suited to the nature of the matter is enough. The rule rests on the idea that a decision reached after both sides have been heard is more likely to be right, and is seen to be fair, and that a person should not be condemned on a case he has had no chance to answer.

Facts: A college council expels Dinesh for alleged cheating in an examination. It does not tell him the charge and does not allow him to explain. The invigilators' reports show clearly that he did cheat. No law excludes a hearing in such cases. Dinesh challenges the expulsion. Decide.

options.A: The expulsion can be set aside, because Dinesh was given no notice of the charge and no chance to be heard
options.B: The expulsion stands, because the invigilators' reports clearly show that he cheated
options.C: The expulsion stands, because colleges have wide powers over their students
options.D: The expulsion is invalid, because expulsion is too harsh a punishment for cheating

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The decision adversely affected Dinesh and was made without notice or hearing; no law excluded a hearing. So it can be set aside even if the cheating was real. Shortcut: no hearing, no valid decision, whatever the merits. Trap (B): Ignoring the condition. The principle says a decision without a hearing can be set aside however correct on the merits. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The principle limits the power to decide adversely without hearing. Trap (D): General morality. The principle concerns the absence of a hearing, not the severity of the penalty.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A will is valid only if it satisfies two formal requirements. First, the maker of the will, called the testator, must sign it, or have another person sign it in his presence and by his direction. Second, the will must be attested by at least two witnesses, each of whom has seen the testator sign the will and each of whom signs it in the presence of the testator. A will which does not meet these requirements is not valid, however clearly it states the testator's wishes. The rule exists to ensure that the document is genuine and that the testator made it freely, and so the law does not allow the formalities to be dispensed with merely because the intention is clear.

Facts: Uma writes a will leaving her house to her nephew and signs it. Only one neighbour, Vijay, sees her sign and signs as a witness; no one else does. After Uma's death, the nephew claims the house under the will. Decide.

options.A: The will is valid, because Uma's wishes are clearly stated and signed by her
options.B: The will is not valid, because it was attested by only one witness
options.C: The will is valid, because Vijay is a trustworthy neighbour
options.D: The will is not valid, because it was not registered with a government office

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The principle requires attestation by at least two witnesses. Only one attested, so the will is not valid. Shortcut: tick each formal requirement; one missing means invalid. Trap (A): Ignoring the condition. The principle says clear wishes cannot replace the formal requirements. Trap (C): General morality. The trustworthiness of a witness does not remove the need for two witnesses. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. Registration is not among the requirements stated in the principle.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal procedure - protection against double punishment
questions.question_text:
Passage: No person who has already been convicted of an offence can be prosecuted again and punished for the same offence. The rule prevents the State from using repeated trials to wear down a person or to obtain a heavier sentence than the court first gave. The bar applies where the second prosecution is for the same offence, or an offence with the same essential ingredients, arising from the same facts. It does not apply when the second charge is for a different offence with different ingredients, or when the earlier proceeding did not result in a conviction or acquittal by a competent court. The question is whether the second charge requires proof of the same essential facts as the first.

Facts: Dev is tried by a competent court and convicted for driving at a dangerous speed on a particular road at a particular time. The State then prosecutes him again for the same act of dangerous driving on that occasion, hoping for a longer sentence. Dev objects to the second prosecution. Decide.

options.A: Dev's objection is invalid, because the State may seek a heavier sentence if the first was light
options.B: Dev's objection is invalid, because dangerous driving harms society
options.C: Dev's objection is valid, because he has already been convicted of the same offence on the same facts
options.D: Dev's objection is valid only if he served the full sentence

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The offence and facts are the same and there was a conviction by a competent court. The bar applies. Shortcut: compare the ingredients of the two charges. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. The principle exists precisely to prevent a second trial for a heavier sentence. Trap (B): General morality. The seriousness of the act is not the test; the same offence is. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle depends on conviction, not on completion of the sentence.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A principal is bound by the acts of his agent which are done within the scope of the authority given to the agent. The authority may be express, where it is stated in so many words, or implied, where it follows from the position the agent holds or the nature of the business. Where the agent acts outside his authority, the principal is not bound unless he later approves the act, which is called ratification. A third party who deals with the agent should act in good faith, and cannot hold the principal liable for an act that the agent had no authority to do, if the third party knew of the limits of the authority.

Facts: The owner of a stationery shop authorises his manager, Nikhil, to buy paper and pens for the shop. Nikhil buys a delivery van for ₹4 lakh from a dealer in the name of the owner. The owner does not approve the purchase. The dealer sues the owner for the price. Decide.

options.A: The owner is not bound, because Nikhil had no express or implied authority to buy a van and the owner did not ratify it
options.B: The owner is bound, because Nikhil was his manager and acted in his name
options.C: The owner is bound, because the shop would have benefited from a van
options.D: The owner is not bound, because a manager can never make any purchase

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Buying a van is outside the authority to buy paper and pens, and there was no ratification. Shortcut: compare the act with the written scope of authority. Trap (B): Ignoring the condition. The principle limits the principal's liability to acts within authority. Trap (C): General morality. Benefit to the shop is not part of the principle. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The principle says acts within authority bind the principal; buying stock would have bound him.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A bailment arises when goods are delivered by one person (the bailor) to another (the bailee) for a purpose, on the understanding that they will be returned or dealt with as the bailor directs. The bailee must take as much care of the goods as a reasonably careful owner would take of his own goods of the same kind. If the goods are lost or damaged because the bailee failed in that care, he must make good the loss. If the loss occurs despite such care, for example through a robbery against which reasonable precautions had been taken, the bailee is not liable. The duty is of reasonable care and not of absolute security.

Facts: Leela leaves her laptop with a repair shop. The shop keeps all items in a locked steel cabinet in a building with an alarm and a night guard. Thieves break in, overpower the guard, and steal all the items in the shop, including Leela's laptop. Leela demands the price of the laptop from the shop. Decide.

options.A: The shop is liable, because the laptop was in its custody when it was stolen
options.B: The shop is liable, because it ought to have insured the goods
options.C: The shop is not liable, because Leela should have kept the laptop at home
options.D: The shop is not liable, because it took the care a reasonably careful owner would take of his own goods

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The shop took reasonable precautions (locked cabinet, alarm, guard). A robbery despite such care does not make the bailee liable. Shortcut: test care against the 'reasonably careful owner'. Trap (A): Ignoring the condition. The principle says a bailee is not liable if he took reasonable care. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. Insurance is not part of the stated duty. Trap (C): General morality. The principle does not turn on what the bailor should have done.

questions.concept_tag: Sale of goods - fitness for purpose
questions.question_text:
Passage: When a buyer makes known to the seller the particular purpose for which he wants goods, and relies on the seller's skill or judgement, and the goods are of a kind which the seller deals in, the goods must be reasonably fit for that purpose. This is an implied condition of the sale. If the goods are not fit, the buyer may reject them and recover the price. The condition does not apply when the buyer chooses the goods himself without relying on the seller's judgement, or where the goods are ordinarily sold under a patent or trade name for a known use. The protection depends on actual reliance on the seller's advice for the stated purpose.

Facts: Mehul tells a hardware dealer that he needs paint for an iron gate exposed to rain. The dealer recommends a can labelled "for indoor walls only". Mehul buys it as advised, but the paint peels off in the first heavy rain. Mehul wants to return the paint and recover the price. Decide.

options.A: Mehul has no remedy, because he chose to buy the paint himself
options.B: Mehul may reject the paint and recover the price, because he stated his purpose and relied on the dealer's advice, and the paint was unfit for it
options.C: Mehul has no remedy, because paint is cheap and ought to be tested before use
options.D: Mehul may recover the price only if the dealer intended to deceive him

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The conditions are all met: the purpose was stated, Mehul relied on the dealer, the dealer deals in paint, and the paint was unfit. Shortcut: check for stated purpose plus reliance. Trap (A): Ignoring the condition. He bought on the dealer's recommendation, relying on his judgement. Trap (C): General morality. The principle imposes the condition on the seller where the buyer relies on his advice. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The condition applies without proof of intent to deceive.

questions.concept_tag: IPR - copyright protects expression, not ideas
questions.question_text:
Passage: Copyright protects the particular way in which an author expresses an idea, not the idea itself. The author's actual words, the sequence in which they are arranged, and the detailed way in which characters and events are presented are protected. An idea, a theme, a general plot or a bare premise is free for anyone to use. Two authors may therefore write stories on the same theme without either infringing the other's rights, so long as the second does not copy the first author's expression. Infringement requires copying of a substantial part of the protected expression, and independent creation of a similar work, without copying, is not infringement.

Facts: Author A publishes a novel about two rival bakers who fall in love. Author B, who has not read A's novel, independently writes a novel with the same basic premise of rival bakers falling in love, but with different characters, plot events, setting and language. Author A sues B for infringement. Decide.

options.A: B has not infringed copyright, because only the same premise was used and not A's expression
options.B: B has infringed, because the premise of the novels is the same
options.C: B has infringed, because A's novel was published first
options.D: B has not infringed, because B will sell far fewer copies than A

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Only the idea is common. B used different expression and did not copy. So there is no infringement. Shortcut: compare expression, not themes. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. The principle says that an idea or premise is free for anyone to use. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. Priority of publication does not matter if only the idea is common. Trap (D): General morality. Sales are irrelevant to infringement under the principle.

questions.concept_tag: IPR - trade mark infringement and related goods
questions.question_text:
Passage: A registered trade mark gives its owner the exclusive right to use the mark for the goods or services for which it is registered. Its infringement occurs when another trader uses an identical or deceptively similar mark, in relation to the same or similar goods, in a way that is likely to confuse ordinary buyers about the source of the goods. Use of a similar mark for wholly unrelated goods, where an ordinary buyer is unlikely to think the two come from the same source, is not infringement under this rule, although other protections may exist for very well-known marks. The test is the likelihood of confusion in the mind of an ordinary buyer and not the mere sameness of a word.

Facts: "Zenix" is registered as a trade mark for motor-vehicle tyres. Another trader opens a small shop selling sweets under the name "Zenix Sweets". The tyre company sues for infringement, claiming that the shopkeeper uses its registered word. Assume "Zenix" is not a famous mark in any other field. Decide.

options.A: There is infringement, because the identical word is used
options.B: There is infringement, because the shopkeeper benefits from the reputation of tyres
options.C: There is no infringement, because sweets and tyres are unrelated goods and ordinary buyers would not be confused about the source
options.D: There is no infringement, because small shops cannot infringe a trade mark

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Infringement needs same or similar goods and a likelihood of confusion. Tyres and sweets are unrelated, so the identical word is not enough. Shortcut: ask whether an ordinary buyer would think both come from one source. Trap (A): Ignoring the condition. The principle requires the same or similar goods and a likelihood of confusion. Trap (B): General morality. The principle depends on confusion for same or similar goods, not on benefit. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle contains no exemption for small traders.

questions.question_text:
Passage: False imprisonment is the total restraint of a person's liberty without lawful justification. The restraint must be complete: the person must be prevented from going in every direction in which he has a right to go. It need not involve walls or locks, since a guard who stands before the only exit and refuses to let a person pass restrains him. But if the person is free to leave by another reasonable way, the restraint is not total, and a mere obstruction of one route is not false imprisonment. The person's liberty is protected, but the protection is not extended to every inconvenience in moving about. A person who chooses to stay, though free to go, is not imprisoned.

Facts: A guard in a showroom stands in front of the main door and tells Charu she cannot leave until she shows a receipt. A side door nearby is open and unguarded, and Charu can see it. She stays for an hour arguing with the guard and then sues the showroom for false imprisonment. Decide.

options.A: There was false imprisonment, because the guard blocked the main door
options.B: There was false imprisonment, because Charu spent an hour in the showroom
options.C: There was no false imprisonment, because the restraint was not total, as Charu was free to leave by the side door
options.D: There was no false imprisonment, because guards may stop anyone they suspect

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The principle requires total restraint. An open side exit means Charu was free to go, so the blockade of the main door was only an obstruction. Shortcut: count the exits: if one is free, there is no total restraint. Trap (A): Half-true. Blocking one route is an obstruction, but total restraint requires blocking every route. Trap (B): Ignoring the condition. The time spent does not matter if she was free to leave. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle does not give guards a power to stop; it turns on total restraint.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - written promise to pay a time-barred debt
questions.question_text:
Passage: A debt cannot be recovered by suit after the period allowed by law has run out, and a mere hope or oral assurance by the debtor does not revive it. However, a fresh promise to pay such a debt is enforceable even though nothing new is given in return for it, provided the promise is in writing and is signed by the debtor. The exception exists because the debtor is treated as having chosen to waive the protection which lapse of time had given him. The promise must be to pay the debt itself, and a bare acknowledgement that the debt once existed is not enough. A promise that is made orally, or that is not signed, falls outside the exception and the general bar continues to apply.

Facts: Rohan owes Sameer ₹40,000, and the period for suing on the debt ended last month. Rohan then writes and signs a letter to Sameer: 'I will pay you the ₹40,000 by December.' He does not pay. Sameer sues. Decide.

options.A: Sameer fails, because the debt was time-barred and Rohan received nothing new for his promise
options.B: Sameer succeeds, because Rohan is morally bound to repay money that he borrowed
options.C: Sameer succeeds, because a signed written promise to pay a time-barred debt is enforceable without fresh consideration
options.D: Sameer fails, because a debtor can be bound only by a promise made before the court

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The general rule bars the suit. The exception applies: the promise is in writing, signed, and is to pay the debt itself, so no fresh consideration is needed. Shortcut: check the three conditions of the exception: written, signed, promise to pay. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. This applies the general bar and forgets the exception for a signed written promise. Trap (B): General morality. The principle rests on a signed written promise, not on moral duty. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. No such requirement appears in the principle.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - restraint of trade and sale of goodwill
questions.question_text:
Passage: An agreement which restrains a person from carrying on a lawful trade or profession is void to that extent. The law favours freedom to work, and a person cannot be made to give up his livelihood merely because he signed a paper. There is one recognised exception: where a person sells the goodwill of a business, he may agree with the buyer not to carry on a similar business within specified local limits, so long as the limits are reasonable for protecting the buyer. The exception does not extend to a restraint which has nothing to do with a sale of goodwill, for example one placed on an employee after he leaves a job simply to keep him out of the market.

Facts: Ila sells her bakery and its goodwill to Joel and agrees not to open another bakery within 5 km of it for three years. Separately, Kunal, her former cashier, signed a promise not to work in any bakery anywhere in the country after leaving her. Both Ila and Kunal later start bakeries in breach. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Neither promise can be enforced, because every restraint on trade is void
options.B: Ila's promise can be enforced as it accompanies a sale of goodwill within reasonable limits, but Kunal's cannot
options.C: Both promises can be enforced, because both persons agreed freely
options.D: Kunal's promise can be enforced but Ila's cannot, because Kunal was an employee who signed in writing

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Ila's restraint belongs to a sale of goodwill and is limited by place and time, so it falls in the exception. Kunal's is a general restraint on an ex-employee with no goodwill sale, so it is void. Shortcut: ask whether goodwill was sold and whether the limits are reasonable. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The goodwill exception saves Ila's promise. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. The principle makes restraints void unless they fall within the exception. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The exception covers the seller of goodwill, not the employee.

questions.concept_tag: Tort - strict liability for escape of dangerous things
questions.question_text:
Passage: A person who, for his own purposes, brings on his land and keeps there something likely to do mischief if it escapes is answerable for all the damage that is the natural consequence of its escape, even if he was not careless. The rule applies only to a non-natural use of land, and not to things that are present in the ordinary course of life. There is no liability where the escape was caused by an act of God, such as an extraordinary natural event which no human foresight could guard against, or by the unforeseeable act of a stranger over whom the keeper had no control.

Facts: A factory stores a large tank of toxic chemicals on its premises for its production. A sudden earthquake of unprecedented force cracks the tank, and the chemicals flow onto the neighbouring farm and ruin the crop. The factory had maintained the tank carefully. The farmer sues. Decide.

options.A: The factory is liable, because it stored a dangerous thing and strict liability does not need carelessness
options.B: The factory is not liable, because the escape was caused by an act of God
options.C: The factory is liable, because the farmer suffered a heavy loss through no fault of his own
options.D: The factory is not liable, because it maintained the tank carefully

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The rule would make the factory liable regardless of care. But the escape resulted from an extraordinary earthquake, an act of God, which is the stated exception. Shortcut: strict liability ignores care; look only for the listed exceptions. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Carelessness is not required, but the exception for an act of God still applies. Trap (C): General morality. The test is the rule and its exception, not the farmer's hardship. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. Care is irrelevant to strict liability; the exemption comes from the act of God.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - necessity as a defence
questions.question_text:
Passage: An act which would otherwise be an offence is not an offence if it is done in good faith to prevent a greater harm to person or property, provided that three conditions are met. There must be no time to seek the protection of law, the harm caused must be less than the harm prevented, and the person acting must not himself have created the danger by his own wrongful conduct. The defence is lost if any one condition is missing. It does not permit a person to take another's life in order to save his own, because a life is never less than a life.

Facts: A fire breaks out in Gopal's neighbour's house at night, and nobody can be reached by phone. To stop the flames from spreading to the whole row of houses, Gopal demolishes the neighbour's empty garden shed, which stands in the fire's path. The shed is valued at ₹10,000, while the houses saved are worth many lakhs. Gopal did not cause the fire. Is Gopal guilty of damaging property?

options.A: Yes, because he destroyed another person's property without permission
options.B: Yes, because he should have waited for the fire brigade, however long it took
options.C: No, because the neighbour has insurance and suffered no real loss
options.D: No, because he acted in good faith, had no time to seek help, caused lesser harm and did not create the danger

questions.pedagogical_explanation: All three conditions are satisfied: no time to seek help, lesser harm than prevented, and Gopal did not create the fire. So necessity defeats liability. Shortcut: tick off the three conditions one by one. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The defence of necessity is available exactly when the stated conditions are met. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. The principle excuses acts where there is no time to seek the protection of law. Trap (C): General morality. Insurance is not part of the principle.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - provocation and culpable homicide
questions.question_text:
Passage: Causing death with the intention of causing death is ordinarily murder. But the offence is reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder if the offender, while deprived of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation. The provocation must not be sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender himself as an excuse for violence, and it must not be given by anything done in obedience to law or in the lawful exercise of a right. The death must also be caused by the provoker and not by an unrelated person, because the reduction depends on the loss of self-control directed at the cause of the anger.

Facts: Hari is mocked in front of friends by Imran in an extremely hurtful and sudden manner. Hari, losing control, strikes Imran with a rod, intending to kill him, and Imran dies. Hari had not sought the quarrel. Under the principle, what is Hari's liability?

options.A: Murder, because Hari intended to kill Imran
options.B: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder, because of grave and sudden provocation
options.C: No offence, because Hari was provoked and lost his self-control
options.D: Murder, because words alone can never amount to provocation

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Intention would make it murder, but the exception for grave and sudden provocation, not sought by Hari, reduces it to culpable homicide. Shortcut: provocation reduces the offence; it does not erase it. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Intention alone makes it murder only when no exception such as grave and sudden provocation applies. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. Provocation only reduces the offence; it does not remove liability. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle says nothing that excludes words as provocation.

questions.concept_tag: Property - transfer by an apparent owner
questions.question_text:
Passage: As a general rule, a person who is not the owner of goods cannot give a better title than he himself has. A buyer from a thief, for instance, gets no title even if he pays and acts in good faith. There is an exception where the true owner, by his own words or conduct, has led the buyer to believe that the seller was authorised to sell, since the owner is then prevented from denying the seller's authority. The exception protects only a buyer who has acted in good faith and who has paid value. A buyer who knew, or had plain reason to suspect, that the seller had no right to sell cannot rely on it.

Facts: Lata leaves her scooter with Mohan's garage for repair and tells all customers at the garage, in the buyer's hearing, that 'Mohan sells my scooters for me.' Mohan sells the scooter to Neel, who pays the full price honestly. Lata claims the scooter back from Neel. Decide.

options.A: Neel keeps the scooter, because Lata led him to believe that Mohan could sell it and he paid in good faith
options.B: Lata gets it back, because Mohan was not the owner and could give no better title
options.C: Lata gets it back, because it is unfair to take an owner's scooter without her consent
options.D: Neel keeps the scooter, because anyone who pays the full price becomes the owner

questions.pedagogical_explanation: General rule: no better title than the seller has. The exception applies since Lata held Mohan out as a seller, and Neel acted in good faith and paid value. Shortcut: look for the owner's own words or conduct creating apparent authority. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. The exception overrides the general rule where the owner held the seller out as authorised. Trap (C): General morality. Fairness is not the test; the principle turns on the owner's conduct. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. Payment alone does not give title; the exception needs the owner's holding-out and good faith.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - undue influence and independent advice
questions.question_text:
Passage: Where one party is in a position to dominate the will of the other, and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage, the contract is voidable at the option of the weaker party. Such a position is presumed to exist where one person stands in a relation of trust, for instance a guardian and ward. In such cases the dominant party must prove that the contract was fair and freely made. A contract is not set aside merely because it was unwise or because the other party was in a weak position, if it was made at a fair price after the weaker person had received independent advice, because the unfairness on which the rule depends is then absent.

Facts: Tara, an elderly widow, is cared for and advised by her nephew Uday, in whom she places complete trust. She sells him her house for far below its worth, without taking any other advice. Later, Tara asks the court to cancel the sale. Decide.

options.A: The sale stands, because Tara signed it herself and nobody forced her
options.B: The sale stands, because the law cannot protect people from their own bad bargains
options.C: The sale is voidable at Tara's option, because Uday dominated her will and has not shown that the sale was fair
options.D: The sale is void from the start, because every sale between relatives is illegal

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A relation of trust gives rise to a presumption of dominance. The price was unfair and no independent advice was taken, so Uday cannot rebut it and the sale is voidable. Shortcut: trust relationship plus unfair terms shifts the burden to the stronger party. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Where a relation of trust exists, the dominant party must prove fairness. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. The principle expressly protects the weaker party from an unfair advantage. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle makes the contract voidable, not void, and does not forbid relatives to contract.

questions.concept_tag: Tort - fair comment on a matter of public interest
questions.question_text:
Passage: A person who publishes a statement of opinion on a matter of public interest is not liable for defamation if the comment is fair, that is, if it is an honest opinion which a person could reasonably hold on the facts stated, and if it is based on facts that are true. The defence protects criticism, not the invention of facts. A comment made out of spite, or one that is presented as a fact which the writer knows to be false, does not qualify. The writer need not be correct in his opinion, since opinions may differ and a harsh review is still fair if it is honestly held and based on true facts.

Facts: Vimal, a restaurant critic, visits a new cafe and finds the coffee cold and the service slow, both of which are true. He writes in a newspaper: 'In my view, this is the worst cafe in town and it should close.' The owner sues for defamation. Decide.

options.A: Vimal is not liable, because his harsh opinion is honest and rests on true facts about a matter of public interest
options.B: Vimal is liable, because his opinion was harsh and caused loss to the owner
options.C: Vimal is liable, because no critic is entitled to say that a business should close
options.D: Vimal is not liable, because newspapers may print whatever they wish
