questions.pedagogical_explanation: The defence needs honest opinion on true facts. Both conditions are met, even though the opinion is severe. Shortcut: test: honest opinion plus true facts means fair comment. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. A harsh opinion is protected if it is honestly held and based on true facts. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The principle contains no such limit. Trap (D): General morality. The protection depends on the conditions of fair comment, not on a press freedom without limits.

questions.concept_tag: Constitutional law - self-incrimination and physical evidence
questions.question_text:
Passage: No person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. This means that an accused cannot be forced to make statements which would prove his guilt. The protection covers testimony, which comes from the knowledge or mind of the accused. It does not cover physical evidence taken from the body of the accused, such as fingerprints, a sample of handwriting or a specimen of blood, because such material is not a statement but a physical fact. The protection also does not apply where the accused speaks voluntarily, as the bar is only against compulsion. The rule therefore asks one question: is the thing demanded a statement drawn from the accused's mind, or a physical fact about him?

Facts: Rakesh is arrested on a charge of forging a signature. The police compel him to say where he hid the forged document, and also take a sample of his handwriting by force of an order of the court. Rakesh objects to both. Decide.

options.A: The compelled statement about the hiding place violates the protection, but the handwriting sample does not
options.B: Both violate the protection, because Rakesh was compelled in each case
options.C: Neither violates the protection, because Rakesh was an accused in custody
options.D: The handwriting sample violates the protection but the statement does not, because writing is a skill of the mind

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A statement of where the document was hidden comes from the mind, so compelling it is barred. A handwriting sample is physical evidence and falls outside the protection. Shortcut: split testimony (mind) from physical evidence (body). Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. The protection does not extend to physical evidence such as a handwriting sample. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. The protection is against compelled testimony by an accused. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle treats the sample as physical evidence and the statement as testimony.

questions.concept_tag: Consumer law - defects open to inspection
questions.question_text:
Passage: A seller who sells goods in the course of business impliedly promises that the goods are of satisfactory quality. If goods are defective, the buyer may reject them or claim compensation. However, where the buyer has examined the goods before buying, there is no such promise in respect of defects which that examination ought to have revealed. The buyer who inspects takes the risk of defects that are obvious, though not of hidden ones that a reasonable inspection would not reveal. The exception does not depend on the buyer's having examined every part, but on whether the defect would have been disclosed by the examination he actually made.

Facts: Dev buys a second-hand mixer from a shop after switching it on and examining it. It turns out that the jar has a visible crack on its outer surface which Dev did not look at, and the motor, which seemed to work, has a hidden internal fault that stops it after a week. Dev claims compensation for both. Decide.

options.A: Dev can claim for both defects, because the seller promised satisfactory quality
options.B: Dev can claim for neither defect, because he examined the mixer before buying
options.C: Dev can claim for the hidden motor fault but not for the visible crack
options.D: Dev can claim for the crack but not for the motor fault, because cracks affect safety

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The crack was visible and an examination of the jar ought to have revealed it, so it is excluded. The internal motor fault is hidden and is covered by the implied promise. Shortcut: separate obvious defects from hidden ones. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. A defect which a reasonable examination would have revealed falls within the exception. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. The exception covers only defects the examination ought to have revealed, not hidden ones. Trap (D): General morality. Safety is not the test; visibility to a reasonable examination is.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - mistake known to the other party
questions.question_text:
Passage: Where both parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a fact that is essential to the agreement, the agreement is void. A mistake by only one party does not by itself make the agreement void, and the mistaken party is generally bound, because the law requires people to look after their own interests. An exception is recognised where the party who is not mistaken knows of the other's mistake and takes advantage of it, since he cannot then insist on enforcement. The mistake must be about a fact essential to the agreement and not about the value or quality of the thing sold.

Facts: Wasim advertises 'old brass vase, ₹900' but the ad was meant to read ₹9,000, a typing slip he did not notice. Yash, who has seen the identical vase on sale elsewhere for ₹9,000, knows that the ad is wrong and quickly accepts it. Wasim refuses to sell. Yash sues for the vase. Decide.

options.A: Yash succeeds, because a one-sided mistake does not make a contract void
options.B: Yash succeeds, because the advertisement was a clear offer at ₹900
options.C: Yash fails, because he knew of Wasim's mistake and tried to take advantage of it
options.D: Yash fails, because Wasim is a seller and the law favours sellers

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A unilateral mistake normally binds the mistaken party. But Yash knew and exploited it, so the exception stops him from enforcing the agreement. Shortcut: unilateral mistake binds unless the other side knew of it. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. This overlooks the exception where the other party knows of the mistake. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. The knowledge exception prevents enforcement against the mistaken party. Trap (D): General morality. The principle favours neither party as such; the knowledge of Yash decides.

questions.concept_tag: Tort - intervening act breaking the chain of causation
questions.question_text:
Passage: A wrongdoer is liable for the damage which his wrong has caused. But if, after the wrong, an independent and unforeseeable act of another person intervenes and itself causes the damage, the chain of causation is broken and the first wrongdoer is no longer liable for that damage. The new act must be free and deliberate and not merely a natural reaction to the situation which the first wrongdoer created. If the later act is a foreseeable consequence of the first wrong, for instance a rescuer's attempt to help or a victim's reasonable effort to escape, the chain is not broken.

Facts: Zoya negligently leaves a ladder blocking a corridor, and Aman trips and breaks his arm. While Aman is waiting in the corridor for help, an unrelated stranger, in a fit of rage, deliberately hits Aman's injured arm, worsening the injury. Aman sues Zoya for the worsened injury as well. Decide.

options.A: Zoya is liable for the whole injury, because it would not have occurred without her negligence
options.B: Zoya is not liable at all, because the stranger was the real wrongdoer
options.C: Zoya is liable for the whole injury, because the law prefers to compensate the injured person
options.D: Zoya is liable for the broken arm but not for the worsening caused by the stranger's deliberate blow

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The trip and break were caused by Zoya. The stranger's deliberate blow was a free and independent act, so it breaks the chain for the worsening only. Shortcut: split the damage by cause: before and after the break. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The chain was broken by the independent, deliberate act. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. The break affects only the later damage; the original injury remains Zoya's responsibility. Trap (C): General morality. The principle limits liability by causation, not by sympathy.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - common intention and acts beyond it
questions.question_text:
Passage: When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of them is liable for the act as if he alone had done it. The common intention must exist before or at the time of the act, and it must be shared by the participants. However, if one participant does something which was outside the common intention, the others are not liable for that extra act. They remain liable for what they had agreed to do, but they cannot be made responsible for an act which they did not plan or foresee and which the actor did on his own.

Facts: Ben, Chirag and Dilip plan to break into a shop to steal cash and agree that nobody will carry a weapon. Inside, Dilip, without telling the others, pulls out a knife he had hidden and stabs the watchman who tries to stop them. Which statement is correct?

options.A: All three are liable for both the burglary and the stabbing, because they acted together
options.B: All three are liable for the burglary, but only Dilip is liable for the stabbing
options.C: Only Dilip is liable for anything, because only he used force
options.D: None of the three is liable for the stabbing, because the watchman was an innocent person

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Common intention covers the planned burglary, so all are liable for it. The stabbing was Dilip's own unplanned act, so only he answers for it. Shortcut: common intention covers only what was planned. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The stabbing was outside the common intention, so Ben and Chirag are not liable for it. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. Each participant is liable for the planned burglary. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. Dilip, who acted on his own, remains liable for the stabbing.

questions.concept_tag: IPR - patent novelty and prior publication
questions.question_text:
Passage: A patent may be granted only for an invention that is new, that is, one that has not been made known to the public anywhere before the date on which the application for the patent is filed. If the inventor himself publishes the details of his invention before applying, the invention loses its novelty and cannot be patented. There is a limited exception: a publication made by the inventor at a notified scientific society, or one made without his consent by another person, will not destroy novelty if the application is filed within twelve months of that publication. Publication in any other way by the inventor himself is not covered by the exception.

Facts: (i) Nina presents the full working of her new water filter at a notified scientific society's meeting in January and files a patent application in June of the same year. (ii) Omar posts the full details of his new water pump on a popular website himself in January and files a patent application in June of the same year. Decide whether each invention is patentable.

options.A: Both are patentable, because each application was filed within twelve months
options.B: Nina's is patentable because of the notified-society exception; Omar's is not, because his own posting is outside the exception
options.C: Neither is patentable, because any publication before filing destroys novelty
options.D: Omar's is patentable but Nina's is not, because a website reaches fewer experts

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Nina's disclosure was at a notified society and her filing was within twelve months, so novelty is saved. Omar's own website posting is not in the exception, so it destroys novelty. Shortcut: an exception covers only the specific disclosures it names. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The twelve-month period protects only the publications named in the exception. Trap (C): Ignoring the exception. A notified-society publication is excused if the application is filed within twelve months. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The principle protects Nina's publication and not Omar's.

questions.concept_tag: Evidence - hearsay and the dying declaration
questions.question_text:
Passage: A statement made by a person who is not before the court is generally not admissible to prove the truth of what it says. This is the rule against hearsay, since the maker cannot be questioned about his statement. There is an exception for a statement made by a person as to the cause of his death or the circumstances which resulted in it, when he is dead, and the statement was made at a time when he believed that death was near. Such a statement may be used in a case in which the cause of his death comes into question. A statement made without any belief that death was near, even if the maker later dies, does not qualify.

Facts: Kabir is accused of stabbing Farid. At the hospital, Farid told a nurse, 'Kabir stabbed me', believing that he would not survive his wounds, and died the next day. In the same trial, a shopkeeper says that Farid's neighbour, who is not called as a witness, told him last month that Kabir was planning violence. Which statement is admissible to prove the facts it states?

options.A: Both statements, because both concern Kabir's violence
options.B: Neither statement, because the makers cannot be cross-examined
options.C: The neighbour's report, because it was made earlier
options.D: Farid's statement to the nurse, and not the neighbour's report to the shopkeeper

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Farid's words concern the cause of his death and were made in the belief that death was near. The neighbour's report is hearsay with no exception. Shortcut: hearsay is out unless an exception, like a dying declaration, fits. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Only the dying declaration is within the exception. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. The dying declaration is an exception to the hearsay bar. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. The earlier date gives the neighbour's report no protection; it is plain hearsay.

questions.question_text:
Passage: When parties to a contract fix in advance a sum payable on breach, the court allows the injured party reasonable compensation not exceeding the sum named. If the sum is a genuine pre-estimate of the loss that breach would cause, it is enforceable as liquidated damages. If it is out of all proportion to any probable loss, and its purpose is only to frighten the other party into performance, it is a penalty and the injured party recovers no more than his actual, proved loss, with the named sum as the upper limit. A sum is not a penalty merely because it is large, if it is a fair estimate of a loss that is hard to measure.

Facts: Om agrees to deliver a stage to Pia for her wedding on a fixed day, under a clause that he will pay ₹5,000 per day of delay, a figure that fairly reflects the cost of renting a substitute. Separately, a clause says that for any breach whatever, even a one-hour delay in delivering a chair, he will pay ₹10 lakh. Both clauses are breached. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both clauses are enforceable in full, because the parties agreed to the sums
options.B: Neither clause is enforceable, because a contract cannot fix damages in advance
options.C: The ₹5,000 per day is enforceable as a genuine estimate; the ₹10 lakh clause is a penalty limited to actual proved loss
options.D: The ₹10 lakh clause is enforceable but the ₹5,000 clause is not, because larger sums deter breach better

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The daily sum is a fair estimate of probable loss and is liquidated damages. The ₹10 lakh sum for a trivial breach is out of proportion and works as a penalty, so only actual loss up to the sum can be recovered. Shortcut: test whether the sum is proportionate to probable loss. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. A sum that is out of proportion to the probable loss is a penalty. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. The principle allows a genuine pre-estimate to be enforced. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. Deterrence is the mark of a penalty, not of liquidated damages.

questions.concept_tag: Tort - liability for animals known to be dangerous
questions.question_text:
Passage: The keeper of an animal which he knows to have a tendency to cause a certain kind of harm is strictly liable if the animal causes harm of that kind. The keeper's knowledge of the animal's dangerous tendency is essential, and an animal's first act of harm, if the keeper had no earlier reason to suspect it, does not by itself make him liable under this rule. The keeper is also not liable where the injured person voluntarily provoked the animal or where the person knew of the danger and chose to run the risk. A keeper may still be liable in negligence if he failed to take reasonable care.

Facts: Rani's dog has bitten two visitors in the past, and Rani knows about it, yet she keeps it unchained in her garden. It bites a delivery boy, who came into the garden to hand over a parcel and did not provoke it. Rani says she is not negligent since she has no way to restrain it. Is Rani liable?

options.A: Yes, because she knew of the dog's tendency to bite, and neither exception applies
options.B: No, because a dog's bite is a natural act for which an owner is not responsible
options.C: No, because she took no step that could be called negligent
options.D: Yes, because dogs are always dangerous animals

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rani knew of the biting tendency. The delivery boy neither provoked the dog nor knowingly ran the risk, so the strict liability applies whether or not she was careless. Shortcut: knowledge of the tendency triggers strict liability. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. The principle imposes strict liability on a keeper with knowledge. Trap (C): Ignoring the exception. Liability under this rule does not depend on negligence. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle needs knowledge of the particular animal's tendency.

questions.concept_tag: Company law - lifting the corporate veil
questions.question_text:
Passage: A company is a separate legal person, distinct from its shareholders. Its debts are its own, and the shareholders are not personally liable for them beyond the value of their shares. The courts respect this separation even if one person holds nearly all the shares. The only exception is where the company is used as a device to commit fraud or to avoid an existing legal obligation, in which case the court may ignore the separate personality and treat the controllers as the persons who acted. The mere fact that a company has been set up to limit the owner's risk is not fraud.

Facts: Sanjay, owner of all shares in Zenith Traders Ltd, fell into heavy debt as a firm in his own name. Whenever creditors came, he said that business was done by Zenith Ltd. Two cases: (i) Zenith Ltd, a genuine trading company, fails and owes Tanu ₹2 lakh. (ii) After a court orders Sanjay personally to pay a debt, he moves his assets to a new company he forms the next day to avoid the order. Which statement is correct?

options.A: In both cases Sanjay is personally liable, because he owns all the shares
options.B: In neither case is Sanjay personally liable, because a company is always a separate person
options.C: In (i) Sanjay is liable but in (ii) he is not, because forming a company is a lawful act
options.D: In (i) Sanjay is not personally liable; in (ii) the court may ignore the company because it was used to avoid an existing obligation

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Case (i) is ordinary limited liability. In case (ii) the company was a device to evade an existing court order, which is the exception. Shortcut: one question: was the company used to cheat or dodge an existing duty? Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Sole ownership alone does not lift the veil. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. The exception applies where a company is used to avoid an existing legal obligation. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. The principle reverses these two outcomes.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - consent and the limits of consent
questions.question_text:
Passage: Consent given by a person above eighteen years, in good faith and without fear or misapprehension, is a defence to harm caused to that person by an act that is done for his benefit or that he agreed to bear. But a person cannot consent to his own death, or to the causing of grievous hurt, except where the act is done for his benefit, as in a medical operation. Consent given by a person under eighteen is not valid for this purpose. An act which causes only slight harm, such as a bruise in a friendly sport, falls within the consent given by joining the sport.

Facts: (i) Ravi, aged 25, agrees to a doctor's operation, which is done in good faith for his benefit, and the doctor causes grievous hurt by making the necessary cuts. (ii) Sonu, aged 25, asks his friend to cut off his finger for a bet, and the friend does so. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The doctor is not liable, because the grievous hurt was for Ravi's benefit; the friend is liable because consent cannot excuse grievous hurt not done for benefit
options.B: Both are liable, because consent never excuses grievous hurt
options.C: Neither is liable, because both Ravi and Sonu consented as adults
options.D: The friend is not liable but the doctor is, because a medical operation is risky

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The surgeon's act is for the patient's benefit and is covered by the exception. The friend's act, done for a bet, is grievous hurt not for benefit, so consent is no defence. Shortcut: consent excuses slight harm; grievous hurt needs a benefit. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. There is an exception for acts done for the person's benefit, such as an operation. Trap (C): Ignoring the exception. Consent does not excuse grievous hurt that is not for the person's benefit. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The principle protects the surgeon and not the friend.

questions.question_text:
Passage: An act done by a person for another without that other's authority may be adopted by the other later, and he is then bound as if he had given authority from the start. This is called ratification. Ratification must be made with full knowledge of the material facts, and it must cover the whole of the act, not only the part that is beneficial. It cannot be used to injure a third party by changing a right already acquired, and it is not possible if the act was one which the principal could not himself have done when it was made. Silence may amount to ratification if it is accompanied by conduct that shows approval.

Facts: Usha, without authority, buys 100 sacks of rice from Vivek in the name of Waman, who runs a shop. Waman, knowing all the facts, tells Vivek in writing that he accepts the purchase of the rice. Later, rice prices fall and Waman says that he was never bound because he gave Usha no authority. Decide.

options.A: Waman is not bound, because Usha had no authority at the time of the purchase
options.B: Waman is not bound, because he may withdraw whenever the price falls
options.C: Waman is bound, because every act of a person who claims to be an agent binds the principal
options.D: Waman is bound, because he ratified the purchase with full knowledge of the facts

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The original act lacked authority, but Waman adopted it in writing with full knowledge. Ratification relates back and binds him. Shortcut: unauthorised act plus informed adoption equals ratification. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Later ratification makes Waman bound as if authority existed from the start. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. Ratification, once made, binds the principal and cannot be withdrawn when it becomes inconvenient. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The principle needs ratification, not the mere claim of agency.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - acceptance by performance of a public offer
questions.question_text:
Passage: An offer made to the world at large, such as a promise of a reward to anyone who does a stated act, can be accepted by any person who performs the act. The performer need not give notice of acceptance, because performance of the act is itself the acceptance. But the performer must have known of the offer when he did the act, since a person cannot accept what he has never heard of. If the offer requires a particular act, doing something different or something only similar does not entitle him to the reward. An offer of this kind may be withdrawn before anyone has performed, but the withdrawal must be made with the same publicity as the offer.

Facts: A company announces in a newspaper that it will pay ₹20,000 to anyone who returns its lost parcel at its office. Pritam, who has not seen the announcement, finds the parcel and returns it to the office. The next day, Quasim, who read the notice, posts the parcel to the office instead of delivering it, and the parcel arrives. Decide who may claim.

options.A: Both can claim, because the company has got its parcel back through each of them
options.B: Pritam alone can claim, because he did the act exactly as stated
options.C: Quasim alone can claim, because he knew of the offer and the parcel arrived
options.D: Neither can claim: Pritam did not know of the offer and Quasim did not do the stated act

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Acceptance needs two things: knowledge of the offer and the stated act. Pritam has the act without the knowledge; Quasim has knowledge without the stated act (posting is not returning at the office). Shortcut: check knowledge and the exact act separately for each person. Trap (A): General morality. Benefit to the company is not the test; knowledge and the stated act are. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. Pritam did the act but without knowledge of the offer, so he did not accept it. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. Quasim knew of the offer but did not perform the stated act of returning at the office.

questions.concept_tag: Tort - eggshell skull rule and remoteness
questions.question_text:
Passage: A wrongdoer must take his victim as he finds him. If a wrongful act causes a kind of injury that was foreseeable, the wrongdoer is liable for the full extent of the harm, even though the victim's special weakness made the harm far more serious than a normal person would have suffered. The wrongdoer cannot say that a healthier person would have suffered less. This rule, however, is about the extent of the harm, not its kind. If the type of harm was not at all foreseeable from the wrong, the wrongdoer is not liable for it, whatever the victim's condition.

Facts: Sunil negligently bumps into Tina on a pavement. A normal person would only be bruised, but Tina has an unusually thin skull and suffers a serious head injury. Separately, Sunil's bump makes Uma drop her phone, which, in a freak sequence, falls into a pot and starts an electrical fire that burns her house. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Sunil is liable for neither, because a normal person would have suffered only a bruise or no harm
options.B: Sunil is liable for Tina's full head injury but not for the fire in Uma's house
options.C: Sunil is liable for both, because he started the chain of events
options.D: Sunil is liable for the fire but not for the head injury, because the injury depended on Tina's weakness

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A bump foreseeably causes bodily injury, so Sunil takes Tina as he finds her. A fire from a dropped phone is a different, unforeseeable kind of harm, so it is too remote. Shortcut: separate the extent of harm from the kind of harm. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The rule makes Sunil liable for the full extent of a foreseeable kind of harm. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. Liability for the fire fails because that kind of harm was not foreseeable. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The rule runs the other way: weakness does not reduce liability for foreseeable harm.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Ordinarily the person who claims damages for negligence must prove it. But where an accident is of a kind that does not happen in the ordinary course unless someone has been careless, and the thing that caused the harm was under the exclusive control of the defendant, the facts themselves raise a presumption of negligence. The defendant is then required to give an explanation consistent with care. The presumption does not arise where the cause of the accident may well be something other than the defendant's want of care, or where the thing was not under his sole control. It makes the defendant explain; it does not decide the case against him.

Facts: A barrel falls from the window of a warehouse and injures a pedestrian, Vinay. The warehouse is run solely by Wasim's company, whose workers alone handle barrels. Nobody else had access. The company says only that it 'knows nothing' about how the barrel fell. Decide.

options.A: The company is not liable unless Vinay proves exactly how a worker was careless
options.B: The company is automatically liable, because Vinay was injured on its premises
options.C: The company must explain how the barrel fell, and its silence leaves a presumption of negligence standing
options.D: The company is not liable, because accidents happen without negligence

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A barrel does not ordinarily fall from a window without carelessness, and the warehouse was under the company's exclusive control. The presumption arises and the company must explain. Shortcut: two triggers: unusual accident, exclusive control. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The presumption relieves Vinay of proving the precise act of carelessness. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. The presumption only requires an explanation; it does not decide the case automatically. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle says this type of accident does not ordinarily happen without carelessness.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - mistake of fact and mistake of law
questions.question_text:
Passage: An act is not an offence if the person does it under a genuine mistake about a fact, and believes in good faith that he is acting as the law permits. A mistake about the law gives no such protection, since everyone is presumed to know the law. The mistake of fact must be one of fact itself, not a mistake about the legal consequences of the facts known to the person. Where he makes a mistake of fact but the act would still be an offence even on the facts as he believed them, no defence arises. The law therefore draws a firm line between what a person believed about the world and what he believed about the rules, and only the first can excuse him.

Facts: (i) At night Wilson takes an umbrella from a stand, honestly believing it to be his own, and leaves; it belongs to another. (ii) Xavier takes a neighbour's bicycle, knowing it is the neighbour's, believing wrongly that the law allows a person to use an absent neighbour's goods for a short time. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Wilson has a defence of mistake of fact; Xavier has none because his mistake is about the law
options.B: Both have a defence, because both honestly believed they were doing nothing wrong
options.C: Neither has a defence, because both took property that belonged to another
options.D: Xavier has a defence but Wilson does not, because Xavier knew whose property it was and acted openly

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Wilson's mistake is about a fact (whose umbrella it is) and is held in good faith. Xavier's mistake is about what the law allows, which is no defence. Shortcut: fact: who, what, where; law: what is allowed. Trap (B): General morality. The honesty of belief is not enough where the mistake is one of law. Trap (C): Ignoring the exception. Wilson's mistake of fact is protected. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. Knowledge of the owner removes Xavier's mistake of fact, and his mistake is about law.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - conspiracy and overt act
questions.question_text:
Passage: When two or more persons agree to do an illegal act, or a legal act by illegal means, they commit the offence of criminal conspiracy. For an agreement to commit a serious offence, the agreement itself is the offence, and no further act is required. For an agreement to commit a less serious offence, some act in pursuance of the agreement must also be done. One person alone cannot conspire, and a person who only pretends to agree, while intending to expose the plan, does not himself become a conspirator, although his pretended partner may be guilty of attempt or of a different offence.

Facts: Yogi and Zubin agree to commit a robbery, which is a serious offence, but do nothing more, and are then arrested. Separately, Anita pretends to join Bipin's plan to forge a document, a lesser offence, only to inform the police, and Bipin, who believes that Anita is really in, makes no move. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Neither pair is guilty, because nothing was done beyond talk
options.B: Yogi and Zubin are guilty of conspiracy; Bipin is not guilty of conspiracy because Anita never really agreed and no act followed
options.C: All of Yogi, Zubin and Bipin are guilty, because each of them agreed to a crime
options.D: Only Bipin is guilty, because forgery is a document offence

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Yogi and Zubin: a real agreement on a serious offence is complete conspiracy. Bipin: there is no agreement because Anita only pretended, and for a lesser offence an act was also needed. Shortcut: two checks: real agreement, and (for lesser offences) an act. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. For a serious offence the agreement alone is sufficient. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. Bipin had no real partner, since Anita only pretended to agree. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle gives no special place to document offences.

questions.question_text:
Passage: No person shall be convicted of an offence except for the violation of a law in force at the time the act was done. Nor can he be given a punishment greater than that which the law allowed at the time of the offence. This bars laws which make a past act an offence, and laws which raise the penalty for a past act. It does not bar a law that reduces the penalty, or a law which changes only the procedure of the trial, for example the court in which the case is to be heard, because neither makes the accused worse off in terms of guilt or punishment.

Facts: In 2015 Chetan did an act that carried a maximum penalty of two years. In 2020 a new law raised the maximum for such an act to five years, and also moved such trials to a special court. Chetan is tried in 2021. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Chetan can be given five years, because he is being tried after the new law
options.B: Chetan cannot be given more than two years, but he can be tried in the special court
options.C: Chetan cannot be tried in the special court, because the new law came after his act
options.D: Chetan cannot be punished at all, because the penalty has been changed since the act

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The enhanced penalty cannot apply to a past act. A change only of court is procedural and permitted. Shortcut: split substance (offence, penalty) from procedure (forum). Trap (A): Reversal of principle. The penalty for the act is fixed by the law at the time of the act. Trap (C): Ignoring the exception. A change of forum is a procedural change, which is not barred. Trap (D): Half-applied principle. The old penalty continues to apply; he can be punished up to two years.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - frustration and money already paid
questions.question_text:
Passage: When, after a contract is made, an event happens which makes performance impossible or unlawful and the event is not the fault of either party, the contract becomes void and the parties are excused from future performance. Money paid before the event can be recovered, but the party who has received a benefit under the contract before the event must compensate the other for it. A party cannot rely on frustration if the event was caused by his own act or choice, or if performance has merely become more costly or difficult, since mere hardship does not frustrate a contract.

Facts: Dhruv hires a hall for a concert from 1 to 3 June and pays ₹50,000 in advance. On 28 May a fire, for which neither party is at fault, destroys the hall. The owner has by then spent ₹5,000 from the advance on setting up chairs at Dhruv's request, which Dhruv benefited from in a rehearsal on 27 May. Decide what Dhruv can recover.

options.A: Dhruv can recover the full ₹50,000, because the contract is void
options.B: Dhruv can recover nothing, because he paid for the hall and it was destroyed
options.C: Dhruv can recover the advance and also damages for the cancelled concert
options.D: Dhruv can recover the advance less a sum for the benefit he received from the chairs and rehearsal

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Fire without fault frustrates the contract. The advance is recoverable, but Dhruv must allow the owner for the benefit he actually received. Shortcut: frustration: refund minus benefit received; no damages. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. A party who received a benefit before the event must compensate for it. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. Frustration allows recovery of money paid, subject to the allowance for benefit. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. Frustration excuses both parties and gives no right to damages.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - anticipatory breach and the right to wait
questions.question_text:
Passage: If a party declares, before the time for performance, that he will not perform his promise, the other party has a choice. He may treat the contract as ended at once and sue for damages, or he may decline to accept the refusal, wait for the time of performance and hold the contract alive for the benefit of both. If he chooses to wait, he keeps his own obligations too, and he runs the risk that events may release the other party, for example a supervening impossibility. Damages are then assessed with reference to the loss at the date for performance, and he must take reasonable steps to reduce his loss.

Facts: On 1 March, Esha agrees to buy 500 kg of wheat from Faraz for delivery on 1 June. On 10 March, Faraz writes that he will not deliver. Esha replies that she will wait for 1 June and hold him to the contract. On 15 May, a government order bans all sale of wheat, making the sale unlawful. Esha sues Faraz for damages for breach. Decide.

options.A: Esha succeeds, because Faraz had already refused to perform in March
options.B: Esha succeeds, because a refusal to perform is always a breach for which damages are due
options.C: Esha fails, because by choosing to wait she kept the contract alive and it was discharged by the later unlawfulness
options.D: Esha fails, because she should have bought wheat elsewhere in March itself

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Esha elected to affirm the contract. A contract kept alive remains subject to events, and the ban made performance unlawful, so both parties are released. Shortcut: affirming the contract means bearing later risks. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Esha chose to keep the contract alive, so Faraz's earlier refusal no longer controls. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. She treated the contract as continuing and so took the risk of later events. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle gives the choice to wait; it does not require immediate substitution.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person who is in open, continuous and hostile possession of another's land, claiming it as his own, for the full period fixed by law acquires ownership and the former owner loses his right to sue. Possession is not hostile if it is with the owner's permission. If, during the period, the possessor acknowledges in writing that the land belongs to the owner, the period starts afresh from the date of acknowledgment. Time does not run against the owner while he is under a legal disability, for example if he is a minor, until the disability ends. The three rules work together: hostility is needed at the start, acknowledgment restarts the clock, and disability only pauses it.

Facts: The period fixed is 12 years. Gagan has occupied Hari's vacant plot openly for 11 years, claiming it as his own. In the eleventh year he signs a letter saying 'I know the plot is yours, but I am using it.' He continues to occupy it for two more years. Hari then sues. Decide.

options.A: Gagan acquires ownership, because he has been in possession for thirteen years
options.B: Gagan acquires ownership, because the 12 years ended before the suit
options.C: Hari succeeds, because the written acknowledgment restarted the period and only two years have run since
options.D: Hari succeeds, because Gagan was never in lawful possession at any stage

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The acknowledgment re-starts the clock. Only two years have run after it, far short of 12, so Hari's right to sue survives. Shortcut: acknowledgment resets the clock to zero. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The acknowledgment in writing restarted the period. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. The period began afresh at the acknowledgment. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. Adverse possession by definition begins without lawful right.

questions.concept_tag: Tort - defamation and publication to a third party
questions.question_text:
Passage: Defamation requires that the false and damaging statement be published, that is, communicated to at least one person other than the person defamed. A statement made only to the person himself, even if insulting, harms no reputation in the eyes of others and is not defamation. A person who sends a defamatory letter that he does not expect anyone else to open is not liable if only the addressee reads it. But if it is reasonably foreseeable that others will read it, for example in an open postcard or a letter to a person whose secretary customarily opens the mail, then publication occurs.

Facts: (i) Ila writes a false and insulting letter to Jatin, sealed and marked 'private', and Jatin reads it alone. (ii) Kavi writes a false, insulting message to Lalit on an open postcard, which the postman and Lalit's neighbour read. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Ila is not liable for defamation but Kavi is, because only in Kavi's case was there publication to others
options.B: Both are liable, because both statements were false and insulting
options.C: Neither is liable, because defamation requires proof of actual financial loss
options.D: Ila is liable but Kavi is not, because a private letter shows greater malice

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Ila's letter reached only the person addressed, so there was no publication. Kavi's open postcard was read by others, so there was. Shortcut: no third-party reader means no defamation. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Publication to a third party is an essential element. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. No such requirement appears in the principle. Trap (D): General morality. Malice is not the test; publication is.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - claim of right in taking property
questions.question_text:
Passage: Theft needs a dishonest intention to take movable property from another's possession without consent. A person who takes property under an honest belief that he has a legal right to it does not act dishonestly, even if his belief is wrong. The belief must be honest, and not a mere pretext. The exception does not cover a person who, having a genuine claim to a smaller thing, takes something larger or different, such as taking goods worth much more than the debt which is due to him, because the extra part is not covered by his belief. The test is applied separately to each article taken, and a general feeling of being wronged is not a claim of right.

Facts: Mohan honestly believes that Naveen owes him ₹2,000 and, in Naveen's absence, takes Naveen's watch worth ₹2,000, which he intends to keep until he is paid. Mohan then, in the same visit, takes Naveen's gold chain worth ₹60,000 'as interest', knowing that no such interest was agreed. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Mohan is guilty of theft for both, because he took property without consent
options.B: Mohan is not guilty of theft for the watch but is guilty of theft for the gold chain
options.C: Mohan is not guilty for either, because he honestly believed that Naveen owed him money
options.D: Mohan is guilty for the watch but not for the chain, because the chain was taken as interest

questions.pedagogical_explanation: For the watch he acted on an honest claim of right. For the chain he knew that no right existed, so the intention was dishonest. Shortcut: check honesty of belief separately for each item. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. An honest belief in a right removes dishonesty for the watch. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. The belief covers only the debt, and he knew the chain was not due to him. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. This reverses the two outcomes.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - past consideration and past request
questions.question_text:
Passage: As a rule, consideration must be given in return for a promise. Something done before the promise and without any request is called past consideration and does not support a promise made later. A promise to pay for a past act is, however, enforceable if the act was done at the promisor's request, and if both parties understood, when it was done, that it would be paid for or rewarded. If the act was voluntary, so that the promisor never asked for it, a later promise to pay is a mere gift and cannot be enforced, unless it falls within some other exception, such as a signed promise to pay a time-barred debt.

Facts: (i) Omkar asks Prem to repair his roof, and Prem does it without any talk of payment. Afterwards, Omkar promises Prem ₹3,000, but later refuses to pay. (ii) Qadir, without being asked, paints a neighbour Rekha's gate while she is away. When she returns, she promises him ₹500, but later refuses to pay. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both can enforce, because each did something useful before the promise
options.B: Neither can enforce, because in both cases the act came before the promise
options.C: Prem can enforce Omkar's promise, since the roof was repaired at his request with an understanding of reward, but Qadir cannot enforce Rekha's
options.D: Qadir can enforce but Prem cannot, because only Qadir acted wholly on his own

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The roof repair was done at Omkar's request and a payment was expected, so the later promise is enforceable. The gate was painted voluntarily, so Rekha's later promise is a bare gift. Shortcut: past act + request = enforceable; past act without request = gift. Trap (A): Half-applied principle. Usefulness alone is not consideration; a request is needed. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. A past act done at the promisor's request is an exception. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. This reverses the principle; a voluntary act is a gift.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person who sets the law in motion against another is liable for malicious prosecution if four things are proved. The prosecution was begun by the defendant, it ended in favour of the plaintiff, it was begun without reasonable and probable cause, and the defendant acted with malice, that is, for a purpose other than bringing an offender to justice. If any of the four is missing, the claim fails. A person who honestly reports facts to the police and leaves the matter to them, without more, does not begin the prosecution, and a case that ended on a technical ground may not count as ending in the plaintiff's favour.

Facts: Sohan, angry over a land dispute, files a complaint with the police against Tarun for theft, knowing that Tarun is innocent. The police investigate and the court acquits Tarun after trial on the merits. Tarun sues Sohan. Sohan says that the police and the court, not he, decided to prosecute. Decide.

options.A: Sohan is not liable, because the police and the court decided to proceed
options.B: Sohan is liable, because he began the prosecution without cause and with malice, and it ended in Tarun's favour
options.C: Sohan is not liable, because Tarun suffered no financial loss
options.D: Sohan is liable merely because the acquittal showed that his complaint was wrong

questions.pedagogical_explanation: All four elements exist: Sohan started the case, it ended in Tarun's favour, there was no reasonable cause as he knew of the innocence, and his motive was malice. Shortcut: tick the four elements; any gap defeats the claim. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Sohan did more than report honestly; he set the law in motion knowing Tarun was innocent. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. No such element is listed in the principle. Trap (D): Half-applied principle. Acquittal is only one of four elements, and the others must also be proved.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A confession made by an accused to a police officer cannot be used against him. This protects the accused from being forced into a confession by fear of the police. There is a limited exception: so much of the information given by the accused while in police custody as leads to the discovery of a fact may be proved, whether it amounts to a confession or not. The part that may be proved is only the part which distinctly relates to the fact discovered. The remainder of the statement, including any admission of guilt, remains inadmissible. The exception is justified because the discovery of a real object confirms that this part of the statement is true and not a product of fear.

Facts: Ujwal, in police custody, tells the inspector: 'I killed Vijay with an axe and hid the axe under the banyan tree behind my house.' The police dig there and find a bloodstained axe. At the trial, the prosecution wants to prove his statement. What can be proved?

options.A: The entire statement, because it led to the discovery of the axe
options.B: Nothing, because a statement made to a police officer is never admissible
options.C: Only the part 'I killed Vijay with an axe', because it shows guilt
options.D: Only the part about hiding the axe under the banyan tree, as it led to the discovery of the axe

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The general bar excludes his confession. The exception allows only the portion that distinctly led to discovering the axe. Shortcut: admit only the discovery part. Trap (A): Half-applied principle. Only the part distinctly relating to the discovery is admissible. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. The discovery exception applies to the part leading to it. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. The admission of guilt is excluded; the discovery part is admitted.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A contract is novated when, with the consent of all parties, a new contract takes the place of the old, so that a new party takes over both the rights and the duties of an old party, who is then released. An assignment is different: the benefit of a contract may be assigned to another, but the burden cannot be transferred without the consent of the other contracting party. The party who assigns his rights remains liable for his own duties under the contract. A person who is to perform a duty cannot escape it by merely arranging for another to perform it.

Facts: Vasu agrees to supply Wendy with 100 chairs for ₹50,000. Vasu then arranges with Xena that Xena will deliver the chairs instead and will take the payment, and informs Wendy, who does not agree. Xena fails to deliver. Whom may Wendy hold liable?

options.A: Xena, because she took over the contract from Vasu
options.B: Both Vasu and Xena equally, because they agreed between themselves to deliver
options.C: Vasu, because the burden could not be transferred to Xena without Wendy's consent
options.D: Neither, because Vasu has handed over the contract and Xena has the money

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Without Wendy's consent there is no novation. Vasu's duty stays with him, and Wendy has no contract with Xena. Shortcut: burden needs consent; benefit can be assigned. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Wendy never consented, so there was no novation. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Xena has no contract with Wendy. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. A burden cannot be transferred without consent, so Vasu remains liable.

questions.question_text:
Passage: An act is not an offence if the person, at the time of doing it, is by reason of unsoundness of mind incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that what he is doing is wrong or contrary to law. The test is the capacity to know at the time of the act. Mental illness alone, or a delusion that did not affect his knowledge of the act, is not enough. A person who knows that his act is wrong but cannot restrain himself, or who knows the act is contrary to law but acts out of rage, does not come within this defence.

Facts: (i) Yash, suffering from a mental illness, strikes a man believing that he is cutting a tree, and is thus unable to know what he is doing. (ii) Zahir, who is undergoing treatment for mental illness, plans an attack on his rival with care, hides his weapon, flees afterwards and lies to the police, though he is plainly angry. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Yash comes within the defence; Zahir does not, because he knew what he did was wrong
options.B: Both come within the defence, because both suffer from a mental illness
options.C: Neither comes within the defence, because the act caused death or injury
options.D: Zahir comes within the defence but Yash does not, because Zahir was being treated

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Yash did not know the nature of his act, so the defence applies. Zahir's planning, hiding and lying show he knew it was wrong. Shortcut: test: knowledge of nature or wrongfulness at the time of the act. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Illness alone is not enough; the capacity to know at the time of the act decides. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The principle contains no such rule about outcomes. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. Treatment is not the test; knowledge at the time of the act is.

questions.concept_tag: IPR - copyright ownership and the employer
questions.question_text:
Passage: The author of a work is the first owner of the copyright in it. There is an exception where a work is made by an employee in the course of his employment under a contract of service, in which case the employer is the first owner, in the absence of an agreement to the contrary. The exception does not apply to a work made by an independent contractor under a contract for services, nor to a work which an employee makes in his own time unrelated to his duties. The independent author keeps the copyright unless it is assigned to the other in writing.

Facts: Aditi is a salaried designer at Brightline Ltd and designs a logo for a client as part of her duties. In her spare time she also draws a comic that has nothing to do with her work. Separately, Brightline hires Bharat, a freelance illustrator, to draw a poster, with no written assignment of rights. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Brightline owns all three works, because it paid or employed each of the three persons
options.B: Aditi, Bharat and Brightline each own a share of every work, because all three took part
options.C: Brightline owns the logo and the poster, but not the comic
options.D: Brightline owns the logo; Aditi owns the comic; Bharat owns the poster

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The logo is an employee's work in the course of employment. The comic is outside her duties. The poster is by a contractor with no written assignment. Shortcut: employee in course of duty vs. outsider or off-duty work. Trap (A): Half-applied principle. Employment covers only works made in the course of employment, and a contractor is not an employee. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. The principle assigns first ownership to one person per work. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. The poster was made by an independent contractor, who owns it unless there is a written assignment.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - quantum meruit for part performance
questions.question_text:
Passage: Where a person has been engaged to do a piece of work for a fixed sum, he ordinarily cannot claim payment until the whole work is done. But if the other party prevents completion by his own act, the worker may claim a reasonable sum for the work he has done. This is called quantum meruit. If, instead, it is the worker who abandons the work without good reason, he cannot claim anything for the part done, unless the other party has accepted the benefit of the part already done with a choice to accept or reject it. The reason for the rule is that a person who prevents performance should not profit from his own act, while a person who abandons the work should bear the consequence.

Facts: Chanda agrees to build a wall for Dinesh for ₹10,000, and builds half. (i) Dinesh then locks the site and refuses to let Chanda continue. (ii) In another contract, Eshan agrees to build a wall for Farhan for ₹10,000, builds half and walks away for a better job; Farhan takes no benefit from the half-built wall, as it must be demolished. What may each worker claim?

options.A: Chanda can claim a reasonable sum for half the work; Eshan can claim nothing
options.B: Both can claim a reasonable sum, because each did half of the work
options.C: Neither can claim anything, because the work was not completed
options.D: Eshan can claim a reasonable sum but Chanda cannot, because Chanda could have gone elsewhere

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Dinesh prevented completion, so Chanda can claim quantum meruit. Eshan abandoned the work and Farhan took no benefit, so Eshan gets nothing. Shortcut: who stopped the work? That decides who may claim. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. A worker who abandons without good reason and gives no accepted benefit gets nothing. Trap (C): Ignoring the exception. Where the other party prevents completion, the worker can claim a reasonable sum. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The principle reverses these outcomes.

questions.concept_tag: Limitation - disability and the running of time
questions.question_text:
Passage: A suit must be filed within a fixed period from the date the right to sue arises, and once the period has run out the suit is barred. If, at the time the right arises, the person entitled to sue is a minor, the period is counted from the date he attains majority. This relief applies only to a person who was under the disability when the right first arose. If a person becomes a minor, or comes under a disability, after the period has started to run, time continues without a break. The extension for disability is also not given to a person who could have sued through a guardian but chose not to; the law gives it by status, not by effort.

Facts: The period for a suit on a debt is 3 years from the date the debt falls due. A debt falls due to Gita, aged 16, on 1 January 2015. She turns 18 on 1 January 2017. Another debt falls due on 1 January 2015 to Hemant, aged 30, who becomes mentally incapable in 2016 and remains so. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Gita can sue until 1 January 2020; Hemant's time ran out on 1 January 2018 despite his later incapacity
options.B: Both can sue until after the end of their disability, because both were disabled during the period
options.C: Neither is entitled to an extension, because the period is the same for all persons
options.D: Hemant can sue until 1 January 2020 and Gita cannot, because Hemant's disability was the greater

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Gita was a minor when the right arose; time runs from her majority (turning 18 in 2017), and three years later is 2020. Hemant's disability began after the period started, so time was not interrupted. Shortcut: check when the disability started relative to the right. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. The extension applies only if the disability existed when the right arose. Trap (C): Ignoring the exception. A minor at the time of the right gets time counted from majority. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The principle favours Gita, who was a minor when the right arose.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A court may, in suitable cases, order a party to perform his promise, instead of merely awarding damages. This is known as specific performance. It is not ordered where the contract is one of personal service, such as a contract of employment, because a court cannot force a person to work or an employer to keep a worker. The court may, however, restrain a person by injunction from working for a rival during the term of a contract if he has agreed in the contract not to do so, provided the restraint is limited to the contract period and does not leave him without any means of livelihood.

Facts: A music company, Glow Records, signs singer Jaya for three years and she agrees not to sing for any other company during that period. After one year she refuses to record for Glow and signs a deal with a rival firm. Glow asks the court (i) to order Jaya to record songs for it, and (ii) to restrain her from singing for the rival. What may the court do?

options.A: Order her to record for Glow and also restrain her from singing for the rival
options.B: Refuse both requests, because the court cannot interfere in a personal service contract
options.C: Restrain her from singing for anyone at all after the contract ends
options.D: Refuse to order her to record, but restrain her from singing for the rival during the three years

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Courts will not compel a person to work, but will enforce a negative promise by injunction for the contract term, provided livelihood is not destroyed. Shortcut: positive duty: no; negative covenant: yes, for the term. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Specific performance of personal service is not ordered. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. The negative covenant can be enforced by injunction during the term. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The restraint is limited to the contract period.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - agreement with a person of unsound mind
questions.question_text:
Passage: The law of contract permits only those persons who are competent to contract to bind themselves by agreement. A person is competent if he is an adult, is of sound mind, and is not disqualified by any law to which he is subject. The requirement of sound mind has a particular meaning. A person is said to be of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract if, at the time when he makes it, he is capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon his interests. A person who is usually of unsound mind, but occasionally of sound mind, may make a contract when he is of sound mind. Conversely, a person who is usually of sound mind, but occasionally of unsound mind, may not make a contract when he is of unsound mind. The test is therefore applied at the moment of the agreement and not by looking at the general state of the person's health. An agreement made by a person who is not competent to contract is void, which means that it has no legal effect from the beginning and cannot be enforced by either side. The rule is meant to protect those who cannot properly protect themselves, and it also gives certainty to the other party, who can know that only an agreement made at a time of understanding will bind. A person's illness, however serious, does not by itself prevent him from making a valid contract on a day when he understands what he is doing. Nor does a person's mere eccentricity, strange habits or poor judgment show unsoundness of mind. What matters is the real capacity to understand the terms of the agreement and their likely consequences at the time of the agreement. The party who claims that the agreement is void for unsoundness of mind must show that the other party was incapable of understanding at that very time. The other party's knowledge of the illness does not change the test, since the question is the capacity of the maker at that moment and not the opinion of those around him.

Facts: Harish suffers from a mental illness that makes him confused for most weeks of the year, but on a particular afternoon his doctor certifies that he was thinking clearly and understood everything he did. On that afternoon, Harish agrees to sell his scooter to Indu for a fair price. Later, Harish's brother says the sale is void because Harish is generally of unsound mind. Is the agreement binding?

options.A: Yes, because Harish was capable of understanding the agreement and its effect at the time he made it
options.B: No, because a person who is generally of unsound mind can never make a valid contract
options.C: No, because it is unfair for Indu to buy from a person who is ill
options.D: Yes, because Indu paid a fair price, whatever the state of Harish's mind

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The test is the maker's capacity at the time of the agreement. Harish understood the agreement and its effect that afternoon, so he was of sound mind for this contract and it binds. Shortcut: apply the test at the moment of the agreement, not to the person's general health. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. The principle expressly allows a usually unsound person to contract during a lucid period. Trap (C): General morality. Fairness to the ill person is not the test; capacity at the moment is. Trap (D): Ignoring a condition. A fair price does not replace the condition that the maker understood the agreement when making it.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - agreements with an unlawful object
questions.question_text:
Passage: An agreement is a contract only if it is made for a lawful object. The object or consideration of an agreement is unlawful if it is forbidden by law, if it is of such a nature that, if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law, if it is fraudulent, if it involves or implies injury to the person or property of another, or if the court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy. Where the object is unlawful in this sense, the agreement is void and neither party can ask the court to enforce it. The rule rests on the idea that the machinery of the courts must not be used to carry out plans which the law itself condemns. The rule also applies where only a part of the consideration is unlawful and the lawful part cannot be separated from the unlawful part. But where the lawful and unlawful parts can be separated, the court may enforce the lawful part. The unlawfulness must exist in the object of the agreement itself. An agreement does not become void merely because one of the parties, or a person connected with him, has behaved wrongly on some other occasion, and an agreement does not become unlawful merely because it is made by a person who intends to use the thing for a wrong purpose which the other party does not know about. The court looks at the common object of the parties, as shown in their agreement. A promise to pay money in return for a forbidden act is the clearest example, because the forbidden act is the very thing for which the promise is given. In such a case the person who has done the forbidden act cannot recover the promised money, and the person who promised it cannot be forced to pay. Courts do not apply this rule to harsh bargains or bad bargains, which are valid if their object is lawful, and the question is always whether the object itself is forbidden by law. The agreement of the parties must also be genuine in the sense that it is made freely, and the court will not enforce an agreement merely because a party says he would have been willing to carry it out.

Facts: Jagan promises to pay Kishan ₹50,000 if Kishan will burn down the shop of Jagan's business rival. Kishan sets fire to the shop and then demands the ₹50,000. Jagan refuses. Kishan sues for the money. Decide.

options.A: Kishan can recover the money, because he did everything that was asked of him
options.B: Kishan cannot recover the money, because the object of the agreement was unlawful and the agreement is void
options.C: Kishan can recover the money, because Jagan has become dishonest by refusing to pay
options.D: Kishan cannot recover the money, because the rival never agreed to the plan

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Burning another's shop is forbidden by law and injures another's property, so the object is unlawful. The agreement is void and no court will enforce it for either side. Shortcut: if the promised act is forbidden by law, the promise is void. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. The performance of an unlawful object gives no right to enforcement. Trap (C): General morality. Dishonest refusal is not relevant when the agreement itself is void. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle does not require the victim's consent or knowledge; it turns on the unlawful object.

questions.question_text:
Passage: For an agreement to become a contract, its meaning must be certain, or capable of being made certain. If the terms of an agreement are so vague that the court cannot say what the parties have actually promised to do, the agreement is void for uncertainty, and no one can be compelled to carry it out. The rule recognises that the court's task is to enforce the promises that parties have made, not to make promises for them. An agreement may, however, be uncertain on its face and still be valid if the parties have supplied some way of making it certain. For example, a promise to sell a quantity of goods at the market rate on a fixed day can be enforced, because the market rate on that day can be found. Similarly, an agreement to sell the whole of a farmer's crop of a given year, at a price to be fixed by a named valuer, is certain since the price will be fixed by the valuer. Words that merely express hope, or leave an essential matter to be settled by further agreement between the parties, are not enough. The question is whether an essential term, such as the price, the subject matter or the time of performance, has been left open in a way that no standard can fill. A vague phrase that does not affect an essential term, or one to which the court can give an ordinary meaning, does not make an agreement void. The court will try to give effect to the agreement where it can, since parties who intend to be bound should not be allowed to avoid a bargain through a minor lack of precision. But the court cannot invent an essential term which the parties themselves never agreed. The same principle explains why the court is slow to rescue a party from a bargain that is merely unwise. A party may be quite free to make a poor bargain, but he is not free to ask the court to enforce an agreement the content of which cannot be known. When examining a claim, the court therefore begins by asking what was promised, and only then asks whether the promise has been broken. If it cannot answer the first question from the words of the parties, from their dealings or from a stated standard, it does not go on to the second.

Facts: Laxman agrees to sell Maya his car 'at a price to be settled between us later on', and no other method of fixing the price is stated. Before any price is settled, Laxman receives a better offer and refuses to go ahead. Maya sues to compel the sale. Decide.

options.A: Maya can compel the sale, because Laxman agreed to sell and the court can fix a fair price
options.B: Maya cannot compel the sale, because the price, an essential term, was left open with no way of making it certain
options.C: Maya can compel the sale, because Laxman acted unfairly in taking a better offer
options.D: Maya cannot compel the sale, because a car is a movable thing and not land

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The price is an essential term, and the agreement supplies no method of settling it. The agreement is therefore uncertain and void. Shortcut: can the essential term be found without the parties' further agreement? Trap (A): Reversal of principle. The court cannot invent an essential term that the parties left open. Trap (C): General morality. Unfairness cannot cure an agreement which is void for uncertainty. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle does not distinguish between movable things and land.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person who, by an act, makes another fear that force is about to be used against him commits the wrong of assault, and a person who actually applies force to another without lawful justification commits the wrong of battery. The two wrongs are separate. In assault, the wrongdoer causes the other person to apprehend immediate unlawful force, even if no force is actually applied. A threat of violence which is to be carried out at some distant time, or in a different place, is not an assault, because the apprehension must relate to immediate force. The words which accompany a gesture may remove the threat. For example, a person who raises his fist and says that he would strike the other if it were not for the presence of the police officers has made it clear that he does not intend to use force at that time. In battery, the slightest touch may be enough, if it is hostile or goes beyond the ordinary touching which everyone accepts in daily life, such as the jostling of a crowded pavement or a light tap on the shoulder to attract attention. There need not be any harm to the victim. A wrongdoer may be liable for battery even though he did not intend to injure, so long as he intended the contact itself. The victim may claim damages for either wrong or for both, according to the facts, and need not show any physical injury for either. Consent of the victim, given freely and for the kind of contact which occurred, removes the wrong. Both wrongs are concerned with the protection of a person's body and his peace of mind against unwanted interference. For this reason, the law treats the apprehension of force as harm in itself, because a person should be free to go about his affairs without being put in fear of violence. A person who is threatened may therefore sue even if the wrongdoer is stopped, or changes his mind, before any force is used. Both wrongs are different from the crime of the same name, which is punished by the State.

Facts: During an argument, Nikhil lifts a stick, walks towards Omar and shouts that he will hit him now. Omar, terrified, ducks and runs away. Nikhil does not touch Omar. Which wrong, if any, has Nikhil committed?

options.A: Battery, because the intention to hit was enough even though no touch occurred
options.B: No wrong, because Omar was not physically injured
options.C: Assault, because Omar was made to fear immediate force, although there was no battery as no force was applied
options.D: No wrong, because Nikhil was merely angry and angry words are lawful

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Nikhil's lifting of the stick and his words caused Omar to fear immediate force, which is assault. No force was applied, so there is no battery. Shortcut: assault = fear of immediate force; battery = actual force. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. Battery requires an actual application of force. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Injury is not required for assault. Trap (D): General morality. The threat of immediate force, not the anger, makes the wrong.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person is liable in tort for harm which he causes by his act when the harm was caused through his intention or his want of care. But a person is not liable for harm that results from an inevitable accident. An accident is inevitable when the harm could not have been prevented by the exercise of reasonable care and caution on the part of the person who is said to have caused it. The defence rests on the idea that people should be answerable for what they could have avoided, and not for what no care could have avoided. The defendant who pleads inevitable accident must show that he took all the care which a reasonable person would have taken in the circumstances, and that the harm occurred despite that care. It is not enough for him to say that he did not intend the harm. Nor is the defence made out where the accident, though unexpected by him, would have been avoided if he had taken ordinary precautions, such as maintaining his vehicle or looking at the road. The standard is not perfection but the care that a reasonable person in the same position would have taken. The same rule applies to accidents arising from natural causes, from the unexpected failure of a machine which was properly inspected, or from a sudden illness which gave no warning. The defence does not apply to those torts in which liability is strict, where the law makes the defendant liable whether or not he was careful. In a case of ordinary negligence, however, an accident which could not have been avoided by care is a complete defence to liability. The defence is therefore narrow and is to be examined strictly by the court. The defendant has to bring evidence of the precautions he actually took, such as inspection, maintenance and attention at the relevant time, and the court will compare those with what a prudent person would have done. Where the evidence shows that careful behaviour would not have prevented the harm, the claim in negligence fails, however serious the loss to the person injured, since the law of negligence punishes fault and does not guarantee safety against every mishap.

Facts: Pavan, a careful driver whose car was serviced a week ago, is driving at a safe speed when a tyre bursts suddenly because of a hidden defect that no inspection could have found. The car hits a roadside stall and damages it. The stall owner claims damages for negligence. Decide.

options.A: Pavan is liable, because his car damaged another person's property
options.B: Pavan is liable, because the stall owner is poor and should be helped
options.C: Pavan is not liable, because the harm was an inevitable accident that reasonable care could not have prevented
options.D: Pavan is not liable, because roadside stalls should not be placed near the road

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Pavan took all reasonable care, and the tyre failure came from a hidden defect that no inspection could reveal. That makes it an inevitable accident, which defeats the claim in negligence. Shortcut: care taken plus unavoidable cause means no liability. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. Liability needs a want of care, and the accident was inevitable. Trap (B): General morality. The principle does not depend on the stall owner's circumstances. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle does not rest on where the stall stood.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - criminal breach of trust
questions.question_text:
