Passage: A person commits criminal breach of trust when he has been entrusted with property, or with dominion over property, and he dishonestly misappropriates it, converts it to his own use, or dishonestly uses or disposes of it in violation of the direction of law or of any legal contract which prescribes the way in which the trust is to be discharged. Two elements are essential. First, there must be an entrustment, which means that the owner has voluntarily placed the property in the hands of the other person for a particular purpose. Second, there must be dishonest misappropriation of that property. Entrustment distinguishes this offence from theft, because in theft the property is taken out of the owner's possession without consent, while here the owner himself has handed it over. The offence is complete when the person to whom it has been entrusted dishonestly deals with the property contrary to the trust. A mere failure to return the property, or a delay in accounting for it, is not by itself breach of trust, if there is no dishonest intention. A temporary use of the property which does not defeat the purpose of the entrustment, and which the person honestly meant to make good, is not enough. But a dishonest use of the property for a purpose which was not intended by the owner shows the offence. The person who is entrusted may be an employee, an agent, a trustee, a banker or any other person who holds the property on behalf of another. The amount involved does not change the nature of the offence. It is also important to see how the offence differs from the nearby offences. Where the person has not been given the property but takes it, the offence is theft. Where he gets the property by deceiving the owner at the outset, the offence is cheating. Criminal breach of trust is the offence where the person is in lawful possession for a special purpose and then turns it to a different, dishonest purpose. The relationship of confidence between the owner and the person entrusted is what the law protects. A person who is in a position of trust is expected to use the property only for the purpose for which it was given to him.

Facts: Qureshi gives ₹1 lakh to his accountant Ravi to deposit in the company's bank account. Ravi, instead, uses the money to pay his own gambling debts and tells Qureshi that the money has been deposited. Which offence has Ravi committed?

options.A: Theft, because he took the money away from Qureshi
options.B: No offence, because the money was handed to him voluntarily by Qureshi
options.C: No offence, because the company's loss can be repaid later
options.D: Criminal breach of trust, because the money was entrusted to him and he dishonestly used it for his own purpose

questions.pedagogical_explanation: There was entrustment, and Ravi dishonestly used the money for his own purpose and lied about it. Both elements of criminal breach of trust are present. Shortcut: entrusted + dishonestly misused = breach of trust. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. In theft the property is taken without consent; here it was entrusted. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Voluntary entrustment is only the first element; dishonest misappropriation is the second. Trap (C): General morality. Intention to repay later does not suit the dishonest use shown here.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person commits extortion if he intentionally puts any person in fear of injury to that person or to another, and thereby dishonestly induces the person so put in fear to deliver to anyone any property, or valuable security, or anything signed or sealed which may be converted into a valuable security. Three elements are therefore involved: an intentional putting in fear of injury, a dishonest inducement, and a delivery of property as a result. The fear need not be of physical harm. A threat to injure a person's reputation or property may also be enough, if it is of such a kind as to make a person of ordinary firmness deliver the property. The offence is complete when the victim delivers the property, and it does not matter that the threat is never carried out. If there is only a threat, but no delivery of anything of value, the offence of extortion has not been completed, although a lesser offence of criminal intimidation may be committed. Where the person who delivers the property does so freely, without being put in fear, there is no extortion. Likewise, a demand for a payment which is owed to the person making it, and which he asks for in an ordinary lawful way, does not become extortion. The distinguishing mark of extortion is that the victim hands over the property himself, under the pressure of the fear, and not that the property is taken from him by force. The fear involved must be fear of injury, and injury in this sense includes harm of any kind illegally caused to a person in body, mind, reputation or property. The threat must be intended to produce the delivery, so that a person who makes an angry remark without any purpose of obtaining something does not commit extortion. It is also relevant that the victim has to hand over the property himself, because this feature separates extortion from robbery, in which force is used on the spot to take the property, and from theft, in which the property is taken without any delivery. Where there is only a threat and nothing is delivered, the lesser offence of criminal intimidation may still be punished, so a threatened person is not left without a remedy in any case.

Facts: Sandeep tells shopkeeper Tej that he knows a secret about Tej's past and will publish it unless Tej hands him ₹20,000. Frightened, Tej gives him the money. Which offence is committed by Sandeep?

options.A: No offence, because Tej gave the money himself and was not forced physically
options.B: Extortion, because Sandeep put Tej in fear of injury to his reputation and dishonestly induced him to deliver money
options.C: No offence, because the threat concerned only a secret and not an act of violence
options.D: Theft, because Sandeep got the money without any lawful claim to it

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Sandeep intentionally put Tej in fear of injury to reputation and dishonestly induced the delivery of money. All three elements are present. Shortcut: fear + dishonest inducement + delivery = extortion. Trap (A): Half-applied principle. Delivery by the victim is part of extortion; fear need not be of physical harm. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. A threat to reputation may be enough. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. Theft requires taking out of possession without consent, but Tej delivered the money.

questions.concept_tag: Constitutional law - freedom of religion and public order
questions.question_text:
Passage: All persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion. This right is, however, subject to public order, morality and health, and to the other provisions dealing with fundamental rights. The State may also make laws regulating or restricting any economic, financial, political or other secular activity which may be associated with religious practice, and providing for social welfare and reform. The freedom therefore covers belief and the essential practices of a religion, but it does not cover every act which is carried out in the name of religion. The State may not ask whether a belief is true or false, and it may not prefer one religion over another. But it may regulate practices that disturb public order, such as a procession that blocks a public road and causes disorder, or that endanger health, such as a practice that spreads disease. Where the State's regulation concerns only the secular side of an activity, for instance the management of money collected by a temple, it does not violate the freedom of religion. A restriction on the exercise of religion has to be imposed by a valid law and must be reasonably connected with the stated grounds of public order, morality or health. A restriction that is merely a matter of the State's dislike of the religion, or an attempt to discourage a faith, is not permitted. Every person is free to practise his religion within these limits, and the freedom to propagate does not include a right to convert others by force or fraud. The courts have also said that the State may regulate the times and places of religious gatherings in public spaces, where this is necessary to protect others, while leaving the beliefs themselves alone. A regulation of this kind must be general and fair, and must not be used against one group. It is also important to note that the freedom is given to every person and to every religion equally, so that the State must treat all groups with the same measure when applying public-order rules, and it may not allow one group to disturb public order while stopping another group from doing the same.

Facts: A religious group holds a festival and insists on carrying a large procession through the main road of the town at peak hours, with loud music, so that the road is entirely blocked and several patients are stopped from reaching a hospital. The authority prohibits the procession on that road at that hour, and permits it on a quieter road at another time. The group says that the order violates their freedom of religion. Decide.

options.A: The order is valid, because the freedom of religion is subject to public order and health, and the procession on that road at that hour disturbs both
options.B: The order is invalid, because the freedom to practise religion is absolute
options.C: The order is invalid, because the State may not interfere in any religious activity
options.D: The order is valid, because the State may prefer to avoid religious festivals altogether

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Freedom of religion is subject to public order and health. The authority's order is reasonably connected to these grounds and still allows the festival at another time and place. Shortcut: freedom is real but limited by public order, morality and health. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. The principle makes the freedom subject to public order, morality and health. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. The State may regulate practices that disturb public order or health. Trap (D): General morality. The principle forbids a restriction based on the State's dislike of religion.

questions.question_text:
Passage: The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, or any of them. The word 'only' is important. A rule that distinguishes between persons on some other basis, which is reasonably related to the purpose of the rule, is not rendered invalid merely because it happens to affect a particular group more than others. A rule fails only if the real and sole ground for the difference in treatment is one of the forbidden grounds. The State is also permitted to make special provisions for women and children and for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes of citizens, since such provisions are meant to remove disadvantages and not to impose them. No citizen shall, on any of the forbidden grounds, be subject to any disability or restriction with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment, or the use of wells, tanks, roads and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds. The rule applies to the State and its agencies as against the citizen, and to the specified public places as against private operators. It does not control every private choice, such as whom a person invites into his own home. Where a difference of treatment is challenged, the court asks what the real ground for the difference is, and whether that ground is one of the grounds forbidden by the rule. The rule is also concerned with the practical effects of State action. The State may have many reasons for treating persons differently, such as age, qualifications, income or health, and none of these is forbidden. What the law forbids is the use of the forbidden grounds as the sole reason for a worse treatment. A court examining a challenge to a rule does not accept the label that the State gives to its decision, but looks at the real reason that explains the difference, and decides whether a forbidden ground was the only reason for it. A person who feels aggrieved may approach the court, and the State must then explain the real reason for its action and show that the reason is not one of the forbidden grounds taken alone.

Facts: A State-run public swimming pool refuses entry to Rehana, who is a citizen, solely because she belongs to a particular religion. Rehana challenges the refusal. Decide.

options.A: The refusal is invalid, because it discriminates against a citizen solely on the ground of religion in a place maintained with State funds
options.B: The refusal is valid, because a swimming pool is not a place of public entertainment
options.C: The refusal is valid, because the State has a right to decide who enters its property
options.D: The refusal is invalid, only because Rehana is a woman and women need special protection

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The refusal rests only on religion, which is a forbidden ground, and the pool is a State-maintained place. So the refusal is invalid. Shortcut: ask: is religion the sole ground? Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. The principle covers public places maintained wholly or partly out of State funds. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. The principle forbids discrimination by the State on the stated grounds. Trap (D): Half-applied principle. The ground stated is religion, and that alone makes the refusal invalid.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person who is arrested shall not be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for his arrest, and he shall not be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice. Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate, and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond that period without the authority of a magistrate. These safeguards exist so that the liberty of a person is not taken away on the mere word of a police officer, and so that an independent authority checks whether the detention is justified. The twenty-four hour limit counts from the time of arrest and not from the time of the person's arrival at the police station. Holidays and weekends do not extend the period, though the time of travel does not count. The safeguards do not apply to a person who is arrested under a law relating to preventive detention, or to a person who is an enemy alien, because separate rules apply to them. A person who is arrested has the right to know why he is held, and he must be allowed to speak to his lawyer. If the police fail to produce him before a magistrate within the time allowed, his continued detention is unlawful. The word 'produced' means that the person must actually be taken before the magistrate, and a paper report by the police to the magistrate does not satisfy it. The purpose is to let the magistrate see the person, hear what he has to say about his treatment and decide whether the person is to be released or sent to custody for a further period. The magistrate's authority for further detention must be given by the magistrate after considering the case, and cannot be obtained afterwards. The right to be informed of the grounds and to consult a lawyer begins at the time of the arrest and continues throughout the detention.

Facts: Sumit is arrested by the police for an alleged theft at 10 am on Monday. The police station is in the same town as the magistrate's court. He is produced before the magistrate only at 4 pm on Wednesday, with no authority from a magistrate for the extra detention. Is the detention lawful?

options.A: Yes, because he was told the reason for the arrest and so the safeguards were met
options.B: Yes, because the police are entitled to take as much time as they need to investigate theft
options.C: No, because he was not produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours of arrest
options.D: No, because a person accused of theft can never be held in custody

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The 24-hour period runs from the time of arrest and Sumit was produced after about 54 hours, with no travel delay and no magistrate's authority. The detention is unlawful. Shortcut: count 24 hours from arrest, excluding only travel time. Trap (A): Half-applied principle. Telling the grounds is only one safeguard; production within 24 hours is separate. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. The principle sets a firm limit of 24 hours without a magistrate's authority. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle does not forbid custody; it requires production before a magistrate in time.

questions.question_text:
Passage: An advertisement is misleading if it gives a false description of a product or service, or gives a false guarantee, or is likely to mislead the consumer about the nature, substance, quantity or quality of the product, or conceals a material fact. A seller who publishes such an advertisement commits an unfair trade practice and may be directed to stop the advertisement, to issue a corrective notice and to pay compensation to the consumers who have suffered loss. It is not necessary that any consumer was actually deceived, since the test is whether the advertisement is likely to mislead an average consumer. The effect of the advertisement is judged from the overall impression it gives and not merely from its literal words. A statement in small print which contradicts the main message of the advertisement does not usually cure a misleading impression. The law distinguishes between a false claim and an obvious exaggeration or 'puffery' which no reasonable consumer would take literally, such as a shop that calls its tea 'the best in the world'. A claim that can be checked, such as the percentage of a mineral in a product or the number of days of a battery's life, must be true. A seller is not allowed to defend a false claim by saying that he made it in good faith, because the rule is concerned with the effect on the consumer and not with the seller's intention. Where the advertisement makes a comparison with a competitor's product, the comparison must also be true and fair, and it must not lower the reputation of the other product without a reason. A seller may emphasise the good qualities of his product, but he may not conceal facts that a reasonable consumer would want to know before buying, such as the presence of an ingredient that might harm health. The regulator may also impose a penalty on a seller who repeats a misleading advertisement after being told to stop. The consumer's right to correct information is treated as a basic right in the law of consumer protection. The seller's duty to give correct information continues for as long as the advertisement is in use, and the later discovery of the falsity places a duty on him to withdraw or correct the advertisement.

Facts: A company advertises its juice drink on television as '100% pure fruit juice, no added sugar'. Tests show that the drink contains only 40% fruit juice and a large amount of added sugar. A consumer organisation complains. The company says that it honestly believed that the advertisement was fair. Decide.

options.A: The advertisement is not misleading, because the company honestly believed it was fair
options.B: The advertisement is not misleading, because every advertisement exaggerates
options.C: The advertisement is misleading only if some consumer proves that he lost money
options.D: The advertisement is misleading and an unfair trade practice, whatever the company's belief, because its checkable claims are false

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The claims of 100% juice and no added sugar can be checked and are false. The test is likely effect on consumers, so the company's good faith is no defence. Shortcut: checkable claims must be true; good faith is no defence. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. Good faith is not a defence; the effect on consumers decides. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Puffery is excused, but checkable claims such as purity must be true. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. Likelihood to mislead is sufficient; actual deception need not be proved.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A consumer who hires or avails of a service for consideration may complain of deficiency in service. Deficiency means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature or manner of performance which is required to be maintained by law or which has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract. Where there is a deficiency, the service provider may be directed to remove the deficiency, to refund the charges and to pay compensation for the loss and injury suffered. A service is not deficient merely because the consumer is dissatisfied with the result, if the provider has performed what he promised with the skill and care reasonably expected of him. For example, a repairer who has used reasonable skill is not liable if a part fails later for reasons that no repair could prevent. The consumer must show a shortfall measured against what the provider promised or what the law requires. A person who gets a service free of charge, and not under any contract for consideration, is not a consumer for this purpose. A promised standard, such as delivery within a set number of days, becomes part of the service which has to be provided, and a failure to meet it may be a deficiency. The provider cannot escape by pointing out that the delay did not cause financial loss, if the promised standard was not met. The remedy that the consumer obtains is intended to put him in the position in which he would have been if the service had been properly done. Therefore a refund of the charges and compensation for the actual loss and inconvenience may be ordered. The provider's own claim that the delay was caused by internal difficulties does not by itself excuse him, unless the delay came from an event which neither party could control and which the provider could not have avoided. The promise and the payment are the starting point of the inquiry, and the consumer is not obliged to prove that the provider acted with bad intention. Where the consumer has paid in advance, the refund of the fee is the simplest remedy, and further compensation is added if the consumer can show that he suffered real loss, inconvenience or distress beyond the fee.

Facts: A courier company promises, for a fee, to deliver a parcel of important documents within two days. The parcel reaches the addressee after nine days, with no explanation, though the senders suffered no financial loss. The sender complains about deficiency in service. Decide.

options.A: There is no deficiency, because the sender suffered no financial loss
options.B: There is no deficiency, because the parcel was eventually delivered
options.C: There is a deficiency, because all courier companies are unreliable
options.D: There is a deficiency in service, because the company failed to meet the promised delivery standard for which a fee was paid

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The company promised delivery in two days for payment and took nine days without explanation. This falls short of the promised standard, which is a deficiency. Shortcut: compare performance with the promised standard. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. The failure to meet a promised standard is a deficiency even without financial loss. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Delivery in the end does not cure the failure to meet the promised time. Trap (C): General morality. The finding rests on the company's own promise and its breach, not on general opinion.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person who sells his goods or services in such a way as to lead customers to believe that they are the goods or services of another person commits the wrong of passing off. The person wronged may obtain an injunction and damages. In order to succeed, the claimant must show three things: that his goods or services have acquired a goodwill or reputation in the market, that the defendant has made a misrepresentation, intentional or not, which is likely to lead the public to believe that the defendant's goods are those of the claimant, and that the claimant has suffered or is likely to suffer damage because of it. The action protects the reputation attached to a name, mark, shape or get-up of goods, and it does not depend on whether the claimant has registered a trade mark. It is not necessary for the claimant to show that any customer has actually been deceived, since the likelihood of confusion is enough. The test is whether an ordinary customer with imperfect memory would be confused. The use of a similar name in a quite different field, in which no confusion is likely, will not usually amount to passing off. A defendant is also free to describe his goods truthfully, for example by saying that his product is a compatible refill for the claimant's product, provided he does not mislead people into thinking that it comes from the claimant. The remedy of an injunction is meant to prevent the continuing damage to the reputation which the claimant has built up over the years, while the damages compensate for the loss already suffered. In deciding whether there is likely to be confusion, the court looks at all the features together, such as the name, the colours, the shape of the packing and the way the goods are sold, and considers how an ordinary customer would see them in a shop. Small differences which a careful buyer would notice do not prevent an action if a hurried customer would be misled. The remedy is available to any trader whose reputation is used by another, and the size of the claimant's business is not important as long as the goodwill exists and the confusion among customers is likely.

Facts: Tara Sweets, a well-known shop in a city, has for forty years sold its sweets in a distinctive red box with a particular logo. It has never registered the logo as a trade mark. A new shop nearby, Tara Sweet House, starts selling cheaper sweets in an almost identical red box with a nearly identical logo, and customers begin to buy them believing that they come from Tara Sweets. Decide.

options.A: Tara Sweets can succeed in an action for passing off, even though the logo is unregistered
options.B: Tara Sweets cannot succeed, because the logo was never registered as a trade mark
options.C: Tara Sweets cannot succeed, because the new shop sells at lower prices which benefit customers
options.D: Tara Sweets can succeed only if it proves that the new shop meant to deceive customers

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Tara Sweets has goodwill, the new shop's get-up misrepresents origin and customers are in fact confused, causing damage. Registration is not needed. Shortcut: goodwill + misrepresentation + damage. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. Passing off protects goodwill whether or not the mark is registered. Trap (C): General morality. Lower prices do not excuse misrepresentation. Trap (D): Half-applied principle. Intention is not required; a likelihood of confusion is enough.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A patent may be granted for an invention, which is a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application. A mere discovery of a scientific principle, or the discovery of a naturally occurring substance, or of a new property of a known substance, is not an invention and cannot be patented. The reason is that nature belongs to everyone, and the person who finds what already exists has not created it. To obtain a patent, the applicant must show that he has done something more than find, for example that he has made a new process of extracting the substance, or a new device that applies the principle for a useful purpose. A new use for a known substance is not patentable merely because it is new, unless it results in a new product or process. Likewise, a mathematical method or a scheme for performing a mental act is not patentable. The inventive step must not be obvious to a person skilled in the art, which means a person who has ordinary knowledge of the subject. A patent gives the owner the exclusive right to make, use, sell or import the invention for a limited term, and in return the invention must be fully disclosed to the public. A patent is not given for the idea alone, but for the specific invention described in the application. The law also distinguishes between a discovery and an invention for another reason: monopoly rights should not be given over knowledge that everyone ought to be free to use. If the first person to notice a natural law could control it, other researchers would be held back from making real products using it. The patent system therefore rewards the person who turns knowledge into a new, useful thing, and leaves the knowledge itself free. An application which only describes what already exists in nature, without any human contribution beyond finding it, is refused for this reason. A person who makes a real invention based on a natural principle, for example a new device, can still obtain protection for that device, so the rule does not discourage genuine research and invention.

Facts: A botanist finds a plant growing wild in a forest and discovers that its leaves naturally contain a chemical which lowers blood pressure. She applies for a patent for 'the discovery that the leaves of this plant lower blood pressure'. Decide.

options.A: The patent must be granted, because nobody had known about this property before
options.B: The patent must be granted, because the discovery will benefit many patients
options.C: The patent cannot be granted, because the botanist did not first publish the discovery in a journal
options.D: The patent cannot be granted for the mere discovery of a natural property of a naturally occurring plant

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The leaves' blood-pressure property is a natural discovery. A patent would need a new process or product, such as a new extraction method. Shortcut: find vs make: discovery is not an invention. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. Newness of knowledge does not turn a discovery into an invention. Trap (B): General morality. Public benefit is not the test for patentability. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The principle does not make publication in a journal a condition.

questions.concept_tag: Sale of goods - passing of property in specific goods
questions.question_text:
Passage: In a contract for the sale of specific goods, which are goods identified and agreed upon at the time of the contract, the property in the goods passes to the buyer at the time when the parties intend it to pass. The intention is to be found from the terms of the contract, the conduct of the parties and the circumstances of the case. Unless a different intention appears, the property in specific goods in a deliverable state passes to the buyer when the contract is made, even if the payment of the price or the delivery of the goods is postponed. If the seller is bound to do something to the goods to put them into a deliverable state, the property does not pass until that thing is done and the buyer has notice of it. The risk usually goes with the property, which means that the person who owns the goods bears the loss if they are destroyed without the fault of anyone. If the property has not passed to the buyer, the loss falls on the seller. The delivery of goods and the passing of property are separate matters, and the property may pass before the goods are handed over. The parties may also agree that the property will pass only on payment, in which case the property stays with the seller until payment is made, regardless of delivery. The rule on the passing of property is important because several other results follow from it. The right to sue a third party for damage to the goods, the right to resell them and the duty to bear their loss all depend on who owns them at the time. Where the parties have said nothing, the law supplies the rule which it thinks the parties would most probably have wished. The court will not presume a contrary intention without some proof, such as a term that ownership will remain with the seller till payment, or a condition that the goods have to be tested before the sale is complete. The court looks at the actual terms agreed and not at labels, so that a clause which says that 'ownership will pass later' has effect only if it is part of the contract made by the parties and shows their intention.

Facts: On 1 May, Uday agrees to buy a particular antique clock from Vivek for ₹30,000, to be paid and taken away on 10 May. The clock is in perfect condition and the agreement says nothing about when ownership passes. On 5 May, lightning destroys Vivek's shop and the clock, with no fault of either party. Who bears the loss?

options.A: Vivek, because the clock had not yet been delivered or paid for
options.B: Vivek, because sellers should always insure their goods against loss
options.C: Uday, because the property in the specific clock in a deliverable state passed to him when the contract was made
options.D: Both equally, because the loss was due to lightning, which was nobody's fault

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The clock is specific goods in a deliverable state and no other intention appears, so the property passed on 1 May. Risk goes with property, so Uday bears the loss. Shortcut: specific + deliverable + no contrary intention = property passes at contract. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. Property passes on the contract, and delivery or payment can be postponed. Trap (B): General morality. The rule is about passing of property, not about prudence. Trap (D): Half-applied principle. Risk goes with property; here it had passed to Uday.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Every partner is liable, jointly with all the other partners and also severally, for all acts of the firm done while he is a partner. This means that a creditor of the firm may recover the whole of a debt from the firm's property, and if that is not enough, from the personal property of any one partner or of all the partners. A partner who pays more than his proper share has a right to claim a contribution from the other partners. The liability continues for the acts done during the period of partnership, even after the partner leaves the firm, unless the creditor agrees to release him. An act of a partner binds the firm when it is done in the usual course of the firm's business and in the firm's name. The rule recognises that each partner acts as the agent of the others in carrying on the firm's business. An act that has nothing to do with the firm's business, or one that was done by a partner for his private purposes, does not bind the firm. A partner may protect himself against liability for acts he does not agree with by giving public notice and by agreement between the partners. But such an agreement between the partners cannot reduce their liability towards an outsider who does not know about it. The reason for this strict rule is that outsiders who deal with the firm cannot see the private arrangements between the partners, and they give credit to the firm trusting the personal liability of all its members. The liability of a partner to the creditors is therefore not a matter of how profits and losses are shared between the partners. The share of each in profit and loss is a matter between the partners, and it is settled afterwards by a claim for contribution. A creditor may choose to sue the firm and all the partners together, or any one of them, and the court allows him to recover the whole amount that is due. A partner who retires continues to be liable for debts incurred while he was a partner, unless the creditors agree to discharge him, and a retired partner who wishes to limit his liability should give notice to the public.

Facts: Nitin, Omkar and Piyush are partners in a firm of building contractors. The firm buys cement worth ₹3 lakh from Qadir for its work, and the firm's assets are only ₹1 lakh. Qadir is unpaid. Omkar and Piyush are insolvent. Whom can Qadir sue for the remaining sum?

options.A: No one, because the debt is that of the firm alone and not of its partners
options.B: Only Omkar and Piyush, because Nitin joined as a partner later on
options.C: Nitin only for one third, because the partners share the debt equally
options.D: Nitin, from his personal property, since each partner is liable jointly and severally for the debts of the firm

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Each partner is liable jointly and severally, so Qadir can recover the unpaid amount from Nitin's personal property. Nitin may then claim contribution from the others. Shortcut: creditor may recover the whole amount from any one partner. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. Partners are personally liable for the firm's acts. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Nothing in the facts removes Nitin's liability. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. Each partner is liable for the whole debt, and may seek contribution afterwards.

questions.concept_tag: Negotiable instruments - dishonour of cheque and notice
questions.question_text:
Passage: When a cheque given by a person to discharge a debt or liability is returned by the bank unpaid because of insufficient funds or because it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account, the drawer is deemed to have committed an offence, provided certain conditions are fulfilled. The cheque must have been presented to the bank within its period of validity. The payee must give a written notice to the drawer, demanding payment of the amount of the cheque, within thirty days of receiving information from the bank that the cheque was returned unpaid. The drawer must then fail to pay the amount within fifteen days of the receipt of that notice. Only when these steps are complete may a complaint be filed, and the complaint must be made within one month from the date on which the cause of action arises. The law protects the drawer by giving him a fair chance to pay after notice, and it protects the payee by giving him a remedy where there is a deliberate or careless issue of an unfunded cheque. The offence relates to a legally enforceable debt or liability, and a cheque issued as a gift or for a debt that cannot legally be enforced does not attract the penalty. A payee who files a complaint without sending the notice does not satisfy the conditions. The three time limits in the provision are strictly counted, and a complaint filed before the time for payment after the notice has expired is premature. The courts have explained that the object is not to put people in prison but to promote the trust which is needed in the use of cheques as a method of payment. For this reason the drawer must be given a fair chance to make good the payment before he is prosecuted. The notice has to be in writing and has to demand the payment of the specific amount of the cheque, and a notice that does not do so is not a sufficient notice under the provision. Both the payee and the drawer are expected to act promptly within the time limits, and the law does not allow a complaint to be revived at a later date merely because the drawer has not paid on his own accord.

Facts: Ramesh gives Seema a cheque for ₹80,000 for goods he bought from her. The cheque is returned by the bank for insufficient funds, and Seema, without sending any notice to Ramesh, files a criminal complaint against him the next day. Decide.

options.A: The complaint succeeds, because the cheque was returned for lack of funds and that is the offence
options.B: The complaint succeeds, because Ramesh behaved dishonestly towards a creditor
options.C: The complaint cannot succeed, because Seema did not give the written notice and wait for the drawer's fifteen days to pass
options.D: The complaint fails, because a cheque is not a legally enforceable debt

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The offence is complete only after notice and non-payment within fifteen days. Seema skipped the notice, so the conditions are not met. Shortcut: dishonour, then notice, then 15 days, then complaint. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. The offence needs the notice and the failure to pay within fifteen days. Trap (B): General morality. Dishonesty alone does not complete the offence. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The debt here was for goods bought and is enforceable.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A gift is the transfer of property made voluntarily and without consideration by one person, the donor, to another, the donee, and accepted by or on behalf of the donee. Acceptance is essential, and it must be made during the lifetime of the donor and while he is still capable of giving. If the donee dies before accepting the gift, the gift is void. A gift of immovable property must be made by a registered instrument signed by the donor and attested by at least two witnesses. A gift of movable property may be made by a registered instrument or by delivery. The donee may accept the gift by words or by conduct, and acceptance of a beneficial gift may sometimes be presumed where the gift is wholly to the donee's advantage and he has no reason to refuse it, but a donee is never forced to accept. A gift made to a person who has not yet accepted may be withdrawn by the donor before acceptance. A gift is also different from a promise to give in the future, which is not a transfer of property, and it cannot be enforced without consideration. A donor cannot take back a completed gift merely because he has changed his mind or because he finds the donee ungrateful, unless the gift was made on a condition which has failed. The law gives particular importance to acceptance because a person cannot be made the owner of property against his will, and because ownership brings duties as well as benefits, such as taxes and the cost of maintenance. A gift is also different from a sale, since there is no payment, and from a trust, where the property is held for the benefit of another. The donor must have capacity to give, and his consent must be free. It follows that a document of gift which is signed and registered, but has not been accepted by the donee, remains incomplete until the acceptance is given, and the donor retains the power to cancel it. The donee may of course refuse to accept a gift, and in that case the property remains with the donor, who is free to deal with it as he wishes, since a person is never obliged to receive a benefit he does not want.

Facts: Tarun signs a registered deed, witnessed by two persons, giving his house to his friend Usha. Before Usha learns of the deed or accepts it, Tarun changes his mind and tears up the deed and tells Usha that there will be no gift. Usha says that the gift was complete. Decide.

options.A: There is no completed gift, because Usha had not accepted it and the donor could withdraw it before acceptance
options.B: The gift is complete, because the deed was registered and witnessed
options.C: The gift is complete, because a promise of a gift binds the donor
options.D: There is no gift, because a gift can only be made to a relative

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A gift needs acceptance by the donee. Until Usha accepted, Tarun could withdraw, so the gift was incomplete. Shortcut: no acceptance, no gift; withdrawal possible before it. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Formalities are needed, but acceptance is also essential. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. A promise to give is not a transfer and cannot be enforced without consideration. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle does not limit gifts to relatives.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Under the polluter pays principle, the person who causes environmental harm is responsible for paying the cost of removing the harm and of restoring the environment, and for compensating those who are injured by it. The principle applies even where the polluter took care and was not careless, because the activity itself is the source of the danger, and those who carry on a hazardous activity for profit should bear its costs instead of passing them to the public. The liability is absolute where the activity is hazardous or inherently dangerous. The amount payable is fixed by looking at the extent of the harm, the cost of repair and the capacity of the polluter to pay. The principle is meant both to compensate and to deter. The polluter may be required to pay, even if a licence has been given for his activity, since a licence does not remove the duty to repair damage caused. It is no defence for the polluter to say that other persons also pollute in the area, if his own activity contributed to the harm. Where the harm is caused by several polluters, each may be made responsible in proportion to his contribution, or the authority may recover from any of them the cost of repair. The principle does not require proof that the polluter intended harm. Courts in applying the principle consider several factors: the nature and scale of the activity, the seriousness of the harm to people and nature, the length of time for which the environment will be affected and the cost of restoring it. The money recovered is used for the restoration of the environment and for compensating the victims. The principle also supports the idea of sustainable development, in which economic activity is allowed on the condition that its costs to nature are met by those who profit from the activity. Where a polluter fails to pay, the authority may take steps to recover the amount from his property. The authority that fixes the amount must also consider the ability of the polluter to pay and the harm to the victims, so that the sum is neither so small that it encourages carelessness nor so large that it ends all lawful business.

Facts: A chemical factory, which holds a valid government licence and uses all the safety measures prescribed, accidentally releases toxic waste into a river, killing the fish on which a fishing village depends. The factory says that it was not careless and that it holds a licence. Decide whether the factory must pay for the harm.

options.A: The factory need not pay, because it took all prescribed safety measures
options.B: The factory must pay for the harm and for restoring the river, because it carried on a hazardous activity and care or licence is no defence
options.C: The factory need not pay, because it had a valid licence for its activity
options.D: The factory must pay, because factories are generally harmful to society

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The polluter pays principle applies even without carelessness for a hazardous activity, and a licence is no defence. The factory must compensate and restore. Shortcut: hazardous activity: liability regardless of care or licence. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. Liability does not depend on carelessness for hazardous activities. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. A licence does not remove the duty to repair. Trap (D): General morality. Liability arises from the harm caused by the hazardous activity, not general opinion.

questions.question_text:
Passage: The burden of proving a fact lies on the person who asserts it and who wishes the court to give judgment depending on the existence of that fact. When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, the burden of proof lies on him. If a person claims that he is entitled to a right which depends on certain facts, he must prove those facts. The burden does not shift merely because the other side denies the claim, and a bare denial need not be supported by evidence. The burden of proof may shift during a case: when the claimant has produced enough evidence to support his claim, the other side must then produce evidence to meet it. In a criminal case, the burden of proving the guilt of the accused lies on the prosecution, and the accused is presumed innocent until proved guilty. The prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. There are a few special situations in which the law places the burden on the accused, for example where he claims that his act falls within a specific exception to an offence, and he then has to bring his case within the exception. But in the ordinary course, the court cannot convict simply because the accused fails to prove his own innocence. A fact which is specially within the knowledge of a person must be proved by that person. The courts apply the rule firmly because the machinery of justice would otherwise become unworkable if a person could win a case merely by making an assertion and waiting for the other side to disprove it. A party must always be ready to produce the evidence which supports his own case, and he cannot expect to win by pointing to weaknesses in the story of his opponent. If the evidence on both sides is equally balanced, or if there is no evidence on a fact, the party on whom the burden lay on that fact loses on that point, since a court cannot decide a case on a mere suspicion. The same approach applies in civil and in criminal courts, but the standard of proof is different: a civil claimant must prove his case on a balance of probabilities, and the prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.

Facts: Wasim claims that Yusuf borrowed ₹10,000 from him last year and has not repaid it. Yusuf simply denies that he ever borrowed anything. Wasim produces no document, witness or other evidence of the loan. Decide the case.

options.A: Wasim's claim succeeds, because Yusuf gave no proof that he did not borrow
options.B: Wasim's claim fails, because he asserts the loan and has the burden of proving it, which he has not done
options.C: Wasim's claim succeeds, because a man should repay what he has borrowed
options.D: Wasim's claim fails, because loans of this size must be made in writing

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The burden of proof lies on the person who asserts a fact. Wasim has no evidence of the loan, so his claim fails, and Yusuf's bare denial is enough. Shortcut: whoever asserts must prove. Trap (A): Reversal of principle. A bare denial needs no proof; the burden lies on the person asserting. Trap (C): General morality. Morality does not supply proof of the loan. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle states nothing about a written form.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - fraud and the duty to disclose
questions.question_text:
Passage: A contract is voidable at the option of the party whose consent was obtained by fraud. Fraud means that a party, or someone acting for him, with intent to deceive the other or to induce him to enter into the contract, does one of several things. He may suggest as a fact something which is not true and which he does not believe to be true, or he may actively conceal a fact of which he has knowledge, or he may make a promise without any intention of performing it, or do any other act fitted to deceive. The party who has been deceived may either rescind the contract or insist on its performance and ask to be put in the position he would have been in if the statement had been true. As a general rule, mere silence about facts likely to affect the willingness of a person to enter into a contract is not fraud. A seller of goods, for instance, is not bound to point out the faults in the goods, and each party is expected to look after his own interests and to make his own enquiries. This is sometimes expressed as the rule that the buyer must beware. There are, however, two exceptions. First, where the circumstances of the case are such that, regard being had to them, it is the duty of the person keeping silence to speak, silence is fraud. Second, silence is fraud where it is, in itself, equivalent to speech, as when a person's conduct or half-statement would make others believe something false unless he spoke further. The party who alleges fraud has to prove it. A mere opinion, a sales talk praising goods in general terms, or a statement of what the person honestly believes, does not amount to fraud, even if it turns out to be wrong. Nor will the contract be set aside if the party who says he was deceived had ordinary means of discovering the truth and did not use them, unless the other party took active steps to prevent the discovery. The right to rescind is lost if the deceived party, after learning the truth, affirms the contract.

Facts: Bhim, who is selling his house to Charu, knows that the house has serious termite damage in its main beams, which cannot be seen. Charu asks only whether the price is fair, and Bhim says 'it is a fair price' and says nothing about the termites. Charu, who has not asked any question about the condition of the beams and who had not had any inspection done, learns of the termites after the sale and wants to cancel it for fraud. Decide.

options.A: Charu cannot rescind for fraud, because mere silence about a fault, without a duty to speak or a misleading half-statement, is not fraud
options.B: Charu can rescind, because Bhim knew of a serious defect and did not disclose it
options.C: Charu can rescind, because a house sale is a matter on which all faults must be disclosed
options.D: Charu cannot rescind, because Bhim told the truth when he said the price was fair

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Silence is not fraud as a general rule. Neither exception applies: Charu asked nothing about the beams, Bhim's remark on price was not a half-statement about the condition, and he took no active step to hide the damage. Shortcut: silence is fraud only if there is a duty to speak or it equals speech. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. Mere silence is not fraud unless an exception applies. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The principle contains no general duty of full disclosure for sale of property. Trap (D): Half-applied principle. Truth of the statement is not the issue; the question is whether silence amounted to a fraud under the exceptions.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - innocent misrepresentation and means of knowledge
questions.question_text:
Passage: A representation which is made innocently, that is, without any intention to deceive and in the honest belief that it is true, may still give the other party a right to avoid the contract if it is false and material. This is called misrepresentation. A positive assertion, in a manner not warranted by the information of the person making it, of that which is not true, though he believes it to be true, is misrepresentation. So is any breach of duty which, without an intent to deceive, gains an advantage for the person committing it by misleading another to his prejudice. The result of misrepresentation is that the contract is voidable, so that the party misled may rescind the contract, though he has no claim to damages as he would in the case of fraud. The party misled must have been led by the statement into making the contract, and the statement must relate to a fact and not merely to an opinion. There is an important limit on the right. If consent was caused by misrepresentation, the contract is voidable, but if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, the contract is not voidable. The idea behind this limit is that the law helps those who are misled, and not those who are careless in failing to use the means of knowledge placed before them. For example, where the seller has shown the buyer the documents of title and the true position appears on the face of them, the buyer cannot later say that he was misled by the seller's contrary statement. But this limit does not apply where the party who made the statement did something to prevent the other from finding out. The right to rescind must be exercised within a reasonable time, and it is lost where third parties have acquired rights in good faith in the meantime. It should be added that the choice between rescinding and affirming belongs to the misled party, and that the law is slower to grant relief when the contract has already been carried out to a considerable extent and the parties cannot be restored to their former positions.

Facts: Dilip sells Esha a plot of land, honestly telling her that it measures 800 square metres. The sale documents, which are handed to Esha and are in plain figures, show 600 square metres, and a quick look at them would have shown the true area. Esha signs without reading them, finds out later, and wants to rescind the sale for misrepresentation. Decide.

options.A: Esha can rescind, because Dilip's statement was false and she relied on it
options.B: Esha can rescind, because Dilip ought to have checked the area before speaking
options.C: Esha cannot rescind, because the true area was available to her with ordinary diligence in the documents handed to her
options.D: Esha cannot rescind, because Dilip honestly believed his statement and so made no misrepresentation

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Dilip's statement was a misrepresentation even though honest. But the documents showed the true area and Esha could have discovered it with ordinary care, and Dilip did nothing to prevent that, so the contract is not voidable. Shortcut: means of discovery with ordinary diligence defeats the claim. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The right is lost where the party had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. The principle does not penalise carelessness of the maker where the other party had the means of knowledge. Trap (D): Half-applied principle. An innocent statement can still be a misrepresentation; the bar here is the means of knowledge.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - discharge of a surety by variation of terms
questions.question_text:
Passage: A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. The person who gives the guarantee is called the surety, the person in respect of whose default the guarantee is given is the principal debtor, and the person to whom the guarantee is given is the creditor. The liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless the contract provides otherwise. This means that the creditor may sue the surety for the whole debt as soon as the principal debtor defaults, without first suing the debtor. A guarantee is, however, a contract of a special kind. The surety agrees to bear a particular risk, and he does so on the basis of the terms which the creditor and the principal debtor have fixed between themselves. Any variance made without the surety's consent in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance. A surety is also discharged by the creditor's act or omission that impairs the surety's eventual remedy against the principal debtor, and by the release of the principal debtor by the creditor. The rule does not give protection where the variation is trivial and plainly benefits the surety, or where the surety has consented to it in advance, whether expressly or by his conduct. Nor does it extend to variations which are immaterial and would not make any difference to the risk that the surety has agreed to bear. The reason for the rule is that the surety is allowed to say that he did not agree to bear the risk under a different contract. A surety who has paid the creditor takes the place of the creditor and may recover from the principal debtor. The courts also say that the surety stands in a special position because he usually receives no benefit from the transaction and acts out of friendship or business connection. For this reason the terms of the guarantee are read strictly in his favour, and the creditor must take care to keep him informed of any change that could increase the burden he has accepted. The creditor is not, however, required to tell the surety about every small administrative step in the dealings with the debtor, as long as the substance of the arrangement remains the same.

Facts: Faisal guarantees the repayment of a loan of ₹2 lakh that Gagan takes from Hari Bank, to be repaid in 24 monthly instalments. Without telling Faisal, the bank and Gagan agree to a new scheme that doubles the interest rate and extends the term to 48 months. Gagan then defaults on the new scheme, and the bank sues Faisal. Faisal had not agreed to the change. Decide.

options.A: Faisal is liable, because the liability of a surety is co-extensive with the principal debtor's
options.B: Faisal is liable, because he benefited from the longer period for repayment
options.C: Faisal is discharged, because banks must not lend to people who cannot repay
options.D: Faisal is discharged from liability for transactions after the variation, because the terms were materially changed without his consent

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A material variation without the surety's consent discharges him as to later transactions. Doubling the rate and doubling the term changes the risk he took, and no exception applies. Shortcut: variation without consent discharges the surety. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Co-extensive liability applies to the contract as guaranteed, not to a materially changed one. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. The principle gives no such basis; the variation increased the risk and he did not consent. Trap (C): General morality. The discharge flows from variation without consent, not from any duty of banks in lending.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A pledge is the bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise. The person who delivers the goods is the pawnor, and the person to whom they are delivered is the pawnee. The pawnee may retain the goods pledged, not only for the payment of the debt or the performance of the promise, but for the interest on the debt and all necessary expenses incurred by him in respect of the possession or for the preservation of the goods. He may not retain them for any other debt or promise, unless there is a contract to that effect. If the pawnor makes default in payment of the debt, or in performance, at the stipulated time, the pawnee may bring a suit against the pawnor upon the debt or promise and retain the goods as collateral security, or he may sell the thing pledged on giving the pawnor reasonable notice of the sale. If the proceeds of such sale are less than the amount due, the pawnor is still liable for the balance, and if the proceeds are greater, the pawnee must pay over the surplus to the pawnor. The right of sale is not exercisable at once: the notice must give the pawnor a fair opportunity to redeem the goods by paying the sum due. The pawnor may redeem the goods at any time before the actual sale by tendering the debt with interest and any additional expenses incurred by the pawnee on account of the default. The pawnee must take as much care of the goods as a man of ordinary prudence would take of his own goods of the same bulk, quality and value. If he uses the goods in a way that was not permitted, he is liable for any loss caused to them. It follows that the pawnor remains the owner of the goods during the pledge, and the pawnee has only a special property in them, which is the right to hold them as security. The pawnee cannot treat them as his own, cannot keep the surplus of a sale and cannot refuse to hand them back when the debt is paid in full. If the pawnee sells wrongly, without proper notice or before the due date, the pawnor may claim damages for the loss caused by the improper sale, and the sale may be challenged by the pawnor as not being made in accordance with the rules governing the pledge.

Facts: Ila borrows ₹30,000 from Jai against the security of her gold necklace, which she hands to him. On the due date Ila fails to pay. Without giving any notice to Ila, Jai at once sells the necklace for ₹28,000, and tells her afterwards that she still owes ₹2,000 and interest. Ila objects. Decide.

options.A: Jai's sale is proper, because Ila had defaulted on the stipulated date
options.B: Jai's sale is proper, because the proceeds were lower than the debt and he acted to reduce his loss
options.C: Jai's sale without reasonable notice is improper, because the pawnee must give the pawnor a fair chance to redeem before selling
options.D: Jai had no right to sell at all, because a pawnee can only sue on the debt

questions.pedagogical_explanation: On default, the pawnee may sue or sell, but a sale needs reasonable notice so that the pawnor can redeem. Jai gave none. Shortcut: default allows sale only after reasonable notice. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Default only allows sale after reasonable notice is given. Trap (B): General morality. The motive of Jai does not remove the need for notice. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The principle gives the pawnee a right to sell on notice.

questions.concept_tag: Tort - trespass to land and removal of trespassers
questions.question_text:
Passage: Every unauthorised entry on the land of another is trespass, and it is actionable without proof of damage. The occupier of land is entitled to remove a trespasser from it, and for that purpose he may use such force as is reasonable in the circumstances. The force must be proportionate to the resistance offered and the danger presented, and it must be used only after the trespasser has been asked to leave and has refused or has failed to go within a reasonable time. A request to leave is not necessary where the trespasser has entered with violence or where a request would be useless or dangerous. An occupier may not use force which is likely to cause serious injury merely to protect his property, and he may not set traps or devices intended to injure trespassers where the harm is out of proportion to the interest protected. A person who enters land by permission may become a trespasser when he stays after the permission has ended, or does something not covered by the permission, but he must be allowed a reasonable time to leave. A person who goes on to another's land to retake his own goods which have been placed there wrongfully may enter peacefully, but he may not break into a house or use force. The remedy of the occupier, if he does not wish to use force, is to bring an action for damages or an injunction. Entry is not trespass where the law gives a right of entry, as where an officer executes a lawful warrant or the entrant has a right of way. The same ideas apply to the occupier of a house or a shop. The occupier is entitled to protect his possession, but the law of tort is concerned that the protection should not become a source of greater harm than the harm it prevents. For this reason, the question for the court is always whether the force used was in proportion to the situation as it appeared at the time. A person who is faced with a violent intruder may use more force than one who faces a quiet and unarmed trespasser, and the court considers what a reasonable occupier would have done in the same position, without applying the standard of perfect calm after the event.

Facts: Jatin, an occupier of a farm, finds Kabir sitting under a mango tree on the farm without permission. Without asking Kabir to leave, Jatin at once strikes him with a heavy club and drags him to the gate, breaking his arm. Kabir had made no threat and had not resisted. Kabir sues Jatin. Decide.

options.A: Jatin is not liable, because Kabir was a trespasser and an occupier may do what he likes to remove him
options.B: Jatin is not liable, because Kabir's trespass caused damage to the farm
options.C: Jatin is liable, because he used excessive force and did not first ask Kabir to leave
options.D: Jatin is liable, because trespass on a farm is not a wrong when it is made without any bad intention

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Kabir was a trespasser, but removal must be by reasonable force after a request to leave. A heavy club against a non-resisting man without any request is excessive. Shortcut: reasonable force, and ask first. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The occupier may use only reasonable force after a request to leave. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. Trespass is actionable without damage, and damage does not allow excessive force. Trap (D): Half-applied principle. Kabir's entry was a trespass; Jatin's liability arises from his excessive force.

questions.concept_tag: Tort - professional negligence and the standard of the skilled person
questions.question_text:
Passage: A professional person, such as a doctor or an advocate, who undertakes work holds himself out as possessing a certain level of skill, and he owes a duty to exercise that skill with reasonable care. The standard is not that of the most highly skilled member of the profession, nor that of an ordinary person, but that of an ordinary skilled person exercising and professing to have that special skill. A professional is not negligent if he acts in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of persons skilled in that profession, even though there is a body of opinion that would take a different view. It is not enough for the patient or client to show that another professional would have done differently, or that the outcome was bad. A failure to attain the best result is not in itself negligence. There is an exception: where the accepted practice is plainly illogical or ignores an obvious risk which any competent professional would see, the court may find negligence in spite of the practice. In judging the matter, the court looks at what was known at the time of the act and not at the knowledge obtained later. A professional who undertakes a task beyond his competence without referring the matter to an expert may also be found negligent. A professional is also bound to tell the client about material risks of a proposed course of treatment or action, so that the client can decide for himself, but need not describe every remote possibility. Ordinary unavoidable risks of a properly carried out procedure do not make the professional liable if they materialise. The law takes this view because medicine and similar professions involve judgment in conditions of uncertainty, and a rule that allowed a court to prefer one opinion over another would lead professionals to practise defensively, carrying out needless tests and avoiding useful but risky treatments. At the same time, the law does not let the profession set its own standards without limit, and the court retains the power to reject a practice that cannot be defended on a reasoned basis. The claimant must prove both the standard and the departure from it, usually with the help of expert evidence from a person of the same speciality as the defendant.

Facts: Dr Leela treats a patient for a fracture using a method that is accepted as proper by a responsible group of orthopaedic surgeons, though some other surgeons prefer a different method. She carries it out carefully, but the bone heals badly, which is a known and small risk of that method that she had explained to the patient. The patient sues, relying on the evidence of a surgeon who says he would have used the other method. Decide.

options.A: Dr Leela is not negligent, because she followed a practice accepted by a responsible body of surgeons and carried it out with care
options.B: Dr Leela is negligent, because another skilled surgeon would have used a different method
options.C: Dr Leela is negligent, because the treatment gave a bad result
options.D: Dr Leela is not negligent only because the patient was told about the risk, whatever method she used

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The accepted-practice standard protects a professional who follows a practice approved by a responsible body, even if others differ. The exception for illogical practices does not apply, and the risk was disclosed. Shortcut: accepted body of professional opinion is the standard. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. A different opinion in the profession does not make an accepted practice negligent. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. A bad outcome is not negligence by itself. Trap (D): Half-applied principle. Disclosure of risk is only part of the duty; the method must also meet the accepted standard.

questions.concept_tag: Tort - liability of a manufacturer to the ultimate consumer
questions.question_text:
Passage: A manufacturer of goods who sells them in a form in which they are intended to reach the consumer without a reasonable chance of intermediate examination owes a duty to the consumer to take reasonable care that the goods are free from defect likely to cause injury to health. The duty is not based on any contract between the manufacturer and the consumer, and it is owed to those whom the manufacturer ought reasonably to have in mind as likely to be affected by his carelessness. The consumer must show that the product was defective, that the defect existed when it left the manufacturer's control, that the manufacturer failed to take reasonable care and that this caused the injury. A manufacturer is not liable where there was a reasonable chance of intermediate examination, because in such a case the person who failed to examine, and not the manufacturer, is the cause of the harm. The manufacturer is also not liable where the injury results from the consumer's own misuse of the product contrary to clear instructions or warnings, or from some interference with the product after it left the factory. The duty extends to foreseeable users, and does not depend on whether the goods were bought by the injured person himself; a member of the buyer's family who is injured has the same right. A manufacturer who has given adequate warnings of a danger that cannot be removed has taken reasonable care in that respect. The question is always whether the harm is the result of the manufacturer's want of care in preparing, packaging or labelling the product. The reason for the rule lies in the position of the ordinary consumer, who cannot inspect the inside of a sealed or packaged article and must rely entirely on the care of the maker. The law therefore attaches responsibility to the person who is in control of the process of manufacture and who profits from the sale, and it does not require the injured person to be in any contractual relationship with that maker. The injured person must, however, prove the connection between the defect and the injury, and must show that the product had not been tampered with by some intermediate person after leaving the factory.

Facts: Manoj buys a sealed bottle of soft drink from a shop and gives it to his friend Naina. The manufacturer had negligently allowed a piece of glass to enter the bottle at the factory. Naina swallows it and is seriously hurt. The bottle had been sealed throughout and neither Manoj nor the shop had any chance to see inside. Naina sues the manufacturer. Decide.

options.A: The manufacturer is not liable, because Naina did not buy the bottle and had no contract with it
options.B: The manufacturer is not liable, because the shopkeeper sold the bottle and should have examined it
options.C: The manufacturer is liable, because large companies should compensate people hurt by their products
options.D: The manufacturer is liable to Naina, because it owed a duty of care to the ultimate consumer and there was no chance of intermediate examination

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The bottle was sealed, so there was no intermediate examination. The manufacturer's lack of care put glass in it, and the duty extends to the ultimate consumer irrespective of contract. Shortcut: duty runs to the ultimate consumer when there is no intermediate examination. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The duty is not based on contract and extends to the foreseeable consumer. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. A sealed bottle gave no reasonable chance of intermediate examination. Trap (C): General morality. Liability depends on the failure of reasonable care and causation, not on size.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - house-trespass and criminal intent
questions.question_text:
Passage: Whoever enters into or upon property in the possession of another with intent to commit an offence, or to intimidate, insult or annoy any person in possession of such property, commits criminal trespass. Whoever enters into any building used as a human dwelling, or for the custody of property, in that manner commits house-trespass. Two things are essential: an unlawful entry or remaining on the property, and the intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy. Mere entry without permission, with no such intent, is a civil wrong, but it is not a criminal offence. A person who enters honestly believing that he has a right to enter, or who enters on a foolish dare with no intention to harm, lacks the intent which the offence requires. The intention must exist at the time of entering or of unlawfully remaining. Where a person enters lawfully, for example as a guest, but remains after being asked to leave, with intent to annoy the occupier, the offence arises from the unlawful remaining. The intent is to be judged from the surrounding circumstances, including what the person did, what he said and the time of entry. A house-trespass becomes more serious where it is committed after preparation for causing hurt, or at night, because the risk of harm is greater. An entry in the exercise of a legal right, such as an officer's entry under a warrant, is not an offence. The offence of criminal trespass is concerned with the protection of the peace and security of those who are in possession of property, and not with the protection of ownership alone. A tenant in possession can complain of an entry by the owner, if it is made with the necessary intent. The intent to annoy is judged objectively, in the sense that the court asks whether a reasonable person in the position of the occupier would have been annoyed by the conduct, and also subjectively, in the sense that the entrant must have intended to annoy. A person who enters with a lawful purpose, such as to deliver a letter or to ask for directions, does not have that intent, even if the occupier is displeased by the visit. The offence is complete as soon as the entry or the unlawful remaining takes place with the required intent, and it does not matter whether the intended harm is in fact carried out.

Facts: (i) Rohan, curious about the new neighbours, climbs over the wall at noon to look at their garden, with no purpose beyond curiosity, and leaves when he is asked to. (ii) Sanjay climbs over the wall of another house at night, intending to frighten the family who had insulted him. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both commit criminal house-trespass, because each entered another's house without permission
options.B: Neither commits an offence, because no property was taken in either case
options.C: Rohan commits criminal house-trespass and Sanjay does not, because Rohan entered in daylight
