options.D: Sanjay commits criminal house-trespass; Rohan commits only a civil wrong, as he had no intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Criminal trespass needs unlawful entry plus the intent. Sanjay had the intent to intimidate; Rohan had only curiosity and committed a civil trespass. Shortcut: entry alone is civil; entry with intent is criminal. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy is an essential element. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. Taking property is not an element of the offence. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. The principle reverses the roles; Sanjay's entry had the necessary intent.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Whoever dishonestly receives or retains any stolen property, knowing or having reason to believe the same to be stolen property, commits an offence. Stolen property includes property whose possession has been transferred by theft, extortion or robbery. The offence needs three elements: the property must in fact be stolen, the accused must have received or kept it, and he must have done so dishonestly, knowing or having reason to believe that it was stolen. The knowledge need not be certain. If the circumstances would lead a reasonable person to believe that the goods were stolen, such as an unusually low price, secret dealing at an odd time or the seller's refusal to give an account of how he got them, the belief is established. A person who receives property honestly and without any reason to suspect that it was stolen is not guilty, even if it later turns out to have been stolen. However, a person who first receives the goods innocently and then learns that they were stolen and keeps them with a dishonest intention may become guilty from the point of knowledge. The offence is separate from theft: the receiver need not have taken part in the stealing. The punishment is more severe where the receiver habitually deals in stolen property. The true owner may also recover the property from the receiver in a civil claim, whatever the honesty of the receiver. The law relating to receiving stolen property is intended to discourage the market for stolen goods, because thieves can dispose of what they steal only if others are willing to receive it. The receiver is considered nearly as dangerous to society as the thief. Even so, the criminal law does not punish a purchaser who has been careful and honest, since the burden of the offence is the dishonest state of mind. When a person is accused, the court considers the price paid in relation to the value, the manner and time of the sale, the character of the seller and the explanation offered by the accused, and from these it decides whether the accused knew, or had reason to believe, that the property was stolen. The conduct of the person after he learns of the theft is also important in deciding whether the retention is dishonest.

Facts: A thief steals a laptop worth ₹60,000 and sells it to Tanuj for ₹5,000 at midnight in a dark lane, refusing to say how he got it. Another buyer, Uma, buys a similar stolen laptop at a fair price from a registered shop, and is later told by the police that it was stolen. Uma returns it at once. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both commit the offence, because both received stolen property
options.B: Tanuj commits the offence, because the circumstances gave him reason to believe the laptop was stolen; Uma does not
options.C: Neither commits the offence, because neither took part in the theft
options.D: Uma commits the offence, because she paid a price close to the real value and so knew it was a valuable item

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Tanuj bought at a tiny price, at midnight, from a person who refused to explain, which gives reason to believe it stolen. Uma bought honestly from a shop and returned it at once on learning the truth. Shortcut: knowledge or reason to believe makes the receiving dishonest. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Honest receipt without reason to suspect is not an offence. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The receiver need not have taken part in the theft. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The principle looks at knowledge or reason to believe, which Uma lacked.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - causing death by a rash or negligent act
questions.question_text:
Passage: Whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide is liable to punishment. A rash act is one done with the knowledge that harm may result, but without intending it and in the hope that it will not. A negligent act is one done without the care and attention that a reasonable person would have given in the circumstances. The distinction from the more serious offences lies in the state of mind: in culpable homicide the offender intends to cause death or bodily injury likely to cause death, or knows that his act is likely to cause death, while in the present offence there is no such intention or knowledge. Mere negligence in the civil sense, however slight, is not enough in criminal law; the negligence or rashness must be of a high degree, a gross departure from the standard of a reasonable person. The act must be the direct and proximate cause of the death, so that the death must be the immediate result of the rash or negligent act, without the intervention of some other independent cause. Where an expert, such as a doctor, acts with the ordinary skill of his profession, he is not criminally liable merely because the outcome is death. Where the act is done under an honest and reasonable belief that it is safe, and the person has taken the care that a reasonable person would take, no offence arises. The fact that death results does not by itself make the act rash or negligent. The degree of care to be expected depends on the risk created. A person who handles a dangerous machine, a vehicle on a crowded road or a hazardous substance is expected to take greater precautions than a person doing something harmless, because the likelihood of grave harm is greater. The court therefore asks what a prudent person would have done, in the same place and at the same time, and compares this with what the accused actually did. The courts have also held that an act is not rash or negligent merely because a more careful person might have avoided the accident, and that the prosecution must show that the accused went well beyond the ordinary lapses of care which happen in daily life.

Facts: Vikas, a truck driver, drives through a crowded village road at a very high speed, ignoring warnings shouted by villagers, because he is late. He does not intend to hurt anyone, but he hits and kills a child who was crossing the road. Under the principle, what is Vikas's liability?

options.A: He is not liable, because he did not intend to kill anyone
options.B: He is guilty of culpable homicide, because a death was caused by his act
options.C: He is not liable, because ordinary negligence in civil law is not enough to convict a person
options.D: He is liable for causing death by a rash or negligent act, as he drove with a high degree of rashness without intending or knowing that death was likely

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Vikas lacked the intention or knowledge needed for culpable homicide. But driving at high speed through a crowded road against warnings is gross rashness, and the death was its direct result. Shortcut: no intent to kill, but gross rashness equals this offence. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Absence of intention takes the case out of culpable homicide but not out of this offence. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. Culpable homicide requires intention or knowledge that death is likely, which is absent here. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. Ordinary negligence is not enough, but his conduct was a high degree of rashness.

questions.concept_tag: Constitutional law - reasonable restrictions on trade and business
questions.question_text:
Passage: All citizens have the right to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business. This freedom is not absolute, since the State may make laws imposing reasonable restrictions on its exercise in the interests of the general public. The State may also prescribe professional or technical qualifications necessary for practising any profession, and may itself carry on, or may provide for the carrying on by itself or a corporation, any trade, business, industry or service, whether to the exclusion of citizens or otherwise. A restriction is reasonable if it has a real connection with the public interest that it is meant to serve, if it is not out of proportion to that object, and if it does not go beyond what is needed. A restriction that amounts to a complete prohibition of a lawful trade is looked at with great care, and is upheld only where the nature of the trade makes a prohibition necessary, for example where it is harmful to the public. The court examines both the substance of the restriction and the way in which it is applied. A rule which gives an official uncontrolled power to grant or refuse permission, without a standard, is likely to be unreasonable. The right does not protect trades which are in their nature dangerous to the community or are immoral, such as trading in harmful drugs. It also does not protect a person from competition, and does not entitle him to a licence if he lacks the qualifications that the law requires. In examining a restriction, the courts take into account several matters, such as the nature of the right, the underlying purpose of the restriction, the extent and urgency of the evil sought to be remedied, the disproportion of the imposition and the prevailing conditions at the time. The State bears the duty of showing that the restriction is reasonable, while a presumption of validity applies to laws made by the legislature. Where a licensing system is used, there must be clear rules to guide the licensing authority, and a refusal of a licence must be based on those rules. Qualification rules for professions such as medicine, law, pharmacy and engineering are upheld because the public must be protected from unqualified persons.

Facts: A law requires every person who wants to practise as a pharmacist to hold a diploma in pharmacy, which is a qualification connected with safe dispensing of medicines. Sudhir, who has no diploma but has worked for years in a medicine shop, challenges the law as a violation of his right to practise any occupation. Decide.

options.A: The law is valid, because the State may prescribe professional qualifications and this one is reasonably connected with public safety
options.B: The law is invalid, because every citizen has an absolute right to practise any occupation
options.C: The law is invalid, because Sudhir's experience in the shop is as good as a diploma
options.D: The law is valid, because the State may ban any trade it dislikes

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The State may prescribe the professional qualifications necessary for a profession, and a pharmacy diploma has a real connection with public safety. The restriction is reasonable and proportionate. Shortcut: qualifications connected to public interest are permitted. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. The right is subject to reasonable restrictions and to qualifications prescribed by the State. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The principle lets the State prescribe the qualifications; experience does not replace them. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. A restriction must be reasonable and connected with public interest.

questions.concept_tag: Constitutional law - procedure for depriving personal liberty
questions.question_text:
Passage: No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. The courts have held that this procedure must not be arbitrary, unfair or unreasonable. It must be a procedure which is just, fair and reasonable, and which satisfies the requirements of natural justice, including the right of the person affected to be informed of the case against him and to be heard. A law which provides for a deprivation of liberty must also itself be valid. The right to life has been understood broadly. It is not merely the right to animal existence but includes the right to live with human dignity, and it includes the freedom from torture and the right to a speedy trial. The protection is available to every person, whether a citizen or a foreigner, against the State. It does not apply against a private person, although the State must protect the right through its laws. The protection is not unlimited, because a person's liberty may be taken away by a law that lays down a fair procedure, as when a person is convicted of a crime after a proper trial. An executive order which lets an officer imprison a person for an indefinite period, without telling him the grounds and without allowing him to be heard, does not satisfy the requirement of a fair, just and reasonable procedure. A procedure may be fair even though it is a summary one, if it allows the person a real chance to present his case. The requirement of fairness comes from the idea that the power of the State over the individual must be exercised according to rules that can be known in advance and applied equally. A procedure that depends only on the will of an officer is considered arbitrary, because it provides no safeguard for the person affected. The court therefore examines both whether there is a law and whether the law itself is fair. If the law lays down a procedure that denies any chance to be heard, or that gives the officer an unlimited power, the court may declare it invalid. The court may also order release of a person who is held in violation of the procedure, through a petition challenging the detention, and the State must then justify the detention before the court.

Facts: An official regulation allows a local officer to confine any person suspected of being a nuisance for up to a year, on his own opinion, without informing the person of the reason and without any hearing. The officer confines Wilfred, a foreign tourist, under the regulation. Wilfred challenges the confinement. Decide.

options.A: The confinement is invalid, because the procedure is arbitrary and unfair and the protection extends to foreigners
options.B: The confinement is valid, because it is made under an official regulation
options.C: The confinement is valid, because Wilfred is not a citizen and has no right to liberty
options.D: The confinement is invalid, because the State may never take away a person's liberty

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The confinement rests on no hearing, no grounds and unlimited discretion, so the procedure is arbitrary. The right under the principle covers every person, including Wilfred. Shortcut: procedure must be fair, just and reasonable, for everyone. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. A procedure must be just, fair and reasonable, not merely set out in a regulation. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The principle protects every person, citizen or foreigner. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The principle allows deprivation by a fair procedure established by law.

questions.question_text:
Passage: All citizens have the right to assemble peaceably and without arms. This right is subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of the country or public order. The right therefore covers meetings, processions and demonstrations that are peaceful and unarmed. A gathering which becomes violent, or in which persons carry weapons, loses the protection. The State may regulate the time, place and manner of assemblies, for example by requiring prior permission for a procession on a busy public road, so that traffic and the safety of others may be arranged. Such regulation is valid so long as it is reasonable and does not amount to a ban in disguise. The grant of permission cannot depend on the arbitrary will of an officer, and the reasons for refusing it must relate to public order. The State may also prohibit an assembly where there is a real danger to public order, but a mere possibility that some persons may oppose the meeting is not enough to deny the right of those who wish to hold it peacefully. The right does not include a right to hold a meeting on private property without the owner's consent, and it does not include a right to a particular public place at any time and for any length of time. It does not include the right to hold a strike, nor does it protect a person who obstructs others by blocking the use of public places in such a way as to cause hardship to the public. The right of assembly is closely connected with the freedom of speech, since meetings and demonstrations are among the ordinary ways in which citizens express their views and bring their grievances to the notice of the government. For this reason the courts examine closely any restriction which stops such activity, and the State must show that the restriction is a necessary and proportionate response to a real danger. Where the State imposes conditions, such as the route of a procession or the time of a meeting, these conditions must be reasonable and must leave the organisers a real chance to hold their meeting. A general prohibition of all meetings in a place for an indefinite period is likely to be treated as unreasonable unless it is supported by exceptional circumstances.

Facts: A trade union informs the authorities that it will hold a peaceful, unarmed rally of 500 persons in a public park from 4 pm to 6 pm. The authorities refuse permission, giving as their only reason that a rival group has threatened to disrupt the rally, though the police have enough force to keep order. The union challenges the refusal. Decide.

options.A: The refusal is valid, because the authorities may refuse any rally which may cause disagreement
options.B: The refusal is valid, because the right of assembly exists only on private property
options.C: The refusal is invalid, because a mere threat by others, which the police can control, is not a ground for denying a peaceful, unarmed assembly
options.D: The refusal is invalid, because the right of assembly is absolute and allows weapons for self-defence

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The rally is peaceful and unarmed. A restriction must be reasonable and related to public order, and a controllable threat from a rival group does not justify a ban. Shortcut: real danger to public order is needed; mere opposition is not. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. A possibility of opposition is not enough to deny the right. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. The principle covers assemblies in public places subject to reasonable regulation. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The right is for peaceful assembly without arms and is subject to reasonable restrictions.

questions.concept_tag: Consumer law - product liability and misuse
questions.question_text:
Passage: A product manufacturer is liable to a claimant for harm caused by a defective product. A product has a defect if there is a manufacturing defect, a defect in design, a deviation from the specifications, a failure to conform to an express warranty, or if the product does not contain adequate instructions or warnings of dangers that are known or ought to be known. The claimant need not prove negligence. It is enough to show that the product was defective and that the defect caused the harm. There are exceptions. The manufacturer is not liable if the harm was caused by the claimant's misuse of the product in a way that the manufacturer could not reasonably foresee or that was against clear warnings given on the product. Nor is the manufacturer liable if the product was altered or modified by a person other than the manufacturer after it left his control, and the alteration caused the harm. Where the product has adequate warnings, and the claimant, after reading them, chooses to ignore them, the manufacturer has no liability. But where the misuse was reasonably foreseeable, for example a child using a household item in a way children commonly do, the manufacturer may still be liable if he did not guard against it. The harm may include injury, damage to property other than the product and mental agony. The claimant may sue the manufacturer, the seller or the service provider, and the court may order compensation proportionate to the harm. A product seller who does not alter the product and who identifies the manufacturer is usually not liable for a manufacturing defect. The purpose of this branch of law is to place the burden of defective products on the manufacturer, who is in the best position to prevent the defect and to spread the cost of accidents through the price of the product, and not on the individual consumer. At the same time, the law does not make the manufacturer an insurer against every misfortune. Where a consumer ignores a clear and sufficient warning, he has himself chosen to take the risk, and the law treats the harm as the result of his own choice. The court therefore examines whether the warning was clear, whether it was placed where a user would see it, and whether the use made of the product was one that the manufacturer could reasonably have expected.

Facts: A company sells an electric kettle with a clear label: 'Never use without water; the element will overheat and may burst into flame.' Rakesh, who reads the label, switches on the kettle empty to test it. The element overheats and sets fire to his curtains. The kettle had no manufacturing or design defect. Rakesh sues the company. Decide.

options.A: The company is liable, because the kettle caused the fire and the claimant need not prove negligence
options.B: The company is liable, because manufacturers must guard against every possible misuse
options.C: The company is not liable, because the harm was caused by Rakesh's misuse against a clear warning of a known danger
options.D: The company is not liable, because Rakesh has suffered only a loss of curtains and not injury

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The claimant need not prove negligence, but the exception for misuse contrary to clear warnings applies. Rakesh read the label and used the kettle empty. Shortcut: clear warning ignored defeats the claim. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The misuse exception applies where the claimant ignored a clear warning. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. The principle limits liability to foreseeable misuse and does not apply to warned misuse. Trap (D): Half-applied principle. Property damage can count as harm, and the reason for no liability is the misuse after warning.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A contract between a seller or service provider and a consumer is an unfair contract if it contains terms which cause a significant change in the rights of the consumer. Examples of such terms are the requirement of an excessive security deposit, the imposition of a penalty on the consumer for breach that is out of proportion to the loss caused, the refusal to accept early repayment of a debt without a penalty, a term which allows a party to terminate the contract without reasonable cause and without notice to the other, and a term which gives the stronger party the right to assign the contract to the detriment of the consumer without his consent. A term which is unfair may be declared null and void by the consumer forum, and the forum may direct that the term not be enforced against the consumer. The test is whether the term gives the seller an advantage that is not balanced by a corresponding advantage for the consumer, taking account of the bargaining power of the parties. A term is not unfair merely because it is unfavourable to the consumer, if it is a reasonable term and reflects a genuine business need. The consumer must also be shown to have had no real chance to negotiate the term, as in a standard-form contract that is offered on a take-it-or-leave-it basis. A term which has been freely negotiated and is properly explained to the consumer is more likely to be held fair. The remaining terms of the contract continue to bind the parties unless the contract cannot operate without the unfair term. The aim of the provision is to correct the imbalance that exists where a consumer must accept the terms prepared by the stronger party in a standard form. The forum looks at the contract as a whole as well as at the particular term and at the surrounding circumstances at the time the contract was made. A term which restricts the right of the consumer to complain, or which requires him to give up important rights without any return, is more likely to be held unfair. The forum may allow a reasonable charge for the cost of a cancellation, so that the business is not left without any protection, but it will not allow the business to collect a penalty that has no connection with its loss.

Facts: Sharmila signs a standard-form gym membership contract on a take-it-or-leave-it basis. One term says that if she cancels the membership at any time, she must pay the gym ₹1 lakh as a penalty, whereas the whole annual fee is only ₹10,000, and the gym's actual loss from a cancellation is small. Sharmila cancels, and the gym demands the penalty. Decide.

options.A: The term is valid, because Sharmila agreed to it by signing the contract
options.B: The penalty term is unfair and can be declared void, as it is out of proportion to the loss and was imposed in a take-it-or-leave-it contract
options.C: The term is void, because the gym ought not to charge anything for a cancellation
options.D: The term is valid, because the gym is a business and businesses may set whatever terms they like

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A penalty out of proportion to loss in a standard-form contract that Sharmila had no chance to negotiate is an unfair term, and the forum may declare it void. Shortcut: disproportion + no negotiation = unfair term. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. A term in a standard-form contract can be unfair even if signed. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The principle allows reasonable charges; it condemns disproportionate ones. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The principle declares unfair terms void whatever the seller's wishes.

questions.concept_tag: IPR - trade marks and descriptive words
questions.question_text:
Passage: A trade mark is a mark capable of being represented graphically and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others. A mark that is devoid of distinctive character, or which consists exclusively of marks or indications that may serve in trade to designate the kind, quality, quantity or intended purpose of the goods, cannot be registered. The reason is that traders should be free to use ordinary descriptive words for their goods, and no one should be given a monopoly over them. A word like 'Sweet' for sugar, or 'Fresh' for milk, therefore cannot be registered as a mark on the first application. There is, however, an exception: a mark that was originally not distinctive may be registered if, before the date of the application, it has in fact acquired a distinctive character as a result of the use made of it, so that the public have come to associate it with the goods of one trader. The evidence needed to show this includes the duration and volume of sales, advertising and the recognition of the mark by consumers. A coined or invented word such as one made up for the purpose, or an ordinary word used for goods with which it has no connection, is inherently distinctive and can be registered readily. The registration of a descriptive mark, when allowed, does not stop other traders from using the same word honestly to describe their own goods, because the exclusive right is limited to use as a trade mark. The owner cannot prevent a descriptive use that is in accordance with honest practices. The reason for the exception is that a word which began as an ordinary description can come, through long and heavy use by one trader, to tell the public that the goods come from a particular source. Once it has this function, the principal reason for refusing registration no longer applies, since the public would be confused if another trader used the same word on his goods. The registrar considers the evidence of use before the date of the application and not afterwards, so that the applicant cannot rely on use that started only after he applied. A newly started business can therefore not rely on this exception, however confident it may be of its future success.

Facts: (i) Zoom Foods applies to register the word 'Juicy' as a trade mark for orange juice, but has just started business and has no sales history. (ii) Ahuja Tea has used the word 'Strong' on its tea packets for thirty years, with huge sales and national advertising, and consumers identify 'Strong' with Ahuja Tea alone. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both applications must fail, because descriptive words can never be registered
options.B: Both applications must succeed, because ordinary words are as good as any other mark
options.C: Zoom Foods can succeed and Ahuja Tea cannot, because Ahuja's use has been going on for too long
options.D: Zoom Foods' application must fail as the word is descriptive and has no acquired distinctiveness; Ahuja Tea can succeed through acquired distinctiveness

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Descriptive words are barred from registration, but the exception allows registration if the mark has in fact acquired distinctiveness. Ahuja has it; Zoom Foods has not. Shortcut: descriptive mark + acquired distinctiveness = registrable. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The exception allows registration after the mark has acquired distinctiveness through use. Trap (B): Importing an outside rule. Descriptive words need acquired distinctiveness; Zoom Foods has none. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. Long and extensive use is exactly what supports acquired distinctiveness.

questions.concept_tag: IPR - copyright infringement and the exception for private study
questions.question_text:
Passage: Copyright in a literary work gives the owner the exclusive right to reproduce the work, to issue copies of it to the public and to adapt it. A person who, without the owner's permission, does any of these acts, or allows a place to be used for such acts for profit, infringes the copyright. It is infringement to reproduce the whole of a work, or a substantial part of it, and substantial is judged by the importance of the part that is taken rather than by its length alone. A short passage which forms the heart of the work may be substantial. There are some acts that are not infringement. One of them is the fair dealing with a work for the purposes of private or personal use, including research, which allows a student to make a copy of a part of a work for his own study. The exception is meant to allow individuals to use works for their own learning, and it does not extend to making copies for sale or for distribution to others as a business. Whether the dealing is fair depends on the purpose, the amount taken, and the effect on the market for the original. A person who makes multiple copies of a whole book for sale to students is not within the exception, even if he says that his purpose is educational. The fact that a work is available free on the internet does not remove the copyright. An act that is permitted under the exception does not become an infringement because the work is later put to some other use by another person. In deciding whether a part is substantial, a court considers the quality of what has been taken as well as the quantity, and asks whether the part taken represents the author's skill and labour in a way that the owner would reasonably wish to protect. The idea behind the exceptions is to balance the owner's right to profit from his work against the public interest in learning and research. For this reason the exceptions are interpreted in a way that serves the stated purpose, and they are not allowed to go so far as to destroy the market for the work. A copy made for private study does not harm the market in the same way as large-scale copying for sale does, and the two cases are accordingly treated differently.

Facts: (i) Tarun, a law student, makes a single photocopy of one chapter of a textbook for his own study. (ii) Uday runs a copy shop which photocopies the whole of the same textbook and sells 200 copies to students at a cheap price, saying that it helps education. The owner of the copyright objects to both. Decide.

options.A: Both are infringement, because both copied the copyrighted textbook without the owner's permission
options.B: Tarun's copy is fair dealing for private study, but Uday's sale of copies is infringement
options.C: Neither is infringement, because both acted for the purpose of education
options.D: Tarun's copy is infringement but Uday's is not, because Uday's price was low

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A single copy for personal study is fair dealing. Reproducing the whole book for sale is outside the exception, whatever the stated purpose. Shortcut: personal study is excused; selling copies is not. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The exception for private study covers Tarun's single copy. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The exception does not extend to making copies for sale as a business. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The principle protects the private student and not the seller of copies.

questions.concept_tag: Company law - contracts made before incorporation
questions.question_text:
Passage: A company is a legal person only from the date of its incorporation. Before that date, it does not exist, and no one can act as its agent. A contract which is made by a promoter on behalf of a company that has not yet been incorporated therefore cannot bind the company, because the company is not a party and could not have authorised the act. The company cannot ratify the contract after its incorporation, since ratification requires that the principal was in existence when the act was done. The promoter who made the contract may be personally liable on it, unless the contract says otherwise, because someone must be bound. But where the company, after it has been incorporated, enters into a fresh contract on the same terms, it is bound by that new contract. Likewise, the law may allow a company to enforce a pre-incorporation contract that is specifically enforceable, if the company has adopted it and the other party agrees. The promoter is a fiduciary: he must not make a secret profit out of his position and must disclose any interest he has in a transaction with the company. A promoter who sells his own property to the company at a large profit, without disclosure, may be made to return the profit. A contract made on behalf of a company before its incorporation is different from a contract of a company already incorporated, in which the officers act within their authority. The other party who deals with a promoter must understand that he is dealing with a person acting at his own risk. The rule reflects the plain logic that a person cannot appoint an agent before he exists, and also the policy that a company should not be committed to arrangements made without the authority of its directors. The result is that the other party must protect himself, by dealing with the promoter personally or by waiting until the company is formed and then contracting directly with it. If the other party and the company later wish to be bound by the terms of the earlier arrangement, they may achieve this by a new agreement, which has effect from the date it is made. Statutory provisions in some systems allow a company to adopt a pre-incorporation contract by a fresh contract in terms, but without a fresh contract no such effect follows.

Facts: Vimal, a promoter, signs a contract with Waman Suppliers on 1 March for the supply of machinery, stating that he signs 'on behalf of Delta Ltd, which is being formed'. Delta Ltd is incorporated on 20 March and, on 25 March, passes a resolution that it accepts the contract. The machinery is not delivered. Waman sues Delta Ltd on the contract of 1 March. Decide.

options.A: Delta Ltd is not bound, because it did not exist on 1 March and could not ratify a contract made before its incorporation
options.B: Delta Ltd is bound, because it passed a resolution accepting the contract
options.C: Delta Ltd is bound, because the contract was clearly made for its benefit
options.D: Vimal is not liable either, because the contract was made for the company

questions.pedagogical_explanation: On 1 March Delta Ltd did not exist and could not be bound or ratify later. The promoter may be personally liable, and a fresh contract after incorporation would bind the company. Shortcut: a company cannot ratify what was done before it existed. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. A company cannot ratify a contract made before it existed. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. Benefit to the company does not make it a party. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The promoter may be personally liable on the contract.

questions.concept_tag: Arbitration - the need for a written agreement and the limits of court interference
questions.question_text:
Passage: An arbitration agreement is an agreement by the parties to submit to arbitration all or certain disputes which have arisen or which may arise between them in respect of a defined legal relationship. It must be in writing. An agreement is in writing if it is contained in a document signed by the parties, or in an exchange of letters or other means of communication that provide a record of the agreement, or in an exchange of claim and defence in which the existence of the agreement is alleged by one party and not denied by the other. A reference in a contract to a document containing an arbitration clause is also an agreement if the contract is in writing and the reference makes the clause part of the contract. The court has only a limited role. Where a party to an arbitration agreement files a suit in court on a matter that is the subject of the agreement, the court must, if the other party applies at the proper time, refer the parties to arbitration, unless it finds that the agreement is null and void. The court does not decide the merits of the dispute, which is for the arbitrator. The application to refer the dispute must be made before the applicant submits his first statement on the substance of the dispute. A party who has filed his defence on the merits without raising the objection is treated as having waived the agreement. Courts may intervene at later stages only on the limited grounds stated by law, such as the arbitrator exceeding his powers. The purpose of the requirement in the law is to encourage the speedy and economical settlement of disputes, and to respect the choice made by the parties at the time they made their contract. A court should therefore not be quick to find that an arbitration clause is invalid, and it should hold the parties to the choice they made unless a clear ground exists. At the same time, a party who has chosen to fight the case in court on the merits cannot later turn round and claim the benefit of the arbitration clause, since this would allow him to use the clause tactically after seeing how the court case was going. The right to have the dispute sent to arbitration is thus a right that must be claimed at the proper time and in the proper way.

Facts: A supply contract between Yash and Zara contains a clause: 'All disputes will be settled by arbitration.' When a dispute arises, Zara files a suit in court. Yash, in his first statement to the court, files a full defence on the merits and only afterwards asks that the dispute be sent to arbitration. Decide.

options.A: The court must refer the matter, because there is a written arbitration agreement
options.B: The court need not refer the matter to arbitration, because Yash filed his defence on the substance before raising the arbitration clause and so waived it
options.C: The court must decide the merits itself, because courts always have power over every dispute
options.D: The court cannot proceed in any case, because arbitration clauses oust the court completely

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A written agreement exists, but the request for reference must come before the first statement on the substance. By filing a full defence first, Yash waived it. Shortcut: apply before the first statement on the merits. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The application must be made before the first statement on the substance. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The principle limits the court's role where there is an arbitration agreement. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. A party can waive the clause by filing his defence on the merits.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - privity and the exception for beneficiaries
questions.question_text:
Passage: Only a person who is a party to a contract can sue upon it. A stranger to the contract, even if the contract was made for his benefit, ordinarily cannot enforce it, and he cannot be made liable under it either. This is the doctrine of privity of contract, and it rests on the idea that a contract is a private bargain between those who made it. Consideration must also move from the person who claims to enforce a promise, which is a related but separate requirement. The doctrine has recognised limits. A person for whose benefit a trust has been created may enforce the trust against the trustee, even though he is not a party to the contract that created the trust, because his right arises from the trust and not from the contract alone. In addition, a member of a family in whose favour a charge on property has been created by a family arrangement, such as a provision for the marriage expenses of a daughter, may enforce it. A person may also sue where the contract was made by another as his agent, since the agent contracts on behalf of the principal, who is the real party. An assignee of the benefit of a contract can enforce the rights assigned, but this arises through the assignment. The mere fact that the contract names a person as the intended recipient of a payment does not, by itself, create a trust in his favour, unless the intention to create a trust is clear from the terms and the surrounding circumstances. A clear intention to create a trust requires more than an expectation that the promisee will pass on the money. Where there is no trust, no charge, no agency and no assignment, the stranger has no remedy under the contract, though the promisee himself may be able to sue for the breach. The rule has often been criticised as technical and as unfair to the intended beneficiary, but it protects the freedom of the contracting parties to change or end their arrangement without needing the consent of strangers. Where a promisee has himself suffered no loss because the benefit was meant for another, the damages that he can recover may be small, and this is one of the reasons why the exceptions, such as trusts, have been developed. A court will require clear evidence that a trust was intended, and the use of words like 'for the benefit of' is not on its own enough to create a trust. The intention must be to create an enforceable obligation in favour of the beneficiary.

Facts: Chetan promises his friend Deepak, for valuable consideration, that he will pay ₹1 lakh to Deepak's niece Eesha on her next birthday. The contract between Chetan and Deepak does not mention any trust or any charge on property, and Eesha is not Deepak's agent. Chetan does not pay. Eesha sues Chetan for the money. Decide.

options.A: Eesha cannot sue, because she is a stranger to the contract and none of the recognised exceptions applies
options.B: Eesha can sue, because the contract was made for her benefit
options.C: Eesha can sue, because Deepak is her uncle and family members can always enforce family promises
options.D: Eesha cannot sue, and Deepak also cannot sue because he suffered no loss from the breach

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Eesha is a stranger to the contract. No trust was declared, no charge on property exists, she is not an agent and no assignment was made, so none of the exceptions applies. Shortcut: check each exception: trust, charge, agency, assignment. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. A stranger cannot sue merely because the contract was made for her benefit. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. The family exception applies to a charge on property created by a family arrangement, not to every family promise. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The promisee himself may be able to sue for the breach, as the principle states.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A promise made without consideration is generally not enforceable. However, a rule of equity has developed under which a party who has made a clear promise intending it to be acted upon, and who knows that the other party will act on it, can be prevented from going back on that promise if the other party has in fact acted on it and has altered his position. This is promissory estoppel. It operates as a shield and not as a sword: it prevents a party from enforcing his strict rights, but it does not create a new cause of action where none existed. The promise must be clear and unambiguous, and the promisee must have relied on it. It is not necessary that he suffered a loss in the sense of detriment, but it must be inequitable to allow the promisor to go back. The doctrine does not apply if the promisee acted in bad faith or has himself failed to fulfil his own obligations. Nor will it prevent a party from doing what the law requires or forbids: a promise cannot be used to compel a party to act against a statute, or to confer on a person a legal status or power which the law does not allow. The promisor can also resume his strict rights after giving reasonable notice to the promisee, if the promisee can resume his position. Where the promisee cannot restore the position, the promise stays binding for the period for which it was acted upon. The doctrine can be used against public authorities too, but is subject to the requirements of public interest, since the authority may show that an overriding public interest requires the promise to be withdrawn. The doctrine is flexible, and the court examines all the circumstances to see whether it would be unjust to let the promisor go back. Factors include the length of time for which the promise was acted upon, the nature of the change in position, and whether the promise was made in a context of an existing legal relationship between the parties. The doctrine suspends rights, and does not extinguish them, unless the promisee's position cannot be restored. Where the promise was made for a temporary reason, the suspension ends when the reason ends, and the promisor may then return to his strict rights after giving the promisee a fair opportunity to prepare for the change.

Facts: A landlord, Falguni, tells her tenant Gopal in writing that she will accept half the rent for the next six months because of a flood. Gopal pays half the rent for three months, using the saved money to repair his shop. In the fourth month, without any notice, Falguni demands the full rent for all the earlier months as well. Decide what she can recover for the first three months.

options.A: Falguni can recover the full arrears, because a promise without consideration is not enforceable
options.B: Falguni can never demand the full rent again, because the promise binds her permanently
options.C: Falguni cannot recover the arrears, because landlords are generally richer than tenants
options.D: Falguni cannot recover the unpaid half for the first three months, because Gopal acted on her clear promise, though she may demand full rent for the future after giving reasonable notice

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The promise was clear and Gopal relied on it. Falguni cannot recover arrears for the period covered, but the principle lets her restore full rent for future months on reasonable notice. Shortcut: estoppel protects the period already relied on; notice restores rights for the future. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Promissory estoppel prevents her from going back on the promise as to the period already acted upon. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. She may resume her strict rights for the future on reasonable notice. Trap (C): General morality. The doctrine rests on reliance on a clear promise, not on wealth.

questions.question_text:
Passage: When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by the breach is entitled to receive compensation for any loss or damage caused to him which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The loss of a kind that was not in the contemplation of the parties when they made the contract is therefore not recoverable, unless the defendant had special knowledge of the circumstances which made such loss likely. If a party gives the other notice of special circumstances at the time of the contract, the other will be liable for the loss which a breach would cause in those circumstances. A second rule is that the injured party must take reasonable steps to reduce his loss: he cannot claim damages for any part of the loss which he could have avoided by reasonable action. The cost of the steps he takes to reduce the loss is recoverable even if the steps fail, provided they were reasonable. The burden of showing that the claimant could have reduced his loss lies on the party in breach. The claimant is not required to take risky steps or steps that damage his business reputation, and the law does not demand that he behave in a perfect manner. Where the claimant has reduced the loss through a step that he was not obliged to take, the party in breach can still claim the benefit of the reduction in the assessment of damages. The two rules work together. The first limits the claim to the losses that a reasonable person in the position of the party in breach would have foreseen as likely, and the second prevents the claimant from making a loss worse through inaction. In applying the first rule, the court asks what the parties knew at the time of making the contract, and not what happened afterwards. In applying the second, the court does not demand that the claimant take extraordinary steps, but only the steps that a prudent person would take in the same situation, and whether he acted reasonably is judged leniently, because the claimant did not choose the breach and should not be criticised with hindsight.

Facts: Hari, a baker, orders an oven from Indra Ltd to be delivered on 1 June, telling Indra only that it is for his bakery. Indra delivers on 20 June. Hari's loss from the delay includes ₹20,000 of ordinary profit lost in those 19 days, and also ₹3 lakh from a special wedding contract, of which Indra had no knowledge. Hari could have rented an oven for ₹4,000 but did not. What can Hari recover?

options.A: The full ₹3.2 lakh, because the whole loss was caused by the delay
options.B: Only the wedding loss of ₹3 lakh, because it was the larger loss
options.C: The ordinary profit lost, reduced by the loss that renting an oven would have avoided; not the wedding contract loss
options.D: The ordinary profit lost in full, because renting an oven was optional and not compulsory

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Ordinary loss from a delay in an oven for a bakery is natural and recoverable, but the wedding loss needed notice of special circumstances. Hari also had to mitigate by renting an oven. Shortcut: two filters: remoteness, then mitigation. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The special loss was not in the contemplation of Indra and is too remote. Trap (B): Reversal of principle. The special loss is not recoverable, and the ordinary loss is. Trap (D): Half-applied principle. Hari must take reasonable steps to reduce loss, and the avoidable loss cannot be claimed.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person may, in an emergency, act as the agent of another without having been appointed, and bind that other person, if certain conditions are satisfied. The conditions are: it must be practically impossible to obtain the instructions of the owner in time; the action taken must be necessary in order to protect the interests of the owner, usually in preventing the loss or destruction of his property; and the person acting must act in good faith, for the benefit of the owner, and not for his own benefit. The agent must also take the course that a reasonable person would take in the circumstances. If these conditions are met, the person who acts is entitled to be reimbursed for his reasonable expenses, and the owner is bound by the contracts made. The rule is most often applied to persons who have the goods of another in their keeping, such as a carrier of perishable goods who has to sell them if they will otherwise rot. The doctrine is narrowly applied, and the courts will not extend it to cases of mere convenience or advantage. If the owner has given instructions, or could easily be reached by telephone or message, the agent has no authority to act without him. A pre-existing relationship between the parties, such as bailment, is usually required, since a stranger who interferes with another's property is not normally allowed to claim reimbursement. Where the agent acts for his own benefit, or where he could have waited for instructions, the owner is not bound. The rule has been confined to cases of real emergency because the law is reluctant to allow one person to interfere with the property of another without authority. Where the agent has the ability to communicate with the owner, even if it is with difficulty, he must try to do so, and he cannot say that the owner was inaccessible if he made no attempt to reach him. The agent must also choose the least harmful course of action available that will protect the owner's interests, and where he has two possible courses he must take the one that is more beneficial to the owner. An agent of necessity cannot make a profit for himself out of the transaction beyond reimbursement of his expenses.

Facts: Jagdish gives a truck driver, Kalu, a load of fresh fish to carry to a distant market. On the road, the truck's refrigeration fails in the heat and, with no mobile signal anywhere near, Kalu sells the fish at a fair price to a local trader to prevent them from rotting. Jagdish later claims that Kalu had no authority to sell. Decide.

options.A: Kalu had no authority, because Jagdish had not given him authority to sell
options.B: Kalu acted validly, because any carrier may sell goods whenever he thinks it convenient
options.C: Kalu acted validly as agent of necessity, because it was impossible to reach Jagdish, the sale was necessary to prevent the loss and he acted in good faith for the owner
options.D: Kalu had no authority, because a driver can never sell goods that he is only carrying

questions.pedagogical_explanation: All three conditions are met: no way of reaching the owner, a sale needed to prevent loss, and good faith. The relationship of bailment also exists. Shortcut: three conditions: impossible to ask, necessary, good faith. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. An agency of necessity arises without appointment if the conditions are met. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. The doctrine is narrow and needs necessity, impossibility of instructions and good faith. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. A carrier of perishable goods may have such authority in an emergency.

questions.concept_tag: Contract - performance of an existing duty as consideration
questions.question_text:
Passage: Consideration for a promise may be anything which the promisor desires to be done, and which the promisee does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or abstain from doing. The consideration must be something which the promisee was not already bound to do under the law or under an existing contract with the promisor. A promise to do what one is already legally bound to do for the promisor is not good consideration for a fresh promise by him, because the promisor receives nothing new. This applies to a promise of additional payment made to a person to induce him to carry out an existing contract. There are exceptions. If the promisee, in return for the promise, does something more than he was originally bound to do, the additional act is good consideration. If the promisor receives a practical benefit from the promisee's performance, and the promise to pay more was given freely, without duress or fraud, the court may treat the benefit as consideration, for example where the promisor wishes to avoid a penalty that he would suffer if the work were not completed. An existing duty owed to a third party, rather than to the promisor, may also be good consideration for a promise by the promisor, because the promisor receives a benefit he was not otherwise entitled to demand. A promise extracted by threat to break the contract, or one obtained through pressure, will not be enforced, even where there appears to be a practical benefit. The reason for the rule is that a contract should not become a means of extracting more money from the other party when no more is given in return. At the same time the law recognises that parties often have good commercial reasons for varying a contract, and so it allows a practical benefit to count when the promise to pay more was freely given. If the promise was obtained by pressure which amounts to economic duress, the contract is voidable. The court looks at whether the party seeking more was threatening a breach, whether the other party had any realistic alternative, whether he protested at the time, and whether he acted promptly to challenge the promise after the pressure was removed.

Facts: (i) Lalit has a contract with builder Madan to build a house for ₹10 lakh. Midway, Madan threatens to stop unless Lalit pays ₹1 lakh more; fearing delay, Lalit agrees, and Madan completes exactly the work in the contract. (ii) Neena, who has already agreed to deliver goods to Om, is promised ₹5,000 by Pritam, a third party who benefits from the delivery, if she delivers on time; she does so. Which claim for extra money is enforceable?

options.A: Both claims are enforceable, because each promisor got what he wanted
options.B: Neena's claim against Pritam is enforceable, because she performed a duty owed to a third party; Madan's claim for the extra ₹1 lakh is not
options.C: Neither claim is enforceable, because performance of an existing duty can never be consideration
options.D: Madan's claim is enforceable but Neena's is not, because Madan did the harder work

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Madan did only what he was already bound to do for Lalit, under pressure, so there is no consideration. Neena's performance of a duty owed to Om is good consideration for Pritam's promise. Shortcut: who is the duty owed to: the promisor or a third party? Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Madan's promise rests on an existing duty and was obtained by threat. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. A duty owed to a third party is good consideration for the promisor's promise. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The principle reverses these outcomes.

questions.concept_tag: Tort - liability of occupiers to child trespassers
questions.question_text:
Passage: An occupier of premises owes a duty to take care that persons entering are reasonably safe. The duty owed to a trespasser is much lower than that owed to a lawful visitor: the occupier must not deliberately injure a trespasser or act with reckless disregard for his presence, but he need not make the premises safe for him. This is because a person who enters without permission takes the premises as he finds them. The position is different in the case of young children. Children are less capable of recognising danger, and an object on the premises that is attractive to children and also dangerous may be treated as an allurement or an invitation. If the occupier knows, or ought to know, that children are likely to come on the land and be attracted by a dangerous thing which is left unguarded, he is under a duty to take reasonable steps to prevent harm, and a child's entry is then not treated as that of a mere trespasser. The duty requires the occupier to consider what a reasonable person would do in knowing that children are likely to be present. The occupier is not required to fence off every danger, and the steps must be reasonable having regard to the cost, the likelihood of harm and its gravity. A warning sign addressed to adults may not be an adequate warning to a young child who cannot read. If the danger is a very obvious one, which a child of the age of the injured child ought to appreciate, the occupier may not be liable. The law on this subject is based on a balance between the freedom of an occupier to use his land as he wishes and the safety of young children who may not understand danger. The balance is struck by looking at what is reasonable for the occupier to do. Where the danger could be removed at small cost, such as by putting a cover over a pit or a fence around it, the court is more likely to find that the occupier should have done so. The age of the child is relevant because older children are expected to appreciate more dangers than younger ones, and parents also have responsibilities to supervise their young children, which the court considers when it decides whether the occupier took reasonable care.

Facts: Qadir owns a vacant lot beside a school and keeps an unfenced, uncovered pit full of deep water there. He knows that children often play in the lot after school. A seven-year-old, Rani, enters the lot to play, falls into the pit and nearly drowns. Qadir has put up a sign reading 'Danger — Keep Out' in English, which Rani cannot read. Rani's father sues. Decide.

options.A: Qadir is not liable, because Rani was a trespasser and the duty to trespassers is low
options.B: Qadir is liable, because he knew that children came to the lot, the pit was a dangerous allurement and the sign did not give a child of seven an adequate warning
options.C: Qadir is not liable, because he put up a warning sign
options.D: Qadir is liable because the owners of land are always responsible for any injury on their land

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The low duty to trespassers is displaced for children where a known, attractive danger is left unguarded. A sign that a seven-year-old cannot read does not meet the duty of reasonable steps. Shortcut: child + known allurement + inadequate warning = duty. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The allurement principle raises the duty owed to young children in such cases. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. A sign that a young child cannot read is not an adequate warning. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The duty is based on knowledge of likely child entrants and reasonable steps, not on ownership alone.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A person who suffers a recognised psychiatric illness as a result of a negligent act may claim damages for what is called nervous shock, but the law limits who can claim. The illness must be a medically recognised condition and not mere grief, distress or fright. The claimant must be someone whom the defendant ought reasonably to have foreseen as likely to suffer such an illness through his negligence. The courts look at the closeness of the relationship between the claimant and the person who was injured, since a person with close ties of love and affection, such as a parent, child or spouse, is more likely to be affected. They look at the closeness in time and space of the claimant to the accident or its immediate aftermath, and at whether the shock came from seeing or hearing the event with his own unaided senses, and not through being told about it by someone else. A rescuer who puts himself in danger to help the victims may also claim, and one who is himself within the zone of danger and fears for his own safety may claim even if not hurt in body. A person who is a mere bystander, who has no close tie to the victim, and who is shocked by seeing a distressing accident cannot usually claim, because the law does not expect persons of ordinary fortitude to be unable to endure the sight of accidents. The claimant who learns of the accident from a telephone call or from the news, hours later, is not usually within the class of persons who can claim. The restriction on claims has been defended on the ground that without it the number of claims would grow beyond what is reasonable, and defendants could be liable to a wide class of persons for a single act of carelessness. For this reason, the courts treat the cases of persons who were present at the scene and who are closely connected with the victim as the central cases. The claimant must also show that the psychiatric illness was caused by the shock of the event and not by the gradual effect of grief or by the stress of looking after the injured person over a long period. The illness must be shown by medical evidence, and the damages are assessed in the same way as for any other personal injury.

Facts: A careless driver, Sagar, runs over a boy, Tarun, outside a school in full view of Tarun's mother, Usha, who is standing at the school gate and sees it happen. Usha develops a recognised psychiatric illness. Separately, a stranger, Vikram, who happens to be walking by and who is shocked by the sight, also becomes upset, and Tarun's father Wasim, who is at work, becomes ill after being told by telephone an hour later. Who can claim?

options.A: All three can claim, because each suffered distress through Sagar's negligence
options.B: Usha and Wasim can claim, because both are parents of the injured boy
options.C: Only Usha can claim, since she is the mother who saw the accident with her own senses; Vikram and Wasim cannot
options.D: Only Vikram can claim, because he saw the accident from the beginning without any bias

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Usha has a close tie, was present and saw the event herself. Vikram is a mere bystander and Wasim was told about it later, so neither fits the class. Shortcut: relationship + proximity + own senses. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Closeness of relationship, perception and proximity are needed. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Wasim learnt of the accident by telephone and was not near the event. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. A mere bystander cannot usually claim.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A statement that would otherwise be defamatory is protected by qualified privilege if it is made on an occasion where the person making it has a duty or an interest in making it, and the person to whom it is made has a corresponding duty or interest in receiving it. Examples are a reference given by a former employer to a prospective employer, a complaint made to a person with authority to deal with it, and a communication made between persons with a common interest. The statement is protected even if it is false, provided it was made honestly. The protection is lost if the claimant proves malice, which in this context means that the dominant motive of the maker was to injure the claimant, or that the maker did not honestly believe the statement to be true, or acted with reckless indifference to its truth. The privilege is also lost if the statement is published beyond those who have the corresponding interest or duty. A statement made to the right person but also broadcast to others who have no interest in it is not protected as to the excess publication. An honest but mistaken belief, even if unreasonable, does not amount to malice. A person who is carelessly mistaken is protected so long as he honestly believed in what he said. The burden of proving malice lies on the claimant. The privilege is qualified and not absolute, and so differs from absolute privilege, which protects statements made in Parliament or in the course of judicial proceedings whatever the motive. The law of qualified privilege reflects a balance between the protection of reputation and the free flow of information that is needed for the proper conduct of social and business life. People should be able to give honest references, to report suspicions to the proper authorities and to share information with those who need it, without fear that a mistake will lead to a heavy liability. At the same time, the law does not allow the privilege to be used as a cover for spite. The question of malice is examined by looking at the words used, the manner of publication, the relationship between the parties, and the evidence of the maker's state of mind, and the claimant must prove it by evidence, not by suspicion alone.

Facts: Yogesh, a former manager, is asked by a prospective employer for a reference on Zubin and honestly writes that Zubin 'was dismissed for stealing', which he believes on reasonable grounds although it later proves to be false. In a second case, Aman gives a reference about Bela to a prospective employer, saying that she is dishonest, though he knows that it is false, intending to harm her. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both are protected, because both statements were references to prospective employers
options.B: Neither is protected, because both statements were false
options.C: Yogesh is protected by qualified privilege; Aman is not, because he acted with malice
options.D: Aman is protected because the occasion was privileged, and Yogesh is not because he made a mistake

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Yogesh made an honest statement on a privileged occasion. Aman knew his statement was false and wished to harm Bela, so malice defeats the privilege. Shortcut: privileged occasion, then check for malice. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Qualified privilege is lost where malice is proved. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Falsity alone does not defeat the privilege if the maker honestly believed it. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. An honest mistake does not defeat the privilege; malice does.

questions.concept_tag: Tort - non-delegable duties and independent contractors
questions.question_text:
Passage: An employer is generally not liable for the wrongful acts of an independent contractor, that is, a person who is engaged to do work on his own account and who is not under the employer's control as to the manner in which the work is done. The reason is that the employer has no control over how the contractor does the work. There are, however, exceptions where the employer remains liable. First, where the work is inherently dangerous, so that it will create a serious danger to others unless proper precautions are taken, the employer cannot escape liability by handing the work to a contractor. Second, where the law imposes a particular duty on the employer, such as the duty of an occupier to keep the premises safe for visitors or the duty of a hospital to take care of its patients, the duty is non-delegable, which means that the employer remains responsible for its proper performance even if he has delegated the performance to another. Third, the employer is liable if he himself was negligent in selecting the contractor or in giving the instructions. The injured person must show that the case falls in one of the exceptions. If the wrong is entirely collateral to the work, such as an unrelated act of carelessness by the contractor's worker which could not have been foreseen, the employer is not liable even in these cases. The employer who is held liable can usually recover the amount from the contractor under an indemnity. The basis of the non-delegable duty is that certain duties are so important or so closely tied to a relationship of dependence or vulnerability that the person who has assumed them cannot be allowed to say that he has fulfilled them merely by choosing someone else to do the work. The duty is to see that care is taken, not merely to take care himself. The question whether a particular duty is non-delegable is decided by looking at the nature of the activity, the control which the defendant had over the situation, and the vulnerability of the persons to whom the duty is owed. Where public highways are involved, the authority has long been held responsible for dangers which arise from works carried out in them.

Facts: A municipal corporation hires a contractor to dig a trench for pipes across a public pavement. The contractor's worker leaves the trench uncovered and unlit at night, and a passer-by, Chandra, falls into it and breaks her leg. The contract left all safety matters to the contractor. Chandra sues the corporation. Decide.

options.A: The corporation is not liable, because the contractor was an independent contractor who controlled the work
options.B: The corporation is not liable, because its contract placed all safety matters on the contractor
options.C: The corporation is liable only if it can be shown to have been selecting a poor contractor
options.D: The corporation is liable, because digging a trench on a public way is work that is dangerous unless precautions are taken and the corporation cannot delegate its duty by hiring a contractor

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The general rule protects employers from contractors' wrongs, but the exception for dangerous work on a public way applies, and the corporation's duty cannot be handed over. Shortcut: dangerous work or non-delegable duty means the employer is still liable. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The exceptions for dangerous work and non-delegable duties apply. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. A contract between them cannot remove the corporation's liability to Chandra. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The first two exceptions do not require negligence in selection.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - dishonest misappropriation of property found
questions.question_text:
Passage: Whoever dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use any movable property commits an offence. The offence is not theft, because the property is not taken out of the possession of anyone, but it is a closely related offence of dishonest misappropriation. A person who finds property which has been lost by another is not guilty merely because he picks it up. If he takes it with the intention of returning it to its owner, or if he does not know who the owner is and has not yet had a chance to find out, he does not act dishonestly. But if, at the time of picking up the property, or at some later time, he knows or has the means of discovering the owner and appropriates the property to himself without taking reasonable steps to find the owner, the offence is committed. The honest finder, who in good faith believes that the owner cannot be found, must still take reasonable steps, such as making a public announcement or informing the police, if the property is valuable. The mere passage of time does not make the appropriation dishonest if the finder is trying to trace the owner. Where the finder keeps the property for himself immediately after finding it, knowing the name of the owner from papers inside it, the intention to appropriate is clear. The value of the property does not affect the nature of the offence, but only the punishment and the care that the law expects. The law also takes account of the practical fact that a person who finds something may not know who owns it and may have difficulty in tracing the owner. For that reason the offence does not apply to every case in which a finder keeps property, but only where the intention to appropriate is dishonest. The intention is judged at the time when the finder decides to keep the property, and from the finder's conduct and the circumstances of the finding. Evidence of efforts to find the owner is very important and indicates that the finder was acting in good faith. Conduct such as hiding the property, destroying the identifying marks or lying about it shows a dishonest intention.

Facts: (i) Dharam finds a wallet in the street with ₹5,000 and a card showing the owner's name and address. He keeps the money at once and throws away the wallet. (ii) Esha finds a ring in a park, has no idea whose it is and asks the park staff, informs the police and keeps the ring safe for six months while waiting for a claimant. No one claims, and then she keeps it. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Dharam commits dishonest misappropriation; Esha does not, because she took reasonable steps to find the owner
options.B: Both commit the offence, because both kept property that did not belong to them
options.C: Neither commits the offence, because both found the property by chance
options.D: Esha commits the offence and Dharam does not, because the ring was worth more than the money

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Dharam knew the owner's name and appropriated the money at once, which is dishonest. Esha made reasonable efforts to find the owner and kept the ring only after they failed. Shortcut: finder: owner known or reachable and appropriated is the offence. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. A finder who takes reasonable steps and cannot find the owner is not dishonest. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. Finding by chance does not excuse keeping property when the owner can be traced. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The value does not determine the offence, and Dharam knew the owner.

questions.concept_tag: Criminal law - harbouring an offender and the exception for a spouse
questions.question_text:
Passage: Whenever an offence has been committed, whoever knowing or having reason to believe that an offence has been committed, harbours or conceals a person knowing or believing that he is the offender, with the intention of screening him from legal punishment, commits an offence. Harbouring includes supplying a person with shelter, food, drink, money, clothes, arms, ammunition or means of conveyance, or assisting a person by any means, whether of the same kind or not, to evade apprehension. There is an exception: the offence does not apply to any case in which the harbour or concealment is by the wife or husband of the offender. The exception is based on the close personal relationship of marriage, and it does not extend to other relatives such as parents, brothers, sisters or children. Three elements are required for the offence to be made out: there must have been an offence; the accused must have known or had reason to believe that the person was the offender; and he must have acted with the intention of screening the person from punishment. If the accused gave shelter without knowing of the offence, or in the belief that the person was innocent, there is no offence. Similarly, a person who merely fails to report an offender, without doing any act to conceal him, does not commit this offence, although other laws might impose a duty to inform. The exception for the spouse applies even where the offence is serious, and is not lost because the spouse acted with the intention of screening the offender. The exception is a narrow one, based on the special position of husband and wife, and the courts do not widen it by analogy.
