The fact that a person has acted out of love or family loyalty is not by itself a defence, though it may be taken into account in deciding the punishment. In deciding whether a person acted with the intention of screening an offender, the court looks at the acts done, such as hiding the person, giving him a false name, destroying evidence or misleading the police, and at the surrounding circumstances. A passive act, such as simply allowing a relative to remain in the house without being aware of the reason, does not satisfy the requirement of knowledge and intention.

Facts: Fatima robs a bank and then goes to hide. (i) Her husband Ghulam, knowing of the robbery, lets her hide in his house for a month to avoid arrest. (ii) Her brother Hamid, knowing of the robbery, also lets her hide in his house for a month to avoid arrest. (iii) Her neighbour Ismat, who does not know of the robbery, gives her a room for the night. Who commits the offence of harbouring an offender?

options.A: Ghulam and Hamid, because both knowingly concealed her
options.B: Ghulam, Hamid and Ismat, because each of them gave her shelter
options.C: Only Ghulam, because a husband has a greater duty to the law than a brother
options.D: Only Hamid, because the spouse is excepted and Ismat lacked knowledge

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Hamid knew of the offence and sheltered Fatima to screen her; the exception does not reach brothers. Ghulam is excepted as a spouse and Ismat had no knowledge. Shortcut: knowledge + intent to screen; only the spouse is excepted. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The exception covers the spouse. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Ismat did not know of the offence, and Ghulam is excepted. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. The exception makes Ghulam not liable.

questions.question_text:
Passage: As a general rule, a person is not guilty of a crime unless he has a guilty mind (mens rea) in addition to doing the prohibited act. The prosecution must therefore prove not only the act but also the required intention, knowledge or recklessness. There is, however, a category of offences, usually created by statutes for the regulation of public welfare, in which the legislature has made the doing of the act itself an offence without requiring proof of any intention or knowledge. These are offences of strict liability, and they are found in fields such as sale of adulterated food, safety standards for machinery and traffic regulation. Whether an offence is one of strict liability depends on the words of the statute, the subject matter, the mischief to be prevented and whether imposing liability without fault will help in preventing it. The court begins with a presumption that mens rea is required, and the presumption can be displaced only by clear words or by necessary implication. Even where an offence is one of strict liability, some statutes provide for a defence if the accused proves that he exercised all due diligence and that he did not know and could not by reasonable inquiry have known of the fact that made his act an offence. Where the statute contains no such defence, a person who did everything in his power to comply may still be liable. The purpose is to place the burden on those who engage in a regulated activity, and not on the public, to ensure compliance. The reasoning behind strict liability is that the harm caused by such acts is serious and widespread, and that it would be very difficult to prove the guilty mind of persons who run large businesses. The imposition of liability without fault is thought to encourage those engaged in the regulated activity to be extremely careful and to set up systems for checking their goods or processes. Critics point out that it may be unjust to punish a person who was not at fault, and for this reason many statutes include defences, and the penalties for such offences are often lighter. A court will also ask whether the accused was in a position to control the thing, and whether he took any step to avoid the commission of the offence.

Facts: A statute makes it an offence to sell food containing a prohibited additive, without referring to knowledge or intent, and provides a defence of 'due diligence and lack of knowledge', to be proved by the seller. Jitu, a shopkeeper, sells a packet of biscuits which contains the additive, without knowing it. He bought the packet from a reputed wholesaler, who certified it as free from the additive, and he had taken all reasonable steps to check. Is Jitu liable?

options.A: Jitu is not guilty, because there was no guilty mind on his part
options.B: Jitu commits the offence, which is one of strict liability, but he can escape liability by proving due diligence and lack of knowledge
options.C: Jitu is guilty and cannot escape, because strict liability allows no defence at all
options.D: Jitu is not guilty, because the wholesaler gave the certificate and the shopkeeper is not responsible for it

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The statute omits mens rea, so the offence is strict. Because it provides a defence of due diligence and lack of knowledge, Jitu can escape by proving it. Shortcut: strict liability: act alone; but use any statutory defence. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. The offence is one of strict liability, and mens rea is not an element. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. The statute provides a due diligence defence which Jitu can try to prove. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The seller commits the offence, though he can rely on the defence given by the statute.

questions.concept_tag: Constitutional law - excessive delegation of legislative power
questions.question_text:
Passage: The power to make laws is given to the legislature, and the legislature cannot delegate its essential legislative functions to another body. The essential functions include laying down the legislative policy and the standards for guidance, and enacting that policy as a rule of conduct. However, it is permissible for the legislature, after laying down the policy and guiding principles, to delegate the working out of the details to the executive or some other authority, because modern legislation is complex and requires detailed rules which the legislature cannot itself supply. This is called conditional or subordinate legislation. The delegate must act within the limits of the policy and cannot go beyond the scope of the statute. A delegation that gives the executive an uncontrolled power to decide what the law shall be, without any standard or guide, is excessive and the law containing it is invalid to that extent. The court asks whether the statute has provided a sufficient standard, such as the object to be attained and the conditions for the exercise of the power. The court does not require a detailed standard if the policy can be understood from the statute as a whole. A rule made by the delegate which is inconsistent with the parent Act, or which goes beyond the power conferred, is invalid. The power to modify the Act itself or to repeal it, if given to the executive, is treated with caution, and is allowed only to a limited degree for adaptation of the Act to local conditions. The principle exists because the Constitution assigns the task of making laws to the elected legislature, and permits the executive to act under such laws, not to make the laws themselves. The legislature must therefore make the central choices of policy and give clear guidance, while the executive fills in the details and applies the law in particular cases. The court gives the legislature a fair amount of room, since it recognises that an elected body cannot foresee all the details of a complex subject. It will, however, strike down a delegation in which the executive is left to decide for itself what the policy should be, because this would change the roles of the two bodies and remove the control that the legislature is meant to exercise.

Facts: A statute says: 'The Government may, by notification, make such rules as it thinks fit and may declare any act to be an offence and fix any punishment for it.' The Government declares by notification that wearing a red shirt in the city centre is an offence, punishable with a year's imprisonment. A shopkeeper challenges the rule. Decide.

options.A: The rule is invalid, because the statute lays down no policy or standard and hands the Government an uncontrolled power to create offences
options.B: The rule is valid, because the Government has been given the power by the legislature
options.C: The rule is valid, because the Government knows what is good for the city
options.D: The rule is invalid, because the legislature may never delegate any power to the executive

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The legislature may delegate details after laying down policy and standards. This statute lays down none and gives uncontrolled power, so the delegation is excessive. Shortcut: policy and standards are essential; details can be delegated. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. The legislature may not delegate its essential functions without a policy or standard. Trap (C): General morality. The test is the presence of a legislative policy and standard, not the wisdom of the Government. Trap (D): Half-applied principle. Delegation of details within a laid-down policy is allowed.

questions.question_text:
Passage: The guarantee of equality before the law and of equal protection of the laws forbids arbitrary State action. An action is arbitrary if it is without a rational basis, if it is capricious, or if it is based on a whim and not on reasons. The State must act fairly and in a manner that treats like cases alike. When the State chooses to treat different groups differently, the classification must rest on an intelligible difference between the groups, and the difference must have a rational connection with the aim of the law. A classification is not invalid merely because it is not perfect or because a few persons are caught who should not have been, since a law may take account of general experience. Where the State makes policy choices on economic or social matters, the courts allow it a wide discretion and do not substitute their own opinions, unless the policy is clearly arbitrary. Even for a single individual, the State may not single out a person for unfavourable treatment without a reason, because the equality principle applies to individuals as well as to groups. State action in awarding contracts or granting benefits must also be fair, and the State may not refuse to deal with a person for a reason that has no connection with the matter. The State is allowed to take account of relevant factors, such as experience and financial soundness, in deciding to whom to award a contract. A decision which meets this standard is not invalid just because another person might think it unwise. The prohibition on arbitrariness is part of the idea of the rule of law, which requires that public power be exercised on the basis of rules and reasons that can be understood and tested. It does not require the State to adopt the best possible decision, but only a decision that is reasoned and fair. The court therefore considers the reasons recorded by the authority, the relevance of the factors considered and whether any relevant factor was ignored. When the authority itself has laid down criteria for a decision, it is expected to follow them, and a departure from them without explanation is a strong sign of arbitrariness. The remedy is generally to quash the decision and to ask the authority to decide again fairly.

Facts: A State agency invites bids for supply of uniforms, with a published condition that bidders must have at least five years of experience. Lena has seven years' experience and the lowest price, but the agency rejects her bid without any reason, and awards the contract to a firm with two years of experience at a higher price, for no stated reason. Lena challenges the decision. Decide.

options.A: The decision is valid, because the State has a wide discretion in choosing its suppliers
options.B: The decision is invalid for arbitrariness, because the agency ignored its own published criteria and gave no rational basis for preferring a less qualified, higher-priced bidder
options.C: The decision is valid, because a bidder has no right to a government contract
options.D: The decision is invalid, because the State may never prefer one supplier to another

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The State may choose suppliers, but a decision that disregards its own criteria and has no rational basis is arbitrary and violates equality. Shortcut: discretion is allowed; arbitrariness is not. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Wide discretion exists for rational policy choices, not for decisions without any rational basis. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. A bidder has no right to the contract but has a right to fair and non-arbitrary treatment. Trap (D): Importing an outside rule. The State may choose among bidders on rational grounds.

questions.concept_tag: Constitutional law - writs against private bodies performing public functions
questions.question_text:
Passage: A writ may be issued to enforce a fundamental right or for any other purpose, against the State and its instrumentalities. The State includes the Government, Parliament, State legislatures and all local and other authorities. An authority is treated as State if it is created by a statute, controlled by the Government in its functioning, financed by the State, and given a monopoly status, or if it performs functions of a public nature closely related to governmental functions. A private body is ordinarily not subject to a writ, because a writ is a remedy against the exercise of public power. A private person who is violating another's rights is dealt with by ordinary suits and not by a writ. However, a writ other than for enforcement of a fundamental right may be issued to a private body, if it performs a public duty or discharges a public function, and the right claimed arises out of that function. A body which performs a public function, such as running an educational institution with public aid or providing an essential public service, may thus be required to act fairly and in accordance with law. The nature of the function is more important than the form of the body. A purely private contract, such as a contract of private employment which is not subject to statutory regulation, is not enforceable by writ. The court considers whether the duty is owed to the public and is imposed by a statute or arises from the public character of the function, before issuing the writ. The extension of the writ to bodies other than the State comes from the idea that public functions should be performed in accordance with law, whoever performs them. Where a private institution has taken over a function that would otherwise be done by the State, such as the provision of education or health services to the public, those who depend on the institution should have a remedy. The court therefore asks whether the body is exercising a public function, whether it is under a statutory obligation, and whether the right which the petitioner relies on arises from that function. Even then, the writ is discretionary, and the court may decline to issue it where an adequate alternative remedy exists, such as an appeal under the statute.

Facts: (i) A private club expels its member Mahesh after a dispute about unpaid dues, under its own rules. (ii) A private college that receives State aid and is bound by a statute to admit students on merit refuses admission to Nisha, who topped the merit list, and gives no reason. Both persons seek writs. Which statement is correct?

options.A: A writ can be issued in Nisha's case, since the college performs a public function under a statute, but not in Mahesh's, which concerns a private matter
options.B: Writs can be issued in both cases, because both involve a violation of a person's rights
options.C: Writs cannot be issued in either case, because both bodies are private
options.D: A writ can be issued in Mahesh's case but not Nisha's, because a club has more members

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The college performs a public function, under statute, with State aid; the writ lies. The club's expulsion is a private matter with no public duty. Shortcut: public function = writ; private matter = ordinary suit. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. A private club in a private dispute is not subject to a writ. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. A private body performing a public function can be subjected to a writ. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The principle supports the writ for the college discharging a public function.

questions.concept_tag: Consumer law - liability of an intermediary platform
questions.question_text:
Passage: An e-commerce platform that provides a marketplace on which independent sellers list and sell goods is generally an intermediary. An intermediary is not liable for the goods sold by independent sellers on its platform, nor for the content provided by them, provided that it does not itself initiate the transmission, does not select the receiver, does not modify the information and observes due diligence. This protection is meant to allow platforms to operate without being held answerable for every listing. The protection is lost if the platform has conspired, abetted or aided in the unlawful act, or if, on receiving actual knowledge or a notice from the authority that the content is unlawful, it fails to remove it promptly. In addition, where the platform has taken on the role of a seller, for instance by selling its own goods or by guaranteeing the quality of the goods, it is treated as a seller and is liable as such. A platform that provides a service such as delivery or payment collection is liable for deficiencies in that service. The platform also has a duty to display the details of the seller and the return and refund policies, and to give the consumer a means to complain. Where the platform actively promotes particular goods and represents them as its own assured products, the consumer may reasonably expect the platform to be answerable. The platform cannot avoid liability by a term of its own that says it is not responsible for anything. The rules about intermediaries try to strike a balance between protecting consumers and allowing digital platforms to grow without bearing the cost of checking every product. The balance depends on the platform's role. The more the platform controls, presents or guarantees the goods, the more a consumer is justified in relying on it, and the less it can claim to be a mere conduit. For this reason, the court looks at features such as the use of the platform's own brand, a promise of quality or authenticity, the handling of payment and delivery, and the way the product is advertised. If the platform takes such an active role, it is regarded as having assumed responsibility to the consumer for the quality of the goods.

Facts: On a marketplace website, an independent seller lists a phone charger, and the platform only carries the listing and passes on the order. The charger is defective and burns a buyer's hand. In a second case, the same platform sells a charger under its own brand name and marks it 'Assured by the platform', and that one burns another buyer. Decide the liability of the platform.

options.A: The platform is liable in both cases, because both items were sold through its website
options.B: The platform is not liable in either case, because its terms say that it takes no responsibility
options.C: The platform is not liable for the independent seller's charger, but is liable for its own assured charger as it acted as a seller
options.D: The platform is liable for the independent seller's charger and not for its own, because its own products are tested

questions.pedagogical_explanation: As an intermediary, the platform is protected for independent listings. When it sells its own product and guarantees it, it becomes a seller and is liable. Shortcut: intermediary protected; seller or guarantor liable. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. A passive intermediary is protected for independent sellers' goods. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. A term cannot remove the liability of a platform that acts as a seller. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. This reverses the position under the principle.

questions.concept_tag: IPR - confidential information and the public interest exception
questions.question_text:
Passage: A person who receives information in circumstances which impose an obligation of confidence cannot use or disclose the information without the permission of the person who gave it. The obligation arises from an express agreement or from the circumstances, for example a relationship such as that between an employer and employee, or a doctor and patient, or where the recipient knew that the information was given in confidence. To succeed in an action for breach of confidence, the claimant must show that the information has the necessary quality of confidence about it, that it was imparted in circumstances importing an obligation of confidence, and that there was an unauthorised use or disclosure of it to the detriment of the claimant. Information which is in the public domain, or which is trivial, does not have the quality of confidence. There is a defence of public interest: a person may disclose confidential information if disclosure is necessary to expose serious wrongdoing, such as a crime or a danger to public health or safety, and the disclosure is made to a person who has a proper interest in receiving it, and not to the world at large. The court weighs the public interest in keeping confidences against the public interest in disclosure. The defence is not a licence to publish any matter that the public is curious about, since public interest means something that is of real importance to the public, and not merely what interests them. Disclosure limited to what is needed to remove the danger is favoured. The basis of the action for breach of confidence is the equitable duty not to take unfair advantage of information given in trust. It is independent of contract, and may bind even a person who is not a party to any contract with the claimant but who received the information knowing of its confidential character. The remedy may be an injunction against disclosure or damages. Courts also recognise that employees may use the general skill and knowledge they gained in a job, and they cannot be stopped from doing so, but they may not use specific confidential information, such as secret processes or customer lists. The public interest defence is applied narrowly and needs a careful balancing in each case.

Facts: Olive, an engineer, learns in confidence from her employer's records that the company is knowingly selling a baby food with a poisonous contaminant. (i) She sends the records to the food safety regulator. (ii) Her colleague Parth learns of the company's confidential plan for a new colourful logo and sells details of it to a newspaper, to be published to the public. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both disclosures are breaches, because both employees had a duty of confidence to the company
options.B: Neither is a breach, because both involve information the public might want to read
options.C: Parth's disclosure is protected and Olive's is not, because the newspaper reaches more people
options.D: Olive's disclosure to the regulator is protected by the public-interest defence; Parth's disclosure is a breach of confidence

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Olive discloses a danger to health to a body with a proper interest. Parth discloses a trivial commercial matter to the public at large, with no public interest. Shortcut: public interest needs serious wrongdoing and a proper recipient. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Olive's disclosure is justified by the public interest exception. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Public interest means real importance, not curiosity; Parth's matter is trivial. Trap (C): Reversal of principle. The principle prefers disclosure to a proper recipient for serious wrongdoing.

questions.concept_tag: IPR - originality and the idea-expression merger
questions.question_text:
Passage: Copyright subsists in original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works. Originality means that the work originates from the author and is not copied from another, and that it involves some degree of skill, judgment and labour in its creation, more than a trivial or purely mechanical effort. The work need not be novel or inventive. The law protects the expression of ideas and not the ideas themselves. If a particular idea can be expressed in only one way, or in so few ways that to protect the expression would be to protect the idea itself, the idea and the expression are said to merge, and the copyright is limited or denied in order to prevent the monopolisation of the idea. A copyright in a compilation of facts exists only to the extent that the author has used skill and judgment in selecting and arranging the facts, and does not extend to the facts themselves, which anyone may use. A mechanical listing of facts in an obvious order, such as an alphabetical list of names, will not have the necessary originality. Facts, news of the day and common data are free for all to use. A person who takes the facts from a compilation and arranges them in his own way does not infringe the copyright in the first compilation, although a person who copies the selection and arrangement itself may do so. The author's labour in collecting the facts is not itself protected, unless the labour was exercised in creating an original expression. The distinction between idea and expression ensures that copyright does not become a barrier to the free development of knowledge and culture. If one author could stop others from using an idea, an obvious method of doing a task or a basic fact, then the progress of learning would be hindered. The law therefore rewards the personal contribution of the author in the form of expression, selection and arrangement, and leaves the underlying material free. Where a work is made up of many parts, the court looks at whether what has been copied is a substantial part of the original and protected contribution, and not merely a piece of common material available to all. The same approach applies to databases, directories and similar collections.

Facts: Quinn compiles a directory of local plumbers by listing all plumbers in the town in alphabetical order with their phone numbers, which he collected by phoning them. Ravi copies Quinn's whole directory page by page. In another case, Sita compiles a guide to 'ten best plumbers', selected and ranked with her own judgment and commentary, and Tej copies her selection and ranking exactly. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Ravi infringes, because Quinn spent labour in collecting the numbers
options.B: Neither infringes, because the numbers and the plumbers' names are facts
options.C: Both infringe, because both copied a compiled work of another
options.D: Ravi does not infringe because an alphabetical list lacks originality; Tej infringes because he copies Sita's original selection and ranking

questions.pedagogical_explanation: An alphabetical list of facts has no skill and judgment in selection or arrangement. Sita's selection and ranking is an original expression, and Tej copied it. Shortcut: facts are free; original selection and arrangement is protected. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. Labour in collecting facts is not itself protected without original selection or arrangement. Trap (B): Half-applied principle. Sita's selection and ranking show originality, which Tej copied. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. Copyright depends on originality, and an alphabetical list lacks it.

questions.concept_tag: Administrative law - legitimate expectation and overriding public interest
questions.question_text:
Passage: A person may have a legitimate expectation of being treated in a certain way by an administrative authority, because of an assurance given by the authority or because of a consistent practice which the person can reasonably expect to continue. A legitimate expectation is not a legal right, but it is a ground on which the court can examine the fairness of the authority's decision. Where the authority intends to depart from the practice or the assurance, it must act fairly, which usually means giving the person a chance to present his case and the reasons for the change. The expectation is protected by procedural fairness in all cases, and in some cases by a substantive benefit, if it would be an abuse of power to defeat it. The expectation must be based on a clear and unambiguous promise or practice, and it must be reasonable. It does not arise from a mere hope. The authority is free to change its policy for good reasons. Where a change of policy is required by an overriding public interest, the authority may defeat the expectation, but the courts will examine whether the reasons were genuine and whether the means used were proportionate. An expectation cannot be used to compel the authority to act contrary to a statute or to ignore its duty. The person claiming the expectation must show that he knew of the assurance and relied on it. A claim based on a representation by an official who had no authority to give it will not usually succeed. The doctrine of legitimate expectation is an aspect of fairness in public administration. Its purpose is to prevent authorities from acting in a way that disappoints those who have reasonably relied on their words or conduct, without giving them a fair chance to respond. The doctrine does not freeze the policies of the government, since public authorities must be able to change course when the public interest requires it. The court's role is not to decide whether the change of policy is wise, but to ensure that the authority has acted with fairness, has considered the expectation and has proportionate reasons for departing from it. An authority which makes an assurance must be held to it unless a sufficient public reason for departing from it is shown.

Facts: For ten years a city authority has renewed the stall licences of street vendors each year after a short application and without any inquiry. Without notice or reasons, it refuses to renew Tanya's licence this year, saying only that it 'no longer wants vendors on that street'. In another case, the authority hears and explains to a vendor, Umesh, that a new road-safety law now requires the removal of vendors from a dangerous junction, and refuses his renewal after giving him a hearing. Decide.

options.A: Both refusals are valid, because a licence is only a permission that may be withdrawn at any time
options.B: Tanya's refusal is open to challenge for want of fairness, as she was denied notice, a hearing and reasons; Umesh's refusal stands because of an overriding public interest and fair process
options.C: Both refusals are invalid, because both vendors had a legitimate expectation of renewal
options.D: Tanya's refusal is valid and Umesh's is not, because Umesh was given a hearing and should have been renewed

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The ten-year practice created a legitimate expectation for Tanya, so the authority must give notice, hearing and reasons. For Umesh, the change was required by an overriding public interest and he had a fair hearing. Shortcut: expectation protects fair process; overriding public interest can defeat it. Trap (A): Ignoring the exception. A legitimate expectation requires fair process before a departure from practice. Trap (C): Half-applied principle. An overriding public interest can defeat the expectation if fairly applied. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The reasoning reverses the outcomes.

questions.question_text:
Passage: An easement is a right which the owner of one piece of land, called the dominant heritage, has over another's land, called the servient heritage, for the beneficial enjoyment of the dominant heritage, such as a right of way. An easement of necessity arises where a person transfers a part of his land and the part transferred is completely enclosed by the remaining land of the transferor or by the land of the transferor and others, so that it cannot be used at all without passing over the retained land. In that case, the law implies a right of way over the retained land in favour of the transferee, because it would be absurd to suppose that the parties intended the transferred land to be useless. The same arises in favour of the transferor if he retains a part that is enclosed by the land transferred. The necessity must be absolute and not merely a matter of convenience. If the transferee has another route, even a longer, more difficult or more expensive one, no easement of necessity arises. The easement lasts only as long as the necessity continues, and ends when the land acquires another way of access. The route is to be that which is the least inconvenient to the servient owner and is reasonably sufficient for the purpose. The easement arises from the transfer and not from mere use before it, and it is not available to a person who bought land knowing it to be landlocked from a stranger who had never owned the neighbouring land. The doctrine of easement of necessity is based on the presumed intention of the parties at the time of transfer, and not on the court's view of fairness to the person who is shut in. It arises only when the land was one before the transfer and was divided by the transfer. Where the dominant owner has acquired land that is landlocked from a person who never owned the land over which he claims a way, the doctrine does not apply, and the owner must seek other remedies such as an agreement with the neighbour or a statutory right of way. The extent of the right is limited to what is necessary, so that it can be used only for the purposes for which the land was granted and not for greater uses.

Facts: Vasant owns two plots, A and B, adjoining a public road only at A. He sells B to Wilma, and B is completely enclosed by A and other private land, with no access to the public road. Wilma claims a right of way over A. In another case, Xavier sells plot D to Yamini, which touches the public road on one side but whose road side is rocky, making a pathway from the road very costly to build; Yamini claims a right of way over Xavier's neighbouring plot E instead. Decide.

options.A: Wilma has an easement of necessity over A; Yamini has none, because her plot already has road access at higher cost
options.B: Both have easements of necessity, because both plots are difficult to reach
options.C: Neither has an easement, because a right of way needs a written grant
options.D: Yamini has an easement and Wilma does not, because Yamini's access cost is higher

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Plot B is entirely enclosed by land of the transferor, so Wilma's easement is implied. Yamini's plot has access to the road, though costly, so there is no absolute necessity. Shortcut: absolute necessity vs mere inconvenience. Trap (B): Ignoring the exception. Necessity must be absolute, not merely inconvenience or cost. Trap (C): Importing an outside rule. The easement of necessity is implied by law and needs no grant. Trap (D): Reversal of principle. The easement is for absolutely enclosed land, so Wilma qualifies.

questions.question_text: A tank is 3/8 full. After 30 litres are poured in, it is 7/8 full. What is the capacity of the tank?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The added water raises the level from 3/8 to 7/8, i.e. by 4/8 = 1/2 of the capacity. So 30 L is half the tank and the capacity is 60 L. Shortcut: subtract the fractions first; the added quantity equals that difference. Trap (A): divides 30 by the initial fraction 3/8 instead of by the added fraction. Trap (B): divides 30 by 1/8 after misreading the difference of 7/8 and 3/8 as 1/8. Trap (C): treats the 30 L as one quarter of the tank.
questions.verify_code:
import math
x = 30/(7/8 - 3/8)
opts = {'A': 80.0, 'B': 240.0, 'C': 120.0, 'D': 60.0}
m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]
answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.concept_tag: Averages - mean of an arithmetic sequence
questions.question_text: What is the mean of the first 15 positive multiples of 4?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The terms are 4, 8, ..., 60 in AP. The mean of an AP is the average of the first and last terms: (4 + 60)/2 = 32. Shortcut: mean of an AP = (first + last)/2. Trap (A): takes the middle position as 7.5 instead of 8, giving 4 × 7.5. Trap (C): adds the first and last terms and forgets to halve. Trap (D): reports the last term instead of the mean.
questions.verify_code:
import math
x = (4 + 60)/2
opts = {'A': 30.0, 'B': 32.0, 'C': 64.0, 'D': 60.0}
m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]
answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.question_text: A rectangular room measures 6 m by 4.5 m. It is to be covered with square tiles of side 30 cm. How many tiles are needed?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Tiles along the length: 6 / 0.3 = 20. Tiles along the breadth: 4.5 / 0.3 = 15. Total = 20 × 15 = 300. (Check by area: 27 m² ÷ 0.09 m² = 300.) Shortcut: convert to the same unit and count along each side. Trap (A): divides the area in square metres (27) by the tile side in metres (0.3). Trap (B): takes the tile's area as 0.03 square metres. Trap (D): reports the area of the room instead of the number of tiles.

questions.question_text: At a meeting, each of 12 people shakes hands exactly once with every other person. How many handshakes take place?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Each handshake is an unordered pair of people: C(12, 2) = 12 × 11 / 2 = 66. Shortcut: divide the ordered count by 2. Trap (A): counts each handshake twice, as 12 × 11. Trap (B): squares the number of people. Trap (C): counts 13 people, C(13, 2).

questions.concept_tag: Geometry - sides from the number of diagonals
questions.question_text: A convex polygon has 20 diagonals. How many sides does it have?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The number of diagonals is n(n - 3)/2. Set n(n - 3)/2 = 20, so n(n - 3) = 40, giving n = 8 (8 × 5 = 40). Shortcut: test n(n - 3) = 2 × diagonals. Trap (A): a heptagon has only 14 diagonals. Trap (B): a nonagon has 27 diagonals. Trap (D): a decagon has 35 diagonals.

questions.concept_tag: Number System - digits used in page numbers
questions.question_text: How many digits are used in numbering the pages of a book from 1 to 120?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Pages 10 to 99 are 90 pages with 2 digits each: 180. Pages 100 to 120 are 21 pages with 3 digits each: 63. Total = 9 + 180 + 63 = 252. Shortcut: split by number of digits. Trap (A): treats every page number as having 3 digits. Trap (C): treats every page number as having 2 digits. Trap (D): counts 20 three-digit pages (100 to 119) instead of 21.

questions.question_text: A solid cube of edge 12 cm is cut into 8 equal smaller cubes. By how much does the total surface area increase?

options.B: 432 cm²
options.C: 864 cm²
options.D: 216 cm²

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The original surface area is 6 × 144 = 864. Each small cube has edge 6, so area 216; eight cubes give 1,728. The increase is 1,728 - 864 = 864. Shortcut: each cut plane adds two faces; three cuts of 144 each add 6 × 144 = 864. Trap (A): reports the new total surface area, not the increase. Trap (B): halves the increase. Trap (D): gives the surface area of one small cube.
questions.verify_code:
import math
x = 8*6*6**2 - 6*12**2
opts = {'A': 1728.0, 'B': 432.0, 'C': 864.0, 'D': 216.0}
m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]
answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.concept_tag: HCF - largest square tile for a floor
questions.question_text: A floor measures 6.6 m by 4.2 m. What is the side, in centimetres, of the largest square tile that can cover the floor exactly without cutting any tile?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In centimetres the floor is 660 by 420. The side must divide both exactly, so it is HCF(660, 420) = 60. Shortcut: convert to the same unit and take the HCF. Trap (B): is a common factor of 660 and 420 but not the greatest one. Trap (C): is a common factor of 660 and 420 but not the greatest one. Trap (D): takes the HCF of 66 and 42 and forgets to convert back to centimetres.

questions.question_text: How many different 3-letter arrangements can be made from the letters of the word LOGIC if no letter is used more than once?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The word LOGIC has 5 different letters. The arrangements of 3 of them: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60. Shortcut: choose positions one by one: 5, 4, 3. Trap (A): counts selections of 3 letters and ignores their order. Trap (C): allows letters to be repeated, 5 × 5 × 5. Trap (D): arranges all 5 letters.

questions.concept_tag: Mensuration - area outside an inscribed circle
questions.question_text: A circle is drawn inside a square of side 14 cm so that it touches all four sides. What is the area, in square centimetres, of the part of the square outside the circle? (Take π = 22/7.)
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The circle has diameter 14, so radius 7 and area (22/7) × 49 = 154. The square has area 196. The region outside is 196 - 154 = 42. Shortcut: the inscribed circle's diameter equals the side of the square. Trap (B): reports the area of the circle. Trap (C): reports the area of the whole square. Trap (D): takes half the area of the square.

questions.concept_tag: Polygons - sides from an interior angle
questions.question_text: Each interior angle of a regular polygon measures 140°. How many sides does the polygon have?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The exterior angle is 180° - 140° = 40°. The exterior angles of any convex polygon add up to 360°, so n = 360/40 = 9. Shortcut: always work with the exterior angle: n = 360/exterior. Trap (A): 3 rounds 360/140 ≈ 2.57 up to 3, treating 140° as the angle at the centre. Trap (C): reports the exterior angle. Trap (D): divides 140 by 10.

questions.question_text: If 2^(x + 3) = 8^(x - 1), what is x?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Write 8 = 2³, so 8^(x - 1) = 2^(3x - 3). Equate exponents: x + 3 = 3x - 3, so 2x = 6 and x = 3. Shortcut: reduce both sides to one base, then equate exponents. Trap (A): writes 8 as 2² and gets 2x - 2 = x + 3. Trap (B): forgets the -1 in the exponent and solves x + 3 = 3x. Trap (D): negates the right-hand exponent and solves x + 3 = -(3x - 3).

questions.question_text: In how many ways can 5 different books be arranged on a shelf so that two particular books are always together?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Glue the two books into one block. Then 4 units can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways, and the block's internal order gives × 2: 48. Shortcut: treat the pair as one object, then multiply by its internal arrangements. Trap (A): forgets that the pair can be ordered in 2 ways. Trap (B): ignores the condition. Trap (C): multiplies by 2 twice.
questions.verify_code:
import math
x = math.factorial(4)*2
opts = {'A': 24.0, 'B': 120.0, 'C': 96.0, 'D': 48.0}
m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]
answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.question_text: What is the value of log₂ 64 - log₃ 81?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: log₂ 64 = 6 since 2⁶ = 64 and log₃ 81 = 4 since 3⁴ = 81. So 6 - 4 = 2. Shortcut: convert each log to an exponent count first. Trap (A): adds the logarithms instead of subtracting. Trap (B): divides 6 by 4. Trap (D): subtracts in the wrong order.

opts = {'A': 10.0, 'B': 1.5, 'C': 2.0, 'D': -2.0}
m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]
answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.question_text: ₹83 equals $1, and €1 equals $1.10. How many rupees equal €100?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: €100 = $110. Then $110 × ₹83 = ₹9,130. Shortcut: convert step by step: euro to dollar, dollar to rupee. Trap (B): divides by 1.10 instead of multiplying. Trap (C): ignores the euro-dollar rate and converts 100 dollars. Trap (D): gives the dollar value of €100 and not the rupee value.

questions.concept_tag: Linear Equations - price of an item
questions.question_text: 5 notebooks and 3 pens cost ₹99, and 2 notebooks and 3 pens cost ₹54. What is the price of one notebook, in rupees?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Subtract the second equation from the first: 3 notebooks cost 99 - 54 = ₹45, so a notebook costs ₹15 (and a pen ₹8). Shortcut: subtract the equations to eliminate the pens. Trap (A): reports the price of a pen. Trap (B): divides ₹99 by 5 as if only notebooks were bought. Trap (C): divides ₹54 by 2 as if only notebooks were bought.

questions.question_text: A 60 L solution contains 40% acid. How much water must evaporate for the solution to become 50% acid?

options.B: 6 L

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Acid = 0.4 × 60 = 24 L and it does not change on evaporation. For 50% acid the total must be 24 / 0.5 = 48 L, so 60 - 48 = 12 L must evaporate. Shortcut: the solute is the invariant: new total = solute / new fraction. Trap (A): treats the 10 percentage points of increase as 10 litres. Trap (B): takes 10% of the 60 L. Trap (D): reports the quantity of acid, not the water removed.
questions.verify_code:

x = 60 - 0.4*60/0.5
opts = {'A': 10.0, 'B': 6.0, 'C': 12.0, 'D': 24.0}
m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]

questions.concept_tag: Coordinate Geometry - reflection in a slanted line
questions.question_text: The point (3, 5) is reflected in the line y = x + 1. What is the x-coordinate of its image?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The point (3, 5) has y - x - 1 = 1. The mirror image has the same distance on the other side: reflection in y = x + 1 maps (x, y) to (y - 1, x + 1). So (3, 5) goes to (4, 4). The x-coordinate is 4. Shortcut: reflection in y = x + c maps (x, y) to (y - c, x + c). Trap (B): reflects in the line y = x and ignores the shift by 1. Trap (C): reflects in the line y = x - 1 instead. Trap (D): leaves the x-coordinate unchanged.

questions.concept_tag: Counting - divisible by 3 but not by 9
questions.question_text: How many integers from 1 to 1,000 are divisible by 3 but not by 9?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Multiples of 3: ⌊1000/3⌋ = 333. Multiples of 9 (which are also multiples of 3): ⌊1000/9⌋ = 111. Required = 333 - 111 = 222. Shortcut: count the larger set, then subtract the subset. Trap (A): counts all multiples of 3 without removing multiples of 9. Trap (B): counts only the multiples of 9. Trap (D): counts the numbers not divisible by 9.

questions.concept_tag: Probability - at least one without replacement
questions.question_text: Two balls are drawn one after the other, without replacement, from a bag holding 5 red and 3 blue balls. What is the probability that at least one of the two balls is blue?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: P(no blue) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56 = 5/14. So P(at least one blue) = 1 - 5/14 = 9/14. Shortcut: use the complement: 1 - P(none). Trap (A): this is the probability that both balls are red. Trap (B): this is the probability of exactly one blue ball. Trap (C): this is the probability of a blue ball on a single draw.

questions.concept_tag: Number System - divisors with a condition
questions.question_text: How many positive divisors of 360 are multiples of 6?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A divisor that is a multiple of 6 is 6 × d where d divides 360/6 = 60. 60 = 2² × 3 × 5 has 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 divisors, so there are 12. Shortcut: divisors of N that are multiples of k = divisors of N/k (when k divides N). Trap (A): counts all divisors of 360. Trap (C): counts the divisors that are multiples of 3 only. Trap (D): divides 360 by 6 and reports the quotient instead of counting its divisors.
questions.verify_code:

x = sum(1 for d in range(1,361) if 360 % d == 0 and d % 6 == 0)
opts = {'A': 24.0, 'B': 12.0, 'C': 16.0, 'D': 60.0}
m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]
answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.concept_tag: Permutations and Combinations - identical items with a minimum
questions.question_text: In how many ways can 10 identical sweets be distributed among 4 children so that each child gets at least one sweet?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Give each child 1 sweet first; 6 remain to be distributed freely among 4 children: C(6 + 3, 3) = C(9, 3) = 84. Shortcut: stars and bars: with a minimum of 1, choose 3 gaps out of the 9 between 10 sweets. Trap (A): allows a child to get none: C(13, 3). Trap (C): uses C(9, 4), choosing the wrong number of dividers. Trap (D): uses C(10, 4).

questions.question_text: Four letters are placed at random into four addressed envelopes, one in each. What is the probability that no letter is in its correct envelope?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Derangements of 4 objects = 4!(1 - 1 + 1/2 - 1/6 + 1/24) = 9. So the probability is 9/24 = 3/8. Shortcut: for n = 4 the number of derangements is 9; memorise 0, 1, 2, 9, 44. Trap (A): treats the four envelopes as independent, each with a 3/4 chance of a wrong letter. Trap (B): gives the probability that every letter is correct. Trap (C): gives the probability that at least one letter is correct.

m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]
answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.concept_tag: Geometry - square in a right triangle
questions.question_text: A square is drawn inside a right triangle with legs 15 and 10 so that one corner of the square is at the right-angle vertex and the opposite corner lies on the hypotenuse. What is the side of the square?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: By similar triangles, if the side is s then s/10 = (15 - s)/15, so 15s = 150 - 10s and s = 6. In general s = ab/(a + b). Shortcut: s = ab/(a + b) = 150/25. Trap (A): takes half of the shorter leg. Trap (B): takes half of the longer leg. Trap (D): takes the mean of the two legs.

opts = {'A': 5.0, 'B': 7.5, 'C': 6.0, 'D': 12.5}
m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]
answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.concept_tag: Logarithms - number of digits of a power
questions.question_text: Given that log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010, how many digits does 5²⁰ have?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: log₁₀ 5²⁰ = 20 × (1 - 0.3010) = 20 × 0.6990 = 13.98. A number with logarithm 13.98 has ⌊13.98⌋ + 1 = 14 digits. Shortcut: digits = ⌊log₁₀ N⌋ + 1. Trap (B): takes the integer part of the logarithm and forgets to add 1. Trap (C): rounds 13.98 up and then adds 1. Trap (D): takes the exponent as the number of digits.

questions.question_text: A function f satisfies f(0) = 0 and f(x + 1) = f(x) + 2x + 1 for every x. What is f(10)?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: f(1) = 1, f(2) = 1 + 3 = 4, f(3) = 4 + 5 = 9. The increments 1, 3, 5, ... are odd numbers, so f(n) = n², and f(10) = 100. Shortcut: telescope: the sum of the first n odd numbers is n². Trap (A): adds the first ten positive integers. Trap (B): multiplies 10 by 11. Trap (C): evaluates 2 × 10 + 1, a single step.

x = f

m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]
answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.question_text: The average mark of 25 students is 60. When the 5 highest scorers, whose average is 80, are removed, what is the average of the remaining students?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total = 25 × 60 = 1,500. Removed = 5 × 80 = 400. Remaining = 1,100 over 20 students, so the average is 55. Shortcut: work with totals, not averages. Trap (A): divides the removed surplus by 25 instead of 20. Trap (B): assumes the average does not change. Trap (D): subtracts the gap of 20 from the original average.

questions.question_text: A loan of ₹21,000 is repaid in two equal annual instalments, the first due after one year. If interest is 10% per annum compounded annually, what is each instalment?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let each instalment be x. Present value: x/1.1 + x/1.21 = 21,000, so x × (110 + 100)/121 = 21,000 and x = 21,000 × 121/210 = 12,100. Shortcut: discount each instalment back to today and equate to the loan. Trap (A): splits the principal equally, ignoring interest. Trap (B): adds one year of simple interest and splits the total. questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed and Distance - round trip with total time
questions.question_text: Asha walks from her home to a station at 4 km/h and returns at 6 km/h. She spends 5 hours walking in all. What is the one-way distance?

options.A: 24 km
options.B: 12 km
options.C: 25 km
options.D: 30 km

questions.question_text: A positive integer N leaves remainder 7 when divided by 9. What is the remainder when N³ + N is divided by 9?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: N ≡ 7 ≡ -2 (mod 9). Then N³ ≡ -8 ≡ 1 (mod 9), so N³ + N ≡ 1 + 7 = 8. Shortcut: reduce to a small negative residue before taking powers. questions.concept_tag: Coordinate Geometry - distance from a line
questions.question_text: What is the perpendicular distance of the point (1, 2) from the line 3x + 4y - 5 = 0?

questions.concept_tag: Probability - conditional on at least one hit
questions.question_text: Archers A and B hit a target independently with probabilities 0.6 and 0.5 respectively, and each fires once. Given that the target is hit at least once, what is the probability that exactly one of them hit it?

questions.concept_tag: Geometry - overlap of two quarter circles
questions.question_text: ABCD is a square of side 10 cm. Quarter circles of radius 10 cm are drawn inside the square with centres A and B, where A and B are adjacent vertices. What is the area common to the two quarter circles?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The two arcs meet at the point 5 cm from AB's midpoint line, forming an equilateral triangle with A and B. The overlap equals two 60° sectors (each 100π/6) minus that triangle (25√3): 100π/3 - 25√3 ≈ 61.4 cm². Shortcut: overlap of two sectors = sum of sectors - the equilateral triangle. Trap (A): reports the full lens of two overlapping circles, not the half inside the square. Trap (B): reports the area of one quarter circle. Trap (D): subtracts twice the equilateral triangle's area.

questions.question_text: A walker moves from (0, 0) to (5, 5) taking unit steps right or up, and never goes above the line y = x (she may touch it). How many such paths are there?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total paths = C(10, 5) = 252. Using the reflection method, the bad paths (that cross above) number C(10, 4) = 210. The good paths are 252 - 210 = 42, the fifth Catalan number. Shortcut: these paths are counted by the Catalan number C(2n, n)/(n + 1). Trap (A): counts all lattice paths, C(10, 5). Trap (B): halves all paths using symmetry, ignoring paths that touch the line. Trap (C): uses the Catalan number for 6 steps.

questions.concept_tag: Expectation - waiting for two consecutive heads
questions.question_text: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly until two heads appear in a row. What is the expected number of tosses?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let E be the expectation from the start and F after one head. E = 1 + (1/2)F + (1/2)E and F = 1 + (1/2)(0) + (1/2)E. From the first, E = 2 + F; the second gives F = 1 + E/2. So E = 2 + 1 + E/2, giving E = 6. Shortcut: set up one equation per state (no head yet, one head). Trap (B): uses 1/p with p = 1/4 for a fixed pair of tosses. Trap (C): uses 2³. Trap (D): gives the expected tosses for three heads in a row.
questions.verify_code:
import math
from fractions import Fraction
x = Fraction(3,2)/(1 - Fraction(3,4))
opts = {'A': 6.0, 'B': 4.0, 'C': 8.0, 'D': 14.0}
m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]
answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.concept_tag: Inequalities - weighted AM-GM with three variables
questions.question_text: Positive reals x, y and z satisfy x + y + z = 12. What is the maximum value of x y² z?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Write x y² z as x · y · y · z and split y into two halves: the four quantities x, y/2, y/2, z have sum 12 and are equal at the maximum: each is 3. So x = 3, y = 6, z = 3 and the maximum is 3 × 36 × 3 = 324. Shortcut: give each variable a share in proportion to its exponent. Trap (A): takes x = y = z = 4. Trap (C): takes x = 4, y = 5, z = 3 without the 1 : 2 : 1 rule. Trap (D): takes x = 2, y = 6, z = 4.

questions.question_text: How many real solutions does the equation ∣∣∣x∣ - 2∣ - 3∣ = 1 have?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: ∣∣x∣ - 2∣ - 3 = ±1 gives ∣∣x∣ - 2∣ = 4 or 2. Then ∣x∣ - 2 = ±4 or ±2, so ∣x∣ = 6, -2, 4 or 0. ∣x∣ = -2 is impossible. The solutions are x = ±6, ±4 and 0: five in all. Shortcut: peel the modulus from the outside in and reject any branch that makes ∣x∣ negative. Trap (A): discards x = 0. Trap (B): counts x = 0 twice and keeps a negative value of ∣x∣. Trap (C): takes both signs at every level without rejecting ∣x∣ = -2.

opts = {'A': 4.0, 'B': 7.0, 'C': 8.0, 'D': 5.0}

answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.question_text: Ravi climbs a moving escalator and takes 15 steps, taking 30 seconds. Tara climbs the same escalator at twice Ravi's stepping rate and takes 20 steps. How many steps are visible on the escalator when it is stopped?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Ravi steps at 15/30 = 0.5 step/s, so Tara steps at 1 step/s and takes 20 seconds. If the escalator moves e steps/s, the visible steps N = 15 + 30e = 20 + 20e, so e = 0.5 and N = 30. Shortcut: N = steps taken + steps carried by the escalator; equate for both people. Trap (B): adds the two step counts. Trap (C): averages the two step counts. Trap (D): takes the mean of 20 and 30.

questions.question_text: Vessel A holds 30 L of milk and vessel B holds 30 L of water. 10 L is poured from A into B and mixed well. Then 10 L is poured from B back into A. How much water is now in A?

options.D: 5 L

questions.pedagogical_explanation: After the first move, B has 40 L: 10 L milk and 30 L water. Pouring back 10 L takes a quarter of B: 2.5 L milk and 7.5 L water. So A now holds 7.5 L of water. Shortcut: the returning 10 L is a quarter of B, so it carries a quarter of each ingredient. Trap (A): reports the milk that came back. Trap (C): assumes the returning litres are all water. Trap (D): takes the average of 2.5 and 7.5.

questions.concept_tag: Coordinate Geometry - shortest path by reflection
questions.question_text: A ray of light travels from A(1, 2) to the x-axis and then reflects to B(7, 4). What is the length of the shortest such path?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Reflect A in the x-axis to A'(1, -2). The shortest path via the axis equals A'B = √((7 - 1)² + (4 + 2)²) = √72 = 6√2. Shortcut: reflect one point across the mirror line and join straight to the other. Trap (A): gives the straight-line distance AB, ignoring the touch on the axis. Trap (B): adds the horizontal distance and the two heights. Trap (D): adds the two heights 2 + 4.

questions.question_text: A number is chosen at random from 1 to 100. What is the probability that it is coprime to 100?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 100 = 2² × 5². Numbers coprime to 100 avoid the primes 2 and 5: 100 × (1 - 1/2)(1 - 1/5) = 40. Probability = 40/100 = 2/5. Shortcut: use φ(n) = n ∏ (1 - 1/p). Trap (A): excludes only the multiples of 2. Trap (C): subtracts 1/2 and 1/5 from 1, double-counting multiples of 10. Trap (D): excludes only the multiples of 5.

questions.question_text: What is the sum of all the digits used in writing the numbers from 1 to 99?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Pair the numbers as 00 to 99. Each digit 0 to 9 appears 10 times in the units place and 10 times in the tens place. Sum = 2 × 10 × 45 = 900. Shortcut: treat 0 to 99 as two-digit strings; every digit is equally frequent in each place. Trap (B): counts only the units digits. Trap (C): 990 multiplies 99 numbers by an assumed average digit sum of 10 instead of adding the digits place by place. Trap (D): leaves out the digit 9's contribution in the tens place.

questions.concept_tag: Progressions - zero term of an AP
questions.question_text: In an arithmetic progression the 5th term is 12 and the 12th term is 5. Which term of the progression is zero?

options.A: 16th
options.B: 18th
options.C: 17th
options.D: 19th

questions.pedagogical_explanation: d = (5 - 12)/7 = -1, so a = 12 + 4 = 16. The nth term 16 - (n - 1) = 0 gives n = 17. (In general a₍ₚ₊q₎ = 0 when aₚ = q and a_q = p.) Shortcut: if aₚ = q and a_q = p then the (p + q)th term is zero. Trap (A): confuses the first term 16 with the position. Trap (B): is off by one after dividing. Trap (D): is off by two.

questions.concept_tag: Combinatorics - subsets with a forbidden difference
questions.question_text: What is the largest possible size of a subset of {1, 2, ..., 20} in which no two elements differ by exactly 5?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Split the numbers by remainder mod 5. Each class forms a chain of four numbers r, r + 5, r + 10, r + 15, in which neighbours differ by 5. From a chain of four, at most 2 can be chosen (alternate ones). So the maximum is 5 × 2 = 10. Shortcut: split into independent chains; in a chain of length k at most ⌈k/2⌉ can be chosen. Trap (A): keeps all numbers except a few, ignoring chain structure. Trap (B): 15 removes only one number from each of the five chains k, k + 5, k + 10, k + 15, which still leaves pairs 5 apart. Trap (C): 8 takes two numbers from only four of the five chains and forgets the fifth chain.

import math
import itertools
total = 0
for r in range(1,6):
    chain = [r, r+5, r+10, r+15]
    best = 0
    for mask in range(16):
        pick = [chain[i] for i in range(4) if mask >> i & 1]
        if all(abs(a-b) != 5 for a in pick for b in pick):
            best = max(best, len(pick))
    total += best
x = total
opts = {'A': 12.0, 'B': 15.0, 'C': 8.0, 'D': 10.0}
m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]
answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.concept_tag: Counting - ordered triples with a given product
questions.question_text: How many ordered triples (a, b, c) of positive integers satisfy abc = 72?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 72 = 2³ × 3². Distribute the three 2s among a, b, c: C(5, 2) = 10 ways. Distribute the two 3s: C(4, 2) = 6 ways. By independence, 10 × 6 = 60. Shortcut: for each prime, count exponent distributions by stars and bars, then multiply. Trap (B): adds the counts for the two primes instead of multiplying them. Trap (C): counts the divisors of 72. Trap (D): treats the three positions as distinct for each prime and double counts.

questions.question_text: Mira starts with ₹2 and plays a fair game, winning or losing ₹1 each round with equal probability, until she has either ₹0 or ₹5. What is the probability that she ends with ₹5?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In a fair game her expected wealth is constant. If p is the chance of reaching 5, then 5p + 0(1 - p) = 2, so p = 2/5. Shortcut: fair game means a martingale: starting wealth = p × target. Trap (A): assumes a fair game gives equal chances of the two ends. Trap (B): gives the probability of ruin. Trap (C): uses 2 out of 3 as the ratio of her money to the distance to ruin.

questions.concept_tag: Counting - isosceles triangles in a polygon
questions.question_text: Three vertices are chosen from a regular 12-gon to form a triangle. How many of the triangles are isosceles but not equilateral?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Count by apex: each vertex is the apex of 5 isosceles triangles (equal sides to vertex pairs at distances 1 to 5 steps), giving 60. Each of the 4 equilateral triangles is counted 3 times, so distinct isosceles triangles = 60 - 2 × 4 = 52. Removing the 4 equilateral ones gives 48. Shortcut: count by apex, then fix the triple-counted equilateral triangles. Trap (A): counts 12 × 5 apex choices, which counts each equilateral triangle three times. Trap (C): subtracts the 4 equilateral triangles only once from 60. Trap (D): counts all isosceles triangles, including equilateral ones.

import math
import itertools
cnt = 0
for a,b,c in itertools.combinations(range(12),3):
    d1 = min(b-a, 12-(b-a))
    d2 = min(c-b, 12-(c-b))
    d3 = min(c-a, 12-(c-a))
    s = sorted([d1,d2,d3])
    if len(set(s)) == 2:
        cnt += 1
x = cnt
opts = {'A': 60.0, 'B': 48.0, 'C': 56.0, 'D': 52.0}
m = [k for k,v in opts.items() if abs(v - x) < 1e-6]
answer = m[0] if len(m) == 1 else 'x'

questions.concept_tag: Inequalities - minimising a product of sums
questions.question_text: For positive reals x and y with x + y = 1, what is the minimum value of (x + 1/x)(y + 1/y)?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Expand: (x + 1/x)(y + 1/y) = xy + 1/(xy) + x/y + y/x. With p = xy ≤ 1/4: xy + 1/(xy) decreases for p < 1 and is smallest at p = 1/4 (value 17/4), while x/y + y/x = (1 - 2p)/p = 2 at p = 1/4. The sum is 17/4 + 2 = 25/4 at x = y = 1/2. Shortcut: by symmetry check x = y = 1/2, since each factor is decreasing in xy. Trap (A): minimises each factor separately using x + 1/x ≥ 2. Trap (B): tests x = 1/3 and stops. Trap (D): adds the two factors at x = y = 1/2 instead of multiplying them.

questions.question_text:
Passage: The green of summer leaves comes from chlorophyll, the pigment that captures sunlight for the tree's food. Yellow and orange pigments are present all along, but the large amount of chlorophyll hides them. As days shorten and nights turn cool, the tree stops making chlorophyll and the existing supply breaks down. The colours that were masked now show through, which is why the leaves of some trees turn yellow. The reds that brighten certain trees are different: they are made fresh in autumn, in leaves that still hold sugars trapped by cold nights and bright days. Brown, meanwhile, comes from waste products left in the leaf after the other pigments fade. The sequence is not a sign that the leaf is dying suddenly; it is the tree drawing useful materials back from its leaves before winter, and the colours are a by-product of that withdrawal.

According to the passage, why do the leaves of some trees turn yellow in autumn?

options.A: The tree makes new yellow pigment when the days shorten
options.B: The chlorophyll that had hidden the yellow pigments breaks down
options.C: Sugars become trapped in the leaf by cold nights
options.D: Waste products build up in the leaf

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says yellow pigments are present all along but masked, and when chlorophyll breaks down they show through. Shortcut: separate the yellow, red and brown explanations. Trap (A): Reversal. The passage says yellow pigments are present all along; it is the reds that are made fresh. Trap (C): Half-true. This explains the reds, not the yellows. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The passage ties waste products to the brown colour.

questions.question_text:
Passage: When tea first arrived in Britain in quantity, it was a luxury sold by the ounce and kept under lock in ornate caddies. Only households with money to spare could afford it, and serving it was a way of showing that one could. Over the next century the picture changed. Heavy duties were reduced, smuggled supplies were squeezed out by cheaper legal ones, and larger ships brought bigger cargoes. Prices fell, and tea moved from the drawing room to the kitchen table. Factory workers began to drink it sweetened and hot, because it was cheap, easy to prepare and gave a sense of warmth and energy through long shifts. By the time the habit had spread to every class, the locked caddy had become a curiosity, and a drink that once marked status had become a daily necessity.

The passage is mainly about

options.A: how tea duties were designed and why smugglers opposed them
options.B: why factory workers in particular came to prefer tea to every other drink
options.C: how tea turned from a status luxury into an everyday drink, and the reasons for the shift
options.D: the way tea has always been a necessity in every class of British society

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage traces a change over time: luxury at first, then falling duties, smuggling and cargo costs made it cheap, and finally it was a daily necessity. The option that captures both the change and the reasons is the answer. Shortcut: a main-idea answer must cover the whole arc, not one stage. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Duties and smuggling are only two of the causes mentioned; the passage does not discuss how duties were designed or why smugglers resisted. Trap (B): Half-true. Factory workers are one stage of the spread, not the whole subject. Trap (D): Reversal. The passage says tea began as a luxury only the wealthy could afford.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Most people know that the tides follow the moon, but the sun also pulls on the oceans, with about half the strength of the moon. When the sun, Earth and moon line up, at new moon and at full moon, the two pulls add together and the sea rises higher and falls lower than usual. These are called spring tides, a name that has nothing to do with the season. A week later, when the moon is at a quarter and the sun and the moon pull at right angles to each other, their effects partly cancel. The tides are then weaker, with a smaller gap between high and low water, and are called neap tides. Harbour authorities publish tables for both, because a ship that clears the harbour mouth with ease at a spring tide may scrape the bottom at a neap tide.

According to the passage, neap tides occur when

options.A: the sun and the moon pull at right angles to each other
options.B: the sun, Earth and moon form a straight line
options.C: the sun's pull on the oceans is absent
options.D: it is the spring season of the year

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says that at a quarter moon the pulls act at right angles and partly cancel, giving neap tides. Shortcut: spot the 'at right angles' phrase tied to neap tides. Trap (B): Reversal. A straight line gives spring tides, when the pulls add. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The passage says the pulls only partly cancel; the sun's pull never disappears. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The passage says the term 'spring' has nothing to do with the season.

questions.question_text:
Passage: In the closing decades of the nineteenth century, the safety bicycle with two equal wheels became cheap enough for ordinary families. Contemporaries noticed at once that it changed more than the way people got to work. A young woman who owned a bicycle could now ride beyond the neighbourhood without a chaperone or a carriage, and could do so on her own timetable. Dress reformers pointed out that long skirts were dangerous near a chain and wheel, and many women adopted looser clothing that did not return to fashion's old forms. Clubs of women cyclists formed, and some newspapers complained that the bicycle was upsetting the established order. Historians still debate how large its effect was, but few doubt that it gave many women a new sense of what they were free to do.

The author's main point is that the bicycle

options.A: was the sole cause of women's freedom in the period
options.B: was invented by women who wanted to travel without a chaperone
options.C: mattered mainly because it made clothing more fashionable
options.D: widened many women's independence in ways that went beyond transport

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage moves from cheap bicycles to independent travel, dress change and women's clubs, ending that it gave women 'a new sense of what they were free to do'. That is a wider independence than just transport. Shortcut: distrust 'sole' or 'only' in answer choices unless the text uses them. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The passage says historians debate its effect; it never claims sole cause. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. The passage says nothing about who invented it. Trap (C): Half-true. Dress change is one effect mentioned, not the main point.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Farmers have lived on the slopes of active volcanoes for as long as there are records, and the reason is not carelessness. Fresh volcanic ash is rich in minerals, and as it weathers it releases them slowly into the soil. A field that is dusted with ash can therefore produce good harvests for years without added fertiliser. The danger is real: an eruption can destroy crops and homes within hours. Yet communities near volcanoes often describe the mountain as a provider, and they treat its occasional violence as the price of a generosity that lasts far longer than any single disaster. Where the soil is poor in the plains below, the choice looks very different. Local sayings record this bargain, and young farmers take up plots on the slopes knowing the history of earlier eruptions.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: Volcanic eruptions are rarely dangerous to farming communities
options.B: Farmers near volcanoes may judge the long-term benefit of mineral-rich soil to outweigh the risk of eruptions
options.C: Farmers on plains never grow crops as successfully as farmers on volcanic slopes
options.D: Fertiliser is harmful to soil that already contains volcanic minerals

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says farmers stay because of the rich ash, treating eruptions as a price worth paying. The first option is a safe restatement of this idea. Shortcut: an inference must be directly supported; prefer the option that restates the logic. Trap (A): Reversal. The passage says an eruption can destroy crops and homes within hours. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The passage only says the choice looks different where plains soil is poor. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. Nothing in the passage suggests that fertiliser is harmful.

questions.question_text:
Passage: The electric telegraph was once the fastest way to send a message over a long distance, and for several decades it had no rival. Operators tapped out words in code, and a message that had taken weeks by ship could now arrive in minutes. Businesses used it to learn prices in distant markets, newspapers used it to collect news, and governments used it to send orders. But the telegraph was costly, since each word was paid for, and a message had to be carried by hand from the office to the person who was to read it. When the telephone spread, people could speak directly and without writing, and the telegraph slowly lost its customers. Most services were closed long ago, but the habit of writing messages in brief, clipped phrases is a memory of the days when each word cost money.

According to the passage, one reason the telegraph lost its customers was that

options.A: operators found the code too hard to learn
options.B: businesses no longer wanted news about distant markets
options.C: governments refused to pay for each word sent
options.D: the telephone allowed people to speak directly without writing out a message

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says the telephone let people speak directly, and 'the telegraph slowly lost its customers'. Shortcut: find the sentence that contains the cause and check the option matches it. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The passage says nothing about the code being hard to learn. Trap (B): Reversal. The passage says businesses used it to learn prices and news; it does not say they lost interest. Trap (C): Half-true. The passage says each word was paid for, but not that governments refused to pay.

questions.question_text:
Passage: High mountain glaciers are often called water towers, and the name is well chosen. In winter, snow piles up on the heights and compresses into ice. In summer, as the weather warms, the glacier releases meltwater that feeds rivers just when the plains below are driest and farms need irrigation most. A glacier thus works like a reservoir that fills in the cold season and empties in the warm, smoothing out the year. Cities and farms downstream may be hundreds of kilometres away and may never see the ice, yet their supply is tied to it. When glaciers shrink, the extra melt first raises river flows, which can look like good news. Over a longer period, with less ice left to melt, flows fall, and the regions that depended on that steady summer supply find that the tower has been drawn down.

The main point of the passage is that glaciers

options.A: are the main source of all the water used by farms
options.B: act as natural storage that supplies river water in the dry season, so their loss threatens downstream users
options.C: are important only for the cities that lie close to them
options.D: melt more quickly in winter than in summer

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage compares glaciers to reservoirs that release water in the dry summer, and warns that when ice is lost the flows fall. This matches the first option. Shortcut: pick the option that covers both the function and the warning. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The passage never says that farms depend on glaciers for all of their water. Trap (C): Reversal. The passage says even distant cities and farms depend on them. Trap (D): Reversal. Snow piles up in winter; the melt arrives in summer.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Certain bamboo species do something that few plants do: they flower together, over a very wide area, only once in several decades. Individual plants of a species may be scattered across many hills, yet they bloom within the same year or two. After flowering, the plants produce huge quantities of seed and then die. The sudden supply of seed feeds rodents, whose numbers rise sharply. When the seed runs out, hungry rodents turn to stored grain in nearby villages, and farmers may face famine. Biologists offer several explanations for the timing. One suggests that flowering so rarely and so suddenly produces more seed than seed-eaters can consume, which allows some seeds to survive and grow. How the plants keep count of the years remains unknown.

According to the passage, the hungry rodents that follow bamboo flowering

options.A: die when the bamboo plants die
options.B: are the reason that bamboo plants flower only once in decades
options.C: turn to stored grain in villages once the seed runs out
options.D: cannot eat bamboo seed because it is too plentiful

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says that when seed runs out, hungry rodents turn to stored grain in nearby villages. Shortcut: answer from the sentence about the rodents' behaviour. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The passage says the bamboo plants die, not the rodents. Trap (B): Reversal. Rodents are a consequence of flowering, not the cause of its timing. Trap (D): Reversal. The passage says the seed feeds the rodents and their numbers rise.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A language borrows words in much the same way that a household borrows tools: because it lacks one and finds a neighbour who has it. When a new object or idea arrives from outside, speakers usually take the foreign name along with it, and the word is gradually reshaped to fit local sounds. English took words for tea, cotton and pyjamas from the lands where they were first met, and many languages of Asia have words from English for machines and offices. Purists sometimes worry that borrowing damages a language, but the record suggests otherwise: languages that borrow freely continue to grow, and the borrowed words often become so ordinary that speakers forget they were ever foreign. Borrowing is, in this sense, a sign of contact and not of weakness.

Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.A: Borrowing words from other languages is a natural result of contact and does not weaken a language
options.B: Languages that borrow from others always lose their original vocabulary
