options.C: Purists are right to warn that borrowing damages a language
options.D: English has borrowed more words than any other language

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage compares borrowing to a household borrowing tools, rejects the purist worry and concludes it is 'a sign of contact and not of weakness'. Shortcut: the last sentence of a passage often states the central idea. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The passage says borrowed words become ordinary; it never says original words are lost. Trap (C): Reversal. The passage says the record suggests otherwise. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The passage gives examples but makes no comparison between languages.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Roman numerals served for centuries in trade, law and the marking of public buildings, yet they were awkward for calculation. The system has symbols for one, five, ten, fifty, one hundred and so on, and numbers are made by combining them. A merchant who wanted to add two long numbers had to rewrite them into a common form before he could total them, and multiplication was slower still. The system also had no symbol for zero, so there was no way to show an empty place. Calculators in Rome relied instead on counting boards, on which pebbles held the places that written numerals could not. When positional numerals with a zero reached Europe much later, sums that had once needed a counting board could be written and worked on paper.

According to the passage, Roman calculators used counting boards because

options.A: Roman law forbade written calculation
options.B: positional numerals were already widely known in Rome
options.C: written Roman numerals had no way of showing an empty place and were awkward for sums
options.D: Roman numerals could not be used in trade at all

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says the system had no symbol for zero and sums were awkward, so counting boards held places that written numerals could not. Shortcut: look for the stated reason, usually after 'because', 'so' or 'instead'. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The passage does not mention any such law. Trap (B): Reversal. The passage says positional numerals reached Europe much later. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The passage says they served in trade and law for centuries.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Long before refrigerators, people kept food from spoiling by changing its chemistry. In pickling with vinegar, the food is placed in an acid that most spoilage organisms cannot tolerate. In fermentation, the process is different: harmless bacteria already present on the vegetable turn its sugars into lactic acid, which in turn protects the food from harmful organisms. Sauerkraut and many traditional pickles are made this way, using little more than salt, which draws out water and favours the helpful bacteria. A fermented food may taste sour and develop new flavours, which many people value, but the sourness is a sign that the process is working. Both methods rely on the same basic idea: make the food unwelcoming to the organisms that cause decay.

According to the passage, in fermentation the protection against spoilage comes from

options.A: the vinegar in which the food is placed
options.B: the salt, which kills every organism in the vegetable
options.C: lactic acid made by harmless bacteria from the food's sugars
options.D: cold storage that slows the growth of bacteria

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage separates vinegar pickling from fermentation, where bacteria turn sugars into lactic acid that protects the food. Shortcut: keep two processes apart: the question names only one. Trap (A): Half-true. Vinegar is the method used in pickling, not fermentation. Trap (B): Extreme scope. Salt only draws out water and favours helpful bacteria; it does not kill every organism. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The passage begins by noting that these methods came before refrigeration.

questions.question_text:
Passage: In some wet hill regions, villagers have built bridges not from timber or steel but from the living roots of fig trees. A young tree is planted beside a stream, and its aerial roots are guided across the water, often along bamboo frames, and allowed to thicken and intertwine over many years. Such a bridge takes a generation to become strong enough to carry a person and can last for centuries, since the roots keep growing and repair themselves. Floods that sweep away ordinary wooden bridges leave these ones standing. The cost is patience: the people who start a bridge seldom live to see it finished, so each bridge is a gift from one generation to the next. Families pass the method down, and a single village may care for dozens of bridges, each trained and repaired by those who use it.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: Living root bridges are quicker to build than timber bridges
options.B: Building a living root bridge requires people to plan for benefits that they themselves may not enjoy
options.C: Floods cannot damage any living root bridge
options.D: Fig trees can grow only beside streams

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says the people who start a bridge seldom live to see it finished, each bridge being a gift to the next generation. This supports the first option. Shortcut: check that the option follows from a sentence rather than adding a new claim. Trap (A): Reversal. The passage says a bridge takes a generation to become strong. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The passage says floods leave them standing; it does not say none can ever be damaged. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The passage says only that the bridges are built beside streams, not that trees need streams.

questions.question_text:
Passage: For most of their history, lighthouses depended on keepers who trimmed the wicks, polished the lenses, wound the clockwork and kept a watch through every storm. The work was lonely and sometimes dangerous, but a light that failed could wreck a ship, so keepers were respected. In the last century, electric lamps and automatic timers made many of these tasks unnecessary, and one by one the keepers were withdrawn. The lights still shine, and ships are probably safer than before, since automatic lights seldom fail. Yet something has been lost: the keepers also reported wrecks, rescued sailors and recorded the weather, and an automatic light does none of these. Automation kept the beam and removed the human watch that had come with it.

The passage is mainly about

options.A: how automation preserved the lighthouse's essential function while removing the human tasks that came with it
options.B: how keepers were mistreated and finally dismissed
options.C: why lighthouses are less safe now than in the past
options.D: the history of lamps and clockwork used in lighthouses

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage describes keepers, shows that automation kept the light, and notes what has been lost: the human watch. Shortcut: identify what the final sentence summarises. Trap (B): Reversal. The passage says keepers were respected. Trap (C): Reversal. The passage says ships are probably safer than before. Trap (D): Half-true. Lamps and clockwork are details, not the point of the passage.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Every year, monarch butterflies in North America make a journey of several thousand kilometres to the same mountain forests in the south, where they spend the winter. Yet no single butterfly completes the round trip. The insects that leave in autumn live for months, but those that return north in spring lay eggs along the way and die, and their offspring complete the next stage. It takes several generations to reach the northern summer range, and the butterflies that start the next autumn migration are great-grandchildren of those that left the forest the spring before. How these insects find a place that none of the living butterflies has ever seen remains one of the puzzles of animal navigation. Several of the forest sites are now protected, and local people welcome visitors who come to see the trees weighed down with resting butterflies.

According to the passage, which statement about the monarch butterflies' round trip is true?

options.A: No single butterfly makes the whole round trip
options.B: Each butterfly makes the whole trip in both directions
options.C: The butterflies that return north in spring live for months
options.D: Scientists have fully explained how the butterflies find the forests

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says no single butterfly completes the round trip, because several generations are needed. Shortcut: watch for 'no' and 'none' in the passage. Trap (B): Reversal. The passage says no single butterfly completes the round trip. Trap (C): Reversal. It is the autumn migrants that live for months. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The passage calls it one of the puzzles that remain.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Coins were once worth their weight in metal, and a merchant could melt one and sell the gold. Paper money asked people to trust something quite different: a piece of paper that is worth something only because others will accept it. The idea probably began as a receipt, when traders who had left heavy coins with a banker carried the banker's note to pay other traders. Over time, governments took over the printing of notes and promised that they could be exchanged for metal. When that promise was dropped, paper money continued to work, held up by the shared belief that it would be accepted tomorrow. Money, on this view, is less a thing than an agreement, and its value rests on confidence as much as on its material.

The passage is chiefly concerned with

options.A: proving that coins were never valuable
options.B: explaining how to print notes that cannot be copied
options.C: the reasons why governments promised to exchange notes for metal
options.D: the way paper money works because of shared trust rather than the worth of its material

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage traces the origin of notes and concludes that money is 'less a thing than an agreement'. Shortcut: the closing sentence states the author's point of view. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The passage says coins were worth their weight in metal. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. Printing methods and counterfeiting are not discussed. Trap (C): Half-true. The promise is one stage in the story, not the main subject.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Charles Darwin spent years watching earthworms and concluded that they were among the most important animals in history. The reason is plain once one looks at what they do. A worm pulls fallen leaves into its burrow and eats them, mixing the plant matter into the soil. As it moves through the ground it makes tunnels that let air and rainwater reach deeper layers. Its castings, the small heaps it leaves on the surface, are rich in nutrients that plants can absorb readily. Over the years, a field with many worms drains better, holds more air, and has a deeper layer of dark topsoil than one with few. Farmers who plough heavily or use certain chemicals can reduce the numbers, and may find the soil harder and less productive as a result.

According to the passage, the tunnels made by earthworms

options.A: are the heaps of nutrients seen on the soil surface
options.B: make the soil harder and less productive
options.C: prevent plants from absorbing nutrients
options.D: let air and rainwater reach deeper layers of soil

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says the tunnels let air and rainwater reach deeper layers. Shortcut: keep tunnels, castings and leaf-eating apart. Trap (A): Half-true. The heaps are the castings, which are different from the tunnels. Trap (B): Reversal. The passage says reduced worm numbers may make soil harder. Trap (C): Reversal. The castings are described as nutrients that plants absorb readily.

questions.question_text:
Passage: In many regions, the oldest form of cinema may be the shadow play. A puppeteer holds flat figures, often cut from leather or paper, between a lamp and a cloth screen, and the audience, seated on the other side, sees only the moving shadows. The same few figures can tell different stories on different nights, since the puppeteer speaks every part and may adapt the tale to the crowd. Traditional plays often draw on epics that audiences already know, and the pleasure lies less in learning the story than in watching how it is told. Despite the arrival of films and television, shadow plays survive where communities value the craft, and their simple means, a lamp, a screen and a voice, show how little a story needs.

The central idea of the passage is that shadow puppetry

options.A: has been completely replaced by films and television
options.B: is a simple but enduring storytelling tradition that survives where communities value it
options.C: requires a different set of figures for every story
options.D: is performed only for audiences unfamiliar with the epics

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage describes how shadow plays work and ends by saying they survive and show how little a story needs. Shortcut: reject options that contradict a stated detail. Trap (A): Reversal. The passage says shadow plays survive where communities value the craft. Trap (C): Reversal. The passage says the same few figures tell different stories. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The passage says audiences often already know the stories.

questions.question_text:
Passage: For centuries, the trade in spices across the Indian Ocean followed the rhythm of the seasonal winds. In summer, the wind blows steadily from the south-west towards the land and in winter it reverses, blowing from the north-east. Sailors learned that a ship leaving the African coast in the right season would be carried across the open sea to India without rowing, and that the return voyage had to wait for the winds to turn. A ship that left at the wrong time might sit in harbour for months. Ports grew rich on this waiting, since sailors needed lodging, repairs and supplies, and merchants used the pause to trade. The winds thus shaped not only voyages but the whole calendar of commerce.

According to the passage, the return voyage across the ocean

options.A: had to wait until the winds changed direction
options.B: could be made at any time of year with equal ease
options.C: was always made by rowing against the wind
options.D: was avoided by merchants because ports offered no supplies

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says the return voyage had to wait for the winds to turn. Shortcut: answer from the sentence that mentions the return voyage. Trap (B): Reversal. The passage says the voyage depended on the seasonal winds. Trap (C): Reversal. The passage says ships were carried by the wind, not rowed. Trap (D): Reversal. The passage says ports grew rich by providing lodging and supplies.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A humble pencil seems like a single object, yet no one person knows how to make it from start to finish. The wood comes from trees felled in one region, the graphite is mined in another, and the metal band that holds the eraser is shaped from ore dug elsewhere. The rubber, the paint and the glue each have their own chain of suppliers, each of whom specialises in one small step. None of these workers is trying to make a pencil, and most have never thought of one. Yet the pencils appear, in great numbers and at low cost. The example is often used to show that coordination across a vast network of strangers can achieve what no central planner could design in detail.

The author uses the example of the pencil mainly to show that

options.A: pencils are the most complicated objects ever made
options.B: one person could make a pencil if given enough time
options.C: complex objects can be made through the coordination of many specialists who need not plan the whole
options.D: workers in each supply chain are paid very poorly

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says no single person knows how to make a pencil and uses it to show coordination among strangers. Shortcut: ask what the example illustrates, not what it describes. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The passage uses the pencil to illustrate, not to rank complexity. Trap (B): Reversal. The passage says no one person knows how to make it from start to finish. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. Pay is never discussed.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A mouse's heart beats several hundred times a minute while an elephant's beats a few dozen. The difference follows from a general pattern: the smaller the animal, the faster its body burns energy for each gram of tissue. A small body has a large surface compared with its volume, and so loses heat quickly; to stay warm it must burn fuel at a high rate, and a fast heartbeat supplies the oxygen. Large animals lose heat slowly and run their bodies at a gentler pace. The pattern is so regular that biologists have noted that, over a lifetime, the hearts of very different mammals tend to deliver a similar total number of beats. Small animals simply spend them faster. Even within a single species, smaller individuals tend to run at somewhat higher rates than larger ones, though the pattern is far less sharp than across species.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: An elephant's body burns more energy per gram than a mouse's
options.B: All mammals live for exactly the same length of time
options.C: A mouse's heart is larger than an elephant's
options.D: A mouse is likely to have a shorter lifespan than an elephant

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If total beats are similar and a mouse's heart beats much faster, it uses up its beats sooner. A shorter lifespan follows. Shortcut: use arithmetic of the passage: fast rate with a similar total means a shorter time. Trap (A): Reversal. The passage says smaller animals burn energy faster per gram. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The passage says only that the total number of beats tends to be similar. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The passage says nothing about the relative size of their hearts beyond the rate.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A seed bank is often described as insurance: store samples of crops in cold, dry vaults and, if disease or drought wipes out a variety in the field, the stock can be replanted. The comparison is apt but incomplete. Insurance pays out the same sum whatever the loss, whereas a seed is only as useful as the knowledge that goes with it. A sealed packet of a rare grain tells a future farmer little about the soil it preferred, how it was sown or how it was cooked, and the people who knew these things may be gone. Seeds also lose the ability to sprout unless they are periodically grown out, and growing out changes them slightly with each cycle. A vault that is forgotten is therefore a slowly spoiling asset. The more durable form of storage is the living one: farmers who keep growing varieties year after year keep both the seed and the skill alive.

The author's argument implies that a seed bank, taken by itself,

options.A: is worthless as protection against crop disease
options.B: is a more reliable guarantee than continued farming
options.C: preserves only part of what a variety needs in order to survive
options.D: needs nothing more than periodic growing out to stay useful

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author says the insurance comparison is incomplete: seeds need knowledge and periodic growing out, and the best storage is living farming. So a bank alone keeps only part of what survival needs. Shortcut: spot the 'but' that limits an analogy; the answer states the limit. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The author calls the insurance comparison 'apt but incomplete', not worthless. Trap (B): Reversal. The author says the living form of storage is the more durable. Trap (D): Half-true. Growing out is needed, but the author also stresses the loss of knowledge, and says growing out itself changes the seeds.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Walk across any campus lawn and you will find a worn line of bare earth that cuts a corner the architect's paving ignored. Planners call such tracks desire paths. One response is to treat them as disobedience and to fence them off. Another is to treat them as data: thousands of walkers have voted with their feet for a route that the design failed to supply. The second response has a cost, since a network of paths drawn by habit may be shorter without always being safe or accessible, and it can leave the lawn a patchwork of mud. Yet the first response has the larger cost, because it assumes that the design was right and the users wrong. A sensible compromise is to wait a season before paving anything, and then to pave what the walkers have already chosen.

The author's attitude to fencing off desire paths is best described as

options.A: approving, because lawns need protection from walkers
options.B: critical, because it assumes without evidence that users are at fault
options.C: neutral, because fences and paths are equally costly
options.D: dismissive of all planning and paving

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Both responses carry costs, but the author concludes that fencing has 'the larger cost' because it presumes the design was right. That is a critical attitude. Shortcut: tone questions: look at the sentence that begins with 'Yet'. Trap (A): Reversal. The author calls fencing the response with the larger cost. Trap (C): Half-true. The author notes costs on both sides but says the first response has the larger cost. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The author recommends paving what walkers have chosen, not abandoning planning.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Translators are often accused of betrayal, as in the old Italian pun that makes the two words nearly identical. The charge assumes that a text has a fixed meaning that can be carried across intact and that anything less is failure. But meaning is not a parcel. A joke depends on the sound of words, a proverb on a stock of shared images, a form of address on social relations that the target language may not mark at all. A translator must choose what to keep: the sense, the music, the register, or the effect on the reader. No choice preserves everything, and the best translators are those who know what they are giving up. Seen this way, a translation is less a copy of the original than an argument about what in it matters most.

Which of the following best captures the author's view of translation?

options.A: It is faithful only when it follows the original word for word
options.B: It involves choices about what to preserve, so it cannot be a perfect copy
options.C: It is inevitably a betrayal of the original author
options.D: It is easiest for jokes and proverbs, which carry little meaning

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author denies that meaning is a parcel and says the translator must choose what to keep: a translation is 'an argument about what matters most'. Shortcut: a view question is answered by the last sentence of the passage. Trap (A): Reversal. The author says no choice preserves everything and a translation is an argument, not a copy. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The author rejects the charge of betrayal as resting on a false idea of meaning. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The author says jokes and proverbs are among the hardest because they depend on sound and shared images.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A master potter can explain the steps of throwing a pot: centre the clay, open it, raise the walls. A novice who follows the steps will still produce a lopsided bowl. What the master knows is not in the instructions but in the hands: the pressure that tells him the clay is about to slump, the sound that signals the wheel is too fast. Philosophers call this tacit knowledge, and it explains why crafts have been taught through apprenticeship rather than manuals. The apprentice watches, copies, fails and is corrected over years, and slowly acquires a feel that no one could have spelled out. Attempts to automate such work often begin with a list of rules gathered from experts and are puzzled when the machine, though it follows every rule, falls short. The expert did not follow rules; the rules were a later summary of what the expert did.

The passage suggests that rule-based attempts to automate a craft often fall short because

options.A: experts deliberately hide part of what they know
options.B: machines cannot follow more than a few rules at a time
options.C: the rules summarise expert practice and leave out the feel that guided it
options.D: experts follow rules strictly, which machines cannot do

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The last sentence says the rules were a later summary of what the expert did. A machine that follows every rule still lacks the tacit feel. Shortcut: find the sentence that explains the puzzle. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The passage says the feel cannot be spelled out, not that it is hidden. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. The passage says the machine follows every rule. Trap (D): Reversal. The passage says the expert did not follow rules.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A pasture open to all is often said to be doomed: each herder gains fully from adding a cow and shares the cost of overgrazing with everyone, so the grass is eaten away. The argument has the force of arithmetic, but it describes only one kind of commons, the kind with no rules. Villages in many places have managed shared pastures, forests and fisheries for centuries by agreeing who may use them, how much, and when, and by posting watchers who are themselves members of the community. These arrangements work when users know one another, when boundaries are clear, and when breakers of the rules are caught and punished by neighbours rather than by distant authorities. Where they fail, the cause is more often an outside force, such as a market that suddenly makes overuse profitable, than the commons itself. The tragedy, then, is not that resources are shared, but that sharing is sometimes left without rules.

The author's main purpose in the passage is to

options.A: show that rules are unnecessary for managing shared resources
options.B: argue that outside markets always harm shared resources
options.C: explain how pastures are divided and fenced among herders
options.D: challenge the view that shared resources are bound to be ruined

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage grants the force of the argument but says it describes only a commons without rules, then shows how rules sustain commons. Shortcut: purpose questions: look for the claim the author sets out to oppose. Trap (A): Reversal. The author says the tragedy is sharing without rules; rules are central. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The passage says failures are 'more often' due to outside forces, not always. Trap (C): Half-true. Agreements on who may use a pasture are mentioned, but fencing is not, and the purpose is wider.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Studies of successful companies often conclude that bold bets lead to success. The companies chosen for study are those that are still thriving, and among them many took large risks. But the studies seldom look at the companies that took the same risks and disappeared. If bold bets are common among both winners and failures, the evidence says nothing about whether they cause success; it shows only that winners are the survivors of a risky process. The same error appears whenever a sample is selected on the outcome: stories of diets that worked are told by those who lost weight, and advice from artists is given by those who became famous. A fair comparison needs the failures as well, though they are harder to find, since few write memoirs or give interviews. Until they are counted, the lesson of the winners is a lesson about luck as much as about method.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument?

options.A: A study that includes failed companies finds that bold bets were much more common among the winners than among the failures
options.B: Many successful companies have written memoirs describing the risks they took
options.C: A study that includes failed companies finds that bold bets were as common among failures as among winners
options.D: Newspapers sometimes report on companies that failed

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author says the winners-only evidence is silent about cause. To weaken this, we need evidence that includes failures and shows that bold bets really do separate winners from failures. Shortcut: to weaken, give the data the author says is missing and make it point the other way. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. This repeats the author's point about winners' stories; it says nothing about the failures. Trap (C): Reversal. This strengthens the author's claim that bold bets do not separate winners from failures. Trap (D): Half-true. This does not show that failures are counted or that their risk-taking differs from the winners'.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Standard spelling is younger than most people think. In the sixteenth century, even careful writers spelled the same word in different ways within a single letter, and nobody thought it an error. Printing, schooling and dictionaries slowly fixed one form for each word, and by the nineteenth century correct spelling had become a mark of education, with errors treated as signs of carelessness or low birth. The attitude is a social judgement dressed as a rule of language: a misspelt word is no less understandable than a correct one. Today software corrects mistakes as we type, and some predict that spelling will matter even less. It may equally harden the standard, since few can now see a deviation without a red line beneath it. Either way, the history suggests that spelling is held up by habit and approval rather than by any need of communication.

The author most likely regards correct spelling as

options.A: a skill that software has now made unnecessary
options.B: a convention sustained by social attitudes more than by any need of communication
options.C: an ancient rule that has always marked the educated
options.D: an invention of dictionary makers alone

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author calls the attitude a social judgement and concludes that spelling is held up by habit and approval, not by communication needs. Shortcut: note the author's own words: 'a social judgement dressed as a rule of language'. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The author says software may equally harden the standard; he predicts neither outcome. Trap (C): Reversal. The author says standard spelling is younger than most people think. Trap (D): Half-true. Dictionaries are one of several forces, including printing and schooling, that fixed spelling.

questions.concept_tag: RC - purpose of a remark (language and dialect)
questions.question_text:
Passage: Travelling along a river valley, a listener hears speech change slowly from village to village. Each neighbour understands the next, yet someone at one end may struggle to follow someone at the other. Where, then, does one language end and another begin? Linguists answer that there is no natural line: the boundary is usually drawn by politics, religion or the border of a state. A well-known quip says that a language is a dialect with an army and a navy. The point of the remark is not cynical; it is that the labels 'language' and 'dialect' describe status more than speech. Two varieties that differ little may be called separate languages because their speakers belong to different nations, while others that differ greatly are called dialects of one language because their speakers share a government and a written standard.

The author mentions the 'army and navy' quip mainly to suggest that

options.A: armies are mainly responsible for spreading languages
options.B: dialects are always harder to understand than languages
options.C: linguists cannot study speech objectively
options.D: the line between a language and a dialect reflects political power more than linguistic difference

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author explains the remark: the labels 'describe status more than speech', drawn by politics and state borders. Shortcut: when a quip is quoted, read the author's own gloss on it. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. The passage does not discuss how languages spread. Trap (B): Reversal. The passage says varieties called dialects may differ greatly or little, so no such rule exists. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The author says the labels describe status; he does not deny that speech can be studied.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Each winter, thousands of amateurs count the birds at their feeders and send the numbers to a central database. Professional ornithologists once dismissed such data as unreliable: the counters are untrained, the feeders are unevenly placed, and enthusiasts tend to report the unusual. But the scale of the effort offsets these flaws. Errors that are random cancel out when there are enough observations, while consistent biases can be measured and corrected by comparing counts from many places. The result is a record of bird populations over a continent and many decades that no team of professionals could afford to collect. The lesson is not that amateurs are as skilled as experts, but that some questions are answered less by skill than by numbers and coverage.

The author's argument depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Amateur counters are as skilled as professionals
options.B: The errors in amateur counts are mostly random or measurable rather than hidden and consistent
options.C: Professional data on birds is never reliable
options.D: Feeders attract only unusual birds

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The case rests on errors cancelling or being correctable. If errors were hidden and consistent, large numbers would not help. This is the negation test: deny the assumption and the argument falls. Shortcut: apply the negation test: deny each option and see if the argument collapses. Trap (A): Reversal. The author says the lesson is not that amateurs are as skilled as experts. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The author never says that professional data is unreliable; only that professionals could not afford this coverage. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The passage says enthusiasts report the unusual, not that feeders attract only such birds.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Ruined castles and abandoned villages attract stories more readily than inhabited ones. A tower with no roof invites a tale of siege; a deserted street invites a tale of plague. The stories are rarely supported by records, yet they are told with confidence, because ruins offer evidence of an ending without evidence of its cause. A visitor sees stone and silence and supplies the missing events from what he already knows of battles and epidemics. Archaeologists often find less dramatic explanations: a stream that moved, a trade route that shifted, a landlord who raised the rent. Such causes leave faint traces and make poor stories. The popular account of a ruin therefore tells us less about the place than about what its visitors expect to find in the past.

According to the author, popular tales about ruins mainly reveal

options.A: the true cause of the abandonment of the places
options.B: the expectations that visitors bring to the past
options.C: the careful findings of archaeologists
options.D: that every ruin was the result of war or plague

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The last sentence says the popular account 'tells us less about the place than about what its visitors expect to find in the past'. Shortcut: the final sentence gives the author's conclusion. Trap (A): Reversal. The author says such tales rarely rest on records and archaeologists often find other causes. Trap (C): Reversal. Archaeologists often find less dramatic causes than the tales suggest. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The author lists quieter causes such as a moved stream.

questions.question_text:
Passage: In hot dry regions, traditional houses are often built around a small courtyard, with thick walls, few outer windows and a well or a tree at the centre. The arrangement is not decoration. At night the courtyard loses heat to the sky and fills with cool air; by day the thick walls keep the sun out and the cool air in. The shade of the tree and the evaporation from the well lower the temperature further. Modern glass buildings in the same regions, by contrast, take in heat through large windows and depend on machines to remove it. Their designers are not careless; they follow fashions and codes devised for other climates. The older houses embody a patient knowledge of local conditions, tested by generations of discomfort, that no single designer could rebuild from principles alone.

The author's attitude to traditional courtyard houses is best described as

options.A: nostalgic for their beauty rather than their function
options.B: contemptuous of modern designers
options.C: respectful of a design that grew out of long experience of the local climate
options.D: indifferent to how much energy buildings use

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author explains each feature's function and ends by praising 'a patient knowledge of local conditions'. That is respect for a design from experience. Shortcut: tone words: 'patient knowledge', 'tested by generations'. Trap (A): Half-true. The author says the arrangement is not decoration; function is the point. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The author says modern designers are not careless. Trap (D): Reversal. The passage contrasts houses that stay cool by design with glass buildings that need machines.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Planting a single crop over a wide area allows machines to sow and harvest cheaply, and yields per hectare can be very high. But a field of identical plants is also an open invitation to pests and disease, which spread easily when every plant is equally vulnerable. Farmers who mix two or more crops in the same field, or alternate them through the seasons, find that pests that favour one crop are slowed by the presence of another, and that one crop may supply nutrients the other needs. The mixed field needs more labour and does not suit large machines. The comparison, then, is not between a productive method and a primitive one, but between high yields in good conditions and steadier yields across varied conditions. Which a farmer should prefer depends on how much risk he can bear.

Which of the following best states the author's conclusion?

options.A: The choice between single-crop and mixed fields depends on how a farmer weighs high yields against stability
options.B: Mixed fields should replace single-crop farms everywhere
options.C: Single-crop farming gives higher yields under all conditions
options.D: Pests never attack fields that grow more than one crop

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author's last sentences frame a trade-off and leave the choice to the farmer's risk tolerance. Shortcut: conclusions often follow 'then' or 'therefore'. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The author says the choice depends on the farmer's tolerance for risk. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The author says single crops give high yields in good conditions only. Trap (D): Half-true. The passage says pests are slowed in mixed fields, not stopped entirely.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Every map leaves things out, and a map that left nothing out would be as large as the territory and as useless. Scientific models work in the same way. A model of a gas that treats its molecules as tiny billiard balls is wrong in many details, yet it predicts how pressure changes with temperature remarkably well. The mistake is to ask of a model whether it is true; the sensible question is whether it is useful for a given purpose and where it breaks down. A model that works well for engineers building a pump may fail for chemists studying a reaction. Disputes between rival models often disappear when it is seen that each was built for a different question. Scientists who forget this may defend a model long after it has stopped helping, as if it were a possession rather than a tool.

The passage suggests that disputes between rival models

options.A: show that only one of the models can be correct
options.B: are always a sign of poor scientific practice
options.C: cannot arise between engineers and chemists
options.D: may fade once the models are seen as answers to different questions

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says disputes between rival models often disappear when each is seen as built for a different question. Shortcut: an inference is often a near paraphrase of one sentence. Trap (A): Reversal. The passage says such disputes often disappear when each model's purpose is understood. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The passage says only that scientists who forget purpose may cling to models; it does not say all disputes are poor science. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. The passage uses engineers and chemists as an example of different purposes, not of impossibility of disputes.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A placebo is said to work even when patients know it is a placebo. In several small trials, patients with persistent pain were told frankly that their pills contained no medicine, but that such pills had helped others. Many still reported relief, more than patients who received no pills. This is puzzling if the effect depends on deception, and it suggests that part of the benefit comes from the ritual of care: attention from a clinician, the habit of taking a pill, an expectation of improvement. It does not follow that placebos can replace medicine. They seem to ease symptoms such as pain and tiredness more than they change the course of a disease, and the trials were small. Still, the finding unsettles an old assumption that honesty in medicine must cost patients some comfort.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: Part of the relief that patients report may come from the care and expectation around treatment rather than from deception
options.B: Placebos can cure serious diseases without any medicine
options.C: Patients who know their pills are dummies never improve
options.D: Doctors should stop prescribing real medicine

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage suggests the benefit may come from 'the ritual of care'. The first option restates this carefully. Shortcut: choose the option that is hedged the way the passage is hedged. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The passage says placebos seem to ease symptoms more than they change the course of a disease. Trap (C): Reversal. The passage says many still reported relief. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The passage says placebos cannot replace medicine.

questions.question_text:
Passage: In a negotiation over price, whoever names a figure first usually shifts the final settlement towards it, even when the figure is arbitrary. In experiments, people who are first asked whether a car is worth more or less than a random number then give estimates close to that number. The effect, called anchoring, is strong because the mind tends to adjust from a starting point and stops adjusting too early. Some negotiators conclude that they should always move first. That advice ignores the risk that an opening offer reveals ignorance: a buyer who opens far too high gives away money that might not have been needed. The advantage of the first offer belongs to those who have prepared well enough to name a figure that is bold but defensible.

The author's reasoning best supports which of the following conclusions?

options.A: Opening figures influence outcomes regardless of how they are chosen
options.B: Anchoring affects only people who are buying cars
options.C: Moving first helps mainly when the opening figure is informed and defensible
options.D: A negotiator should never name the first figure

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author accepts anchoring but rejects the advice to 'always move first': an uninformed opening gives money away. Shortcut: note which advice the author rejects and what he qualifies it with. Trap (A): Half-true. Anchoring works even for arbitrary figures, but the author says the advantage in negotiation goes to the well prepared. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. The car is an experimental example, not a limit on the effect. Trap (D): Reversal. The author says the first offer can be an advantage for the well prepared.

questions.question_text:
Passage: The tale of a clever youngest child who outwits a powerful rival appears in cultures that have had little contact with one another. Scholars have long argued over why. One school holds that the tales spread from a single source along trade routes, changing as they travelled. Another holds that they arose independently because they answer a common need: communities with little power tell stories in which the small defeat the great. The two accounts are not exclusive. A story may begin in one place, but it survives in another only if it fits something the listeners already feel. What is striking is how often the details differ while the shape remains. The cunning is the same; the hero is a fox in one land and a hare in the next.

The author's main purpose is to

options.A: present two explanations for a pattern and suggest that they may be complementary
options.B: prove that the tales all came from a single source
options.C: show that the tales differ completely from one culture to another
options.D: argue that the choice of animal hero is unimportant

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage sets out two schools and then says 'the two accounts are not exclusive'. Shortcut: purpose = what the author does with the views, not which one is chosen. Trap (B): Reversal. The author says the two accounts are not exclusive and does not prove either. Trap (C): Reversal. The author says the shape remains while details differ. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The animals are mentioned only as an example of differing details.

questions.question_text:
Passage: People who are short of money or time do not merely have less; they think differently. A person who must stretch a small income through the month devotes attention to each purchase, and this focus makes them careful in what they notice. But the focus has a cost: attention fixed on the pressing problem is not available for others, such as a letter that needs answering or a long-term plan. Experiments suggest that thinking about a looming bill reduces performance on unrelated tests. This does not show that poorer people are less intelligent; it shows that any person under pressure has less spare capacity. The practical lesson is for those who design public services: forms that are long, deadlines that are strict and rules that are intricate demand the very mental capacity that scarcity has used up.

The passage implies that complicated application forms

options.A: prove that poorer people are less intelligent
options.B: are deliberately designed to exclude poor applicants
options.C: affect all applicants equally whatever their circumstances
options.D: weigh most heavily on people whose attention is already taken up by scarcity

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The last sentence says complex forms demand the mental capacity that scarcity has used up. Shortcut: an implication follows the 'practical lesson' sentence. Trap (A): Reversal. The author says this does not show that poorer people are less intelligent. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. The author makes no claim about the designers' intentions. Trap (C): Reversal. The author argues they demand capacity that scarcity has used up.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A highway that cuts across a forest does not simply remove a strip of land; it divides a population. Animals that once ranged freely now face a barrier they cross at great risk, and each fragment becomes an island. Small populations are more vulnerable to disease and chance events, and when a fragment's numbers fall, new animals cannot easily arrive from outside to replace them. Conservationists therefore build bridges and tunnels over and under roads. These structures work only when they are placed where animals already travel, and when fences guide them towards the entrances. A bridge put in the wrong place, however handsome, will be ignored. Success, in this field, is measured not by the cost of the structure but by the number of animals that use it.

According to the passage, a wildlife bridge is effective only if

options.A: it is placed where animals already travel and fences guide them to its entrances
options.B: it is costly and handsome
options.C: it spans the full width of the forest
options.D: animals never attempt to cross roads elsewhere

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage names two conditions: location where animals already travel, and fences guiding them to the entrances. Shortcut: conditions follow 'only when'. Trap (B): Reversal. The passage says a handsome bridge in the wrong place will be ignored, and success is not measured by cost. Trap (C): Out-of-scope. Width is not discussed. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The passage says animals do cross, at great risk.

questions.question_text:
Passage: People who photograph an experience often remember it less well than those who simply look. When visitors to a museum were asked to photograph objects, they later recalled fewer details of them than visitors who had only observed. The explanation offered is that the camera takes over the work of remembering: a person who knows that a record exists feels free to stop encoding the scene. Yet the effect reversed in one condition: those who were asked to zoom in on a particular detail remembered more of it. Taking a picture, then, can either replace attention or direct it, depending on how it is done. The finding should not be read as an argument against photography, but as a reminder that a tool which stores memory for us may also weaken our own.

Which of the following is best supported by the passage?

options.A: People who take photographs always remember less than those who do not
options.B: Museums should ban cameras from their galleries
options.C: Photographing can weaken memory when it replaces attention but strengthen it when it directs attention to a detail
options.D: Zooming in on a detail makes people forget the whole scene completely

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says photographing can 'either replace attention or direct it'. The first option states this. Shortcut: look for the 'either... or' sentence. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The passage says the effect reversed when people zoomed in on a detail. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. The author says the finding is not an argument against photography. Trap (D): Reversal. The passage says zooming in improved memory of the detail; it makes no claim about forgetting the whole scene.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Before standard units, a pound of grain might differ from one market to the next, and buyers carried their own measures or learned the local custom. The variation was not mere confusion. Units were often tied to the work they measured: a field was measured by how much seed or labour it took, not by area, which told a farmer more than a number of square metres would. Standard units replaced this with a single scale that was easy to trade across regions but said less about the work involved. The gain was real: contracts became easier to write and cheating harder. The loss was subtler, since a measure that once carried local knowledge was reduced to a bare number. Reformers who celebrated uniformity seldom noticed what the older units had been telling people.

The author's attitude to the standardisation of units is best described as

options.A: wholly hostile because it made trade harder
options.B: indifferent because units carry no real value
options.C: enthusiastic because it removed all confusion
options.D: appreciative of its benefits but mindful of what was lost

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author lists a real gain ('easier trade') and a subtler loss ('reduced to a bare number'). That balance is the answer. Shortcut: a balanced attitude shows both a gain and a loss in the text. Trap (A): Reversal. The author says trade and contracts became easier. Trap (B): Reversal. The author says older units carried local knowledge. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The author says the variation was not mere confusion and that something was lost.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Historians are wary of 'what if' questions. What if a battle had gone the other way? Such speculation seems unscientific, since the alternative can never be observed. Yet the wariness is oddly selective, because ordinary historical explanation depends on counterfactuals. To say that a harvest failure caused a revolt is to say that without the failure the revolt would not have happened, or would have been smaller; to say that a minister's decision mattered is to deny that events would have run the same way anyway. A historian who refuses all counterfactuals must also refuse all claims of cause. The real choice, then, is not between speculating and sticking to the facts, but between making one's counterfactual assumptions explicit and testable against what is known of the period, and leaving them buried in the narrative where no one can examine them. Disciplined speculation is not a departure from history but the form that its causal claims must take if they are to be honest.

The author's central argument is that

options.A: causal claims in history already rest on counterfactuals, so these should be stated openly and checked against evidence
options.B: historians should devote most of their work to imagining what would have happened
options.C: counterfactual speculation is unscientific but harmless
options.D: historians who avoid 'what if' questions thereby avoid error

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The chain is: causal claims imply counterfactuals; refusing counterfactuals means refusing causes; so the honest course is to state and test them. Only the first option states this chain. Shortcut: central-argument questions: find the claim that the rest of the passage supports, usually flagged by 'then' or 'the real choice'. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The author wants counterfactuals explicit and tested, not made the main work of history. Trap (C): Half-true. The author grants that the alternative cannot be observed, but denies that the practice can be avoided or is harmless when hidden. Trap (D): Reversal. The author says such historians cannot avoid counterfactuals; they only hide them.

questions.concept_tag: RC - function of an example (fallacy of composition)
questions.question_text:
Passage: When a household faces hard times, saving more is prudent. It does not follow that the same is wise for a whole economy. If every household cuts spending at once, shops sell less, firms reduce output and pay, and incomes fall; and since saving is made out of income, total saving may fall even as each household tries to raise it. What is sound for one is self-defeating for all, because the one acts on the assumption that the rest will go on spending. Economists call this a fallacy of composition: to assume that what is true of each part is true of the whole. The error is a general one and not confined to economics. A person standing up at a concert sees better, but when everyone stands, no one does. The point is not that individual prudence is foolish, but that some goods depend on what others do, and a rule that works for any single person need not work as a rule for everybody.

The author mentions standing at a concert mainly to

options.A: show that the fallacy of composition arises outside economics
options.B: suggest that standing is always a mistake at concerts
options.C: prove that households should never save
options.D: explain why total saving may fall when incomes fall

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sentence before the example says 'the error is a general one and not confined to economics'. The concert is offered as a non-economic case. Shortcut: function-of-example: read the sentence just before the example. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The example concerns what happens when everyone stands, not standing in general. Trap (C): Reversal. The author says individual prudence is not foolish. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. That point is made earlier, in the household example, not by the concert example.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Mathematicians often speak of proofs as elegant, and some insist that beauty is a guide to truth: a conjecture that is beautiful is more likely to be right. The claim is easy to ridicule. Beauty, after all, is a matter of taste, and taste has misled many in other fields. Yet the claim may be less naive than it sounds. What mathematicians call elegance is largely economy: a proof that explains many facts by a single idea, or reveals an unexpected connection between distant areas. Such a proof is not merely pleasing; it shows that the result is no accident, and so gives reason to expect that neighbouring results also hold. Seen this way, beauty is a short-hand for explanatory power, and a feeling for it is a trained judgement of where structure is likely to be found. The feeling can still be wrong, as any trained judgement can; but it is not arbitrary.

Which of the following best describes the author's position on beauty as a guide to truth in mathematics?

options.A: It is naive, because taste has no place in mathematics
options.B: It is infallible, because a beautiful result always reveals real structure
options.C: It is cautiously defensible, since elegance reflects explanatory economy that trained judgement can detect
options.D: It is irrelevant, because proofs are judged only by whether they are valid

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author moves from ridicule ('easy to ridicule') through a defence ('less naive') to a caution ('can still be wrong'). The answer must carry both defence and caution. Shortcut: for 'position' questions, the right option usually matches the passage's hedges. Trap (A): Reversal. The author says the claim may be less naive than it sounds. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The author says the feeling can still be wrong. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The author is concerned with how elegance guides expectation of truth, not with how validity is judged.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Online marketplaces rely on ratings to let strangers trust one another, and for a while the system seems to work. Over time, however, the ratings drift upward until nearly every seller scores close to the maximum, and the numbers no longer separate good from poor. The usual explanation is dishonesty, but the cause is more mundane. A buyer who gives a low rating risks a retaliatory low rating in return, or feels guilty about harming a seller's livelihood for a minor fault. A buyer who gives full marks incurs no such costs. Each rater, acting reasonably, pushes the average upward, and the scale loses the information it was designed to carry. Some platforms respond by hiding who rated whom, or by asking buyers to compare sellers rather than to grade them. These measures help because they remove the private cost of honesty. The lesson is that a signal is only as good as the incentives of those who send it.

The author's explanation of rating inflation rests on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Most sellers deliberately deceive their buyers
options.B: Raters experience honest low ratings as personally costly, while full marks cost them nothing
options.C: Buyers cannot tell good sellers from poor ones
options.D: Platforms earn more money when ratings are high

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If honest low ratings carried no cost for the rater, the push upward would disappear. The explanation therefore depends on that cost. Shortcut: negation test: if raters faced no cost for low ratings, would the explanation survive? Trap (A): Reversal. The author says the usual explanation is dishonesty, but the cause is more mundane. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The argument is that buyers can tell but choose not to say so. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. Platform profit is never mentioned as a cause.

questions.question_text:
Passage: When a city changes the name of a street or a town, the objection usually heard is practical: maps must be redrawn, addresses changed, habits relearned. Defenders of the change reply that the cost is small beside the symbolic gain. Both sides treat the name as a label whose only job is to point. But names also store memory, and the memory they store is a selection. An old name may preserve a language no longer spoken in the town, a trade long gone, or the name of a founder whom later generations judge differently. To rename is to edit that store. The question is not whether editing is permitted, since every generation edits, but whether the edit is made with awareness of what is deleted. A name replaced in haste can remove the only trace of something its replacers would have wished to keep.

The author's main concern is that

options.A: renaming of streets and towns should be prohibited
options.B: renaming may erase stored memory unless it is done with awareness of what is lost
options.C: the practical costs of renaming outweigh its symbolic gains
options.D: old names always honour people whom later generations admire

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author sets aside both practical and symbolic arguments and adds a third angle: names store a selection of memory, so editing it needs awareness. Shortcut: when two sides are described, the author's own point usually begins with 'But'. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The author says every generation edits and the question is awareness. Trap (C): Half-true. This is the view of the first side, which the author says treats names only as labels. Trap (D): Reversal. The author notes a founder may be judged differently by later generations.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Informed consent is a cornerstone of medical ethics, and in practice it often means a long form that patients sign without reading. Critics conclude that consent is a sham. The conclusion is too quick. The form is poor evidence of consent, but consent was never meant to be a signature; it is a process in which a patient is given understanding, free of pressure, of what is to be done and what the alternatives are. A short, plain conversation, in which the patient is asked to say back what they have understood, serves the purpose better than ten pages. This suggests that the failure is one of method, not of principle: institutions, anxious about liability, have replaced the process with the paper, because paper can be filed and a conversation cannot. A reform that makes forms longer and more precise only deepens the error, for it moves further from what the principle requires.

Which of the following would the author most likely endorse?

options.A: Dropping consent because patients rarely read the forms
options.B: Lengthening consent forms so that every risk is spelled out
options.C: Replacing lengthy forms with brief conversations in which patients explain what they have understood
options.D: Treating a signed form as sufficient proof of consent

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author's remedy is the process (a short conversation with the patient repeating understanding) in place of the paper. Shortcut: for 'would endorse' questions, find the author's own remedy. Trap (A): Reversal. The author says the failure is of method, not of principle. Trap (B): Reversal. The author says longer and more precise forms deepen the error. Trap (D): Half-true. The author calls the form poor evidence of consent.

questions.question_text:
Passage: It is a curious fact that old technologies often improve most rapidly when a rival appears. Sailing ships reached their finest form after steamships had begun to take their cargoes, and the last great sailing vessels were faster and more efficient than any before them. The usual reading is that the old technology made a final effort. A more careful reading notes that the improvements came partly from applying the rival's methods and materials: iron frames, better rigging, even small auxiliary engines. The old form survived by becoming partly new. Defenders of established industries often cite such improvements as proof that they have little to fear from competition, but this inverts the lesson. The improvement is evidence that competition produced the gains, and that survival, when it comes, is usually of a hybrid.

The author's final sentence suggests that

options.A: established industries can safely ignore their rivals
options.B: sailing ships were abandoned as soon as steamships appeared
options.C: all old technologies survive unchanged in some corner of the market
options.D: gains made by an old industry are evidence of the pressure rivals exert, not of its immunity to them

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The defenders say improvement shows they need not fear competition; the author says competition produced the improvement. That is the first option. Shortcut: identify who is being answered in the last sentence and what is inverted. Trap (A): Reversal. The author says this inverts the lesson. Trap (B): Reversal. The passage says sailing ships reached their finest form after steamships had begun to take their cargoes. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The author says survival is usually of a hybrid.

questions.question_text:
Passage: It is tempting to think of taste as something we have, like an ear for pitch, and good taste as something we are born with or acquire by refinement. But the evidence of fashion makes the picture doubtful. What is thought tasteless in one decade becomes charming in the next, and the people who lead such changes are as often those who know the rules well enough to break them as those who know nothing of them. This suggests that taste is a relation rather than a possession: a way of positioning oneself among others, who also position themselves. A person who admires a plain white cup may be responding to its proportions, but also to what the cup says about the person who chooses it. The two cannot be pulled apart, and the attempt to find a pure aesthetic response, free of all signalling, may be a search for something that was never there.

The author's view of 'good taste' is that it

options.A: is inborn, like an ear for pitch
options.B: is nothing but pretence with no genuine pleasure behind it
options.C: changes only when people are ignorant of the rules
options.D: involves social positioning that cannot be cleanly separated from the pleasure taken in an object

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author says taste is a relation and that the aesthetic and the signalling parts cannot be pulled apart, though the person may genuinely respond to proportions. Shortcut: avoid options with 'nothing but' or 'only' unless the text says so. Trap (A): Reversal. The author calls this picture doubtful. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The author allows that a person may respond to the cup's proportions. Trap (C): Half-true. The author says those who lead change are as often people who know the rules well enough to break them.

questions.concept_tag: RC - main point of a sentence (metaphor in science)
questions.question_text:
Passage: Scientists like to say that their language is literal and that metaphors belong to poets. Yet the history of science is full of figures of speech that did real work. Early students of electricity spoke of a 'fluid' that flowed through wires, and the picture guided experiments, even after it was found that nothing flowed like water. A good metaphor suggests what to measure and what to ask; when it is used up, it is dropped or turned into a technical term, often so quietly that no one remembers it was a figure at all. The danger lies elsewhere: a metaphor carries more than its owner intends. To speak of genes as 'selfish' invites talk of motives that genes do not have, and arguments about the metaphor can displace arguments about the evidence. A metaphor is a loan, and like any loan it must be repaid, by checking what has been borrowed along with it.

The main point of the last sentence is that

options.A: scientists should avoid metaphors altogether
options.B: users of a scientific metaphor should check what unintended implications come with it
options.C: metaphors should be turned into technical terms as quickly as possible
options.D: poets use metaphors more carefully than scientists

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The loan metaphor means that something has been borrowed with the figure; repaying means checking the extra baggage. The first option states this. Shortcut: a closing figure of speech needs to be unpacked in plain terms. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The author credits metaphors with doing real work. Trap (C): Half-true. The author says metaphors often become technical terms quietly, but does not advise hastening this. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. No comparison of care between poets and scientists is made.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A speed limit is a rule: drive no faster than a stated number. A requirement to drive at a reasonable speed is a standard. Rules are cheap to apply and predictable, but they are blunt: they forbid safe driving at a high speed on an empty road and permit reckless driving at the limit in fog. Standards fit the case, but they cost more, since each decision needs a judge, and they invite inconsistency. Law tends to choose rules where situations are common and errors cheap to correct, and standards where circumstances vary widely. This is why traffic codes mix the two: a numerical limit, with an overriding standard of care. The mixture is not a compromise born of indecision; it exploits each form where it is strongest and uses one to patch the other's failures. Drivers who know only the number tend to treat the law as a promise of safety rather than a minimum.

The author mentions driving 'at the limit in fog' to illustrate

options.A: how standards produce inconsistent decisions
options.B: why high speeds are always dangerous on empty roads
options.C: how a rule can permit conduct that is unsafe in particular circumstances
options.D: why traffic codes avoid numerical limits

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The example comes in the sentence about the bluntness of rules: they forbid safe fast driving on empty roads and permit reckless driving at the limit in fog. Shortcut: an example illustrates the nearest general claim. Trap (A): Out-of-scope. Inconsistency is a weakness of standards, but the fog example is about a rule. Trap (B): Reversal. The author says rules forbid safe high-speed driving on an empty road. Trap (D): Reversal. The author says traffic codes include a numerical limit alongside a standard.

questions.question_text:
Passage: When wolves were removed from a large park, the deer population rose, and the browsing of the deer stripped young trees along the streams. Without trees the banks eroded and the streams widened, with fewer birds and beavers. When wolves were later returned, many observers reported a recovery, and the story has become a favourite of conservationists: a single predator restoring a whole landscape. The account is attractive but too simple. Deer numbers were also affected by hunting and by weather, and the return of vegetation proceeded unevenly, being strongest where other conditions had also changed. The wolves were one cause among several; to call them the cause is to choose the single actor that makes the best story. Conservation needs such stories to win support, but it should not mistake them for explanations.

The author's attitude to the wolf story is best described as

options.A: appreciative of its value in winning support but sceptical of it as a full explanation
options.B: dismissive, since wolves had no effect on the park
options.C: enthusiastic, since it proves the power of a single predator
options.D: indifferent, since stories cannot influence conservation

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author grants the story's attraction and usefulness ('conservation needs such stories') while denying that it explains the recovery. Shortcut: tone questions with mixed signals have mixed answers. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The author calls wolves 'one cause among several'. Trap (C): Reversal. The author says the account is too simple. Trap (D): Reversal. The author says conservation needs such stories to win support.

questions.question_text:
Passage: The theory of comparative advantage shows that two countries can gain from trade even if one of them is better at making everything. Each should specialise where its relative advantage is greatest and exchange the surplus. The result is a larger total output than would have been possible with no trade. The argument has a quiet assumption, however: that the workers and machines released from the industries that shrink can move easily to those that grow. In practice, a weaver cannot become a software engineer by the next quarter, and a region built around a single factory does not relocate. So the theorem says that the winners could compensate the losers and still be better off; it does not say that they will, or that losers will recover. Whether they are compensated is a political question that no theorem can settle. Critics who conclude that the theory is false, and supporters who conclude that trade harms no one, have both gone beyond what it states.

The author's point is that the theory of comparative advantage

options.A: is false because workers cannot easily change industries
options.B: shows gains in total, but does not show that every group gains or that losers will be compensated
options.C: shows that trade harms no one
options.D: assumes that every country is better at making everything

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author accepts the theorem (total gains) and rejects both over-readings (it is false; it harms no one). Shortcut: when the author criticises both extremes, the answer is the middle statement. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The author says critics who conclude the theory is false have gone beyond what it states. Trap (C): Reversal. The author says supporters who conclude this have gone beyond what the theory states. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. The theory shows that gains arise 'even if' one country is better at everything; it does not assume it.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Most of what any of us knows we have not found out ourselves. We believe that distant countries exist, that medicines work and that the earth is old, mainly because others have told us. Philosophers who regard knowledge as something that must be checked by one's own senses find this embarrassing, since it makes knowledge depend on trust. But the dependence is not a defect; it is how knowledge grows. No individual could verify more than a sliver of what a society knows, and a person who trusted no one would know less, not more. What matters is not whether we trust but whom, and on what grounds: whether the source had the means to know, has been right before, and has no stake in misleading us. The ideal is not self-reliance but well-placed reliance.

The author would most likely agree that

options.A: dependence on testimony is unavoidable, so the task is to judge sources well
options.B: a person who trusts nobody gains the most reliable knowledge
options.C: trust in others should be limited to what can be checked personally
options.D: sources with a stake in the matter are always lying

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author argues that dependence is how knowledge grows and recommends judging whom to trust. The first option is a direct restatement. Shortcut: the last sentence usually gives the thesis in compact form. Trap (B): Reversal. The author says such a person would know less, not more. Trap (C): Reversal. The author says no individual could verify more than a sliver. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The author says only that a stake in misleading is a ground for caution.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Calculus was developed independently by two mathematicians at about the same time, and examples of this kind abound: the same element isolated by two chemists in different countries within months, the same theory of evolution proposed by two naturalists. A romantic view treats a discovery as the achievement of a lone genius who saw what others could not. Simultaneous discovery weakens this view. It suggests that when the necessary tools, data and questions have accumulated, a discovery is ready to be made, and several people near the frontier will make it. This does not diminish the discoverers; it changes what they are credited with. The genius is not the one who sees what no one else could see, but the one who sees it first, or best, or says it so that others take notice. The distinction matters for credit, which is often settled by priority disputes that the facts hardly justify.

The author uses examples of simultaneous discovery to argue that

options.A: discoverers deserve no credit for their achievements
options.B: lone geniuses never exist in the history of science
options.C: discoveries become possible when conditions mature, not only through one person's unique insight
options.D: priority disputes are always settled correctly

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author claims that readiness of tools, data and questions explains multiple discoveries; the lone genius view is weakened, not refuted. Shortcut: the example supports the 'It suggests that...' sentence. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The author says it changes what they are credited with, not that they deserve none. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The author says the view is weakened and revised, not that it is never true. Trap (D): Reversal. The author says priority disputes are often not justified by the facts.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Words for sensitive subjects wear out. A term introduced to be polite or respectful gradually takes on the shadow of the thing it names, and after a generation it sounds as harsh as the one it replaced. Another term is then found, and the cycle begins again. Observers sometimes conclude that changing words is pointless, since the stigma only transfers. This misreads the process. The word is not the cause of the stigma; it is the place where the stigma becomes visible. Changing the word may signal a wish to treat people differently, and may help change habits, but it cannot do the work of changing attitudes. Where attitudes do change, the old words often lose their sting without being replaced. The words follow the attitude; they do not lead it.

The author's view is that new terms for sensitive subjects

options.A: express a wish for change but cannot by themselves alter underlying attitudes
options.B: are pointless because stigma only transfers to them
options.C: cause the stigma that attaches to the people they name
options.D: always lose their sting after one generation

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The word is where the stigma becomes visible, not its cause. Changing words may signal intent but attitudes lead. Shortcut: two-sided passages: the author rejects both extremes. Trap (B): Reversal. The author says this misreads the process; the word may signal a wish for change. Trap (C): Reversal. The author says the word is not the cause of the stigma. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The author says the old words lose their sting when attitudes change, not on a fixed schedule.

questions.question_text:
