Passage: After an accident, the causes seem obvious. The warning signs were there; why did no one see them? This sense of obviousness is the product of hindsight: knowing how things ended, we pick out the signals that pointed that way and forget the many others that pointed elsewhere or nowhere. Investigators who judge the people involved by what is clear now are likely to conclude that they were careless or incompetent, and to recommend punishment. Yet the people involved did not know the outcome. They were weighing ambiguous signals under pressure, and most of the time that weighing leads to a safe result. A more useful question than 'why did they not see it?' is 'why did their actions seem reasonable at the time?' The second question leads to changes in procedures, displays or workloads; the first leads to the removal of an individual and leaves in place the conditions that will produce the next accident.

The author recommends that investigators

options.A: identify the careless individual and remove him from his post
options.B: ignore the warning signs present before the accident
options.C: treat every accident as unavoidable
options.D: ask why the actions seemed reasonable at the time, so as to improve working conditions

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author contrasts two questions and prefers the one that leads to changes in procedures, displays or workloads. Shortcut: a recommendation is the remedy contrasted with a criticised practice. Trap (A): Reversal. The author says this leaves the conditions in place for the next accident. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The author does not ask that warning signs be ignored, only that they not be judged with hindsight. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The author wants changes that reduce future accidents.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A slogan says that if you are not paying for a service, you are the product. It is memorable, and it points to something true: services that charge users nothing often earn their money by selling the attention or data of those users to others. But the slogan presents as new a model that is very old. Newspapers sold readers to advertisers for a century, and nobody concluded that a reader was a commodity in the way that a bale of cotton is. The slogan also hides a difference. A newspaper sold the attention of readers in general; a service that records each user's behaviour sells something about that particular person. The first is closer to renting a billboard; the second begins to resemble a file kept on the individual. The worry is real, but it is a worry about the file, not about the absence of a price.

The author's reservation about the slogan is that it

options.A: is false because free services never earn money from users
options.B: overstates the harm done by newspapers
options.C: treats an old model as new and fails to separate selling general attention from selling information about individuals
options.D: ignores that users like free services

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author grants the slogan's truth, then adds two reservations: it is old, and it blurs a difference between general attention and individual files. Shortcut: qualified agreement: find what the author concedes, then what he adds. Trap (A): Reversal. The author says it points to something true: such services earn money from attention or data. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. The author does not claim newspapers did harm; he uses them as a precedent. Trap (D): Out-of-scope. User preferences are not mentioned.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A forensic test that matches a suspect's sample to a crime-scene sample with a one-in-a-million chance of a false match is often taken to mean that there is only a one-in-a-million chance that the suspect is innocent. This is a mistake. The false-match figure tells us how often an innocent person would match; it does not tell us how many innocent people there are to be tested. In a city of ten million, about ten innocent people would match by chance alone. A suspect who matches is therefore one of roughly eleven people who fit, only one of whom committed the crime, unless other evidence narrows the field. The test is still valuable, since it reduces millions to a handful. But it is the start of an argument, not its end. Courts are misled less by the test than by a habit of reading a small probability as a verdict.

The author uses the example of a city of ten million to show that

options.A: the forensic test is of no value in criminal investigation
options.B: the probability of a false match is higher than one in a million
options.C: a suspect who matches must be one of exactly ten innocent people
options.D: a rare chance match can still occur in many innocent people when the pool is large, so a match alone does not prove guilt

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Ten million × one in a million gives about ten innocent matches, plus the guilty one: roughly eleven fit. A match alone cannot single out the guilty. Shortcut: convert the rare chance into expected counts over the whole pool. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The author says the test reduces millions to a handful and is still valuable. Trap (B): Reversal. The author accepts the figure and shows that it is misread. Trap (C): Half-true. The suspect would be one of roughly eleven who fit, only one of whom is guilty, unless other evidence narrows the field.

questions.question_text:
Passage: People who delay an important task are commonly described as lazy or as poor managers of time. Both descriptions may mislead. Studies suggest that procrastination is more often a way of escaping an unpleasant feeling aroused by the task: anxiety about doing it badly, boredom, resentment at being asked. Putting off the task relieves the feeling at once, which rewards the delay, even though the long-term cost is higher. Seen this way, the standard remedies look misplaced. Timetables and reminders address a problem of scheduling, but the person already knows when the task is due; what they lack is a way to bear the discomfort of beginning. Methods that help are those that make the first step small and kind: working for ten minutes, forgiving earlier delays, deciding where to start. They work not because they organise time, but because they lower the emotional price of starting.

The passage implies that advice to 'manage your time better' is

options.A: always successful because deadlines are the real cause of delay
options.B: likely to fail because it treats a problem of feeling as a problem of scheduling
options.C: useful mainly for people who are lazy
options.D: harmful because it makes people more anxious

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author says timetables address scheduling while the real problem is the discomfort of beginning. Shortcut: see which standard remedy the author calls 'misplaced' and why. Trap (A): Reversal. The author says the person already knows when the task is due. Trap (C): Reversal. The author says the label of laziness may mislead. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The author says it is misplaced, not that it causes harm.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Larger cities are not simply bigger versions of small ones. When a city doubles in population, its roads, pipes and cables increase by less than double, because shared infrastructure is used more efficiently. But its output, its inventions and, unhappily, some of its crimes increase by more than double. The explanation lies in what grows faster than the number of people: the number of possible contacts among them. Each new resident adds to the people who can be met, and the meetings in which ideas are exchanged, deals made or quarrels begun rise much faster than the headcount. The same arithmetic explains why a city cannot simply settle into a comfortable size. Its extra output must be spent on handling extra friction, and to keep ahead it needs ever fresh sources of invention. A city that stops inventing does not stay still; it declines.

Which of the following best captures the author's explanation of why larger cities produce disproportionately more innovation?

options.A: Infrastructure grows more slowly than the population
options.B: Larger cities attract only the most inventive residents
options.C: Crime rises in step with innovation and thus drives it
options.D: The number of possible contacts among residents grows faster than the population itself

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Contacts among N people grow roughly as N squared, so doubling population more than doubles meetings. This explains both extra output and extra crime. Shortcut: ask what grows faster than headcount. Trap (A): Half-true. This explains why roads and pipes per person fall, not why innovation per person rises. Trap (B): Out-of-scope. The passage says nothing about who is attracted to cities. Trap (C): Reversal. The author notes that both rise faster than population, but gives contacts as the cause of both, not crime as the cause of innovation.

questions.concept_tag: Arithmetic Progression - sum of n terms
questions.question_text: The first term of an arithmetic progression is 7 and the common difference is 3. What is the sum of its first 20 terms?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: S = n/2 × [2a + (n - 1)d] = 10 × [14 + 57] = 710. Shortcut: use S = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d] directly. Trap (A): forgets the factor 1/2 in n/2 × (first + last). Trap (B): uses the 20th term as 7 + 20 × 3 = 67 instead of 7 + 19 × 3 = 64. Trap (D): sums only 19 terms.

questions.question_text: What is the sum to infinity of the geometric progression 18, 6, 2, 2/3, ...?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The ratio is 6/18 = 1/3, so S = a/(1 - r) = 18/(2/3) = 27. Shortcut: S = a / (1 - r) when |r| < 1. Trap (A): takes the common ratio as 1/2 instead of 1/3. Trap (C): adds only the first three terms. Trap (D): divides by r = 1/3 instead of 1 - r = 2/3.

questions.question_text: What is the value of x that satisfies log₃(x + 2) + log₃(x - 4) = 3?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Combine: (x + 2)(x - 4) = 27, so x² - 2x - 35 = 0, giving x = 7 or -5. For x = -5, x - 4 < 0, which is not allowed. So x = 7. Shortcut: combine logs, solve, then check the domain. Trap (A): is the second root of the quadratic but makes x - 4 negative, so it is rejected. Trap (C): solves x + 2 = 3³ and ignores the second logarithm. Trap (D): adds the arguments instead of multiplying them: (x + 2) + (x - 4) = 27.

questions.question_text: A team of 2 boys and 2 girls is to be chosen from 5 boys and 4 girls. In how many ways can the team be chosen?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Boys: C(5, 2) = 10. Girls: C(4, 2) = 6. Independent choices multiply: 10 × 6 = 60. Shortcut: choose each group separately and multiply. Trap (B): chooses any 4 of the 9 students and ignores the 2 + 2 split. Trap (C): counts ordered selections, 5P2 × 4P2. Trap (D): adds C(5, 2) and C(4, 2) instead of multiplying.

questions.concept_tag: Probability - second throw larger than the first
questions.question_text: A fair die is rolled twice. What is the probability that the second number is greater than the first?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Of 36 equally likely outcomes, 6 have equal numbers. The remaining 30 split equally, so 15 have the second greater. Probability = 15/36 = 5/12. Shortcut: remove the ties, then halve. Trap (A): assumes the second is greater or smaller with equal chance, forgetting the ties. Trap (B): gives the probability of getting equal numbers on the two throws doubled wrongly. Trap (C): counts the cases where the second is greater than or equal to the first.

questions.question_text: The point P divides the line segment joining A(1, 2) and B(7, 8) internally in the ratio 2 : 1, with AP : PB = 2 : 1. What is the sum of the coordinates of P?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: P = ((2 × 7 + 1 × 1)/3, (2 × 8 + 1 × 2)/3) = (5, 6). The sum is 11. Shortcut: weight each endpoint by the opposite part of the ratio. Trap (A): uses the midpoint (4, 5). Trap (B): reverses the ratio and gets (3, 4). Trap (C): adds the coordinates of B's side only, 7 + 6.

questions.question_text: How many of the positive divisors of 72 are even?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 72 = 2³ × 3². An even divisor needs 2 to the power 1, 2 or 3 (3 choices) and 3 to the power 0, 1 or 2 (3 choices). So 3 × 3 = 9. Shortcut: fix at least one factor of 2, then count. Trap (B): counts all the divisors of 72. Trap (C): 6 counts only the divisors that are multiples of 4 (4, 8, 12, 24, 36, 72) and misses those with a single factor 2. Trap (D): leaves out the divisor 72 itself.

questions.question_text: What is the 10th term of the geometric progression 3, 6, 12, ...?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The nth term is a × rⁿ⁻¹ = 3 × 2⁹ = 3 × 512 = 1536. Shortcut: the exponent is n - 1. Trap (A): uses 3 × 2¹⁰ instead of 3 × 2⁹. Trap (C): gives the 9th term. Trap (D): treats the sequence as arithmetic with difference 3.

questions.question_text: What is the coefficient of x² in the expansion of (1 + x)⁶?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The coefficient of x² is C(6, 2) = 6 × 5 / 2 = 15. Shortcut: the coefficient of xʳ in (1 + x)ⁿ is C(n, r). Trap (A): uses C(6, 1). Trap (C): uses C(6, 3). Trap (D): multiplies C(6, 2) by 2.

questions.question_text: What is the value of sin 75° cos 15° + cos 75° sin 15°?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: sin A cos B + cos A sin B = sin(A + B) = sin 90° = 1. Shortcut: recognise the compound angle formula. Trap (A): evaluates cos 90° instead of sin 90°. Trap (B): evaluates sin 30° by halving 60°. Trap (D): uses the difference sin(75° - 15°) = sin 60° instead of the sum.

questions.question_text: How many integers x satisfy ∣2x - 3∣ < 7?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: -7 < 2x - 3 < 7 gives -4 < 2x < 10, so -2 < x < 5. The integers are -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, which is 6 integers. Shortcut: remove the modulus, then count the strict integers. Trap (A): drops one end of the integer range. Trap (B): includes the end value 5. Trap (D): counts only the positive integers.

questions.question_text: If f(x) = 2x + 3, what is the value of f(f(2))?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: f(2) = 2(2) + 3 = 7, and f(7) = 2(7) + 3 = 17. Shortcut: work from the inside outwards. Trap (A): computes 2 × f(2) = 2 × 7. Trap (C): adds 3 to f(2) wrongly as f(2) + 3. Trap (D): 23 adds 3 to f(2) to get 10 and then applies f, giving f(10) = 23.

questions.concept_tag: Circles - radius from the general equation
questions.question_text: What is the radius of the circle x² + y² - 6x + 8y = 0?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Complete the squares: (x - 3)² + (y + 4)² = 9 + 16 = 25. So r = 5. Shortcut: r² = g² + f² - c, where the circle is x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0. Trap (A): reports r² and not r. Trap (B): takes twice the correct radius. Trap (C): adds the coefficients 3 and 4.

questions.question_text: In how many distinct ways can the letters of the word LEVEL be arranged?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: LEVEL has 5 letters, with L twice and E twice. Arrangements = 5!/(2! × 2!) = 120/4 = 30. Shortcut: divide by the factorial of each repeat. Trap (B): treats all the letters as different. Trap (C): divides only by 2! for the repeated L. Trap (D): divides by 2! × 2! × 2!.

questions.concept_tag: Exponents - express in a common base
questions.question_text: If 2ˣ = 5, what is the value of 4ˣ⁺¹?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 4ˣ = (2ˣ)² = 25. So 4ˣ⁺¹ = 4 × 25 = 100. Shortcut: write 4ˣ as (2ˣ)². Trap (A): computes 4 × 5, using 4ˣ = 5. Trap (B): computes 10 × 5. Trap (C): squares 5 and adds 4.

questions.question_text: Four arithmetic means are inserted between 3 and 28. What is the third of these means?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 3, m₁, m₂, m₃, m₄, 28 form an AP with 6 terms, so 5d = 25 and d = 5. The means are 8, 13, 18, 23. The third is 18. Shortcut: the number of terms is the number of means plus 2. Trap (B): reports the fourth mean. Trap (C): reports the second mean. Trap (D): adds 5 to the first term three times and then adds 2.

questions.question_text: The sum of the geometric progression 3 + 6 + 12 + ... to n terms is 189. What is n?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Sₙ = 3(2ⁿ - 1) = 189, so 2ⁿ - 1 = 63 and 2ⁿ = 64, giving n = 6. Shortcut: divide by the first term, add 1, read the power of 2. Trap (A): gives S₅ = 93. Trap (B): gives S₇ = 381. Trap (D): reports the value of 2ⁿ - 1 instead of n.

questions.concept_tag: Logarithms - change of the unknown base
questions.question_text: If log_x 27 = 3/2, what is the value of x?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: log_x 27 = 3/2 means x^(3/2) = 27, so x = 27^(2/3) = (27^(1/3))² = 3² = 9. Shortcut: convert to exponential form and invert the power. Trap (A): takes log₃ 27 = 3 and ignores the 3/2. Trap (B): computes 27^(4/3). Trap (C): multiplies 27 by 2/3 instead of raising it to the power 2/3.

questions.question_text: Using each of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 exactly once, how many 5-digit numbers can be formed in which the digits 1 and 2 are not next to each other?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total = 5! = 120. Treat 1 and 2 as a block: 4! arrangements × 2 orders = 48 numbers with them adjacent. Required = 120 - 48 = 72. Shortcut: total minus the glued case, remembering both orders. Trap (B): counts only the numbers in which 1 and 2 are adjacent. Trap (C): subtracts only 24, treating 1 and 2 as a block in one order. Trap (D): counts the arrangements of the block with the other digits in one order.

questions.concept_tag: Probability - conditional on at least one ace
questions.question_text: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard pack of 52. Given that at least one of the cards is an ace, what is the probability that both are aces?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: P(both aces) = C(4, 2)/C(52, 2) = 6/1326. P(at least one ace) = 1 - C(48, 2)/C(52, 2) = 198/1326. Conditional probability = 6/198 = 1/33. Shortcut: divide the favourable count by the count of the reduced sample space. Trap (A): gives the unconditional probability of two aces. Trap (C): gives the probability that the second card is an ace given that the first is. Trap (D): gives the probability that a single card is an ace.

questions.question_text: A line passes through the point (1, 2) and makes equal intercepts on the two axes (both positive). What is the area of the triangle which it forms with the axes?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Equal intercepts a: x/a + y/a = 1, so x + y = a. The point (1, 2) gives a = 3. Area = 1/2 × 3 × 3 = 9/2. Shortcut: equal intercepts means x + y = constant. Trap (B): forgets the factor 1/2. Trap (C): reports the intercept and not the area. Trap (D): halves the area twice.

questions.concept_tag: Number Theory - HCF, LCM and sum
questions.question_text: Two numbers have HCF 12 and LCM 504, and their sum is 156. What is the larger number?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Write the numbers as 12m and 12n with m and n co-prime, so mn = 504/12 = 42. Also m + n = 156/12 = 13. The pair is 6 and 7, so the numbers are 72 and 84. The larger is 84. Shortcut: HCF × LCM = product; divide by the HCF to get co-prime parts. Trap (A): reports the smaller number. Trap (C): takes half of the sum. Trap (D): divides the LCM by 3.

questions.concept_tag: Quadratic Equations - roots in a given ratio
questions.question_text: If one root of x² - 9x + k = 0 is twice the other, what is k?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let the roots be r and 2r. The sum is 3r = 9, so r = 3 and the roots are 3 and 6. The product k = 18. Shortcut: use sum and ratio to get both roots. Trap (A): takes the roots as 4 and 5. Trap (B): takes the roots as 2 and 7. Trap (C): takes the roots as 3 and 9.

questions.concept_tag: Binomial Theorem - term independent of x
questions.question_text: What is the term independent of x in the expansion of (x² + 1/x)⁹?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The general term is C(9, r)(x²)⁹⁻ʳ(1/x)ʳ = C(9, r)x¹⁸⁻³ʳ. For no x: 18 - 3r = 0, so r = 6. The term is C(9, 6) = 84. Shortcut: set the power of x to zero. Trap (A): uses C(9, 4) or C(9, 5). Trap (B): uses C(9, 2). Trap (D): uses C(9, 1).

questions.concept_tag: Functions - linear function from two values
questions.question_text: A linear function f(x) = ax + b satisfies f(1) = 5 and f(3) = 11. What is f(10)?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: a + b = 5 and 3a + b = 11, so a = 3 and b = 2. f(10) = 32. Shortcut: slope = change in f / change in x. Trap (A): uses the slope 3 with intercept 5. Trap (B): drops the constant term. Trap (D): 38 adds 3 for each of the 9 steps from x = 1 to x = 10 but starts from f(3) = 11 instead of f(1) = 5 (11 + 27).

questions.question_text: If a and b are positive numbers with ab = 36, what is the minimum value of 4a + 9b?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: By AM-GM, 4a + 9b ≥ 2√(4a × 9b) = 2√(36ab) = 2√1296 = 72, with equality at 4a = 9b, i.e. a = 9, b = 4. Shortcut: AM-GM on the two weighted terms. Trap (A): forgets the factor 2 in AM-GM. Trap (C): takes a = b = 6. Trap (D): doubles the correct minimum.

questions.concept_tag: Trigonometry - from tan to sin and cos
questions.question_text: If tan θ = 3/4 and θ is acute, what is the value of sin θ + cos θ?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take the right triangle with sides 3, 4 and hypotenuse 5. sin θ = 3/5 and cos θ = 4/5, so the sum is 7/5. Shortcut: use the 3-4-5 triangle. Trap (A): uses the identity sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 for the sum itself. Trap (C): inverts the correct value. Trap (D): gives the product sin θ cos θ.

questions.concept_tag: Series - telescoping with a gap of two
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 1/(k(k + 2)) = (1/2)(1/k - 1/(k + 2)). The terms telescope, leaving (1/2)(1 + 1/2 - 1/21 - 1/22) = (1/2)(3/2 - 43/462) = 325/462. Shortcut: write each term as half a difference with gap 2. Trap (A): gives the sum to infinity instead of 20 terms. Trap (B): uses the pattern of 1/(k(k + 1)). Trap (C): keeps only the first half of the telescoping terms.

questions.question_text: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other, with replacement. What is the probability that the two balls are of different colours?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: P(red then blue) = 3/5 × 2/5 = 6/25, and P(blue then red) = 6/25. Total = 12/25. Shortcut: count both orders. Trap (A): counts only one order, red then blue. Trap (C): gives the probability that the balls are of the same colour. Trap (D): gives the probability of a red ball on one draw.

questions.concept_tag: Circles - length of a common chord
questions.question_text: The circles x² + y² = 25 and (x - 6)² + y² = 25 intersect at two points. What is the length of their common chord?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Subtract the equations: 12x - 36 = 0, so x = 3. Then y² = 25 - 9 = 16 and y = ±4. The chord joins (3, 4) and (3, -4), so its length is 8. Shortcut: subtract the two circle equations to get the chord line. Trap (A): reports the half-chord. Trap (B): takes the diameter. Trap (C): reports the distance between the centres.

questions.question_text: Ten points lie in a plane, of which exactly four are collinear and no other three are collinear. How many triangles can be formed with vertices among these points?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total triples = C(10, 3) = 120. Triples from the four collinear points = C(4, 3) = 4, and these do not give triangles. So 120 - 4 = 116. Shortcut: subtract the degenerate triples. Trap (B): ignores the collinear points. Trap (C): subtracts 8 instead of 4 collinear triples. Trap (D): subtracts 20, counting C(6, 3).

questions.concept_tag: Matrices - determinant of a scalar multiple of a product
questions.question_text: If A = [1, 2; 3, 4], what is the determinant of 2·A·Aᵀ, where Aᵀ is the transpose of A?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: det A = 4 - 6 = -2 and det Aᵀ = -2. So det(A Aᵀ) = 4. For a 2 × 2 matrix, det(2M) = 2² det M = 4 × 4 = 16. Shortcut: det(kM) = kⁿ det M for an n × n matrix. Trap (A): takes det(2M) = 2 det M instead of 4 det M for a 2 × 2 matrix. Trap (B): drops the scalar 2. Trap (D): takes det(2M) = 8 det M.

questions.question_text: What is the sum of all real values of x that satisfy 4ˣ - 5·2ˣ + 4 = 0?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let t = 2ˣ. Then t² - 5t + 4 = 0, so t = 1 or 4. So x = 0 or 2, and the sum is 2. Shortcut: substitute t = 2ˣ and convert back. Trap (A): takes only the solution x = 0 of 2ˣ = 1 and misses x = 2. Trap (B): adds the values 1 and 4 of 2ˣ, not of x. Trap (D): takes the larger value of 2ˣ as the sum.

questions.concept_tag: Number System - trailing zeros of a factorial
questions.question_text: How many zeros are there at the end of 75! ?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The number of zeros = ⌊75/5⌋ + ⌊75/25⌋ = 15 + 3 = 18. Shortcut: count the factors of 5, including 25s. Trap (B): counts only the multiples of 5. Trap (C): adds 1 for the single multiple of 75. Trap (D): 20 divides by 15 instead of 25 in the second step: 75/5 + 75/15 = 15 + 5.

questions.question_text: How many ordered pairs (x, y) of positive integers satisfy x² - y² = 45?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: (x - y)(x + y) = 45 with x + y > x - y > 0. Factor pairs: (1, 45), (3, 15), (5, 9). All have both factors odd, so x and y are integers: (23, 22), (9, 6), (7, 2). That is 3 pairs. Shortcut: factorise and match the parity of the two factors. Trap (B): counts each factor pair in both orders. Trap (C): 4 counts the divisors of 45 that are at most 9 (1, 3, 5, 9) instead of the factor pairs d × e with d < e. Trap (D): 5 counts the divisors of 45 other than 45 itself (1, 3, 5, 9, 15).

questions.concept_tag: Number Theory - sum of reciprocals of divisors
questions.question_text: What is the sum of the reciprocals of all the positive divisors of 28?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sum of reciprocals of the divisors of n = σ(n)/n. σ(28) = 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 + 28 = 56, so the sum = 56/28 = 2. Shortcut: pair each divisor d with n/d. Trap (A): sums the divisors, not their reciprocals. Trap (C): counts the divisors. Trap (D): doubles the correct answer.

questions.question_text: In how many ways can 20 be written as the sum of three positive integers if the order of the parts does not matter?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Order the parts a ≤ b ≤ c and fix the smallest part a. Then b + c = 20 - a with a ≤ b ≤ c: a = 1 gives 9 pairs, a = 2 gives 8, a = 3 gives 6, a = 4 gives 5, a = 5 gives 3, a = 6 gives 2. Total = 33. Shortcut: order the parts so a ≤ b ≤ c and count by the smallest part. Trap (A): counts ordered triples. Trap (B): counts ordered triples with each part at most 9. Trap (D): 24 counts only the partitions with three different parts (33 minus the 9 with two equal parts).

questions.concept_tag: Probability - no two identical letters adjacent
questions.question_text: All the distinct arrangements of the letters of AABBC are listed. If one arrangement is chosen at random, what is the probability that the two A's are not next to each other?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total distinct arrangements = 5!/(2!2!) = 30. With the two A's glued, we arrange AA, B, B, C: 4!/2! = 12. So the A's are apart in 30 - 12 = 18 arrangements, a probability of 18/30 = 3/5. Shortcut: glue the pair, count, and subtract. Trap (A): gives the probability that the A's are adjacent. Trap (B): assumes that adjacent and non-adjacent are equally likely. Trap (D): halves the correct probability.

Write k·k! = (k + 1)! - k!. The sum telescopes to 7! - 1! = 5040 - 1 = 5039. Shortcut: k·k! = (k + 1)! - k!. Trap (A): reports 7! - 1 + 1 by forgetting to subtract 1. Trap (C): 4999 rounds 7! to 5000 and then subtracts 1. Trap (D): subtracts 7 from 7! instead of 1.

questions.question_text: What is the value of log₂ x · log_x 5 · log₅ 8, for x > 0, x ≠ 1?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: By the chain rule, log_a b · log_b c = log_a c. So the product is log₂ x · log_x 5 · log₅ 8 = log₂ 8 = 3. Shortcut: chain rule: log_a b · log_b c = log_a c. Trap (A): assumes that the chain of logarithms always cancels to 1. Trap (B): reports the argument of the last logarithm. Trap (C): reports the argument of the middle logarithm.

questions.question_text: In an arithmetic progression with a non-zero common difference, the sum of the first 7 terms is equal to the sum of the first 13 terms. What is the sum of the first 20 terms?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: S₁₃ - S₇ = 0 means that terms 8 to 13 sum to zero, which gives 2a + 19d = 0. But S₂₀ = 10(2a + 19d) = 0. Shortcut: S_m = S_n implies S_(m+n) = 0. Trap (A): reports the number of terms. Trap (B): multiplies 7 and 20. Trap (C): reports the sum 1 + 2 + ... + 13.

questions.question_text: How many integers from 1 to 200 leave remainder 1 when divided by 3 and remainder 2 when divided by 5?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The conditions together mean x ≡ 7 (mod 15): 7, 22, 37, ..., 187. The count is (187 - 7)/15 + 1 = 13. Shortcut: combine the congruences into one modulo the LCM. Trap (B): counts one extra term at the end of the progression. Trap (C): leaves out the first number, 7. Trap (D): counts the numbers leaving remainder 2 when divided by 5.

questions.question_text: How many ordered triples (x, y, z) of positive integers, each at most 9, satisfy x + y + z = 20?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Without the limit: C(19, 2) = 171. Triples with some variable at least 10: put x = 10 + x', giving x' + y + z = 10 with positive y, z, x' ≥ 0, which is C(11 - 1, 2) = 45 for each variable. Two variables cannot both exceed 9. So 171 - 3 × 45 = 36. Shortcut: count all, then subtract the cases breaking a limit. Trap (A): ignores the upper limit of 9. Trap (B): reports the number of triples removed, not the number left. Trap (D): 45 counts the triples in which one particular variable exceeds 9 and reports that count, not the number left.

questions.question_text: How many real values of x satisfy (x² - 5x + 5)^(x² - 9x + 20) = 1?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The value is 1 when: (i) base = 1: x² - 5x + 4 = 0, so x = 1 or 4. (ii) exponent = 0 with base non-zero: x² - 9x + 20 = 0, so x = 4 or 5. (iii) base = -1 with an even exponent: x² - 5x + 6 = 0, so x = 2 or 3, and the exponents at x = 2 and x = 3 are 6 and 2, both even. The solutions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 give 5 values. Shortcut: think: base 1, exponent 0, base -1 with even exponent. Trap (B): counts only the cases of base 1 and exponent 0 and misses base -1. Trap (C): misses one root of the second equation. Trap (D): counts only the cases where the base is 1.

questions.concept_tag: Geometry - maximum area of an inscribed rectangle
questions.question_text: What is the maximum possible area of a rectangle inscribed in a circle of radius 5?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The diagonal of the rectangle is the diameter, 10. For sides a and b, a² + b² = 100, and the area ab ≤ (a² + b²)/2 = 50, with equality when a = b (a square). Shortcut: a² + b² is fixed, so ab is largest when a = b. Trap (B): takes the area of the circumscribing square. Trap (C): takes r² as the area. Trap (D): reports the area of the circle itself, with π = 3.14.

questions.concept_tag: Inequalities - integer solutions of a quadratic inequality
questions.question_text: How many integers n satisfy n² < 2n + 15?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: n² - 2n - 15 < 0 gives (n - 5)(n + 3) < 0, so -3 < n < 5. The integers are -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, which is 7 integers. Shortcut: factorise and read the strict interval. Trap (A): includes the root n = 5 where equality holds. Trap (B): includes both the roots n = 5 and n = -3. Trap (C): leaves out n = 0.

questions.concept_tag: Probability - expected number of fixed points
questions.question_text: The six letters of a word, all different, are arranged in a random order. What is the expected number of letters that end up in their original position?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let each letter have an indicator variable for being in its place. Each has probability 1/6. By linearity of expectation, the expected number of fixed letters is 6 × 1/6 = 1. Shortcut: use linearity of expectation with indicator variables. Trap (A): assumes every letter stays in place. Trap (B): reports the probability for a single letter. Trap (C): 1/2 adds the chance 1/6 for only three of the six letters (3 × 1/6).

questions.concept_tag: Counting - arrangements with no two adjacent
questions.question_text: In how many ways can 3 identical red balls and 2 identical blue balls be arranged in a row so that the two blue balls are not next to each other?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Place the 3 red balls first, which leaves 4 gaps. Choose 2 gaps for the blue balls: C(4, 2) = 6. Shortcut: place the free items first and use the gaps. Trap (A): counts all the arrangements. Trap (C): counts the arrangements with the blue balls together. Trap (D): treats the blue balls as different.

questions.question_text: What is the sum to infinity of 1 + 2/3 + 3/9 + 4/27 + ... ?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The series is Σ n·rⁿ⁻¹ with r = 1/3. Its sum is 1/(1 - r)² = 1/(2/3)² = 9/4. Shortcut: Σ n rⁿ⁻¹ = 1/(1 - r)². Trap (A): gives the sum 1/(1 - r) of the plain geometric series. Trap (C): 3 doubles the plain geometric sum 3/2, taking the average weight of the terms as 2. Trap (D): uses 1/(1 - r)³.

questions.concept_tag: Counting - digit sum of a four-digit number
questions.question_text: How many four-digit numbers have a digit sum equal to 9?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let the digits be d₁ d₂ d₃ d₄ with d₁ ≥ 1. Put d₁' = d₁ - 1, so d₁' + d₂ + d₃ + d₄ = 8 with all digits at least 0. No digit can exceed 9 as the total is only 8. The count is C(8 + 3, 3) = C(11, 3) = 165. Shortcut: reduce the leading digit by 1 and use stars and bars. Trap (B): allows the first digit to be zero. Trap (C): uses C(10, 3). Trap (D): uses C(9, 3).

questions.question_text: If x - 1/x = 2, what is the value of x³ - 1/x³?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: x³ - 1/x³ = (x - 1/x)³ + 3(x - 1/x) = 8 + 6 = 14. Shortcut: use a³ - b³ = (a - b)³ + 3ab(a - b) with ab = 1. Trap (A): cubes the given value. Trap (B): reports 3 times the given value. Trap (C): uses 8 + 4, mis-evaluating the middle term.

questions.question_text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: A ________ record-keeper, Sudha never missed a single entry in the ledger, however small.

options.A: careless
options.B: meticulous
options.C: hasty
options.D: indifferent

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The clause 'never missed a single entry, however small' describes extreme care over detail. 'Meticulous' means showing great attention to detail. Shortcut: use the clue after the comma. Shortcut: use the clue in the sentence to find the sense. Trap (A): Opposite meaning. 'Careless' is the reverse of the sense required by 'never missed a single entry'. Trap (C): Opposite meaning. A hasty person would be likely to miss entries. Trap (D): Opposite meaning. An indifferent person does not take care over details.

questions.question_text: Select the word closest in meaning to the word in bold: The beauty of the rainbow is **ephemeral**; it lasts only a few minutes.

options.A: short-lived
options.B: eternal
options.C: colourful
options.D: misleading

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Ephemeral' means lasting for a very short time, and the clause after the semicolon gives the clue 'lasts only a few minutes'. Shortcut: use the explanatory clause after the semicolon. Trap (B): Antonym. 'Eternal' means lasting for ever, the opposite of the sense required. Trap (C): Related word. This relates to a rainbow's colours, not to how long it lasts. Trap (D): Unrelated word. Nothing in the sentence suggests that the rainbow misleads.

questions.question_text: Select the word most nearly opposite in meaning to the word 'scarce'.

options.A: rare
options.B: limited
options.C: plentiful
options.D: precious

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Scarce' means in short supply; its opposite is 'plentiful', meaning available in large amounts. Shortcut: pick the word that reverses quantity. Trap (A): Synonym. 'Rare' is a synonym of 'scarce'. Trap (B): Synonym. 'Limited' is close in meaning to 'scarce'. Trap (D): Related word. 'Precious' means valuable, which is a different idea from quantity.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct option: Each of the boys in the class has submitted ________ project on time.

options.A: their
options.B: they
options.C: his
options.D: our

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Each' refers to one boy at a time, so the pronoun is singular. 'His' agrees with 'boys' as a male group. Shortcut: 'each' and 'every' take singular pronouns. Trap (A): Plural pronoun. 'Each' is singular, so it takes a singular pronoun in standard Indian-exam English. Trap (B): Wrong case. 'They' is a subject pronoun and cannot stand before a noun. Trap (D): Wrong person. The sentence refers to the boys, not to the speaker's group.

questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: Aman's grandmother is ________ honest woman who is respected by everyone in the village.

options.A: a
options.B: an
options.C: the
options.D: no article

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The article depends on the sound: 'honest' starts with the vowel sound /ɒ/, so 'an' is used. Shortcut: go by sound, not spelling. Trap (A): Wrong article. 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound because the 'h' is silent, so 'an' is needed. Trap (C): Wrong article. The woman is introduced for the first time, so the definite article is not suitable. Trap (D): Omitted article. A singular countable noun needs an article here.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct preposition: Rohit cannot eat peanuts because he is allergic ________ them.

options.A: with
options.B: from
options.C: for
options.D: to

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The adjective 'allergic' is followed by 'to', as in 'allergic to dust'. Shortcut: learn the fixed adjective-preposition pairs. Trap (A): Wrong preposition. 'Allergic' takes 'to', not 'with'. Trap (B): Wrong preposition. 'Allergic from' is not used. Trap (C): Wrong preposition. 'Allergic for' is not used.

questions.question_text: Choose the option that best explains the idiom in bold: During the weeks before the examination, Leela had to **burn the midnight oil** to complete her syllabus.

options.A: to waste a lot of electricity
options.B: to sleep very early
options.C: to light a lamp for a festival
options.D: to work late into the night

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'To burn the midnight oil' means to work or study late at night. The context of preparing for an examination confirms this. Shortcut: use the context to avoid the literal meaning. Trap (A): Literal reading. This takes the words literally. Trap (B): Opposite meaning. The idiom refers to staying awake and working. Trap (C): Out of context. This does not suit the context of studying for an examination.

questions.question_text: Choose the option that best explains the idiom in bold: Losing the job at first seemed a disaster, but it proved to be a **blessing in disguise** because it led Karan to start his own successful business.

options.A: something that is good and also looks good
options.B: something that seems bad but turns out to be good
options.C: a prayer said in secret
options.D: a wish that does not come true

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sentence moves from 'seemed a disaster' to a successful outcome, which is the meaning of 'a blessing in disguise'. Shortcut: look for the turn from bad to good. Trap (A): Half-true. The idiom needs an initial appearance of misfortune. Trap (C): Literal reading. This takes the words literally. Trap (D): Reversal. The idiom speaks of a good result.

questions.question_text: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: 'a person who walks in his sleep'.

options.A: insomniac
options.B: somnambulist
options.C: misanthrope
options.D: optimist

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Somnambulist' comes from Latin 'somnus' (sleep) and 'ambulare' (walk). An insomniac suffers from sleeplessness, which is different. Shortcut: split the root: somnus = sleep, ambulare = walk. Trap (A): Confusable word. An insomniac is a person who cannot sleep. Trap (C): Unrelated word. A misanthrope is a person who dislikes people. Trap (D): Unrelated word. An optimist expects good outcomes.

questions.question_text: Choose the correctly spelt word.

options.A: embarassment
options.B: embarrasment
options.C: embarrassment
options.D: embaressment

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Embarrassment' has double r and double s. A memory aid: it takes two r's and two s's to be embarrassed. Shortcut: remember both double letters. Trap (A): Single r. The word has a double r and a double s. Trap (B): Single s. The word has a double r and a double s. Trap (D): Wrong vowel. The syllable is spelt with 'a', not 'e'.

questions.question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.A: He does not know the answer to the question.
options.B: He do not know the answer to the question.
options.C: He does not knows the answer to the question.
options.D: He not know the answer to the question.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'He' is third-person singular, so the auxiliary is 'does', followed by the base form 'know'. Shortcut: auxiliary agrees; the main verb stays in base form. Trap (B): Subject-verb agreement. A singular third-person subject takes 'does', not 'do'. Trap (C): Double marking. After 'does', the main verb stays in its base form. Trap (D): Missing auxiliary. The negative requires the auxiliary 'does'.

questions.question_text: Identify the correct sentence.

options.A: Meena is more taller than her sister.
options.B: Meena is tall than her sister.
options.C: Meena is taller than her sister.
options.D: Meena is most tall than her sister.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A short adjective forms the comparative with '-er'. Adding 'more' as well is a double comparative error. Shortcut: one comparative marker only. Trap (A): Double comparative. 'Taller' is already comparative, so 'more' is not needed. Trap (B): Missing comparative form. Comparison with 'than' needs the comparative form. Trap (D): Wrong degree. 'Most' is for the superlative degree.

questions.question_text:
Passage: The village school had only one classroom and a single teacher. Even so, the children arrived each morning with great enthusiasm. They sat on jute mats and learned to read from a few worn books. The teacher believed that a lack of resources should never stop a child from learning. She often told the parents that curiosity was the one thing a school could not buy and a child could not be taught to lose. When visitors from the town once offered to donate a set of new desks, she thanked them politely but asked first for story books, since the children read every page twice.

Which of the following best completes the passage?

options.A: Therefore the children's progress depended less on the building than on the dedication of the teacher.
options.B: Therefore the school should be closed immediately.
options.C: However, the children disliked reading.
options.D: As a result, the village planned to build a cinema hall.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage stresses enthusiasm and the teacher's belief in learning despite limited resources. The concluding sentence should follow this idea. Shortcut: continue the main idea of the passage. Trap (B): Out of scope. The passage describes enthusiasm and dedication, not a reason to close the school. Trap (C): Reversal. This contradicts the stated enthusiasm. Trap (D): Out of scope. Nothing in the passage points to a cinema hall.

questions.question_text: Choose the word that correctly fills the blank: The new traffic rules have had a positive ________ on road safety.

options.A: affect
options.B: affection
options.C: effect
options.D: affects

questions.pedagogical_explanation: After 'a positive', a noun is needed. 'Effect' is the noun meaning result. 'Affect' is the verb: 'The rules affect road safety.' Shortcut: noun: effect; verb: affect. Trap (A): Confusable word. 'Affect' is usually a verb meaning to influence. Here a noun is needed after 'positive'. Trap (B): Confusable word. 'Affection' means fondness and does not suit the sentence. Trap (D): Confusable word. This is the verb form and does not fit after 'a positive'.

questions.question_text: Choose the best option to complete the sentence: Although it was raining heavily, the players ________.

options.A: abandoned their bats happily
options.B: were therefore delighted by the weather
options.C: complained about the sunshine
options.D: continued the match

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Although' introduces a contrast, so the second clause should show something unexpected despite the rain, namely that they continued. Shortcut: 'although' needs a contrasting clause. Trap (A): Wrong connector logic. 'Although' signals contrast with the rain, so the result should be unexpected. Trap (B): Wrong connector logic. 'Therefore' reverses the contrast needed by 'although'. Trap (C): Contradiction. The first clause says it was raining.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct word: If the pain continues for more than two days, you ________ see a doctor.

options.A: shall
options.B: would
options.C: might to
options.D: should

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Should' expresses advice or recommendation, which suits the sentence. Shortcut: 'should' is the modal for advice. Trap (A): Wrong modal. 'Shall' for the second person suggests a command or promise, not advice. Trap (B): Wrong modal. 'Would' suggests a hypothetical result or a past habit. Trap (C): Wrong form. 'Might' is not followed by 'to'.

questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the word in bold: The scientist's claim was met with **scepticism** by many of her colleagues, who asked for more evidence.

options.A: doubt
options.B: applause
options.C: anger
options.D: curiosity

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The clue 'asked for more evidence' shows that the colleagues doubted the claim. 'Scepticism' means a doubtful attitude. Shortcut: use the clue about asking for evidence. Trap (B): Opposite meaning. Colleagues who ask for more evidence are not applauding. Trap (C): Related word. They are asking for evidence, not expressing anger. Trap (D): Related word. Curiosity is not the same as doubt, and the demand for evidence points to doubt.

questions.question_text:
Arrange the sentences in the correct order.
P. The seeds were then planted in rows.
Q. First, the farmer ploughed the field.
R. Finally, the crops were harvested in autumn.
S. Later, he watered the field regularly.

options.A: PQRS
options.B: QPSR
options.C: QSPR
options.D: SPQR

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sequence words give the order: 'First' (Q), then planting (P), 'Later' watering (S), and 'Finally' harvest (R). So QPSR. Shortcut: start from 'First', end with 'Finally'. Trap (A): Wrong order. The seeds cannot be planted before the field is ploughed. Trap (C): Wrong order. Watering before planting does not follow the sequence. Trap (D): Wrong order. Watering cannot be the first step.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A small library opened in a village that had no bookshop. At first, only a few children visited it. Within a year, the number of readers had tripled, and several adults were seen borrowing books for the first time. The librarian noticed that the most popular books were those about local history and farming. She also noted that many borrowers came back within days to ask whether new titles on these subjects had arrived. A few of the older readers began to share what they had read with neighbours in the evenings, and the small reading room soon became a regular meeting place for the village.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: The villagers were interested in books that related to their own lives
options.B: All the villagers now read books every day
options.C: The village still has no bookshop
options.D: Children are no longer interested in books

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The most popular books were about local history and farming, which suggests interest in material connected with local life. The other options go beyond the facts. Shortcut: stay within what the passage states. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The passage says only that readers tripled and some adults borrowed books. Trap (C): Out of scope. The passage does not say whether a bookshop has since opened. Trap (D): Reversal. The passage says the number of readers tripled.

questions.question_text: Choose the sentence that is grammatically correct.

options.A: The news of the team's victories was received with great joy.
options.B: The news of the team's victories were received with great joy.
options.C: The news of the team's victories are received with great joy.
options.D: The news of the team's victories have been receive with great joy.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'News' is singular although it ends in 's'. The plural noun 'victories' in the phrase is not the subject. So the verb is 'was received'. Shortcut: find the head noun, ignore the phrase after it. Trap (B): Subject-verb agreement. 'News' is a singular noun, so it takes 'was'; the plural 'victories' is only part of the phrase after it. Trap (C): Subject-verb agreement. 'News' is singular and takes a singular verb. Trap (D): Verb form. This combines a plural auxiliary with a wrong verb form.

questions.question_text: Choose the sentence in which the items in the list are in parallel form.

options.A: Neha enjoys swimming, cycling and running on weekends.
options.B: Neha enjoys swimming, to cycle and running on weekends.
options.C: Neha enjoys to swim, cycling and to run on weekends.
options.D: Neha enjoys swimming, to cycle and run on weekends.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Items in a list should have the same grammatical form. 'Swimming, cycling and running' are all gerunds after 'enjoys'. Shortcut: make every list item the same form. Trap (B): Faulty parallelism. The list mixes gerunds with an infinitive. Trap (C): Faulty parallelism. The list mixes infinitives with a gerund. Trap (D): Faulty parallelism. The list mixes a gerund with infinitives.

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly conveys that Ravi eats vegetables on no other day than Sunday?

options.A: Ravi only eats vegetables on Sundays.
options.B: Only Ravi eats vegetables on Sundays.
options.C: Ravi eats only vegetables on Sundays.
options.D: Ravi eats vegetables only on Sundays.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Only' should sit next to the word it limits. To limit the day, place it before 'on Sundays'. Shortcut: place 'only' right before what it limits. Trap (A): Misplaced modifier. This can suggest that Ravi does nothing with vegetables other than eat them. Trap (B): Different meaning. This says that no one else eats vegetables on Sundays. Trap (C): Different meaning. This says that on Sundays he eats nothing but vegetables.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct form of the verb: By the time we reached the station, the train ________.

options.A: already left
options.B: has already left
options.C: had already left
options.D: is already leaving

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Two past events: the train's leaving came before our arrival, so the earlier event takes the past perfect. Shortcut: earlier past event takes the past perfect. Trap (A): Tense sequence. The earlier of two past events needs the past perfect. Trap (B): Tense sequence. The present perfect does not fit a past reference point. Trap (D): Tense sequence. The sentence is about a completed past event.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best fills the blank to complete the passage? 'Many people believe that taking notes during a lecture makes a student a passive listener. Research suggests the opposite. When students put ideas into their own words, they must decide what matters and how the points connect. ________'

options.A: Therefore, students should avoid listening to lectures altogether.
options.B: Note-taking can therefore be an active process that deepens understanding.
options.C: Hence, all notes are equally useful whatever their quality.
options.D: However, taking notes always lowers marks in examinations.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage reverses the common belief and explains how putting ideas in one's own words involves decisions. The conclusion should state that note-taking can be active and helpful. Shortcut: complete the direction of the argument. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The passage does not suggest that lectures should be avoided. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The passage speaks of notes made in a student's own words. Trap (D): Reversal. This contradicts the direction of the passage.

questions.question_text: Choose the option that best explains the idiom in bold: Although he disagreed with several of the new rules, the manager chose to **toe the line** in front of his staff.

options.A: to stand at the edge of a boundary
options.B: to follow the accepted rules or policy
options.C: to challenge the management openly
options.D: to leave the office quickly

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Although he disagreed' sets up a contrast: despite his disagreement, he conformed. 'To toe the line' means to obey the rules. Shortcut: 'although he disagreed...' signals conforming. Trap (A): Literal reading. The idiom is not about a physical edge. Trap (C): Reversal. The manager did not challenge; he conformed. Trap (D): Out of context. Nothing in the sentence concerns leaving.

questions.question_text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: Asked to describe his holiday, the ________ traveller replied in a single word, 'Wonderful'.

options.A: garrulous
options.B: effusive
options.C: laconic
options.D: candid

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The clue 'replied in a single word' points to someone who uses few words. 'Laconic' means using very few words. Shortcut: use the clue of the one-word reply. Trap (A): Opposite meaning. 'Garrulous' means talkative, which is the opposite of the sense needed. Trap (B): Opposite meaning. 'Effusive' means gushing in expression, which does not match a one-word reply. Trap (D): Related word. 'Candid' means frank and does not capture the brevity of the reply.

questions.question_text:
Passage: The town's cooperative dairy began paying farmers according to the fat content of their milk instead of paying a flat rate per litre. Within a year, the average fat content of milk delivered to the dairy had risen noticeably, even though the farmers had not changed their breed of cattle. A dairy officer remarked that farmers had begun to pay closer attention to the quality of fodder given to the animals. Meanwhile, the total volume of milk delivered rose only slightly, which the officer saw as a fair price for better quality.

Which of the following is best supported by the passage?

options.A: The farmers earned less money after the new payment method began
options.B: Fodder quality is the only factor that decides fat content
options.C: The new payment method gave farmers a reason to improve the quality of milk without changing the breed
options.D: The total volume of milk fell sharply after the change

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The payment change was followed by better fat content without a change of breed, and the officer linked it to fodder, so the incentive for quality is best supported. The other options go beyond or against the passage. Shortcut: choose the option closest to the evidence given. Trap (A): Out of scope. The passage gives no figures on earnings. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The passage reports a remark on fodder but does not say it is the only factor. Trap (D): Reversal. The passage says that volume rose slightly.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Some educators argue that schools should begin the day an hour later because teenagers are naturally inclined to sleep late. They point out that students who get more sleep concentrate better and make fewer errors in class. A principal has therefore proposed starting classes at 9:30 am instead of 8:30 am, arguing that this will improve academic performance in the school without any other change in the timetable. The proposal will apply to all classes from the next term, and the school has said that the later start will not reduce the number of teaching hours because the afternoon break will be shortened.

Which of the following is an assumption on which the principal's argument depends?

options.A: Teenagers are more intelligent than younger children
options.B: Students will actually use the extra hour for sleep and not for staying up later at night
options.C: Every student in the school sleeps late at present
options.D: The school day will be shortened by an hour

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Negation test: if students simply stay up an hour later, they get no extra sleep and the benefit disappears. So the argument depends on the extra hour becoming extra sleep. Shortcut: negate the option and see if the proposal fails. Trap (A): Out of scope. Intelligence is not part of the argument. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The argument needs only that the extra hour will lead to more sleep for enough students. Trap (D): Out of scope. The principal proposes a later start, not a shorter day.

questions.concept_tag: Short passage - function of a sentence
questions.question_text:
Passage: Public libraries are often described as quiet places for solitary reading. That description is increasingly incomplete. In many cities, libraries now offer language classes, job-seeking workshops and spaces where elderly residents can learn to use smartphones. These activities draw people who may never borrow a book. Yet the lending desk remains the heart of the library, because it is the shared collection that gives the other activities their purpose and their public character. A library with workshops but no books, one librarian remarked, would be little more than a community hall with a good reputation.

What is the primary purpose of the passage?

options.A: To show that libraries have widened their role while the shared collection remains central
options.B: To argue that libraries should stop lending books
options.C: To criticise public libraries for becoming noisy
options.D: To prove that most visitors never borrow a book

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author notes the new roles, and then asserts the continuing centrality of the lending collection. That is the primary purpose. The other options reverse or exaggerate. Shortcut: combine the two halves of the passage: widened role plus continuing core. Trap (B): Reversal. The passage calls the lending desk the heart of the library. Trap (C): Out of scope. The passage does not criticise; it describes expansion. Trap (D): Extreme scope. The passage says that some visitors may never borrow, not that most do not.

questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (P) Neither of the two proposals (Q) were accepted (R) by the board (S) at its last meeting.

options.A: (P) Neither of the two proposals
options.B: (R) by the board
options.C: (S) at its last meeting
options.D: (Q) were accepted

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Neither' is singular, so the verb should be 'was accepted'. The error is in part Q. Shortcut: 'neither' and 'either' take singular verbs. Trap (A): No error. 'Neither of the two proposals' is correct as a subject phrase. Trap (B): No error. 'By the board' correctly shows the agent. Trap (C): No error. 'Its' correctly refers to the singular board.

questions.question_text: Choose the pair of words that correctly fills the blanks: The ________ of the school said that honesty was the guiding ________ of the institution.

options.A: principle, principal
options.B: principal, principle
options.C: principal, principal
options.D: principle, principle

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A 'principal' is a head of a school; a 'principle' is a basic rule or belief. So 'principal, principle'. Shortcut: principal = person (pal), principle = rule. Trap (A): Swapped words. 'Principle' is a rule and 'principal' is the head of a school; they are swapped here. Trap (C): Repeated word. The second blank needs a noun meaning a rule or guiding idea. Trap (D): Repeated word. The first blank needs a person: the head of the school.

questions.question_text: Choose the sentence that is free from redundancy.

options.A: The officials decided to return to the village the next day.
options.B: The officials decided to return back to the village the next day.
options.C: The officials decided to again return back to the village the next day.
options.D: The officials decided to revert back to the village the next day.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Words that repeat an idea already contained in another word should be removed. 'Return back' is such a repetition. Shortcut: delete a word that repeats another. Trap (B): Redundancy. 'Return' already means to go back, so 'back' is superfluous. Trap (C): Redundancy. 'Again' and 'back' both repeat the idea of 'return'. Trap (D): Redundancy. 'Revert' already includes the sense of 'back'.

questions.question_text: Which sentence expresses the meaning most clearly? Rita told Sonia that Sonia's essay had won the first prize.

options.A: Rita told Sonia that she had won the first prize with her essay.
options.B: Rita told Sonia that her essay won the first prize, which she liked.
options.C: Rita told Sonia it had won the first prize.
options.D: Rita told Sonia, 'Your essay has won the first prize.'

questions.pedagogical_explanation: When two people of the same gender are mentioned, 'she' and 'her' can be ambiguous. Direct speech avoids the doubt. Shortcut: two same-gender antecedents make 'she' ambiguous. Trap (A): Ambiguous pronoun. 'She' and 'her' may refer to either person. Trap (B): Ambiguous pronoun. 'Her' and 'she' may refer to either person. Trap (C): Ambiguous pronoun. It is not clear what 'it' refers to.

questions.question_text: Four of the following five sentences form a coherent paragraph. Choose the one that does not belong. (1) Bamboo is one of the fastest-growing plants in the world. (2) Some species can grow almost a metre in a single day. (3) This rapid growth makes bamboo a renewable building material. (4) The panda is a bear found in China. (5) Builders in several countries use it for scaffolding and flooring.

options.A: Sentence (2)
options.B: Sentence (4)
options.C: Sentence (3)
options.D: Sentence (5)

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 are about bamboo's growth and building use. The panda sentence changes the topic. Shortcut: find the sentence that changes the topic. Trap (A): Supporting detail. This gives a detail about the speed of growth, which supports sentence (1). Trap (C): Link in the argument. This explains the importance of the growth rate. Trap (D): Supporting detail. This gives examples of the building use mentioned in (3).

questions.question_text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The judge, being ________ in the dispute, had no stake in either side's success and could decide it fairly.

options.A: uninterested
options.B: interested
options.C: indifferent
options.D: disinterested

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Disinterested' means impartial, having no personal stake. 'Uninterested' means bored or lacking interest. Shortcut: disinterested = impartial. Trap (A): Confusable word. 'Uninterested' means showing no interest, which is a different idea from having no stake. Trap (B): Opposite meaning. This would suggest that the judge had a stake. Trap (C): Related word. 'Indifferent' suggests not caring, which does not capture neutrality because of having no stake.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.B: Unless you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.C: Unless you will hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.D: Unless you hurried, you will miss the bus.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not'. So the verb that follows should be affirmative and in the present tense for a future result. Shortcut: 'unless' = 'if not', so no extra 'not'. Trap (B): Double negative. 'Unless' already carries the sense of 'if not', so a second negative reverses the meaning. Trap (C): Wrong tense. A future form is not used in the 'unless' clause. Trap (D): Tense mismatch. The past tense in the 'unless' clause does not fit a future result.

questions.question_text:
Passage: The company's annual report describes the past year as 'a period of consolidation', a phrase that, one suspects, was chosen with care. Sales fell for the third year in a row, two factories closed and the share price is half of what it was. Yet the chairman's letter is warm, confident and filled with talk of 'foundations' and 'future readiness'. One admires the optimism, though one may wonder whether shareholders would not prefer a little less of it and a little more of the truth.

The author's attitude to the report is best described as:

options.A: enthusiastically supportive
options.B: angrily hostile
options.C: gently ironic
options.D: neutral and uninterested

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Phrases such as 'one suspects' and 'one admires the optimism, though...' show mild, polite mockery. So 'gently ironic'. Shortcut: spot softened criticism. Trap (A): Reversal. The author hints that the language hides bad news. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The tone is mild and humorous, not angry. Trap (D): Reversal. The author comments pointedly on the choice of words.

questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'cogent', as used in: The lawyer presented a cogent argument.

options.A: persuasive
options.B: clear
options.C: unconvincing
options.D: forceful

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Cogent' means clear, logical and convincing. The opposite is 'unconvincing'. Shortcut: three options are synonyms; pick the odd one. Trap (A): Synonym. 'Persuasive' is close in meaning to 'cogent'. Trap (B): Related word. 'Clear' is close in sense to 'cogent'. Trap (D): Related word. 'Forceful' is close in sense to 'cogent'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Less people attended the lecture this time, and there was fewer noise in the hall.
options.B: Less people attended the lecture this time, and there was less noise in the hall.
options.C: Fewer people attended the lecture this time, and there was fewer noise in the hall.
options.D: Fewer people attended the lecture this time, and there was less noise in the hall.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Use 'fewer' with countable nouns (people) and 'less' with uncountable nouns (noise). Shortcut: fewer for things you can count. Trap (A): Swapped quantifiers. 'Fewer' is used with countable nouns and 'less' with uncountable nouns; here they are swapped. Trap (B): Wrong quantifier. 'People' is countable, so it needs 'fewer'. Trap (C): Wrong quantifier. 'Noise' is uncountable, so it needs 'less'.

questions.question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.A: I wish my brother was here to see the result.
options.B: I wish my brother is here to see the result.
options.C: I wish my brother will be here to see the result.
options.D: I wish my brother were here to see the result.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A wish about an unreal present uses the past subjunctive, and for 'be' the form is 'were' for every subject. Shortcut: unreal present: 'were' for all subjects. Trap (A): Subjunctive missed. After 'wish', an unreal present takes 'were' for all persons in formal usage. Trap (B): Wrong mood. 'Wish' expresses an unreal situation, so the indicative 'is' is wrong. Trap (C): Wrong form. 'Wish' does not take 'will be' for an unreal present.

questions.question_text: Choose the sentence that makes a logical comparison.

options.A: The population of Delhi is larger than that of Mumbai.
options.B: The population of Delhi is larger than Mumbai.
options.C: Delhi's population is larger than Mumbai.
options.D: The population of Delhi is more larger than Mumbai's population.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The comparison should be between like things: population with population. 'That of Mumbai' stands for 'the population of Mumbai'. Shortcut: compare like with like. Trap (B): Illogical comparison. This compares a population with a city. Trap (C): Illogical comparison. This also compares a population with a city. Trap (D): Double comparative. 'More larger' is a double comparative.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A city council wants to reduce the use of private cars in its crowded centre. It has announced that parking charges in the centre will be tripled from next year. The council's transport officer says, 'Because the cost of parking will rise sharply, fewer people will drive into the centre, and the roads will become less congested.' The officer adds that the extra revenue will be used to improve bus services, though this is a separate matter from the question of congestion.

The officer's reasoning about congestion depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Parking in the centre is currently free of charge
options.B: Bus services in the city are already excellent
options.C: Most of those who stop driving into the centre will not be replaced by other drivers on the same roads
options.D: Everyone who drives into the centre can afford the new charges

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Negation test: if drivers who stay out are replaced by others using the same roads, congestion would not fall. So the claim needs the roads to stay freer. The bus improvements are said to be a separate issue. Shortcut: ask what must hold for the cause to produce the effect. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The argument speaks of raising charges, so parking need not be free now. Trap (B): Out of scope. The officer calls the bus improvement a separate matter from congestion. Trap (D): Reversal. If everyone could afford them, the rise might have no effect on driving.

questions.concept_tag: Short passage - what must be true
questions.question_text:
Passage: A report on rural employment notes that, among households that received training in tailoring, the share with a second source of income rose from one-fifth to two-fifths within three years. Among nearby households that did not receive training, the share stayed close to one-fifth. The report cautions, however, that the households which received training had themselves applied for it, while the others had not. It adds that the trained households were also, on average, located closer to the main road and its markets, and that the survey was conducted only once at the end of the three years, so no comparison with their income before training is available.

Which of the following statements is best supported by the passage?

options.A: Tailoring training is the only way to earn a second income
options.B: The training definitely doubled each trained household's income
options.C: The households that sought training may differ from the others in ways that also affect their income
options.D: Untrained households have no wish to find a second income

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The report's caution that trained households applied for it themselves suggests that self-selection may explain part of the difference. The other options claim more than is stated. Shortcut: read the final caution: it signals the limit of the evidence. Trap (A): Extreme scope. The passage does not say that it is the only way. Trap (B): Extreme scope. The passage speaks of the share of households with a second source, not each household's income. Trap (D): Out of scope. The passage does not report any such wish.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Maps are not neutral. Every map leaves things out, because a map that included everything would be as large and as confusing as the land itself. What a mapmaker chooses to show, such as roads, borders or rivers, depends on the purpose of the map. A hiking map and a political map of the same region will look very different. The first marks slopes, streams and campsites; the second marks the lines that separate one state from another and may leave out the hills altogether. Neither can be called wrong, since each answers a different question that someone has put to the land. ________

Which of the following best completes the paragraph?

options.A: A map therefore reflects the decisions of its maker as much as it reflects the land.
options.B: Every map should therefore include all the details of the land.
options.C: A hiking map is always more accurate than a political map.
options.D: Mapmakers rarely think about the purpose of their maps.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage argues that selection depends on purpose. The best conclusion is that maps reflect the maker's choices as well as the land. Shortcut: finish the argument in the same direction. Trap (B): Reversal. The passage says that including everything would make the map confusing. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The passage says they differ in purpose, not that one is more accurate. Trap (D): Reversal. The passage says that purpose determines what is shown.

questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to the word in bold: The humid afternoon heat seemed to **enervate** the workers, who moved more slowly with every hour.

options.A: energise
options.B: weaken
options.C: annoy
options.D: excite

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Enervate' means to cause a loss of energy or vitality. The clue is that the workers moved more slowly. The word looks like 'energise' but means the opposite. Shortcut: beware of look-alike words: enervate is not energise. Trap (A): Opposite meaning. 'Enervate' is often mistaken to mean 'energise', but it means the reverse. Trap (C): Related word. This does not fit the clue that the workers moved more slowly. Trap (D): Opposite meaning. This is the reverse of the effect described.

questions.question_text: Choose the option that best explains the idiom in bold: Asked whether the new policy was good or bad, the minister chose to **sit on the fence**, giving neither approval nor criticism.

options.A: to avoid taking a side in a dispute
options.B: to rest after a long day's work
options.C: to protect a property from outsiders
options.D: to oppose a policy secretly

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The clue 'neither approval nor criticism' gives the meaning: remaining undecided or neutral. Shortcut: use the clue after the comma. Trap (B): Literal reading. The idiom does not concern resting. Trap (C): Literal reading. The idiom does not concern guarding a boundary. Trap (D): Wrong sense. The minister gave neither approval nor criticism.

questions.question_text: Choose the sentence that is correct in parallel structure.

options.A: Anita prefers to walk to the office rather than driving.
options.B: Anita prefers walking to the office rather than to drive.
options.C: Anita prefers to walk to the office rather than to be driving.
options.D: Anita prefers to walk to the office rather than drive.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Rather than' joins two items that must have the same form. 'To walk ... rather than drive' keeps both in the base form. Shortcut: the two items around 'rather than' must match. Trap (A): Faulty parallelism. 'To walk' is an infinitive and 'driving' is a gerund, so the items are not parallel. Trap (B): Faulty parallelism. 'Walking' is a gerund and 'to drive' is an infinitive. Trap (C): Faulty parallelism. The progressive form does not match 'to walk'.

questions.question_text:
Passage: It is tempting to praise a politician who 'never changes his mind'. We call such a person steady, loyal to principle. But consider what that steadiness may hide. A doctor who never revises a diagnosis, whatever the test results, is dangerous. A scientist who never revises a theory is no scientist. Changing one's mind in the light of new evidence is not weakness; the real question is whether the change is honest, and whether the reasons for it are open to scrutiny.

Why does the author mention the doctor and the scientist?

options.A: To show by analogy that refusing to revise a view can be a fault, not a virtue
options.B: To suggest that politicians should be trained as doctors
options.C: To prove that politicians never change their minds
options.D: To argue that doctors and scientists are always right

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The doctor and scientist are analogies that show that refusing to revise a view on new evidence is a defect. That supports the author's point about politicians. Shortcut: identify what the example is used to prove. Trap (B): Out of scope. The passage makes no such suggestion. Trap (C): Reversal. The author's point is about the value of changing one's mind. Trap (D): Reversal. The author uses them as examples of people who ought to revise views.

questions.question_text: Which word best describes the tone of the following remark? 'Our train arrived only forty minutes late, which, by the standards of this railway, one must regard as a triumph of punctuality.'

options.A: jubilant
options.B: wry
options.C: bitter
options.D: reverent

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Wry' describes dry, mildly mocking humour. The remark praises lateness as a 'triumph', which is ironic and gentle. Shortcut: dry humour means 'wry'. Trap (A): Reversal. The remark is not joyful; it quietly mocks the usual delays. Trap (C): Extreme scope. The remark is mild and humorous, not bitter. Trap (D): Out of scope. There is no respect for the railway in the remark.

questions.question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.A: The secret must remain between you and I.
options.B: The secret must remain between you and myself.
options.C: The secret must remain between your and mine.
options.D: The secret must remain between you and me.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Between' is a preposition and takes object pronouns: 'between you and me'. Shortcut: preposition + object pronoun. Trap (A): Wrong case. After a preposition, the objective case 'me' is needed. Trap (B): Wrong pronoun. The reflexive 'myself' is not used when no 'I' appears as a subject in the clause. Trap (C): Wrong form. Possessive forms cannot follow 'between' in this way.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Some farmers in a dry region have begun growing millet instead of rice, claiming that millet uses far less water. A farmers' association argues that if all farmers in the region switched to millet, the falling groundwater level would stop declining, because the region's farming would then use much less water than it does now. The association's argument rests on the premise that rice farming is the main use of groundwater in the region. It also states that the farmers who have already switched report no fall in their total yearly income, though the association has not yet published the figures, and it expects the remaining farmers to follow once they see that millet can be grown with the same equipment.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the association's argument?

options.A: Millet sells at a lower price than rice in the region
options.B: Many farmers in the region prefer the taste of rice
options.C: Studies show that rice farming accounts for most of the groundwater drawn in the region
options.D: The region receives less rain than other parts of the country

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The argument needs rice farming to be the main user of groundwater.
