A study showing that it accounts for most of the groundwater drawn directly supports the premise and the conclusion. Shortcut: strengthen the stated premise. Trap (A): Out of scope. The price of millet does not bear on groundwater. Trap (B): Out of scope. Taste does not bear on water use. Trap (D): Out of scope. This describes the region but does not link rice farming to groundwater depletion.

questions.question_text: Choose the sentence in which 'notwithstanding' is used correctly.

options.A: The match was played, notwithstanding of the heavy rain.
options.B: Notwithstanding that it rained heavily it, the match was played.
options.C: The match was played notwithstanding, the heavy rain it.
options.D: Notwithstanding the heavy rain, the match was played to a finish.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Notwithstanding' means 'in spite of' and is followed directly by a noun phrase: 'Notwithstanding the heavy rain'. Shortcut: 'notwithstanding' + noun, no 'of'. Trap (A): Wrong construction. 'Notwithstanding' is not followed by 'of'. Trap (B): Wrong construction. This is awkward and ungrammatical. Trap (C): Wrong construction. The word order is broken.

questions.question_text:
Passage: After a city introduced a ban on single-use plastic cups in its markets, the amount of waste collected from the markets by the municipality fell by about one-third. A year later, though, a survey found that the number of tea and juice sellers in the markets had risen, and that more cups of drink were being sold each day than before the ban. Officials are puzzled that the waste collected has stayed lower even though more drinks are sold. They are considering what could explain this.

Which of the following, if true, best explains the puzzle?

options.A: Tea and juice sellers earn more than other sellers in the market
options.B: The ban was announced in the newspapers
options.C: Sellers switched to reusable steel cups and to paper cups that are collected separately by recyclers
options.D: The number of cups sold fell after the ban

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If sellers moved to reusable cups and to paper cups collected by recyclers, the waste handled by the municipality could fall even with more drinks sold. That resolves the puzzle. Shortcut: explain how both facts can be true. Trap (A): Out of scope. Earnings do not explain waste volumes. Trap (B): Out of scope. Publicity does not explain lower waste. Trap (D): Reversal. The passage says that more cups of drink are being sold.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Rashmi is one of the students who has scored full marks in the test.
options.B: Rashmi is one of the student who have scored full marks in the test.
options.C: Rashmi is one of the students who is scoring full marks in the test.
options.D: Rashmi is one of the students who have scored full marks in the test.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: In 'one of the students who ...', the relative pronoun refers to the plural 'students'. So the verb is plural: 'have scored'. Shortcut: 'one of the Xs who' takes a plural verb. Trap (A): Subject-verb agreement. 'Who' refers to 'students', which is plural, so the verb is 'have'. Trap (B): Noun number. After 'one of the', a plural noun is needed. Trap (C): Tense and agreement. The verb is both singular and in the wrong tense.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: I live in this town for ten years.
options.B: I have lived in this town for ten years.
options.C: I have lived in this town since ten years.
options.D: I am living in this town for ten years.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A period running up to the present uses the present perfect with 'for' + a length of time. 'Since' goes with a starting point. Shortcut: for + duration; since + starting point. Trap (A): Tense error. A period continuing up to now needs the present perfect. Trap (C): Wrong preposition. 'Since' needs a point in time, and 'for' is used with a period. Trap (D): Tense error. The continuous present does not suit a completed span to now in this way.

questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to 'perfunctory', as used in: The inspector gave the machinery only a perfunctory glance before signing the certificate.

options.A: thorough and detailed
options.B: hasty and without real care
options.C: suspicious and angry
options.D: admiring and pleased

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Perfunctory' means done as a duty with little care. Signing the certificate after a quick glance fits that sense. Shortcut: think of 'doing it just to say it was done'. Trap (A): Opposite meaning. This is the reverse of the sense of 'perfunctory'. Trap (C): Wrong sense. The sentence suggests lack of attention, not suspicion. Trap (D): Wrong sense. The sentence says nothing of admiration.

questions.question_text:
Passage: A coaching institute claims that its new online course improves the scores of its students. As evidence, it points to the fact that students who completed the entire course scored on average 20 marks more in the mock examination than students who enrolled but stopped after the first week. The institute concludes that completing the course raised students' scores, and that all students should therefore be encouraged to finish it. The institute adds that it will use the result in its next advertising campaign and that it has no plans to collect the students' earlier scores, since it regards the mock examination as a fair and sufficient measure of what the course delivers.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the institute's conclusion?

options.A: The course costs the same for every student who enrols
options.B: Some students who stopped early lacked a laptop at home
options.C: The students who completed the course were already scoring higher than the others before they enrolled
options.D: The mock examination was held in the same month for every student

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If the completers were already higher scorers, the 20-mark gap may reflect who stayed in the course, not the effect of the course. That undermines the causal conclusion. Shortcut: look for an alternative explanation of the gap. Trap (A): Out of scope. The cost does not affect the comparison of scores. Trap (B): Out of scope. This may explain why they stopped but does not weaken the claim about scores. Trap (D): Out of scope. This supports a fair comparison, which if anything helps the institute.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct sentence.

options.A: Neither the teacher nor the students were aware of the change in the schedule.
options.B: Neither the teacher nor the students was aware of the change in the schedule.
options.C: Neither the teacher nor the students is aware of the change in the schedule.
options.D: Neither the teacher nor the students has been aware of the change in the schedule.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: In 'neither ... nor' constructions, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. 'Students' is plural, so 'were'. Shortcut: agree with the nearer subject. Trap (B): Subject-verb agreement. With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, which is plural. Trap (C): Subject-verb agreement. The nearer subject 'students' is plural, so 'is' is wrong. Trap (D): Subject-verb agreement. The nearer subject is plural, so 'has' is wrong.
